item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：战争不是政策失败，而是政策本身

Dixon 这段访谈里最刺耳的真话被他轻描淡写地丢了出来——"我不认为任何人在试图结束这场战争"。多数评论者假设乌克兰战争是一个"失控的局面"，需要外交去修补。但如果你把 Dixon 整个框架倒过来读，会发现一个令人不适的结论：从 FIC（金融工业复合体）的损益表角度看，乌克兰战争并没有"失败"，它运行得完美。它消灭了欧洲的廉价能源、迫使欧洲各国政府提高军费（即扩大债务）、把能源定价权交回到美国 LNG 出口商和军工承包商手里、同时让俄罗斯被迫转向东方——这是双赢，只不过"赢家"不在你以为的那张谈判桌上。

欧洲人以为自己是棋手，其实是棋盘本身。

二、跨领域连接：法国不是在"政治危机"，而是在被杠杆收购

这是我在整理时突然看到的一个结构同构（structural isomorphism）：Dixon 描述的"资产剥离期"剧本，和私募股权的杠杆收购 playbook 一模一样，只是执行标的从中型企业换成了主权国家。

PE 收购一家公司的四步是：(1) 加杠杆直到现金流紧绷；(2) 制造管理层危机（"旧班子不行"）；(3) 剥离非核心资产、裁员提升"效率"；(4) 包装后转手或 IPO。

现在对比法国：(1) 10 年期国债收益率破 5%、与德债利差回到 2011 年水平——加杠杆完成；(2) Macron 失去街头、极左极右同时崛起——管理层危机就位；(3) 税收升级、Box3 式的财富税在邻国试点、AI 替代结构性失业——资产剥离在进行；(4) 国有企业私有化压力、关键基础设施（能源、芯片、港口）向跨国私人资本敞开——退出通道正在搭建。

法国人以为自己在经历"民主危机"。更准确的描述是：他们正在经历一场敌意收购，只是这次的"目标公司"是一个共和国。

三、历史的闭环：荷兰作为中央银行的诞生地，正在成为它的试验场

这一点听完访谈后我才意识到有多讽刺——荷兰在 1609 年创立了阿姆斯特丹 Wisselbank，这是现代中央银行的原型，是整个"债务即货币"范式的起点。四百年后，正是荷兰议会在用 Box 3 方案把自我托管的黄金和比特币纳入"未实现收益税"——也就是说，中央银行范式的发源地，正在亲手测试这个范式的最后一道闸门：连逃离闸门本身都要收税。

这不是巧合，这是一种制度性的"回归均值"。一个金融架构从哪里诞生，就会从哪里完成它的终局测试，因为那里的政治、法律、精英网络最熟悉这套语法。想想英国 1844 年银行法、再想想 2008 年雷曼倒在纽约——金融深水区的试验从来不发生在边疆。

四、一个让人睡不着的隐藏对应：比特币的中心化路径 ≈ 1913 美联储的创建路径

Dixon 列出的"比特币被俘获的四个向量"——ETF 托管集中、矿业公司国有化（上市化）、开发者团队被收编、节点运行成本上升——听起来像加密货币专有问题。但如果你读过 1910 年 Jekyll Island 的会议纪要，你会发现美联储的建立路径几乎是同一个子程序在跑：先把私人银行券（greenbacks, state bank notes）通过税收打击使其运行成本变高、再把铸币权集中到少数公众持股机构、再通过"稳定性"叙事招安学术/技术话语权（经济学家 = 开发者）、最后用一次恐慌（1907）锁定终局。

同一套 playbook，中间差了 113 年。这说明的不是"阴谋"，而是更深的东西：一旦债务型法币体系存在，它就会以热力学般的必然性去俘获任何形式的硬通货对手盘，无论那个对手盘是黄金、是绿背票、还是比特币。它不需要一个中央委员会去协调，因为激励结构本身就是重力场。

这才是整场访谈里最阴冷的洞察：Dixon 讲的所有"操纵"，其实都不需要操纵者。

📝 转录文本

Simon Dixon: It's Not WW3, It's a Strategic Retreat

开场定调：被包装成三战的，其实是战略撤退

"It will be framed as World War III, but in actuality, this is, I believe, a strategic retreat. And we're just starting to see the narrative right now on the American political scene that they're starting to say, 'We will no longer protect the Gulf.' And that's why I don't think this war ends. I don't think anyone's trying to end it cuz the more you can weaken Europe, the more it benefits um the stock markets and decouples the economies um from the private sector."

Alex Adriaanse: Welcome to the MicroSMEs Podcast. My name is Alex Adriaanse. I'm your host, and today I'm joined by the one and only Simon Dixon for a second interview. Pleasure to welcome you back, Simon.

Simon Dixon: Thanks for having me.

Alex: Simon, today is the 22nd of October 2026 — still, we're not in 2027 yet. Last time we spoke was in June, so that's a few months ago. You described the West as entering an asset-stripping phase and the global financial system as moving towards a new multipolar order. If we look at everything that has happened over the past 4 months, what's the single most important development that has strengthened your conviction?

一、资本成本飙升与四大"复合体"的协同收割

Simon: Well, look, it's a moving target. If the money tells me that that's the direction we're heading, I think we're still heading in that direction. So what are we actually seeing?

(1) 资本成本上升 — 债权人对借款人的财富转移

Well, we're seeing firstly, the cost of capital going through the roof. Government borrowing, which then impacts mortgages, which then impacts auto loans, credit card loans. The cost of borrowing is increasing across the West. In fact, it's increasing everywhere but China at the moment. That really has one impact: it is a wealth transfer from those that are borrowing or those that have interest as their primary cost, over to those that are issuing the loans or are the creditors on the other side of it — which is the financial industrial complex that we talked about last time.

(2) 高能源价格 — 消费者向能源寡头的财富转移

What else? Well, high energy prices. What does high energy prices do? It really impacts the bottom line of the small-to-medium-sized business and the average person that's heavily dependent upon a reasonable cost of energy. We're seeing a big transfer of wealth from those that consume energy over to those that refine oil or refine energy or produce energy. Those are also the same companies that are public companies in the financial industrial complex.

(3) 两线战争升级 — 军工复合体的订单引擎

What's the third thing we're seeing? We're seeing escalations of wars across two major fronts — one being Iran and the other being Ukraine. Both of those are impacting the cost of energy, but also fueling expenditure for the second complex, the military industrial complex. The concern of America's depletion of weapons is not a consideration. It is churning orders. It is selling weapons. That's what drives those valuations, and they're all public companies as well.

(4) 技术工业复合体 — AI、无人机、媒体操控的试验场

But what are they also doing? Well, they're testing technology for the technical industrial complex, as AI integrates with drones, as more warfare is a function of data, as artificial intelligence and decisions are being made based upon the efficient use of data. But also media manipulation.

二、法国作为"制造型民不聊生"的典型样本

What we're seeing across France right now is manufactured civil unrest — i.e. you make the cost of living to the point where it creates civil unrest. You utilize immigration policy as a hot button topic, at the same time as feeding people content that makes them more and more angry and points to an "other" for the source of their problem. And then you get what happens in France.

What's the byproduct of what's happening in France right now?

  • You burden the government with more debt
  • You increase the police and surveillance state
  • You're able to purchase assets on the cheap as governments go more and more into paying more / facilitating more interest
  • The private equity departments are able to purchase those small businesses and roll them up through the investment banking division into large multinational public companies

So all of that is happening — through the controller of capital, through the control of these different complexes — you're able to manufacture the environment that optimizes the portfolio value for the financial industrial complex, optimizes centralization, and civil unrest just becomes a tool for subordinating governments to the debt capital market.

The dollar vigilantes rule, the central banks are determining the short-term cost of borrowing, the large central banks are demanding more yield from governments, and energy prices are renegotiating every contract. And who's the net loser? It's definitely Europe. Europe is being subordinated further. And who is Europe subordinate to? The private companies that are floated on the European, UK, and American stock markets.

三、能源杠杆与地缘大棋盘：从中东到"西亚"

Alex: How would you say — now if we look at more detail at the conflict in Ukraine — Russia has been hit by drones increasingly from Ukraine. Trump also said, "Hey, Zelensky, please stop doing that, because our diesel prices are going up and he has midterms coming up around the corner." There's a bit of defiance at the moment, actually — a more public one, at least. We don't know what happens in the background.

In the meantime, in the Gulf region, the Houthis started also striking Saudi Arabia, striking key infrastructure, refineries, airports, civilian infrastructure. If you look at the map, it's actually a very clear line going all the way up north through Russia, all down to basically Yemen and the Gulf area — through Palestine, Israel, and so on. There's a clear line being drawn here. How is this interconnected to the geopolitical grand chessboard — who is controlling the energy lever in the end?

石油禁运与"佩特罗美元"的历史起点

Simon: The energy lever is controlled by those that can control the military to escalate tensions and manipulate energy prices, as well as the derivatives and financial tools — so that's the MIC (military industrial complex), FIC (financial industrial complex). But also those that own the energy: Russia, Iran, the Gulf countries, and China has built significant reserves and is in the position to ride this out on the short term and medium term.

What is that represented by? Exxon, Chevron in America, then Total, British Petroleum — the seven major oil companies. But then you've got the sovereign wealth funds and the nation-states that actually have nationalized energy. Now, they're represented by OPEC.

The relationship from the last oil embargo in the '70s was the petrodollar — the 1974 petrodollar agreement. What were both sides of that?

  • An agreement from the energy-producing countries (OPEC — Iran, the Gulf countries, Venezuela, various others) to coordinate on the amount of oil they release
  • On the other side, to price it in dollars, but recycle those dollars into purchasing US government debt, in order to roll over the debt after they came off of the gold standard
  • Then you take the yields on those bonds and purchase military equipment, which gives the West bases in the countries where the oil comes from — effectively a protection racket, like a mafia: "We will no longer destroy you, as long as you continue to buy energy and purchase our debt"

美国退守西半球，中国领衔的 BRICS 填补真空

Now, the Russia side and the NATO side — what do you benefit from these two different factors? If you can utilize NATO to get all the European countries to increase their budgets and bankrupt the governments, then in the end you've got the private interests and the Russian interests. Right now, Russia and the financial industrial complex are in a negotiation via Trump, which represents the private interest there.

My larger thesis of what I think we're seeing is that America is retreating to the Western Hemisphere, which is dominated by private capital interests in those complexes. China is a rising power, which is aligned with the BRICS countries — Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa — and the plus countries: Iran, UAE, Ethiopia, Egypt.

Iran has destroyed the bases. The state-sponsored militias — different types all across the region (some represent Western interests, some Gulf, some Turkey, some Iranian, some Russian with Wagner across Africa) — all of those are in a territorial change, I believe, to be integrated into state armies and the state political system.

从 "Middle East" 到 "West Asia" — 一个殖民框架的终结

With the Houthis, you're seeing the passage of Israeli and American ships, but targeting Saudi Arabia ships. Why? Because Saudi Arabia is one of the hegemonic powers in this new regional order — alongside Turkey, Egypt, and Iran.

If the bases in America are going, and the petrodollar half the equation is no longer needed, and China is producing and consuming the energy, then you've really changed the dynamics of the petrodollar.

What you're seeing overall is what we used to be called the "Middle East" — because you would stand from London and look eastward, and it would be the middle of the world — changing to what it was before colonialism, which is "West Asia". The money and the manufacturing base is coming from the East. But the intellectual property, the artificial intelligence, the weapons purchases for defense are coming from the West.

It will be framed as World War III, but in actuality, this is, I believe, a strategic retreat. We're just starting to see the narrative on the American political scene that they're starting to say, "We will no longer protect the Gulf." Iran has had this — America's had this Suez Canal moment for the British Empire, but having this with the Strait of Hormuz.

The regional armed militia groups are providing leverage for state sponsors in order to set this world order. We had the Mecca agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey. And we recently had a soft introduction from Egypt, at the same time as Preobrazhensky (who represents the Iranian government reformist side) saying they think it's a good thing and would consider joining it in the future.

To me, this is the regional alliance model. The military in the West has just been used by the financial industrial complex to make sure they get their cut and their protection racket — if West Asia is going to be the growth area once the West has decided they can no longer sustain the forever-war model.

四、多极化、QE的必然性与"K型经济"

Alex: So it's basically the West — the US — knowingly leaving the security architecture of the Middle East, where Israel is still the strongest ally. And then also, since the Ukraine conflict, the threat of retracting from Europe as a whole. The question is: if the FIC does not have control over China, nor Russia per se — are the conflicts we still see now actually a direct result of trying to revive the petrodollar in one way or another? And if it's not being revived, are we seeing the rise of a new type of ex-ba-ba-dollar — a petro-something?

从黄金本位到国债本位，再到流动性极限

Simon: I think we're entering into a world of multipolarity. What does that actually mean?

The Western financial system backed by the dollar — the original transition — you had the Vietnamese war that bankrupted the US government, which meant they came off the gold standard when their gold reserves went from 20,000 tons to 8,000 tons. When France put their ships out saying "give me my gold" and Switzerland did the same, you had the Nixon shock and the removal of the gold standard. Then that entered into the '74 agreement after the oil embargo (Syria and Egypt went to war with Israel over Palestine), and you had the petrodollar agreement to recycle these treasuries.

Now we entered into the phase where the liquidity of the US debt is what determines how long the system can continue, because the system has to roll over the debt. For all intents and purposes, the backbone of the entire banking system is US Treasuries.

Right now we're still seeing significant liquidity, but we're seeing foreign central banks that are selling down some of their treasuries for gold. We're also seeing some of the sources of liquidity dry up — i.e. the Japan carry trade, where Japan's increasing their rates and therefore the cheap money that was recycled into treasuries via Cayman Islands for the FIC is drying up.

36万亿美元货币 vs 40万亿美元债务：永动庞氏的数学

At the same time, we've got about $21 trillion within the Federal Reserve system and about $15 trillion of eurodollars — that's got nothing to do with Europe, that's dollars created outside the Federal Reserve system via the City of London and various banks and central banks that have access to these derivatives and FX swap lines.

Put that together, you've got about $36 trillion in the money supply (roughly, there's double counting there) and $40 trillion of debt. Because there's more debt than money, you have to keep the Ponzi scheme going.

But what is the cost of that debt? Currently it's about 3.3% on average. Why did Treasury intervene? Because foreign central banks are selling down those bonds. When you sell down bonds, yields go up. So the cost of the government debt is increasing — it's the largest amount on the balance sheet right now.

财政部与美联储的拉锯 → 唯一出口：QE

Scott Morrison (sic) and Treasury came in and said: "We'll backstop those 20-year auctions, 30-year bonds, and we'll buy them to supplement those auctions. And we'll issue more debt at the short end." But now the Federal Reserve has come up and said: "Well, we'll put our rates up on the short end."

So now you've got the bondholders demanding higher rates, the Federal Reserve demanding higher rates. The only solution to that is eventually quantitative easing. And QE requires a crisis in order to allow for it — whether it be the AI bubble, the funding bubble, whatever stress points there.

核心公式：只要名义增长 > 债务成本，游戏就能继续

What determines whether the dollar's liquidity continues? As long as the US economy can grow — and growth can be any way possible. It doesn't have to be genuine growth. It can be print money, spend it into the markets, and that increases GDP. That's what we're seeing on both the war side, the technical side, and the financial side if you ever get quantitative easing.

The key metric here: the cost of the debt is about 3.3% and going up — the growth rate of the US economy has to be larger. As long as it grows above 3.3%, you can continue this. If it goes below that, or the cost goes above that, then you start to hit the unwinding — and you have to sacrifice the currency, weaken the currency, which then pushes capital out towards these multipolar nodes.

If you're setting up for multipolarity, you want to invest into as much weakness as possible, accumulate as much assets as possible, then flow the capital out — but you want to have as much leverage. The military is just getting as much leverage, in my opinion, into these multipolar nodes while maximizing what you can squeeze from the K-shaped economy in the West.

五、对冲通胀的三条路径：加税 / 制造需求毁灭 / AI 替代人力

Alex: But I mean, if the nominal growth might increase, from a real perspective it might get eaten up by inflation, which is already higher. The Fed is also stuck — it cannot raise rates much more. And in the meantime we have energy shocks creating chokes that also are reflected in energy cost rising. So do you understand — are they engineering a crisis and a pretext to activate QE?

Simon: On the inflation side, people need to understand — how can you offset inflation as a result of all of this increase in the money supply rolling over the debt?

(1) 加税: One way is to actually tax more. That's what's happening across the European countries, the UK, various others — because when you tax people, remember the government is funded by debt, not tax. Unless it has an actual surplus, which most countries in the West don't. When you tax people, you take money out of the supply and it offsets some of the inflationary impact across Europe. That has demand destruction forces — only the wealthy are able to supplement the economy. Much of the economy is supplemented by the top 10% of earners.

(2) 制造危机 → 需求毁灭: You could have a crisis that creates demand destruction. If you have really high energy prices, the way to handle shortages is to have higher prices, which means less people consume. More people stay at home — you have lockdowns (which happened in Pakistan as energy, beta-tested in Cuba) — various things you can create demand destruction as an offsetting force, which benefits wealth transfer up to the asset holder.

(3) AI 大规模替代人力: The other way is through massive productivity improvement — that's the artificial intelligence trade. If you replace as many humans with AI as possible, it creates a lot of unemployment, but massive productivity increases from the companies that are able to be way more productive, have bigger earnings, get more stock market valuations. Then all you need to do is figure out what you're going to do with all those people that don't have jobs — that's the central bank digital currency, universal basic income, programmable money trade that we're creeping into. Manufactured civil unrest really helps as well.

Look, whether it's coordinated or adjusting to incentives, the root of the whole thing is: our fiat currencies are debt-based Ponzi schemes, which has implications. Those that get to print the money have significantly more incentives to benefit from the system than those on the wrong side of the debt cycle.

六、法国的死循环与欧元区的终局

Alex: Now if we look at the case of France specifically — you can't ignore it. I'm French, I'm from Paris. I see the images and the tension in our country is more divided than ever. The French 10-year yields reached more than 5%, and more importantly, the spread with the German bonds has widened towards 174 basis points — something we haven't seen since the Eurozone sovereign debt stress levels in 2011. And we're talking about the second most important country in the Eurozone. Where do you see it going? Could the ECB still offset with the TPI (transmission protection instrument)?

"厄运循环"：社会动荡 → 社会主义政策 → 债务爆炸 → 央行干预 → 更多财富转移

Simon: You've only got a couple of choices.

选项一 — 继续展期庞氏: One is that you can roll over the Ponzi, increase debt to GDP, supplement it through more socialist policies, tax higher, have AI replace some of the structural unemployment, and then have universal basic incomes.

选项二 — 把国家推入困境再政权更替: The other is you take the country into severe distress. You then regime-change the leadership. If Macron's getting very unpopular, then you just replace him with another one. These violent cycles tend to coincide with election cycles. If you can get the government to the point where it's in distress — and the euro is still the second-most important currency — you can either do it through the European Central Bank and intervention, or you can do IMF / more global multinational bailouts.

So you could end up in a situation where civil unrest justifies more socialist policies → more socialist policies blows out the debt to GDP → debt to GDP requires central banking intervention → that drives more wealth transfer. That's the doom loop. Then you can come in with an IMF loan or bailout, which requires austerity → austerity has economic contraction → the Fed can then purchase up these assets.

法国与非洲去殖民化 / 承认巴勒斯坦 / 新能源协议的时间线

It's interesting in the France case. If you look at the order with the geopolitical situation — you've had a big movement away from French decolonization across Africa. Niger, Chad — the French were expelled from previous colonial times and replaced with more Russian partnerships and Russian bases. Also Gulf partnerships: Saudi Arabia hosted much of their different economic agreements in France.

After that, you got a wave across Europe — France, England, Canada, various others — recognizing Palestine. We know that's very theatrical, but it coincides. And now you're getting new energy agreements where Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE are signing new energy agreements because of the diesel crisis happening right now. Then you get civil unrest and regime change.

You either think this is reaction, or you can see this is all part of a longer-term strategy.

前情：Nord Stream、关闭核电、风能税 — 欧洲对自己经济的"自杀"

What also preceded that was the Russia-Ukraine war: destroy Europe by taking away all of its cheap energy. We had the blowing up of the Nord Stream pipeline. Germany shutting down its nuclear power plants. UK introducing windfall taxes for climate energy policies and various other things.

Leading up to that, we had what would be suicide for the economy — create a strategic dependence upon Russia, and then choke off the pipelines and choke off Europe of its energy. Ever since then, the economic situation — and now they're hitting these severe energy shortages — can only lead to more draconian policy.

Sadly, there's no bullish case for Europe, for any of these countries. What you're witnessing right now, I think, is a reflection, and I think it gets worse in the years and decades ahead. I don't see any other plan other than austerity or European Central Bank debt rollover. Europe has launched their digital euro. Everything's about programmability, surveillance state — and it just so happens that the more civil unrest you have, the more it ties to accelerate those trends.

七、政治家不是傻瓜：他们知道自己为谁打工

Alex: The violence creates a precedent to justify a more controlled authoritarian state. And maybe I could link that with the digital euro — what we've seen with Christine Lagarde, who will leave her role as president of the ECB very soon for very strategic reasons.

Simon: The way I see it, the politicians that are in power are the ones that are able to come off the back of "we need change." There's a narrative where new leadership comes in saying: "You're corrupt, I'm going to do the opposite, we're going to fix everything, the world needs change, we're coming in with that change."

That narrative requires lobby money to build a marketing campaign to build favor with the people. The people then give you your vote — but once you're in power, you work for the lobby that funded your campaign. The lobby that funded your campaign is the real power structure of the country, which in the case of France is military power, London financial power, and American corporate power. Or you have partnerships with China — these different alternative rails or alternative energy rails.

New leadership does not mean change. It means a new marketing campaign to pretend you're going to change for the people, while you serve the lobby power. When you serve your sentence, the people realize you work for them — then you start the process again, and again, and again, until people just stop falling for it and stop believing you can vote your way out of this. At those stages, you get these kind of uprisings and revolutionary situations — which they're already prepared for, with the police and surveillance state.

Lagarde 提前离任与下一任 ECB 行长的"锁定"

Alex: What I was getting at with Christine Lagarde is that she's stepping down before the end of her term for very obvious reasons: in France, very likely it will be Marine Le Pen or Jean-Luc Mélenchon — more likely Le Pen. In Germany it will be the AfD, a very right-wing party. They would be putting someone at the head of the ECB which needs to be in accordance with Germany and France. This is done in the intent to not let any of those new governing leaders choose who the head of the ECB will be.

欧洲内部裂痕与"右派-俄罗斯"轴线的可能性

Simon: We're starting to see Europe kind of split between the Baltic states, which are investing severely in these new military budgets and this new European-based military industrial complex. You could end up with a right-leaning AfD Germany that may be aligned with Russia, and those that are not aligned with Russia — you end up having that fractioning.

A bit like you're seeing in America right now, where Russia's clearly aligned with China in the BRICS corridor, but you're getting sanction relief to solve the diesel crisis, and many people are accusing the Trump administration of being aligned with Russia and Putin. That creates that whole left-and-right type of divide — pragmatism versus those that have been radicalized by narrative, thinking that Putin's "the Hitler" or whatever it may be in their mind.

You can see where who is going to be aligned with Russia — and that's why I don't think this war ends. I don't think anyone's trying to end it, because the more you can weaken Europe, the more it benefits the stock markets and decouples the economies from the private sector.

八、数字欧元：不是货币走向数字化，而是权力集中

Alex: Do you see things like Pontus — the new system that is kind of the predecessor of the first rails of the digital yuan being implemented, concerning actual companies and commercial entities — as really the acceleration on the ECB side to lock down the control in Europe?

Simon: Look, we already have digital currencies. Many people talk about separating money and state. The central banks and the banks already did that. Most fiat currencies are created by private banks — it's not that the state creates it. The most important central bank is the Federal Reserve, and the Federal Reserve is owned by the banks.

Now, the European Central Bank is part of a European Union structure, which came from a project by the Bank for International Settlements between World War I and World War II. By having one currency in the European Union, you get way less state autonomy, but more power within the European Central Bank / European Union.

One of their dreams has been to have: - Capital markets union - Monetary union (the euro) — already achieved - Fiscal union — one tax policy, one capital market across Europe

The longer-term project is mass centralization of power into the European Central Bank, which feeds back into the Bank for International Settlements (the central bank of central banks), which represents the global Western financial industrial complex. It's about removing state autonomous power and loading those governments up with debt. Then when you manufacture crisis, you can come along with your digital rails.

CBDC vs 现有的"数字货币"：所有权的变化，而非技术的变化

What is the difference between a digital currency, which we currently have — banks create money every time they issue a loan, is all digital, is online, and a tiny percentage you can go to an ATM and redeem for physical cash — and a central bank digital currency? You transfer all of that power away from those private banks and over to one central bank. It's not that it's going digital — you're just changing it.

If you do it on blockchain rails and integrate it with social credit scores and artificial intelligence, then you can have these agentic autonomous policies, which would move towards a central bank fiscal union. Then you tokenize all the assets — a capital markets union by tokenizing everything, CBDC the currency, and a fiscal union by automating tax collection.

九、荷兰 Box 3：财富税作为"剥离期"的终极工具

Alex: Talking about tax collection — in the Netherlands, kind of a first in terms of OECD countries, they're in parliament right now discussing this "Box 3." For listeners not familiar: it's a reform where ETFs and financial securities would generally be taxed on capital gains when sold, while investors holding physical investments like gold and Bitcoin and other cryptos in their own custody directly could still be taxed annually on unrealized gains during a transitional period — which is insane. If anything, this is maybe the epitome of financial repression. Is the Netherlands — one of the most developed countries in the world — a test bed for closing the exit valves of anything left?

Simon: Correct. Look, politicians aren't idiots. They just know who they work for. Most of your job as a politician is to be a battering ram where everyone thinks you're crazy, you're an idiot — "why would you do that, socialism doesn't work," all of that. The politicians know that. They just work for power that is going through some kind of suppression of assets for a distressed acquisition.

资产剥离期的政策工具箱

The way you do asset-stripping at kind of end of empire — once you've burdened as much government debt as you can upon the government — you implement asset-destruction policies: wealth taxes, exit taxes. It's not like capital controls from China where the central bank and the government are trying to keep it in their own closed-loop system. This is: you've already privatized all the assets, now you use increased prices and inflation while at the same time increasing taxes, which means you create selling pressure on those assets. That's the asset-stripping phase.

为什么是荷兰？—— 中央银行的发源地、能源与芯片的关键节点

What you're also noticing is that it's cracked. The Netherlands is kind of an important country. It was where the central banking model was born. It was a very important trade route for liquefied natural gas — you had the "Dutch disease" where the economy was too concentrated on energy. Now it's got a very important part of the chip manufacturing supply chain.

If you can try and get those assets on the cheap, if you can introduce wealth taxes and some kind of financial oppression, then you can beta-test these different impacts.

英国的"源头扣税"实验与 OECD 全球税

One of the things they're beta-testing in the UK now is introducing that the bank actually pays the tax at source, and then you need to claim back the money if you don't think you owe the tax. Now they're going to be taking the tax directly out of your account. Programmable money is the ultimate way of doing that.

There is also a global tax that's been proposed by the OECD, where rather than having different jurisdictional arbitrage, they're trying to gradually beta-test global taxes via these transnational institutions.

十、什么条件下 Simon 会卖掉所有比特币换黄金？

Alex: You've also had a conversation with Natalie Brunell very recently, where you mentioned there would be certain conditions in which you would actually sell all your Bitcoin and buy gold. Do you see this as something — like, cutting the escape routes, cutting the escape valves — something that is likely to happen?

三种主权资产

Simon: You've got three sovereign assets that exist:

  1. Cash — will be inflated away if you're saving in cash
  2. Gold — most people, because it's hard to store and hard to spend, end up just buying an ETF or putting it in custody. You end up subject to your own custodian depending on how you purchase gold
  3. Bitcoin — allows you to own money without a bank, spend it without government permission, in an innocent-until-proven-guilty system. They can seize it, they can confiscate it, but it has to play within the confines of the law. Practically it's hard. And a fixed money supply means the money supply is set without a central bank

Obviously I can't hold cash at scale. I hold some cash, but it's going to be worth nothing in the future. It allows you to transact at the local level. We're starting to see lots of hacks and PHP things — we're definitely in a crazy time. We're seeing all these AI hacks, and the banks were closed yesterday trying to patch PHP and stuff like that.

To me, Bitcoin still is a sovereign asset, as long as you play within the confines of the law — you're able to store it outside the system, send it peer-to-peer, and there will only ever be 21 million.

导致 Simon 换仓的四个"中心化向量"

What Natalie was asking me is what would be the circumstances where I'd sell? Well, there is a trend to try and centralize Bitcoin:

  • (1) 托管集中化: Trying to own as much Bitcoin in custody (like gold) rather than people self-custody. About 30% is in custodian exchanges, 70% is outside
  • (2) 开发者团队被收编: Any type of control over competing developer teams and implementations
  • (3) 矿业国有化（上市化）在美国: Trying to make all of the Bitcoin mining companies public companies in one country, like America
  • (4) 让运行节点变贵: Making it expensive to run nodes. We've had wars over this — those wars are won, it's still cheap to run nodes

We've had more centralization of mining in China. That moved over to American public companies. Now they're pivoting over to AI, so it's getting more and more distributed — that's moving in the right direction. More and more people are centralizing their Bitcoin. Fortunately, it's proof of work rather than proof of stake, so it doesn't necessarily matter — but it does give short-term price manipulators more tools to manipulate the short-term price rather than the long-term price. I think there's been a lot more attention on developers, which I think is a very positive thing.

什么时候 21M 的上限会变得"微不足道"？

If we had fully compromised developers, very expensive nodes where only a few nodes matter, if all of the mining is centralized within the financial industrial complex as public companies, and everyone stops owning Bitcoin in self-custody and owns it via an ETF — then that would be the set of parameters where I think the 21-million cap, the ability for me to own my money and spend my money, might be trivial for the financial industrial complex to change.

I'm watching that trend. I don't think we're anywhere near it yet, but we have been moving in the wrong direction. I want to draw attention to it.

收尾

Alex: Thanks, Simon. As always, a pleasure to speak with you. As a note to the listeners, obviously Simon has a YouTube channel where he also has regular live streams, interviews — go check it out. Also Substack. Also on X. Very active online. Thank you, Simon, for your time.

For the listeners and viewers, I just want to remind you — 80% of you are not subscribed. It's obviously a trend in most channels out there, but it would mean a lot if just a few of you could actually hit the subscribe button if you follow or enjoy our interviews. And I will see you in the next episode of the Macroscopic Podcast. Thanks a lot, Simon.

Simon: Thank you.

Dixon 这段访谈里最刺耳的真话被他轻描淡写地丢了出来——"我不认为任何人在试图结束这场战争"。多数评论者假设乌克兰战争是一个"失控的局面"，需要外交去修补。但如果你把 Dixon 整个框架倒过来读，会发现一个令人不适的结论：**从 FIC（金融工业复合体）的损益表角度看，乌克兰战争并没有"失败"，它运行得完美**。它消灭了欧洲的廉价能源、迫使欧洲各国政府提高军费（即扩大债务）、把能源定价权交回到美国 LNG 出口商和军工承包商手里、同时让俄罗斯被迫转向东方——这是双赢，只不过"赢家"不在你以为的那张谈判桌上。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Jon Rahm 的"损失一亿美元"是本世纪最被误读的头条

表面上，社交媒体在传播一个"赔了一亿美元"的悲情故事。但若把他的位置看成一张资本结构表上的坐标，就会发现他其实做了可能是整个 Liv 故事中最聪明的一笔资本配置：

  • 作为规模最大的无担保债权人，他在重组瀑布流（waterfall）里处于最底端——理论回收率接近于零；
  • 他交出的，是一张几乎不可能兑付的应收账款；
  • 他换回的，是肖像权、赛程自由、以及重返大满贯通道——这些资产的净现值，在他这个年龄段，远超一亿美元。

媒体把它叙述成一次"放弃"，但从公司金融的角度，这更像是一次债转股失败后的理性注销：你不是放弃了钱，而是放弃了"你本来就拿不到的那笔钱"去换"你本来可能永远拿不回来的职业生涯"。真正的头条应该是：一位球员第一次用破产程序给自己做了杠杆收购。

二、Liv 2.0 的真正产品不是高尔夫——是税务损失

这是整段分析里最被低估的洞察。Ted Goldthorp 是 BC Partners 的债务合伙人，不是股权合伙人。一个债务人在估值归零的资产里出现，只有一种可能：他看中的根本不是这家公司的运营价值。

Charles 已经点破：Liv 累计 50 亿美元净运营亏损 (NOL)。按美国约 20% 的企业所得税率，这是一个面值 10 亿美元的税盾。BC Partners 用 3 亿美元"债务注资"，换取的是一张可以嫁接到自己整个体育组合（包含类 CVC 模式潜在收益）上的巨额抵税凭证。

跨领域连接：这不是体育故事，这是 1980 年代以来私募股权经典剧本的翻版—— - 与 Section 382 下的 "NOL shell play" 完全同构（典型案例：早年多家航空公司破产重组后被作为"税壳"收购）； - 与好莱坞税收抵免证券化（film tax credit funds）在数学上几乎同构：真实业务是不是赚钱并不重要，重要的是会计损失能否被跨主体转移使用； - 与 Donald Trump 1990 年代通过亏损抵免未来二十年所得的操作，逻辑完全一致。

换句话说：Liv 本质上已经从"沙特软实力项目"折旧为了一个税务特殊目的实体 (SPV)。打球的人，是让这个 SPV 保持"仍在营业"必备的生物性道具。

三、Bryson–GSE–BC Partners 三角：这是一场"自己给自己颁奖"的 WeWork 时刻

一个连 Charles 自己都承认是推测，但一旦看破就无法 unsee 的结构：

角色 关系
Bryson（唯一能撑估值的明星） 由 GSE Worldwide 代理
GSE Worldwide 由 BC Partners 持有重大股权
BC Partners 为 Liv 2.0 提供 3 亿美元"债务"

这是一个关联交易闭环：Bryson 的存在是让 2.0 看起来可行的唯一星光；而他的经纪人就是其金主。这意味着 BC Partners 几乎必然会以某种方式让 Bryson 参与到税务上行的分成中——因为他的留下既是产品，也是估值合法性的来源。

令人意外的类比：这不是体育赞助，这是 Adam Neumann 把自己名下地产租给 WeWork 的那个结构。它甚至更干净——因为所有人都在高尔夫球场上，没有人在看审计意见书。

四、Dean Burmeister 的"小孩和犀牛"不是搞笑——是诊断性症状

当参与者无法用经济语言解释自己为何加入某个结构时，他们会退回到道德与慈善的叙事。这是 Robert Cialdini 关于"social proof + 权威"操纵的教科书前兆，也是传销学术研究中著名的 "charitable halo deflection" 模式。

Dean 说不出 token economics、说不出 cap table、说不出 vesting schedule——他说"小孩和犀牛"。这不是傻；这是认知不协调下的叙事避险。而在他身后，Wall Street 的西装们正在计算 20% 的联邦企业税可以被抵消多久。

五、系统性真相：高尔夫选手正在被"证券化"

把这几件事放在一起看，Liv 2.0 的本质就显现了：

  • 球员 = 底层资产（underlying asset）
  • "股权" = 为了让底层资产留在产品里的激励代币
  • 税务损失 = 真正的现金流产品
  • BC Partners = 结构化金融机构
  • Scott O'Neil / Ted Goldthorp = 产品销售

这就是过去四十年发生在次级住房贷款、音乐版权、好莱坞片单、专业体育特许经营权上的同一套"实物资产金融化"模板，第一次被完整地移植到了"职业运动员的生涯中期"这个新资产类别上。

Jon Rahm 之所以是这个故事里唯一的真正赢家，是因为他是唯一一个意识到自己不是股东、而是抵押品的人。

📝 转录文本

Why we're still talking about Liv

...onto something which traditionally we've been very sceptical about entirely. In fact, I would say no one has sipped the Kool-Aid of Live Golf more than us, Charles. [laughter] Um, we — we — we are the evangelists. We are the ones who, even as the flame flickers...

bell ringing for our addiction to come. Yeah.

Flame flickers in the great, and still we — we're the ones here still. The way I put it, I know some people think we've been critical of Live Golf, but at least we're still talking about it, whereas most people have stopped talking about it.

I know. Um, and the reason why —

well —

obsessed.

It probably won't be for much longer.

Um, why are we talking about it?

We're talking about it because there are some important dates coming up to do with Liv 2.0. Is it 2.0? 2.0. 2.0. I think you're right. 2.0. Okay. Right.

Jon Rahm walks away from $100M

So, um, and just say — last week, Jon Rahm, there was a big, you know, number whacked all over social media and news sites, etc. saying Jon Rahm has given up $75 million —

dollars. No, hundred million. Yeah. $100 million. Rough. These were the rough numbers. They said he was the biggest unsecured creditor —

key word there, which is I think is one of the reasons why he did it. So, you know, being an unsecured creditor means you're pretty much at the bottom of the pile [clears throat]. Being the biggest one of those is not a good place to be.

Him doing that, I would imagine, comes from the reality that under BC Partners's new refinancing structure, players' debts are getting converted into equity. Rahm's team found that unacceptable, which is why he's left the tour. The likelihood of him actually getting that money back was therefore incredibly small, and as the biggest creditor it would have probably dragged on for a very long time.

This deal has freed him of all of the ties that he's had. He's got his name, image, likeness rights back. He's now got the freedom to go and make the moves on to tours that he wants to play on if they'll have him. And let's be honest, he's made a lot of money out of it already. So for him, while that number is standout, it seems to make sense to clear this and let him focus on the next part of this.

Absolutely. Right. But I think we need to put it in context of what's going on here. So —

Well, no, I do. I agree. But it's important because that needed to happen for this next bit to move on.

Scott O'Neil, BC Partners, and the $300M lifeline

Yeah. So, um, Scott O'Neil, who has been for the last year, year and a half the chief executive of Liv, um, has been for the last couple of months trying to find a way to get funding for Liv 2.0. Um, he's managed to rustle up a financial partner in BC Partners, um, which is an American finance house. Um, and reputedly BC Partners have agreed to put forward $300 million um to support Liv 2.0. And indeed the partner concerned at BC Partners, a guy called Ted Goldthorp — I think, is that right, Charlie? — um, was doing a conference with Scott O'Neil in London a couple of weeks ago, when they were both talking as if there's a brand new thing, you know, amazing concept. Everyone should get really, really excited. And I think a lot of people were sort of reaching for the sick bag. But —

100 million franchises, players. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You know, "we're going to create an amazing team golf sport, you know, sort of blah blah blah. All new, all new." And everyone's like, "well, we sort of heard that story before, when there was 5 — when there was 5 billion behind it, not 300 million." But whatever.

The October 25 deadline

Now what happened was: BC Partners effectively set a deadline of October the 13th for golfers who are currently on Liv to recommit to 2.0. When that wasn't proving to be as easy as perhaps they thought, they delayed the deadline to October the 25th, and we are recording this, Charlie, on October the —

20th.

20th. So, we're talking about this weekend, effectively. By this weekend, golfers who want to be on Liv 2.0 need to stick their hand up and say, "I'm on board. I'm with you. Um, Mr. Goldthorp, I'm part of your gang." Right.

The four buckets of players

So, we've speculated before about who would sign up. Um, if you remember, do you remember our buckets, Charlie?

I do. I love the buckets.

We had our buckets. And our buckets were basically:

Bucket 1 — Serious current golfers. There was one bucket which was serious current golfers who still have aspirations to win majors, who still would back themselves to get back on the European Tour and the US PGA Tour thereafter, um, who were only ever really on Liv, as you famously put it, to "play less golf for more money," and who are now like, "Okay, well, if that's not going to be the case, I'm going to go back off to the traditional tours." So, you know, we said at the time, you know, Jon Rahm and so on and so forth. These types of guys — Joaquin Niemann, Tyrrell Hatton.

Yeah, there's actually a bit of a question mark over Joaquin Niemann. I think —

I think he'll stay.

Well, it's not clear. Um, anyway, there's that.

That's a shame. He's one of the most exciting ones.

Well, let's see. It's not clear yet. Anyway, there's that group.

Bucket 2 — The OAPs. Then there is the OAP group. Um, the Phil Mickelson, Lee Westwood, Ian Poulter — these types of guys. And it's broadly assumed that if there's still more money going on Liv 2.0 than there is on the seniors tour, then that's fine by them.

Yeah. And fair play — again, you know, no one's judging anyone here. It is, you know, people do the best for themselves.

Bucket 3 — Bryson, on his own. The third bucket being, um —

Bryson —

being Bryson on his own, right? Just being the only big high-profile golfer who seems to be quite committed to this concept. And reminding people that Bryson's agency, the agency who looks after Bryson, is also owned by BC Partners — or GSE Worldwide.

GSE Worldwide. BC Partners have a significant stake in GSE Worldwide. So clearly wheels within wheels there.

Bucket 4 — The journeymen. And then the fourth bucket being the journeyman — the ones who came over to Liv basically because it was a steady, very lucrative steady wage. Didn't have to worry about missing cuts. Didn't have to worry about dropping, you know, finishing below 100th in the money list and therefore losing your card. You could just keep on going, earning lots of money, making — every week — making money because of no cuts and guaranteed prize money and so on and so forth.

Um, and we speculated to about three weeks ago that basically Liv 2.0 would be a mixture of the three buckets other than bucket one —

right? Some veterans, some journeymen, and Bryson —

and big bad Bryson.

And it actually looks like that is what it's going to be: that all the serious golfers other than Bryson are out. We'll come on to the fifth bucket in a moment. I know I'm holding —

Yeah, we'll come on to Dean Burmeister in a moment. So, let's just park him for one side, because when you're talking about the greatest star on the planet, you have to, you know, take what he says seriously.

The European Tour hardens its line

Um, meanwhile, the European Tour has said that whereas before they would allow Liv golfers to sometimes play on the European Tour if they paid their fines effectively — European Tour have said from now on that's off the table. Anyone who plays for Liv can't play on the European Tour.

There was some quite funny stuff going on during the Chapter 11 bankruptcy hearings in New Jersey, where Liv lawyers were claiming that the European Tour is — in quotations — "attempting to interfere with Liv's survival." No, Sherlock. [laughter] I think that's a fair thing to say.

Pot, kettle.

Well, [laughter] talking about pot, listen to this one. The Liv lawyer said, bemoaning the fact that the European Tour is trying to control where the players can and can't play:

"Player freedom is the reason Live Golf was created, and it's the foundation of Live Golf 2.0. It's unfortunate that another tour is taking the opposite view and pressuring our players with false choices."

Player freedom. Do I think that player freedom is the cornerstone of Live Golf? No. This is a tour which, when you signed up to it, you were banned from playing in any other event in the world when there was a Live Golf event on, and where you had to sign over all of your image and media rights to the tour and couldn't exploit them yourself at all. This was a tour that was precisely against player freedom. It was paying players a vast amount of money in return for them totally, totally releasing their freedom. I mean, the hypocrisy is utterly extraordinary.

The debt vs equity puzzle: what is Ted Goldthorp really doing?

I just want to ask you one other question, Charlie, since you have a sort of financial fund management side to your life. Um, Ted Goldthorp, this guy from BC Partners — he, um, is a debt partner there, which is to say that he invests money as debt. This feels to me like under normal circumstances this would be an equity investment, and yet the fact that it's Ted Goldthorp from BC Partners suggests that it's a debt investment. How does that work? How can you — because equity value's non-existent, right?

Okay. Well — but do you remember we were kind of laughing about this, weren't we? We were joking. Do you remember when the news first came out, we were going — we didn't really know anything about anyone. We said: this cannot be an equity play. There has to be another financial motive, with very intelligent people running various types of financial institutions recognizing an opportunity to gain some value off the misfortune of Live Golf and/or the people that have been left on the shelf.

So what do you think Ted's doing?

The NOL tax-shield theory

The point is that they have recognized that off the losses that Liv made — 5 billion —

5 billion —

that presents a significant opportunity for them to gain some tax exemptions in the future. So they've — 5 billion in net operating losses, as they call it. And this is where it gets technical. So trying to keep it for myself and everyone else simple:

Uh, you can offset those net operating losses — the taxes associated with future profits that you make in your portfolio — against net operating losses in other ventures that you're involved in. So governments traditionally did this to try and remove some of the distress on struggling businesses, to give them an opportunity to recover. Private equity has been taking advantage of this because they know they can front cash to get companies out of situations. What they want to do is look at their broader portfolio and say: right, so in this case, if BC and its sports portfolio — it kind of wants to run a CVC-type model — let's say they made 5 billion in profits over the next few years. They could offset the corporate tax (corporate income tax, which is about 20%); they could offset 1 billion of that against the 5 billion losses that would be associated with Liv's debt currently. I.e., they pay no tax.

Right? So, effectively the deal here, what you're saying — and this answers really well a question that's been lurking ever since I saw Ted's face, thinking "what the hell is a debt guy doing in this?" — okay, so what you're basically saying is that BC Partners is potentially buying 5 billion of tax credits in return — which nets out at 1 billion, because it's 20%. Effectively 1 billion of tax credits in return for 300 million of debt.

Like that, right? They're feeding this money in as well, most likely. So, you know, I think it's a 50 million — they put 4 million up at the beginning to cover some of the bankruptcy. I think that could extend to 50 million. I'm not sure, but I think these challenges they've got now around when they can pull out — or, you know, if certain players aren't signed, or if they don't get to the stage they need to to continue — they can pull that money. If no more than 50 million would be committed. If they do get to the stage, then the 300 million is still on the table.

But absolutely, from what it looks like, the real value to BC Partners is for the money that they can save in the future on a broader sports portfolio by offsetting the taxes of any future profits on their other businesses. Now, if you look at it like that —

then it's a good deal for them, not a bad —

and that explains a lot.

Why this is being mis-sold to players

But then what we don't want to see — and I think where you have the challenge, and where we know golfers have the challenge — is: don't sit on a panel and spin it to us as a 100 million equity investment and an opportunity for players who are sitting there facing um —

massive losses —

massive losses, because they've had to convert their cash into equity if they want anything to do with this. This is why I find it a bit distasteful, because some players — particularly golfers — actually are quite smart, but some are not, and some can be easily taken in. And these are years of their life which are the critical earning years. And these people, in some cases, should be going off and making their career back again on the main tours, qualifying for majors, cementing legacies, and all this type of stuff.

And you've got slightly slimy, slick-suited Americans sitting on panels at sports conferences, talking about how this is going to be this amazing new equity play, and the players are so lucky to be involved — when in actual fact it's ultimately, potentially (and I must say potentially, because we don't know), but it's potentially a piece of financial structuring, really, where if it does come off, great, but if it doesn't come off, then BC Partners win anyway.

The fifth bucket: Dean Burmeister, "kids and rhinos"

And actually, that's when I want to bring in the quote from our favorite global star.

biggest star on the planet —

biggest star on the planet: Dean Burmeister. The fifth bucket —

the top bucket.

All right, this is the South African player Dean Burmeister, who Scott O'Neil, the chief executive of Live Golf — and we'll come back on to him in a moment — um, described memorably as "the greatest star on the planet." Um, sorry, just every time I say that, I have to just take two deep breaths.

It's just — nothing on Dean. This is all —

poor Dean, right? [laughter] So, this is Dean um talking about the new Liv 2.0 and the wonderful equity opportunity it presents to people like him:

"It's obviously beneficial from a player perspective because we will own a huge chunk of it. I can't think of any other sport where it is that way. The trickle-down effects of all of this is going to do massive things all over the world — like for kids and rhinos."

Sorry. So, I'm just quoting him. [laughter] So, it gets weirder. Sorry, sh— stop it. Stop it. Right. Just let me —

Did it say "for kids and rhinos"?

Yes. I think he might be talking about his foundation or something. Anyway — kids and rhinos. Um:

"It's not just about golf. I think golf is just a part of life. All of this is way bigger than life. It's probably above my pay grade. Long may it continue."

Yeah.

Just seems to me like a very confused man. [laughter] Um — "it's not just about golf. I think golf is just a part of life. All of this is way bigger than life." What?

Yeah. So, sorry. Just — kids and rhinos. This is charity, I'm guessing —

seems like a very odd pairing to lump — even if he's South African, [laughter] still.

The kids and the rhinos are going to benefit. I didn't think Ted Goldthorp was thinking about the rhinos when —

Oh, yeah. You can see Ted — Ted's all over the rhinos. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Ted gets up in the morning and all he thinks about is saving the rhinos.

I can — when I saw Ted on that panel, that's why I thought Ted's a WWF Worldwide Life Fund — and no. The reason — sorry, just the reason why I read that out, Charlie, is because that outlines why I think that this whole proposal is —

dodgy —

Right. Which is: you've got a guy here who is not the greatest golf star on the planet, but who, before coming to Liv, did have a progressive, good career going on on the main tours, right? And who's still young enough to have the time to rebuild his career. And he's being told, "No, no, no — this is unbelievable, you're going to save lots of kids and rhinos, you know, all this type of stuff." And meanwhile, in the background are, you know, sort of slick-suited executives from Wall Street going, "Well, I tell you what, you know, this could be a really interesting piece of financial engineering here."

Just doesn't sit well with me. You know, if everyone's out front and they say, "Look, this is a debt investment. This is the reason why we're doing it. We do think it's got a chance, but I want to be really clear about how this is happening and why this is happening and all this type of stuff — and you guys need to know that you are taking a risk" — it's like when people advertise financial offerings in this country, you know, or even gambling, actually have to say, "by the way, you know, this is a risk. You do know that you are taking a risk, right? You do understand that this is not a slam dunk."

It seems to me that this has been sold to the players — in fact, not even "it seems to me." I know, from speaking to players who have had it sold to them, who said no, who perhaps are a little bit more worldly than Dean Burmeister, who have said it's basically just sold to you as being, "you'd be fools not to." You'd be fools not to buy in. This is an amazing opportunity.

And if you're in the journeyman bucket, that may be true. If this pretty much guarantees a few hundred thousand pounds of cash and prize money each year, or participation fees or whatever, if it comes with equity ownership — whatever that is — that could be better than the alternatives for you on other tours. So, the question is: does that deal make sense to BC, Liv 2.0 and what they want this product to be?

But I think, you know, as you said, the point is: you should just come out and explain it. You say, look, if we want to give you this opportunity, this is how it needs to be done. There are lots of different incentives at stake here for all of the people involved. If it works well and we do our job, you are going to benefit from it. But being pitched as "you'll be a fool not to be a part of it" is where we fall from reasonable justification to kind of fanciful.

I don't think it's overegging it to say that is how it's been pitched, because that is also how it was pitched at Sportico, the conference two weeks ago, right? It was not pitched as "this is going to be very challenging, but we could pull it off." This was pitched as "this is the greatest thing ever."

Yeah. Which was the problem. It made you feel stupid for thinking that this couldn't hit 100 million team valuations very quickly, which was why we had a problem with it last week — or a couple of weeks ago. So —

Speculation: a Bryson–BC Partners joint venture?

Now I'm just going to do a bit of speculation here, and I want to make it very clear that it is speculation. Which is: we mentioned the groups of people for whom this is obviously not a slam dunk, but it may be their only option — right? The journeyman and the veterans. The person for whom it's not obviously a slam dunk is Bryson.

  • Bryson's agency, who he's very close to, is GSE.
  • Who is the major shareholder in GSE? BC Partners.
  • Who is going to benefit massively if we're right about the financial structuring around this? BC in its portfolio.
  • What's the one thing that might potentially make this some sort of a success? Bryson.
  • What can they not offer Bryson? Loads of money — because there isn't loads of money to offer.

Is it possible that Bryson derives some portion of the benefit that BC Partners potentially are deriving from all of this? Is this effectively a joint venture between BC Partners and Bryson?

And this is speculation. I'm asking the question, because everything has been so opaque, so lacking in transparency. I'm asking the question: if this is effectively a JV between BC Partners and Bryson — on the upside it could be —

well — I'm just talking about how they — because if BC have got their own downside protected, have they also therefore protected Bryson's downside?

Possible. Because look, Bryson — we did say Bryson probably got most of his money out, right, from the initial deal. But let's say any debt that he had left in there — that, not so much. It's the opportunity cost, isn't it? The next two or three years.

Exactly. If you can find the right ways to go about it and legally structure that properly, then again that would make sense. It would make sense for BC to say, "Look, we need you here. You've burnt a lot of your bridges elsewhere, so — and we know you don't really want to go back really, right? So why not stay? This is the opportunity we're trying to exploit. If we pull it off, you'll be a very rich man. And if you don't, you're no worse off."

No, I think better than that. And if you don't, we may cut you in on part of the downside protection that we have in terms of the tax credits. I'm just speculating. I'm speculating on: if I was Bryson —

Do you remember how hard Bryson was trying to drive that deal with Liv in January? "You need to give me 500 million bucks. Yeah. Right. Or else I'm off."

Yeah. He's got all the cards again. So —

right. He's got the cards, but they don't have much cash to give him —

and they share effectively — share an agency anyway.

No, look, if I was — that's what I'd be doing, right?

So — yes. Good.

## 一、Jon Rahm 的"损失一亿美元"是本世纪最被误读的头条
表面上，社交媒体在传播一个"赔了一亿美元"的悲情故事。但若把他的位置看成一张**资本结构表**上的坐标，就会发现他其实做了可能是整个 Liv 故事中最聪明的一笔资本配置：
- 作为规模最大的**无担保债权人**，他在重组瀑布流（waterfall）里处于最底端——理论回收率接近于零； - 他交出的，是一张几乎不可能兑付的应收账款； - 他换回的，是**肖像权、赛程自由、以及重返大满贯通道**——这些资产的净现值，在他这个年龄段，远超一亿美元。
媒体把它叙述成一次"放弃"，但从公司金融的角度，这更像是一次**债转股失败后的理性注销**：你不是放弃了钱，而是放弃了"你本来就拿不到的那笔钱"去换"你本来可能永远拿不回来的职业生涯"。真正的头条应该是：*一位球员第一次用破产程序给自己做了杠杆收购*。
## 二、Liv 2.0 的真正产品不是高尔夫——是**税务损失**
这是整段分析里最被低估的洞察。Ted Goldthorp 是 BC Partners 的**债务合伙人**，不是股权合伙人。一个债务人在估值归零的资

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Do Chip Fabs Even Need Clean Rooms?
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的瓶颈不是光刻机，而是"组织性恐惧"的复利

这段对话最反直觉的一刻，是当 Dwarkesh 开玩笑说"让人在实验室里一边吃汉堡一边抽雪茄，看看良率会怎样"时，Intel 高管的反应——他没有否认这个实验可能揭示洁净室的部分冗余，而是说"没有现任者会愿意去做"。这里暴露了半导体行业一个被严重低估的事实：它的最大成本不是 EUV，而是"不敢做实验的成本"。

一家 fab 每损失一天产能就是数百万美元，这个数字本身成了认知的囚笼——它让"验证旧假设"的边际成本看起来远高于"保留旧假设"的边际成本。但如果洁净室的某些等级其实只对 10% 的工艺步骤关键呢？没人知道，因为没人敢付代价去知道。这是一种独特的工业形态：知识的更新速率，被资本的沉没规模反向压制。

二、跨领域连接：半导体 fab 和中世纪的大教堂建造

这里有一个让我停下来思考很久的类比。中世纪的大教堂往往要花 80–120 年才能建成，建造者早在完工前就已死去。久而久之，石匠的技艺变成了"配方式传承"——"祖父这么做，父亲这么做，所以我也这么做"。没人敢在圆顶上做结构实验，因为失败意味着整座教堂塌掉、整个城市破产。

半导体 fab 已经进入了同样的"大教堂阶段"：建造周期 5–7 年、资本 400 亿美元、工程师从入职第一天就被教导"流程就是流程"。Intel 高管说得非常坦率——"有新工程师进来，他们把工艺流程当作圣经。" 这不是比喻，这是真实的宗教学结构：当资本足够重、周期足够长，工程就会退化为仪轨。

而当年打破中世纪建筑停滞的，不是更好的石匠，而是预算小得多、风险承受力大得多的"异端建造者"——文艺复兴早期那些建自家小礼拜堂的佛罗伦萨商人。这正是埃隆的 Terrafab 在半导体世界里的隐喻位置：他不是来做得更好，他是来被允许失败的那个人。

三、被掩盖的"反摩尔定律"：fab 成本的几何爆炸终将先于物理极限杀死进步

对话里埋了一个数字炸弹，但两人滑过去得太快：fab 建造成本每 4–5 年翻一倍，光刻模块的成本翻倍更快。按这个速率外推——"四年后光刻一个工艺节点要花 8 亿美元"——Intel 高管自己笑说"没道理"。

但这里有个更大的洞察：整个半导体产业其实在同时跑两条摩尔定律。一条是正向的（晶体管密度每两年翻倍），一条是反向的（建造成本每四五年翻倍）。两条曲线在数学上注定相撞。而撞点早于物理极限——晶体管还能继续缩小，但没人付得起缩小它所需的 fab。

这解释了为什么 Intel 和 Elon 的合作在战略层面比表面看起来更深：这不是产能合作，而是在赌"谁能第一个跳出成本的指数曲线"。Elon 的议价能力在于他可以说"我愿意不要洁净室试试"，而 Intel 不能。这种"愿意承担异端成本"的能力，可能比资本本身更稀缺。

四、一个意外的旁注：这次对话本身是一次"公开认错"

Intel 高管在最后一句话里悄悄说了一件惊人的事——"如果我们早知道今天的需求，一年前就该多买设备。而知道我们现在知道的，我们会继续多买。" 翻译过来是：我们一年前判断错了 AI 的 silicon 需求曲线。

这句话的真正含义不是"我们错了"，而是"在一个资本周期 5–7 年、认知修正窗口只有 12 个月的行业里，所有现任者都在系统性地低估需求"。这才是 Nvidia 的 Jensen 用数百亿美元合同锁死 HBM 内存的那个决策的底层逻辑——他不是在供应链上下赌注，他是在赌"所有保守主义都会以同一个方向、同一个速度错下去"。

对我们这些观察者来说，这句话值得留在耳边——它是一种反向指标：当一个资本最密集的行业的领导者当众承认"我们一年前该下更大的注"，意味着这个波段还远远没有结束。

📝 转录文本

关于与 Elon 合作的 Terrafab

Dwarkesh： I think it'll be interesting to discuss the partnership you guys have with Elon on Terrafab. What's going on there?

Intel： Well, I think Elon's publicly talked about his desire to build a fab.

"We either build the Terrafab or we don't have the chips. And we need the chips. So we're going to build Terrafab."

So, the same thinking — he's seeing just an enormous increase in demand for silicon, for compute and for memory. And I think he came to the conclusion that his own businesses are going to require a lot of silicon. So he thought maybe he should just do it all on his own. Unlike building a car, for example, this is such an intricate and complicated process. We thought we could work together to help accelerate his bringing up his fab.

工具瓶颈真的是唯一瓶颈吗？

Dwarkesh： But because of the bottleneck at the tool level, it seems like the net amount of silicon in the world won't increase. It's just that maybe if somebody were to start a new fab, they would get access to guaranteed supply in a way that they wouldn't have if they're working with another person's foundry.

Intel： It's actually not just tools. A fab does require a lot of power, a lot of water, a lot of consumables — there are many other input variables as well.

Dwarkesh： But those can be scaled in the way that tools cannot.

Intel： Yeah, some more than others, but yes. In one sense, yes, we need a lot more equipment, but it is true — we also need a lot more just raw fab space, raw clean room capacity.

Fab 的经济学：一条正在失控的指数曲线

Dwarkesh： So if you think of a foundry like Intel, which has to build these expensive facilities, buy expensive tools, I wonder what you think the economics of that fundamentally could look like — whether it could get more economical, whether it could scale faster.

Intel： Like I described earlier, this is an extremely capital-heavy business. If you just plot how much it costs to build a fab over the last 20, 30, 40 years, it's doubling every four to five years. Even inside the fab, if you look at the cost to do lithography — which is the most expensive module, just patterning — that itself is doubling at more than that rate.

So today a high-end EUV scanner and all its associated equipment is like $400 million. What does that mean? If that rate were to continue, four years from now the cost of patterning is going to be like 800 million — it doesn't really make sense, right?

一个"从零开始"的思想实验

I think a very interesting thought exercise is to say: are there things that could be very radically different that we could do today that we perhaps couldn't do 20 years ago?

This is a very risk-averse industry, for very good reason. You put in tens of billions of dollars and you really don't want to take any risks. So you want to keep doing things the way they've been done for literally decades. This is not just true of semiconductors, but of everything really.

But if you've just kept doing that for decade upon decade, many things just become — you know, you just become indoctrinated. There are engineers who work at Intel who come in and they're taught: "This is how the fab, this is the process flow," and they just take that as gospel. That's just how it is done.

But is that really the best way to build a chip today? It's a really valid question.

不只是光刻——晶体管、流程、乃至洁净室本身

Dwarkesh： I'm very curious what you're hinting at, because it could be anything from "we can figure out ways in which we use fewer litho passes and economize on the expensive component" to "maybe we need to rethink the transistor." What is the level of —

Intel： I think all of the above.

Transistor architecture — the silicon transistor has continued to evolve over 30–40 years, and that will continue. You've seen the evolution from the planar transistor to FinFETs to now gate-all-around transistors. That roadmap exists and it's pretty well defined, with a lot of people working on it.

But there are things like: do you really need a clean room today? Does the infrastructure need to be as sophisticated, as complex, as it is today?

汉堡与雪茄：一个（不会被允许的）实验

Dwarkesh： Surely one can run an experiment where you just have people eating hamburgers and smoking cigars in the research lab and see what happens to yield.

Intel： That would be a great experiment to run, but no incumbent — Intel, TSMC, Samsung — nobody would want to just willingly do that. That's what I meant by this being a very risk-averse business, for good reason. Every one day lost in productivity is like, I don't know how many dollars.

Dwarkesh： But you save so much money in not having to build clean rooms in the future.

Intel： It's really the fear of the unknown. Nobody is going to willingly take that risk. That's why I think sometimes it's good to just start with a clean slate and rethink everything.

The same thing applies to chip design, by the way. Many of the ways we do CPU design were probably locked in 30 years ago. Does that mean it's still smart to do it the same way? Probably not. But this is a very complex problem. Chip design — the capacity to take risk is maybe higher. This one, less so. But given where the economics is today, it's a very valid question to ask: maybe there's a smarter way to do this.

收尾：Intel 应该如何回应这场 AI 需求浪潮？

Dwarkesh： To close out, maybe we'll start off at the same question we began the interview with. Which is: how does Intel respond to this crazy AI demand that's incoming and has already arrived?

It sounds like what Intel ought to do — if the ultimate bottleneck is that you guys already have these foundries, you guys already have the ability to expand these foundries, but what you will eventually lack is the tools from upstream in the supply chain — is to raise as much capital as possible right now. The same way that Nvidia has locked down memory and other components for reportedly hundreds of billions of dollars worth of commitments. Intel should maybe do the same thing, make all these commitments, so that over the coming years the US is in a good position to have the bulk of semiconductor manufacturing at the most advanced levels happening here.

Intel： You're suggesting maybe we should be buying a lot more tools, right?

Dwarkesh： Yeah, because it sounds like — well, in a couple of years otherwise you'd just be in a position where you're like, "Oh man, we could be making trillions of dollars right now, but all the tools are in Taiwan."

Intel： Yes. Had we known what we know today, we would have invested more like a year ago. Knowing what we know now, I think we'll be investing more.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

这段对话最反直觉的一刻，是当 Dwarkesh 开玩笑说"让人在实验室里一边吃汉堡一边抽雪茄，看看良率会怎样"时，Intel 高管的反应——他没有否认这个实验可能揭示洁净室的部分冗余，而是说"**没有现任者会愿意去做**"。这里暴露了半导体行业一个被严重低估的事实：**它的最大成本不是 EUV，而是"不敢做实验的成本"**。
一家 fab 每损失一天产能就是数百万美元，这个数字本身成了认知的囚笼——它让"验证旧假设"的边际成本看起来远高于"保留旧假设"的边际成本。但如果洁净室的某些等级其实只对 10% 的工艺步骤关键呢？没人知道，因为**没人敢付代价去知道**。这是一种独特的工业形态：**知识的更新速率，被资本的沉没规模反向压制**。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一所高中教室漏水，如何烧掉一座 143 年的市政厅？

表面上这是"法国人爱抗议"的又一次重演，但真正值得注意的是触发链的物理学：导火索不是失业、不是通胀、不是移民政策，而是一所学校的数学课没有老师。这个细节比任何宏观数据都更危险——因为它暴露了一个被忽视的系统性真相：当一个国家把 57% 的 GDP 投入公共服务，却连一名高中数学老师都派不出来时，崩溃的不是财政，而是"交换契约"本身。

学生举着那块牌子——"如果你不出钱弄好我的学校，我就不付你的退休金"——不是情绪宣泄，而是一次代际合同的公开违约声明。这是整个事件最被低估的瞬间：一个 16 岁的孩子，用一句话精准地识破了法国福利国家的庞氏结构（现役劳动人口供养退休人口），并当众宣布拒绝签字。这种清醒，比燃烧的汽车可怕得多。

跨领域连接：法国街头正在上演一场"流动性危机"

这里有个让人意外的类比——法国目前的政治状况，在结构上与 2008 年的雷曼时刻惊人地相似，只不过抵押品不是次级房贷，而是"社会信任"。

想想银行的运作：银行只需要维持一小部分准备金，因为储户相信"随时可以取钱"，所以他们大多数时候不取。福利国家也一样——政府承诺"从摇篮到坟墓"的保障，是建立在"没有人同时来兑现"的前提上。一旦人们开始怀疑承诺的可兑现性，就会出现挤兑。

学生、黄背心、工会、无政府主义者——他们表面诉求不同（要老师、要加薪、要降油价、要砸店），但本质上都在同一个时刻"挤兑"同一张合同。这才是为什么一所郊区高中的事能在两周内蔓延到 1027 所学校：这不是模仿，是系统性信任的级联失效，和银行一家倒闭引发全面挤兑是同一个数学模型。

更妙的是，日本三井住友已经抛光了法国公债——金融市场的挤兑和街头的挤兑，是同一场挤兑的两个侧面。债券利率上升和市政厅着火，是同一个"信任准备金"耗尽的两个外显指标。

一个最反直觉的观察：法国的"进步传统"正在吞噬它自己

大多数评论会说法国问题出在"保守"（不愿改革）或"激进"（太爱抗议）。但真正的悖论是——法国正在被它自己最引以为傲的两样东西反噬：世俗主义（laïcité）与大革命精神。

  • 世俗主义本是启蒙的武器，用来把宗教赶出公共领域、保障平等。但在 2026 年的移民后代眼中，它变成了"只针对我的头巾、却从没针对过教堂钟声"的歧视工具。启蒙的普世语言，被 29% 的非欧裔二代读成了"文化不认同我"的密码。
  • 1789 年的革命精神教会法国人：街头是政治的合法场所，断头台可以斩首国王。这是法国人的骄傲。但这个 DNA 现在的副作用是——任何改革都会被当作"路易十六时刻"来反抗。想把退休年龄从 62 调到 64？百万人上街。因为法国人从历史里学到的教训不是"妥协"，而是"反抗奏效"。

换句话说，法国正在被自己最成功的两次历史胜利困住：它赢得了政教分离，于是无法与新移民的信仰共处；它赢得了反抗君主的权利，于是无法让人民接受任何牺牲。

这就是为什么邦妮说"可能无解"——不是因为问题太难，而是解决方案本身被这个国家最神圣的两条教义禁止。一个国家最大的危险，往往不是来自它的弱点，而是来自它过度成功的强项。

一条留给思考的裂缝

那个撒谎说老师歧视穆斯林、最终导致老师被斩首的 13 岁女孩——她当天根本没去上课。这或许是整个法国困境的最小单元：一个关于"我没在场"的谎言，杀死了一个"在场"讲言论自由的人。而今天街头 55 万人中的大多数，也许根本没真正弄清自己为什么愤怒——他们只是感到"自己没在场"于这个国家的许诺之中。

📝 转录文本

一、开场：法国在烧什么？

你一定有看过这些法国烧起来的新闻画面——示威游行、暴力抢劫、零元购，各大精品百年历史的建筑被喷得乱七八糟，还有被烧到金光。法国他到底在吵什么？他们到底想要争取什么？为什么一个高中缺老师的问题，最后会演变成几十万个人上街、政府建筑被烧掉？

看完这支影片就会知道这场法国的暴动完整的来龙去脉，整个事件背后四个长久以来社会延伸出的矛盾情景：

  1. 政府财政跟社会福利
  2. 贫富跟世代的利益
  3. 移民、宗教，还有国家的认同
  4. 人民跟政府之间长期累积的不信任

这些问题到底有多严重？你跟我的钱包又怎么样被这场暴动影响？

请不吝点赞订阅、转发、打赏，支持明镜与点点栏目。

Hello 我是 Bonnie，喜欢这种把复杂故事线跟历史爱恨情仇说清楚的影片，记得要订阅按赞，谢谢你的鼓励。

二、火光中的市政厅：事件现场

2026 年 10 月 17 号，法国中部的城市叫做礼魔日，有一座 143 年历史的市政厅正在熊熊的燃烧。这栋建筑呢是 1883 年建成的，经历过两次世界大战都还屹立不摇。但是就在 2026 年的这一天，一群蒙面的暴动者闯进了市政厅，从地下室和一楼开始纵火，还威胁要杀死市政厅里面的工作人员。火势迅速的蔓延到屋顶，到了晚上这座高达 43 公尺、象征着城市历史的市政厅终于受不了了，在众人面前轰然倒塌。

也就在同一个夜晚，法国的其他城市也开始陷入了混乱：

  • 巴黎：街上有汽车被点燃，蒙面的暴动者朝着警方丢石头，还发射烟火，甚至还有人趁乱砸商店的玻璃，冲进精品店、名表店、手机店去抢劫。警察一边放催泪瓦斯，一边试图要阻止人群继续往前进。
  • 里昂：有人放火烧掉了旅游服务中心。
  • 马赛：暴动者闯入了市政厅，破坏设施，留下了无政府主义的涂鸦。

这一天全法国到底有多少人上街呢？法国的内政部是说 55 万人，但是呢，工会说实际人数是高达 80 万人。大部分参加的人都是和平的在示威，但是随着暴力的冲突慢慢的扩大——烧汽车、抢商店，还有火爆的警民冲突——这些画面开始占据了全世界的新闻版面。

最让人完全无法想象的是，这一场席卷全国的社会动乱，竟然是巴黎郊区的一所高中里面的高中生开始的。

三、导火索：一所没有数学老师的高中

我们得要先从 2026 年的 9 月开始说起。

时间倒回到 2026 年的 9 月 18 号，巴黎郊区有一所叫做圣修伯利的公立高中，一群学生一大早就来学校门口，但是他们今天呢并没有打算要进去上课。学生拿来一大堆东西就把校门口堵住。

为什么呢？因为前一天学校的老师才刚刚发动罢工而已。原因就是新学期都开始了，学校竟然还有将近十个教职员的职位没有补齐——没有数学老师、没有法文老师、没有副校长、护理师，还有负责安排学生实习的行政人员都没有。

去年一整年呢，这一所高中只有三个月有数学老师；今年开学竟然直接没有数学老师。还有学生因为学校缺行政人员，连实习都没有办法正常安排。有些教室跟公共设施都已经坏了很久，也都没有人修。

这不是小问题——这是对法国模式的质疑

这个时候就有人要说啦："学校缺老师，那你就好好讲啊，有必要把学校封起来这干嘛呢？"

法国它是全世界公共支出最高的国家之一，政府每一年要花掉 GDP 57% 的钱，老百姓缴的税呢也是在欧洲名列前茅。法国政府是长期承诺"我们会从教育到医疗到退休保障，都要提供完善的公共服务"。结果呢，这些学生连老师都不够，那大家交这么多税是干嘛呢？

而且问题还不只是老师不够。这一所高中呢大概有 1500 个学生，但是连护理师都没有。所以很多家长说如果有学生突然发生医疗状况，到底谁来照顾呢？

法国公立学校的老师呢受到公务员的制度保障，校长没有办法直接开除老师。所以呢，如果老师长期请假，学校又找不到人带课的时候，最后受影响的就是学生。法国的教育部统计，从 24 年到 25 年公立国高中有 7.5% 的教学时数，是因为老师缺席又找不到人带课而泡汤。

四、从一所学校到全国罢课

学生最后受不了了，决定自己站出来。这些高中生呢他们拿手机去拍影片抗议，原本大家只是想要逼教育部注意这些事情，结果呢其他的学校学生也都看到这个影片了，开始也都纷纷分享自己的遭遇。

  • 有一些学校的同学抱怨："教室好挤哦。"
  • 有些人说："天花板会漏水，教室很热，还有老鼠会出没。"

让很多高中生更不爽的是呢，法国申请大学要参考高中的成绩还有老师的评语。但问题就是有一些学生他可以正常上课，有一些学生是连数学老师都没有。所以同样要竞争大学的名额，学校提供的教育资源差这么多，这样的竞争哪有公平可言呢？

反正很快啊，TikTok、Snapchat、Instagram 上面开始都出现了各种抗议的影片，一所接着一所的高中同学都加入。

一句意味深长的标语

有高中生在抗议的时候举着标语，上面写着：

"如果你不出钱弄好我的学校，我就不付你的退休金。"

这一句话意味深长。因为法国的退休制度呢，很大一部分就是靠着现在工作的年轻人缴纳社会保险费，支撑已经退休的人的那些费用。可是今天以学生的角度来说，他连基本的教育资源都没有完整的保障，凭什么被要求要承担这么多的责任呢？

我们要记住这个重点，因为接下来还会扯出一大堆法国非常严重的世代跟财政矛盾。

两个星期：四分之一的高中沦陷

到了 10 月 1 号，距离最刚开始的抗议两个礼拜之后呢，整场的运动已经蔓延到了法国全国了。根据法国的内政部统计，全国大概 3700 所高中，当天有 1027 所出现同学在抗议还有罢课的行动，其中有 222 所甚至是被学生用各种物品直接封锁校门，让师生都没有办法正常进出。也就是说，短短两个星期，全法国超过四分之一的高中都出现了抗议的活动。

随着参与的人数慢慢增加，部分的学校周边也开始出现了暴力的冲突：有人开始烧垃圾桶、烧脚踏车，甚至还朝警察发射烟火。警察开始部署了防暴部队，用催泪瓦斯去驱赶人群。学生抗议的焦点，也从改善教育的资源慢慢延伸到抗议警察的执法方式了。

五、政府让步，但火已经烧不住了

政府眼看着事情越闹越大，终于让步了。10 月 8 号，法国的教育部长宣布要调派 3000 名代课老师，优先支援全国里面大概 500 所问题最严重的高中。政府也开始跟学生代表协商，试图想要平息这场抗议。教育当局也赶快把原本发起抗议的圣修伯利高中补上缺少的教职员，在 10 月初他们就恢复正常上课了。

所以这个时候，最先开始抗议教育资源的那一所学校的学生已经回到教室正常上课了。可是后来其他加入的学校越来越多人去加入抗争，甚至连不是学生的人都出现了。

黄背心归来

法国的街头开始出现一群穿着黄色反光背心的人。如果你还记得 2018 年的法国新闻，应该对这个画面很熟悉，也就是当年让马克宏政府陷入严重的政治危机的黄背心运动。2018 年那个时候呢，这群人是因为反对燃油税上涨走上街头，后来呢就演变成持续好多个月的全国性抗争。

那就在现在这个时刻也太刚好了吧，燃油的价格跟生活成本又再次变得很高，所以这些黄背心运动的支持者又加入了这场学生的行动。

接着法国部分的工会开始动员了，像是公共部门的员工、对薪资不满的劳工、反对政府财政政策的左翼团体，都陆续走上街头。大家要的东西不太一样：

  • 学生要老师
  • 工人要加薪
  • 黄背心要求政府减轻生活负担
  • 还有人直接要求"马克宏你给我下台"

就这样，一场原本发生在校园里面的抗议，逐渐变成了一个全国性的反政府示威。

黑衣集团登场

不过这时候街头又出现了另外一群人，他们是全身穿着黑衣服、蒙着脸，有一些人还带着护目镜跟防毒面具。这种集体行动方式叫做黑衣集团战术（Black Bloc），经常出现在欧洲的激进示威活动里面。他们支持的是反资本主义或者是无政府主义的立场，会透过破坏企业跟政府的设施来表达政治的诉求。

六、广告段落：MyTrade

在我们继续讲故事之前呢跟你说，现在到资讯栏，只要完成指定的任务复合资格，就可以得到频道的 200 美金 USDT 粉丝福利红包，不过这个限量的名额呢先到先得。

MyTrade 拥有全世界四大监管机构的交易牌照，股票、外汇、加密货币、指数，还有大宗商品跟 ETF 都可以交易。MyTrade 是一个 CFD 差价合约的交易平台，你交易的不是标的本身，而是透过合约参与它的价格涨跌。MyTrade 可以信用卡跟 USDT 直接出入金，交易本身免佣金，点差偏低，还可以做多做空双向交易，涨跌都有机会获利。交易门槛只要 5 美元就可以开始交易，它内置了 TradingView 的指标免费使用，平台里面还有很多的资讯、新闻跟交易策略可以参考。

想要完成任务得到 200 USDT 美金的奖励，一定要透过下面频道的专属注册连结，这样才符合活动的资格，赶快到下面的资讯栏看时间跟活动的规则。

七、暴动的黑夜：巴黎街头实况

你听到这里不会觉得很奇怪吗？一场从高中教室开始的抗议，到底怎么会演变成这么大的暴力冲突呢？

10 月 17 号礼拜六，法国各地有 55 万个人走上街头，其中巴黎就有 11 万人。

一通打不通的报警电话

我先带你到巴黎的这间手机店。10 月 17 号晚上，巴黎马真塔大道，大概有 20 个蒙面男子拿着一大堆工具开始攻击一家手机店。店主叫做 Azam，他眼看情况不对了，赶快跟员工一起把店关起来，但是还是被攻击了。他在短短一个小时里面打了五通电话跟警方求救，但是得到的回应就是：警察现在没有办法派人过去。

结果这一群人呢砸店、开门，搬走了 50 支 iPhone、70 支的三星手机，还有 50 台电脑，另外呢也搜刮了收银机里面的 8000 欧元现金，总共损失呢至少 14 万欧元。

在同一条马路上面呢，还有其他的手机店、超市跟银行都被破坏了，有人去砸碎玻璃，有人放火。

为什么警察到不了？

你可能会想，这警察到底去哪里了呢？原来是暴动的人分成不同的小团体在城市的各处移动，警察刚赶到一个街区，另外一个地方又开始有人纵火、砸店。在巴黎呢，甚至还有暴动者一度逼近总统府附近，让警方是不得不调动更多的警力。

到了 10 月 19 号，法国已经有超过 2400 个人被逮捕。这场暴动呢也冲击到了大型的连锁企业，比如说家乐福就有 50 间门市受到很严重的影响，预估全年的营业利润减少 8000 万到 2 亿欧元。

10 月 19 号，法国的内政部长纽涅斯公开承认说警方在部分的主要城市确实是失去控制了，他还跟马克宏总统提出辞呈，结果马克宏呢拒绝他，因为现在才是最需要有人继续指挥警力的时候。

不过这场暴动也让法国的警方执法的方式受到质疑。在圣爱蒂安有一个 17 岁的示威者在警民的冲突里面失去了一只手，警方使用的防暴武器呢因此就成为调查的重点。

八、矛盾一：钱去哪儿了？——法国的财政黑洞

政府收了这么多，所以为什么还可以搞成这样呢？政府的钱到底去哪里了呢？

2025 年法国政府各级的公共部门总共花了 1.71 兆欧元，收入却只有 1.56 兆，所以光是一年就出现了 1500 亿欧元的财政缺口。

一个夸张的数字

法国的公共支出占他们整个 GDP 57% 左右。这个数字到底有多夸张？我们来对比一下：

  • 美国：约 38%
  • 日本：约 37%
  • 中国：约 33%

也就是说，同样是 100 块钱的经济产出，法国政府的支出规模就比日本、美国还有中国高出大概 20 多块钱，这真的很多。

退休金吃掉四分之一

那为什么法国政府要花这么多钱呢？很大一部分就是法国引以为傲的社会福利制度。里面最贵的一个开销就是退休金——法国每一年光是退休金呢就相当于 GDP 的 14% 左右，吃掉四分之一的公共支出。

更严重的就是法国人口在老化，所以退休的人越来越多，大家的负担也就越来越重。2023 年马克龙政府决定要把法定的退休年龄从 62 岁提高到 64 岁，结果立刻引发全国的大罢工，上百万人走上街头。这改革最后虽然通过了，但是到 2025 年国会又决定要暂缓这个部分的调整。

债务螺旋

截至 2026 年中，法国政府的公共债务已经累积到了 3.6 兆欧元，相当于 GDP 的 119%。而且随着投资人是越来越担心法国的财政，法国政府借钱的成本也就开始上升了。

现在法国政府提出了明年 2027 年的预算，光是支付公债的利息，预计就要花掉 9120 亿欧元。同一年，法国国民教育的预算草案大概是 655 亿欧元。也就是说，法国政府明年要支付利息的金额，已经超过了国民教育年度预算的规模。

九、矛盾二：有钱人减税，普通人延退——世代与阶级的愤怒

而且法国人呢还有另外一个原因是非常生气。2018 年马克宏政府呢是缩小了原本针对富人多种的资产税的财富税范围，改成主要针对房地产来课税。那政府希望用这种方式来吸引投资。

但就像我们刚刚讲到了，2023 年他又要求一般劳工要延后退休。所以站在一般民众的角度来说——有钱人得到减税，普通人却要工作更久、退休得更晚，那大家就会觉得不公平。这也就是为什么那时候的黄背心运动示威者长期把马克宏当作是一个偏袒有钱人的总统。

为什么法国人这么爱抗议？

法国人很爱抗议，这其实是有历史原因的。早在 1789 年，法国政府呢就曾经因为债务沉重、物价上涨，各种不公平的原因引发了人民强烈的反弹，最后爆发了震惊世界的法国大革命，当时的国王路易十六甚至是被送上断头台。

对很多法国人来说，走上街头就是一个很熟悉的政治手段。

十、矛盾三：谁才算"真正的法国人"？——移民与世俗主义之痛

不过这一场现在在发生的暴动，很多人会归咎的问题是移民的问题，说是移民太多造成的。那我们来看看究竟是什么样的人才会被算作是真正的法国人。

殖民遗产

法国他曾经统治阿尔及利亚长达 132 年。在二战之后呢，法国需要大量的劳动重建经济，所以呢有很多阿尔及利亚、摩洛哥、突尼西亚这些人来到法国。几十年过去之后呢，这些移民的孩子跟孙子很多都是法国土生土长了，他们说法文，接受法国的教育，还有法国的国籍。

但是根据法国国家统计局的调查，在非欧洲移民的下一代当中，超过 29% 的人认为说其他人也就是法国社会的其他人，并没有真的把自己当成是法国人。这可能是他们自己主观的感受，也可能是真实发生的状况，我们也就是用数据在推敲。

世俗主义（Laïcité）的争议

而且不只是种族而已，一旦碰到宗教问题，哇那又更敏感了。

法国有一个非常重要的传统叫做世俗主义。法国强调国家跟宗教是分离的，尤其是在公立学校里面，学生必须要遵守一套共同的世俗规则，有点像是我们上学要穿制服一样。

  • 2004 年：法国通过了一个法律，禁止学生在公立的中小学佩戴显著的宗教标志，比如说回教的头巾、犹太教的小圆帽，还有大型的十字架都不可以。
  • 2010 年：法国进一步禁止了在公共场合遮盖脸部，这当然影响到有一些回教女性穿戴尼卡布跟罩袍。
  • 2023 年：法国政府宣布公共学校禁止学生穿着被认定具有宗教象征的 Abaya 长袍。

当然这些原因就是政府觉得学校是要维持宗教中立，避免学生受到宗教的压力，所有人都应该要遵守共同的规则。但是对有一些回教女性来说，佩戴头巾就是自己的信仰的选择，政府反而去限制她们的穿着，这不就是侵犯了宗教自由吗？

一位被斩首的历史老师

2020 年法国发生了一个震惊全国的命案。有一个 47 岁的历史老师叫做 Samuel，他在课堂上面讨论言论自由的时候，展示了查理周刊登一个回教先知 Muhammad 嘲讽的漫画。他还事先告诉学生说："如果你们觉得不舒服，可以选择不要看。"

没想到有一个 13 岁的女学生告诉父亲说，学校的老师歧视穆斯林的学生，还要求他们离开教室。那这老爸就非常愤怒了，在网路上面公开指控老师做了不好的事情，甚至要求学校要立刻开除他。但是后来调查发现——这个女学生当天根本没有上那一堂课，而且整个指控都是她自己编造的。

但这件事情已经太迟了，这个谎言已经在网路上面传开。有一个 18 岁的伊斯兰极端主义者就来到这个学校，斩首了这个历史老师。

"白人的罪恶感"

到了 2026 年的 10 月，法国又引发了一个争议。有一个影片就秀出法国西部旺代省的一座天主教堂里面，有 9 个大概 12 到 14 岁的青少年闯入这个教堂破坏东西，还跟着一首饶舌歌大声唱出赞扬两名恐怖分子的歌词。这两个恐怖分子呢，其中一个是在 2012 年在法国杀掉七个人，另外一个就是参与 2015 年巴黎的恐怖攻击。

而且这些青少年呢看起来都像是白人。那就有评论学者把这个现象叫做"白人的罪恶感"（White guilt），他们分析说部分的西方年轻人呢因为对殖民的历史有点罪恶感吧，开始同情甚至是美化反西方的激进暴力。

十一、矛盾四：这场暴动如何影响全世界的钱包？

那这个法国暴动究竟会对世界的经济造成什么样的影响呢？

风险一：法国的财政危机

法国政府已经欠了 3.6 兆欧元，每一年都需要借新钱来支付政府新的开支跟偿还到期的旧债。但是现在人民反对去削减福利，那在这个暴动的情形之下，国会又很难决定说要加税或者是删减预算。未来要借钱给法国政府的人，就会提出"你们要给更高的利息才愿意借钱"。

所以最惨的恶性循环就发生了：政府缺钱就需要改革，但是人民反对，政治就越不稳定，政府借钱就越贵。

风险二：企业的投资

像刚刚说的家乐福已经因为暴动面临很大的损失。如果很多的企业都担心政治不稳定，决定要把工作机会搬到其他国家，那法国人民就会失去很多工作机会，未来的税收呢也会变少。

风险三：观光业

法国是全球旅游人数最多的国家，2025 年吸引超过 1 亿个国际观光旅客，带来 775 亿欧元的观光收入。而且很多人去法国旅游同时就要买很多精品嘛，对不对？光是 2024 年，非欧盟的旅客在法国办理退税的金额就高达 84 亿欧元——这是退税金额。

那我们看暴动越久呢，外国的旅客就越不想去法国购物。即便想，也去不了，觉得不安全。

风险四：金融市场

你看日本的银行、保险公司跟投资机构手上都有很多法国的公债，但是呢他们可能越来越不想要这些公债了。日本三井住友 DS 资产管理的全球债券投资团队呢已经卖光了投资组合里面的法国公债，把资金转往买德国的公债还有短期日本的公债，他们很明确就说啦，就是担心法国的财政状况。

风险五：欧洲银行

过去六个礼拜，法国三大银行的股价下跌大概 17%。法国央行最新的调查也发现 41% 的中小企业反应借钱的成本上升了。真正危险的就是如果政府公债是继续暴跌，银行承受不住损失，融资成本又会上升，最后呢就迫使这些企业贷款缩减。最惨的状况呢，就是引发类似 2011 年欧债危机的这种连锁反应。

当然这些呢都是风险警告，还没有说它会发生，我们也不想要它发生。只是想说一场在法国街头的政治危机，最后可能怎么样去影响全世界的经济。

十二、结尾

如果你觉得这支影片呢让你对法国的暴动多一点认识，请你帮我按赞按下订阅，这会鼓励我们继续制作这样的内容。如果你对这一起事件有什么想法，也欢迎在留言区留下你的想法，大家一起讨论。我们在市场上继续努力，下次见，拜拜。

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一所高中教室漏水，如何烧掉一座 143 年的市政厅？
表面上这是"法国人爱抗议"的又一次重演，但真正值得注意的是**触发链的物理学**：导火索不是失业、不是通胀、不是移民政策，而是**一所学校的数学课没有老师**。这个细节比任何宏观数据都更危险——因为它暴露了一个被忽视的系统性真相：**当一个国家把 57% 的 GDP 投入公共服务，却连一名高中数学老师都派不出来时，崩溃的不是财政，而是"交换契约"本身**。
学生举着那块牌子——"如果你不出钱弄好我的学校，我就不付你的退休金"——不是情绪宣泄，而是**一次代际合同的公开违约声明**。这是整个事件最被低估的瞬间：一个 16 岁的孩子，用一句话精准地识破了法国福利国家的庞氏结构（现役劳动人口供养退休人口），并当众宣布拒绝签字。这种清醒，比燃烧的汽车可怕得多。
## 跨领域连接：法国街头正在上演一场"流动性危机"
这里有个让人意外的类比——**法国目前的政治状况，在结构上与 2008 年的雷曼时刻惊人地相似**，只不过抵押品不是次级房贷，而是"社会信任"。
