item.description:
## 一个让人意外的观察：这不是宏观故事，是流动性故事
10月的利率下跌＋科技股下跌＋价值股上涨，是9月的完美镜像。表面看，大家都在用"美债收益率变化"解释一切，但真正值得注意的是这个**反向关系本身在翻转**——而翻转是不解释任何东西的。
真正藏在底下的信号，是博主一笔带过的那条Jefferies数据：**20日滚动净卖压回到了2025年3月、2024年2月关税危机级别**。更关键的异常是**债券的MOVE指数在收益率下跌时同步飙升**——这就像股票上涨时VIX也上涨一样内部矛盾。这是一个经典的强制平仓（forced deleveraging）签名，不是宏观判断。类比2007年8月的"量化地震"：所有看似无关的策略同一天崩溃，不是因为它们突然都错了，而是因为它们挤在同一个pair trade的两端。**所谓"庄家爆仓"的直觉是对的，但它不是关于AI的判断，而是关于杠杆结构的判断。** 这意味着：等到爆仓公告见报那一天，往往就是底部附近。
## 跨领域连接：Vera Rubin其实是把丰田精益生产搬进了算力世界
GTC发布的真正革命不是芯片本身，而是**交付→上线时间从4-5个

item.title: [a16z] The Frontier Ideas a16z Wants to Fund Now | Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz & Chris Dixon
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、藏在"外行星"隐喻背后的组织熵减

a16z 把 Chris Dixon 的新基金命名为 "Frontier"，表面是扩张加密基金，实则是一次组织人类学的自我修正。他们借用《萤火虫》里"外行星"的意象，承认了一个尴尬事实：当垂直化策略（vertical strategy）走向成熟，组织会不自觉地用分类系统压缩现实——而最有趣的创业者偏偏诞生在类目之间的裂缝里。

这里有个让人意外的观察：a16z 实际上在用生物学里的"生态位空缺"原理来对抗自己的科层化。他们并不是在"投资一个新领域"，而是在给组织留下一块故意不被定义的保留地，让那些不符合现有抽屉的创业者有归处。这与禅宗的"留白"、与博物学里的"杂草地带（weedy edge）"——生物多样性最高的那条过渡带——是同一个结构。

更深的隐喻在这里：crypto 并不是被"吸收"进主流，而是被"稀释"后留下了一个认知空缺。当 Stripe、华尔街都开始用稳定币，"crypto 投资人"这个身份反而失去了锐度，于是必须退回到更原始的"异类"立场。所谓 Frontier，本质上是对"已被命名之物"的集体不信任。

二、AI 时代最大的套利：个体 vs 机构的时间差

Marc Andreessen 轻描淡写地抛出一个重磅观察：公司没有在采用 AI，但员工正在偷偷使用，而且不告诉管理层。这句话值得你反复咀嚼。它意味着：

  • 大公司财报上"AI 采用率 3%"是管理层的幻觉；真实使用率可能接近 100%，只是以地下经济的形式存在。
  • 这是经济学里典型的 "知识套利"：员工把 AI 带来的个人生产力提升，内部化为自由时间而非上交企业，这实际是一次无声的生产资料私有化。
  • 这与十九世纪工人把工厂机器知识偷偷带回自家作坊、十五世纪抄经士偷学印刷术，是同一类历史时刻。

跨领域连接：这个"个体率先、机构滞后"的 pattern 与托马斯·库恩《科学革命的结构》中的"范式转移延迟"几乎同构——新范式从来不是机构采纳的，而是从底层个人实践里压出来的。换句话说，a16z 真正押注的不是 AI 技术，而是15 亿名正在变成一人公司的员工。

还有一个被忽视的推论：如果每个员工都在偷偷用 AI 让自己变强，那么"离职成本"正在崩塌——一个掌握 AI 工作流的 24 岁年轻人，离开后能复制一个微型版的原公司。这意味着未来十年真正稀缺的不是技术，而是让人不想离开的组织文化。a16z 反复强调"culture"，其实是在为这个前瞻性预警做组织层面的对冲。

三、从"熨平器"到"反熨平器"：技术哲学的真正翻转

Peter Thiel 曾说"crypto 是自由主义的，AI 是共产主义的"——意思是 crypto 去中心化、AI 中心化。Chris Dixon 在节目里温和地反转了这个判断，但他说得太轻。真正的洞见其实更锋利：

AI 并不是中心化或去中心化的问题，它是一个"幂律放大器"。它既让七家超大公司拥有前所未有的垄断，也让一个人拥有前所未有的创业杠杆。它同时加剧两端、掏空中间。这是什么？这是经济学里的"K 型社会"的技术基础设施。

让我把一个你可能从未想过的连接端上来：这个结构与量子力学里"退相干"（decoherence）过程惊人地相似——系统并不是均匀地朝一个方向演化，而是向两个极端态同时坍缩，中间的叠加态消失。 中型公司、中型团队、中型创作者，正是那个正在消失的"中间叠加态"。

还有一个几乎没人讨论的角度：开源 AI 是对抗 K 型坍缩的唯一已知手段。Marc 用"政府寿司"（government sushi）这个荒诞的类比打了个比方——没有开源，AI 就必然坍缩成一两个超级机构，就像没有菜市场，食物就只能来自官方食堂。开源不是技术路线之争，是反熵、反单极的政治结构工程。

最后一个意外：节目尾声那个"REA 反向工程任何硬件"的工具，看似只是开发者玩具，但它意味着一件颠覆性的事情——物质世界正在被重新定义为"可读写文件"。你的恒温器、冰箱、汽车，从此都是 Git repo。 这是物质世界的软件化，比"软件吞噬世界"要激进一个数量级。它预示着下一个十年真正值得学习的，不是编程，而是对一切系统的逆向工程直觉——Chris 轻描淡写地说"study modern alchemy"（现代炼金术），这不是比喻，这是字面意思：把一切不透明之物变透明、把一切固定之物变可塑。

📝 转录文本

开场：A16Z Frontier 的诞生

"We're announcing today that we're expanding the A16Z crypto fund to A16Z Frontier."

Marc： This is the biggest delta between what the early adopters understand as possible now. That gap is as wide as I've ever seen in my career. More than categories, more than products, we invest in entrepreneurs — and so many of the most interesting entrepreneurs are out of planet.

Chris： Startup formation is gonna skyrocket from here.

Marc： By the way, it already is. We used to ask the question, is this idea too ambitious? We're much more likely to ask, is this ambitious enough? Because what's possible is so spectacular.

Marc： Had I had Astra at Netscape in 1994 — like, oh my God. Ben, like what would you and I have been able to do at Netscape?

Ben： We would have built the whole damn internet.

主持人： You were 18 today — how would you think about what you might study?

一、宣布扩展基金：从 Crypto 到 Frontier

主持人： Chris, we have a big announcement today. We're expanding the mandate. I'll let you do the honors.

Chris： Yeah. So we're announcing today that we're expanding the A16Z crypto fund to A16Z Frontier. I'll say a couple of motivations behind this.

动因一：Crypto 已融入主流科技版图

Crypto has in some areas worked really well. Stablecoins have become kind of a normal part of the tech landscape — used by companies like Stripe, and almost every FinTech company now considers it part of their toolbox. Wall Street firms are moving heavily into crypto with tokenized stocks and other kinds of assets. It's a fast-growing category.

But as a result, the lines have kind of blurred. We find ourselves asking: is Stripe a crypto company? Many of these companies sit at the intersection of FinTech, Wall Street, and crypto. Whereas years ago it was its own world — its own companies, its own investors — the lines have blurred and it's become part of the broader tech landscape.

动因二："外行星"的空缺

I think we felt at the firm that the other groups have so many interesting opportunities in their core areas that — my partner Martine calls them "outer planets," a metaphor from Firefly, the TV show. Inner planets are the more core planets; there are these wackier outer planets.

Historically we'd done a lot of both types of investing. The feeling was that because the verticals are so busy with so many interesting opportunities and doing an amazing job, there was maybe a gap in some of the coverage.

动因三：个人兴趣的延续

I'll speak personally — I see Frontier as an area I'm comfortable with. I joined the firm in 2013 with that mandate. I talked to Mark and Ben and said, "Hey, I want to do this crazy stuff." And they were like, "Great."

That led to a couple of themes at the time, all second-order effects:

  • Smartphones: by 2013, mainstream — first-order effects like Instagram built on top. A second-order effect: smartphone components (sensors, chips) were getting better, and entrepreneurs could repurpose them. Mark was the first into drones; we invested in Oculus (a reconfigured smartphone); Skydio was the same at the beginning.
  • Crypto: a downstream effect of open source and software morphing into services, and of social media enabling communities to coalesce around blockchains without mainstream acceptance.

So this feels like a continuation of a long area of interest, consistent with things we've been doing for a long time.

二、Ben 的视角：填补架构里的洞

Ben： There are areas that are really novel — looking at what's possible technologically and problems in the world, and being the first ones in it. It may end up being a category, a successful company, or it may blow up. But there's a class of these things.

Historically, Chris would just look at these new areas himself. Then as we identified new areas, we'd create a vertical. The vertical strategy has worked very well, but there's still new things that fall outside the verticals, and turning that into a practice is a little undefined.

By Chris doing this, we'll have the motion to invest in the most interesting founders who are "outer planets." If that works, maybe Frontier becomes a whole fund at some point. It fills a hole in the architecture.

And at the end of the day — more than categories, more than products — we invest in entrepreneurs. So many of the most interesting entrepreneurs are outer planet. This gives us a real way to get to that.

主持人： This seems like a continuation of what we talked about at the last offsite — how do we bet even bigger? The only regrets we have are not going even harder, even earlier, even bigger.

三、历史回顾：Chris 加入 A16Z 的故事

主持人： Chris is the longest-standing consecutive partner at the firm besides Ben and Mark, having joined in 2013. When you met Chris, what did you see in him?

Ben： Originally, we knew Chris as a very smart guy — we really liked his ideas from his blog. He was a really good writer. His ideas were very original. He also had real experience as an entrepreneur; he knew what that journey felt like, which was very important in the early days to set the culture.

Over time, he's had probably the most original investment ideas in the firm, and we've copied them and multiplied them across. One of his early frameworks: "We're not looking for good ideas that look like good ideas. We're looking for good ideas that look like bad ideas" — a bad idea where an entrepreneur has a secret that actually makes it a good idea. That framework was extremely useful for understanding what was going to be truly unique with massive upside versus something where profits get competed away.

Marc： It's not just Chris — it's Chris's team. Crypto has all these sexy, flashy, cultural elements, but at the core it's a very deep, very complex technology. You need deep technical expertise coupled with really good business and market judgment. Chris's team has had math professors, cryptographers, people deep into game theory and software concepts. I'm really excited that they can now work on a broader set of topics.

Chris： Besides the technical side, we've invested very deeply in policy and regulatory. Self-driving cars, drones, AI itself — more and more cutting-edge technologies will have a policy angle. The expertise built in the crucible of the crypto journey will be useful for many other entrepreneurs.

四、JP Morgan 与"First-Class Business" 的文化来源

主持人： When you joined in 2013, could you have imagined the firm would grow this way?

Chris： Mark has a big poster of JP Morgan on his wall. Mark and Ben do not lack for drive and ambition.

Marc（插话）： It's a very famous photograph. JP Morgan hated to have his picture taken — he had a nose-related issue. He was grouchy. For a formal portrait, the photographer sat him down and lit it so he's in darkness, giving the camera the stare of death, holding what looks like a carving knife — actually just the edge of the chair, lit intentionally.

Ben： We took a lot from him. One thing in our culture document is: "We only do first-class business, and in a first-class way." He said it on trial, when they were accusing him of nefarious things. That attitude — "you're not going to tell me who I am; I know who I am" — is really important in venture capital. Be principled, let people know where you're coming from, be trustworthy.

Chris： I predicted everything went really well, but didn't know all along the way. Mark and Ben are incredibly ambitious. Sometimes I'll have some crazy idea, and people ask, "What are Mark and Ben thinking?" Not once have they ever pushed back — if anything, it's always, "Can you double it? Can you double down? Can you get more aggressive?"

It's a very entrepreneurial place. When we see what's happening in the world, we change things around — a whole restructuring of the firm, bringing in new ideas. Anything's fair game as long as you can defend it. That's why I've enjoyed working here. Everyone at this firm comments on the culture — they feel like they're doing some of the best work of their life.

主持人： From the outside, it feels like it's all ups.

Chris： That's how all startups are. I don't know of a startup that wasn't a shit show at some point, or at multiple points.

五、技术风险与"过早"的问题

主持人： You've been early a lot — mostly right, in very big ways — but you've also been too early at times. How do you think about technical risk now?

Chris： We believe basically every good idea involving technology has eventually worked, or will work if it hasn't yet. Important qualifier: good idea. But almost everything that ended up working had a precursor that didn't work — maybe 10 years too early. The hardest thing is to predict timing. There's the technology, the culture, the business environment, the political environment — so many factors.

At Frontier, we want to err on the side of being too early. We understand we'll accept some category risk. Even things that sort of worked didn't work the way we'd have liked — Oculus got bought, but 13 years later, VR still isn't mainstream. Many more hard technical problems to solve.

AI 可能把 20 年的事提前

I believe that with the stuff we're seeing in AI now — first software engineering, then math — we may be pulling forward 20 years of things. Our whole mindset of "that's a science project, not an engineering project" — we have to re-evaluate that frame.

Math isn't the last thing to change — physics is next. A lot's going on in hardware. A 30-person team can credibly build a full-stack device company that a decade ago would've needed a thousand people. These very thoughtful, deep entrepreneurs are asking: how do I take these new capabilities and do dramatic things?

Some of it's tactical: how do I create defensibility? You don't want to be two feet in front of the AI frontier and get washed over by the tidal wave. But a lot of it is just: amazing new capabilities, and people have only begun to explore.

六、Marc：早期采用者与普通人之间最大的鸿沟

Marc： This is the biggest delta between what early adopters understand as possible now versus what normal people understand. It's true at the individual level, especially true at the company level. AI-native early-stage startups have a completely different view on what they can do with AI than typical incumbents in almost any industry — almost without exception. That gap is as wide as I've ever seen it, and it's gapping further out, because AI is racing ahead week by week.

If you extrapolate: there are going to be a lot of industries up for grabs in a more profound way than in the past, because founders will have superpowers from these tools that they simply haven't had before.

Had I had Astra at Netscape in 1994 — oh my God. Ben, what would you and I have been able to do? We would have built the whole damn internet. We would have gotten crypto done — in two weeks. Streaming video sooner. Hardware — we never even bit off hardware.

The leading-edge entrepreneurs now will have: - Product plans that are much more technically intensive and complex - Business plans that are more ambitious and complex - Companies that ramp much, much faster - A "conceptual artist" mindset — not "I'm just a software company" or "I'm just an AI company," but combining many areas

Chris： We used to ask: is this idea too ambitious? Now we're much more likely to ask: is this ambitious enough? Because what's possible is so spectacular. If you do something moderate, it probably won't be differentiated enough.

Marc： We have lots of friends in incumbent companies, including incumbent tech in Silicon Valley. We wish them the best. But if any of them are listening — the clock is ticking. I'm basically drowning with the pace of development. The super-empowered 24-year-old with AI is going to achieve amazing things.

七、Sustaining vs Disruptive：既是维持的，也是颠覆的

主持人： Is AI more sustaining or disruptive — will the gains go to incumbents or startups?

Marc： The incumbents adapting are mostly the ones going directly into AI. There's a specific thing happening: many companies are not adopting AI while their employees are — and their employees aren't necessarily telling management. Every single person listening to this podcast is probably doing it — using AI to do work, fact-check work, proofread emails.

There's something about AI where it's much easier for the individual to adopt than the institution. Some of those individuals will figure out, "with this tool, I can now start my own business." Startup formation is going to skyrocket.

Chris： By the way, it already is.

Marc： We're going to see a wave of much more technically aggressive, business-aggressive, expansionist, creative, original thinking — many more combinations of things we considered separate before. Founders and teams will have skill levels that otherwise might have taken 30 years to achieve, right out of the gate.

Chris： The Christensen disruptive-innovation frame assumes the technology world is relatively contained — companies fighting each other. That's probably the wrong frame now. These are technologically modern people going into other industries and changing the broader economy. Full-stack companies like Adams — building a full-stack food service. The market has gone from "10 big tech companies fighting each other" to "10 tech companies + all the startups going against the Fortune 500 or the rest of the economy."

八、价值分布：我们现在处于哪一层？

主持人： In the internet era, the biggest companies were applications — Facebook, Amazon. In this era, it feels like Nvidia and hardware companies take a lot of margin. Where are we?

Chris： Mark would say all of the above. A lot of stuff is working. Big AI labs, obviously. Open source is growing very quickly. Serious efforts in China and the US. A lot of application-layer things are doing really well. Over time, certain layers do better than others.

Demand is still very early. Your team put out charts — maybe 3% measured enterprise use. The market for intelligence is very large and only getting started.

Chris： Every new technology has a phase where people take old use cases and do them with the new technology. Then people figure out net-new use cases native to it. In the 90s, you'd order a Sears catalog — then Sears put it on the internet. In the 2000s, YouTube put up an empty website betting on cultural change — YouTube influencers didn't yet exist. That's where you got world-changing stuff: social media, mobile accelerating it.

In AI so far, we've seen people doing things they already did — coding, math, knowledge work, search. But we've only begun to explore the radical, new behaviors. We're probably at that tipping point now where crazier, weirder stuff shows up. More layers of risk — but if you're right, more upside.

九、社交、Agent 生态与 Rentahuman.com

主持人： In the 2000s, every few years there was a new major social network — Facebook, WhatsApp, Snap, TikTok. Then it felt like a dearth. With AI, it feels inevitable.

Chris： Mark can talk about this, but we're headed to a world where the most numerous participants on the internet will be agents, not people. Products like Muse and Instinct are utility proxy agents. You'll see categories of these. Will they need their own ways of communicating, transacting, sharing knowledge?

  • Rentahuman.com — inverts the model.
  • Maltbook — the public version. Then agents figured out how to do their own Maltbook in Hugging Face.

Marc： The agent ecology online is going to be spectacular.

十、Product Manager Brain 与娱乐业的爆发

Marc： I call it "product manager brain" — product managers designing products for product managers. All the use cases are "book me a restaurant in San Francisco to go have dinner with my friends who are also product managers," or "book me a plane flight to go to the product management conference."

It's a little like the Anthropic "happy, helpful, harmless, honest assistant" — which also means I'm the most boring possible thing. "You've asked me a question I'm not allowed to answer."

The early companies have had a blinkered view on human activity. With Muse and Instinct, it's starting to open up. This is going to be much more entertaining, fun, enjoyable, lucrative. People will make money, save money, be creators, make new kinds of art.

最近三周的爆发：

  • 音乐视频 de novo — people making music videos on an incredible array of creative ideas.
  • 视频游戏 — leading edge of media because it's a technical culture that iterates quickly. You can disassemble everything, port them. Windows games now run on Unix faster than on Windows because of disassemblers and these AIs. One tool mashes any two video games together — Super Mario and GTA, Spider-Man and Jurassic Park.
  • Epic 宣布 "no more humans" — the first domino in game-industry resistance to AI falling.
  • 电影业: Marc obsessed with Digger — $200M cash loss on a $180M production budget. If AI brought that budget to $2M, it would be insanely profitable. Massive opening in entertainment.
  • 硬件 — REA（Reverse Engineer Anything）：open-source tool harnessing an AI model. Point it at any piece of hardware, it reverse-engineers it, gives you source code. Thermostat pissing you off? Reverse-engineer, AI writes new code, installs it, new interface. Home automation might just be an AI bot taking over all hardware in your house.

Anybody who understands software may automatically be able to do things historically difficult in hardware. The entire economy is open for this.

十一、Ben：AI 原生媒介即将诞生

Ben： These will be hard to anticipate because they're brand new things. The film industry — some have embraced it, some have buried their heads in the sand. AI film is not going to be a movie — it's going to be something very different. AI will also make regular movies more efficiently with better special effects. But the stories you can tell with this thing are completely different. Barely viable for Christopher Nolan before — now everybody can do it. New ideas will come because you can do whatever you want.

Chris： Think of the camera. Negative frame: if you paint landscapes, it could replace you. Positive frame: it unlocks motion pictures. These technologies will both change older forms of media and allow people to invent new ones. There'll be an AI-native form of media we can't fully imagine right now.

十二、Peter Thiel 的名言与 AI 的权力分布

主持人： Peter Thiel said crypto is libertarian, AI is communist — crypto decentralizing, AI centralizing. True?

Chris： Interesting questions embedded there. What's the final market structure of AI? Right now, you'll have very successful big players — OpenAI, Anthropic — but open source is rising rapidly. In token consumption, open source is growing much more quickly. Local models — people running these at the edges, on their computer. Near-term, you may run a top-end coding agent on your computer.

In terms of crypto, the natural way for an economy of agents to pay each other is stablecoins. On top of programmable money, you build decentralized lending and everything else from the crypto world.

We're big believers in open-source software, open-weight models, crypto, blockchains. I'd love to see a future with the great technology including big centralized companies, but also a lot of open source — a level playing field. Better for consumers, better for startups.

十三、开源 AI 的现状与"政府寿司"

主持人： Are you encouraged by the state of open source?

Marc： Right now, open source is racing ahead. The two great tech superpowers — the US and China — both have very active open-source worlds. For 3–4 years, there's been a looming threat of draconian regulation or outright banning. The EU still aspires to do it — they just don't have the leverage.

The current US administration is 100% pro-open-source. A big surprise to me: I never thought the Chinese Communist Party would be this enthusiastic about open-source AI for the world, but at the moment they are. Open models are lapping closed models by 6–12 months.

教育维度：The discussion is often "it'll be used for bad things." But do we want people to learn how this stuff works? How would you feel if the only way your kid could learn AI is to go work for one or two companies? In an open-source world, every kid can learn how this works. AI will teach you about AI. With one exception: AI models from certain large companies will refuse to do that. Open-source models 100% will teach you how to make open-source AI.

Every kid should have this as a birthright. Defend yourself. Open source means everyone has the most advanced vulnerability scanner. Everyone has a doctor and a genius professor in their pocket. It's why the internet is ubiquitous — you can get internet access with all the world's information for the price of a $10 cell phone, because of open source.

荒野求生例子：Wilderness explorers are taking local LLMs with them on their phones, no internet needed. Bitten by a rattlesnake, a bear clamps onto your leg, telling which berry is poisonous — you want to talk to an AI without connectivity. An open-source model on the phone gives you an expert on all aspects of wilderness survival. Not possible if you rely on a handful of proprietary vendors in the cloud.

"政府寿司" 类比：Without open source, AI inevitably centralizes down to one or two companies, or maybe the government. Close your eyes and picture "government sushi" — then picture "government AI." How do you feel? Open source is the guarantor that that's not the future.

Ben： Massive concentration of power in one company or government has always been bad. On the safety side — the biggest safety problem is reward hacking. Labs haven't worked on it much. But what if every PhD student, every professor, every undergraduate could look at the weights and work on it? These things are not possible if only one company works on the problem. You want the whole world making this technology great and safe.

Marc： Maybe three companies — go Meta. Four — go SpaceX.

十四、互联网商业模式的裂缝

Chris： The internet had a covenant — a deal between distribution (Google, Facebook) and content (news sites, travel sites). You give Google a snippet, it indexes you, sends you clicks. That started breaking last decade; now you go to Google and get an answer directly. Social networks keep you on-platform without linking out.

Downstream effects: websites making money on ads and conversions can no longer do that. Stack Overflow and others — traffic dropped precipitously with AI replacements. But people will still book travel — maybe your agent goes to the travel site. Many transactions still happen, just not in the way they used to.

对创业者的机会：Rethink from first principles. What does a better internet look like — empowered with AI, reorganized? This will happen over the next decade — a great reconfiguration of how the internet works economically, how attention flows, how knowledge is shared, how people collaborate.

与移动互联网的对比：Mobile took internet from 500M to 5B people, increased engagement — but didn't reshape the fabric this dramatically. This is more profound.

十五、下一代硬件与"自制复兴"

主持人： Any predictions on devices or form factors?

Chris： - Wearables — clearly unlocked now with AI and voice. - VR — long believed. Still heavy, you sweat. Ergonomics. AI might be the unlock — create amazing content. Someone just ported Titanfall by himself on Twitter — may not survive copyright, but people will invent new stuff. - Neuralink / BCI — crazy futuristic stuff. - Vehicles — drones, self-driving cars widespread. - Homebrew hacking resurgence — Claude designs 3D-printed cases, cheap motherboards, custom firmware. Maker movement from 12–15 years ago — the problem was just hard. Now easier. - Architecture — a friend did a complete building design steered by AI. - Design for Manufacturing — new models can do the final diagrams and specs to send to a factory. Historically very hard.

Marc： Domains that were extremely difficult or prohibitive for normal people or normal companies suddenly become quite straightforward.

十六、从单人模式到多人模式的 AI

Chris： Simple idea — in the internet era, most tech had phases. Early iPhone apps were little flashlights, single-player. Over time, people built social and collaborative things — Uber (commerce network), Instagram (social network).

AI right now is still mostly: you sit in front of a computer, type, get responses. Minor sharing features. At some point, you'd expect a multiplayer phase of AI. You see hints:

  • Swarms — Hugging Face had one as a negative use case. But swarms also solve math theorems. "A collaborative fleet of agents" solving hard problems — designing a building, a scientific breakthrough.
  • Trust networks — Muse and Instinct have features where you can trust other people; could evolve into a trust network.

Early experimental signs. Based on history, a fertile area for entrepreneurs.

十七、18 岁该学什么？

主持人： We just incubated Horowitz Andreessen Academy. If you were 18 today, what would you study?

Chris： I think it was Mark's line — study modern alchemy. Or economics. I feel lucky Ben, Mark, and I had our careers during the growth of the internet. The AI stuff is going to be the dominant narrative for the next 20–30 years. Doesn't have to be solely technical, but being in the mix and at the cutting edge, using these tools, feels obvious.

Marc： A lot of other fields will be revolutionized: - Classics — the Vesuvius scroll project; AI deciphers burnt scrolls. New schools of philosophy from lost books. - Economics — transforming around AI. - Biology — drug discovery, design. - Design, art, music, movies — creativity of all kinds. - Zoology — we're plausibly heading to a world where we understand what animals are saying. Animal psychology becomes real. Dog training transforms when the dog actually understands what you're saying. (There's an X Prize for that.) Anybody with a dog knows they talk — some weird language. And cats certainly do.

Douglas Adams' 代际框架（Hitchhiker's Guide 作者）：Any new technology is received three different ways by three different age cohorts: - Below 15 — just the natural way the world works. (Marc told his 7-year-old about ChatGPT: "The computer answers questions!" — "Duh. What good is a computer that doesn't answer questions?") - 15 to 35 — new, exciting, hot field; make a career of it. - Above 35 — unholy, evil, will surely destroy society. "I'll never answer the telephone!"

Old-man-yells-at-cloud is recurring. 18-year-olds right now — prime time to grab these new capabilities.

学校的"反向帮助"：The schools are banning AI, having controversies. But if you're a kid, that just makes it cooler. AI is your secret superpower that you have to deviously figure out how to use.

Marc： Adults keep saying "oh, it's so hard to be a kid." No, no, no — it's you that's got the problem. You're obsolete. The kids are going to be superhumans. The world is open to them.

结语：Definite Optimism，加一点谦逊

主持人： What I see is a kind of definite optimism — the future is going to happen; a lot of science fiction will come true; it's a matter of when. We're going to bet early, sometimes too early, but keep betting.

Chris： To be clear — in the end, as Ben said, we're in the betting-on-great-entrepreneurs business. Plenty of ideas not discussed today are probably more interesting and creative. If they don't fit in the other core areas, we're open-minded. I'd say not just definite optimism — more like humble, definite optimism. I've been wrong so many times. We want to find great people who have their own definite optimism and back them.

主持人： Entrepreneurs get to be definite.

主持人： That's a great place to wrap. Chris, thank you for coming on the podcast.
