item.description:
# 关于 Modal 与 Erik Bernhardsson 对话的系统性洞察
## 一、"矩形诅咒"：Modal 的真正商业本质不是卖算力，而是在做"时间形状转换"
Erik 不经意间透露的一个比喻值得反复咀嚼——"GPU 都是以三年矩形的方式出售的"。这个"矩形（rectangle）"是整个对话最深的隐喻：供给侧是三年期、固定容量的刚性长方形，而真实需求是波浪形、锯齿形、脉冲形的。
**出人意料的洞察**：Modal 本质上不是云计算公司，而是一家 **"算力期限错配经纪商"**——它和华尔街的"久期转换"（duration transformation）银行业务同构。银行通过把长期存款变成短期贷款（或反过来）赚取久期利差；Modal 把三年期的刚性 GPU 容量，经过多租户聚合，拆成毫秒级的 serverless 函数调用，赚取的是**"形状差"（shape premium）**。NeoCloud 们融资的方式——拿客户的三年合同去华尔街贴现——证明了 GPU 已经在被证券化。换句话说，当下 AI 基础设施行业最隐蔽的真相是：它正在悄悄演变成一个影子银行系统，Nvidia

item.title: [Odds on Open] Hedge Fund Manager David Orr: Investing is 99% Talent
item.dc:creator: Odds on Open
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：David Orr 的真正产品不是"收益率"，而是"税务时间机器"

大多数人把 David 当成一个"50% 年化、Sharpe 2.1"的超额收益奇才。但如果仔细听他谈 PM 招募策略，你会发现一个被几乎所有人忽略的核心商业模式：

他运营的根本不是对冲基金，而是一台跨策略的递延税收引擎。中频交易者的短期资本利得（最高税率档）在他的结构里可以被基本面长线策略的未实现亏损"吸收"掉，变成基金层面的递延。换句话说，他把两种在税务上互斥的 alpha 焊接成了一个在税后指数级放大的复合体。

这创造了一个外部投资者几乎无法复制的"自然垄断"：任何单一策略的 PM 加入他之后，税后收益会比独立运营高出一个数量级——不是因为他投研更强，而是因为不同 PM 的策略在税务拓扑上互为对冲。这是我见过的最优雅的"策略间套利"结构之一。

二、跨领域连接：扑克的"元游戏"、米其林主厨的强迫症、与 Nike 创始人的银行博弈——同一种心智

David 看似在聊三个毫不相关的东西： - 扑克里"edges go away"（边缘会消失） - 《Kitchen Confidential》里那位亲自称量食材的纽约餐厅老板 - 《Shoe Dog》里 Phil Knight 不让银行限制自己、同时游说 30 家银行

但这三者在他脑中其实是同一个认知原型：对"系统边界条件"的偏执监控。

扑克教他的不是赌博，而是"元游戏"的概念——你赢的不是牌，而是"规则正在怎么变"。餐厅主厨教他的不是经营，而是"信任链上的每一个节点都要亲自验证"（他对 PM 的track record验证流程，几乎就是餐厅主厨称量进货的翻版）。Phil Knight 教他的则是"不接受任何预设的capacity约束"——这正是他为什么敢对"小众 PM"下重注、也为什么他的 broker 自建逻辑如此激进。

最意外的洞察：他真正的核心能力不是"选股"，而是在任何系统里识别出"约束不是真的约束"的瞬间。这就是为什么他能同时在扑克桌、500 支股票的组合、十个 PM 的协调中保持清醒——他只在意一件事：哪里的约束是幻觉？

三、隐藏的系统性真相：他正在无意识地构建一个"反脆弱雇佣契约"

注意他谈到的一个细节："即使 PM 的 edge 消失了，我会解雇他，但他的资金会继续留在机器里复利。"

这是一个在传统金融业根本不存在的契约结构。普通对冲基金里，被解雇意味着彻底出局；在他这里，被解雇反而是财务上最优的退休路径——因为"剩下还在赢的 PM"会继续替退休者复利，且仍享税务递延。

这实际上是把 Nassim Taleb 的"反脆弱"概念偷偷嵌入了雇佣合同： - PM 面临的下行是有限的（最差情况：失去工资，但资本继续增值） - PM 的上行是无限的（carry + 他人复利 + 税务递延）

更深层的系统洞察是：他把"员工"和"LP"的身份合并了。这个合并消解了传统多经理基金最大的内生矛盾——PM 和基金之间的利益错位。Millennium 之所以必须靠规模和品牌招人，是因为它维持的是"雇佣关系"；David 招的人则是在加入一个"长期财富共同体"。

四、一个让你坐立不安的预测

他说"today you just want to focus on growth, not moat"——这句话配上他 400% 杠杆、500 持仓、零 AI 因子相关性的操作画像，暴露了一个他本人可能都没完全意识到的信念：

他相信当下世界的"认知折旧率"已经高到让任何可持续优势都变成一种税收。 任何试图建立 moat 的人，都是在为一个正在崩溃的时间框架付成本。

这不仅是投资哲学，这是一种对现实本身节奏的押注。如果他是对的，那么大多数读商学院、建品牌、搞长期战略规划的人——包括大多数对冲基金——正在系统性地支付一笔隐形的"稳态幻觉税"。而他的整个基金结构，本质上是对这笔税的空头头寸。

📝 转录文本

David Orr 访谈：投资 99% 靠天赋

开场金句精选

"你的表现仍然让我震惊——50% 年化、Sharpe 2.1。"

"我整个工作方式在公司研究层面已经完全改变了。"

"拥抱这个新事物，学会非常高效地使用它，你很可能对那些人拥有巨大优势。"

"每年我都做几百笔独立下注，这比大多数对冲基金经理一辈子的次数还多。"

"我跑的是大约 400% 杠杆的组合，所以我必须非常关心多头端的下行风险。"

"你 7 月涨了 9%，对吧？" "每当东西在崩的时候，我们往往表现最好。"

一、AI 如何改造投资流程

Jack：David，非常感谢你再次来到播客。

David：好，感谢再次邀请我。

Jack：你的表现仍然让我震惊——50% 年化、Sharpe 2.1，今年也很棒。你用 AI 做什么？在投资流程的哪些部分？

David：风险系统可能是推动最大的那个。上次采访我可能提过——我其实已经有这个系统，它会自动把财报翻译成英文并总结。这节省了一些时间。但现在我们重建了工具，比以前好得多。AI 会实际地对当天的不同财报或新闻条目进行排序，所以我现在只需要看前 5 或 10 条；等你到中段，基本上就是噪声了。这能节省大量时间。

Jack：这个风险系统具体包含什么？

David：它有几层。我的合伙人 Sam 买了一个专业系统，它从几个不同角度做测试，但我不太喜欢那个。而 Mike 做的那个——它是自定义因子。我们可以看它和传统因子的相关性，但我们现在用 AI 构建自定义的股票篮子。它会给人们组合里的股票分类，还会给它们起有趣的名字——比如"做得好的银行"是多头部分，"收益率陷阱"是空头部分。AI 以它自己的方式把这些搞清楚了。

自定义因子到底在做什么

Jack：谈谈这些自定义因子，风险系统包含什么？你试图做什么？

David：相关性是关键，而相关性变化非常快。所以这个系统每天更新并重新计算篮子。结果是，即使组合本身完全没变，篮子大小也可能因为底层相关性的变化而增长或收缩。如果我要同时追踪 10 个组合经理，这是不可能的。即使在我自己的分区里本来就很难——我做得挺好，而且随着时间推移越来越保守，所以有一个很大的安全缓冲。

但现在有了新的组合经理，我需要理解：也许他们以为 25% 的仓位——在杠杆组合里是个大赌注，但没事。可如果相关性在一两周内把它推到了 45%，我需要很快知道。

二、如何招募到比自己更强的 PM

Jack：你怎么能招到这么多你认为比你自己还强的 PM 的？

David：头两个——Mike 和 Rodrigo——相对容易。Rodrigo 把自己的结果发在 Twitter 上，是公开的。我不懂为什么没别人先给他 offer。而 Mike 是 2019 年因为我的 Seeking Alpha 文章联系我的。当时我住在泰国，他来清迈旅行，就是想一起喝啤酒。我们见面聊股票，他对所有股票都了如指掌。即使在 2019 年，我就能看出他有真正的热情。

筛选新 PM 的网络

David：新来的那些，我们布了一张网——他们可能在我的 Twitter 或网站上找到我，Sam 也在用另一种方式找。这些 track record 送上门来，95% 完全是垃圾，然后 5% 里，可能不是严格意义的欺诈，但——我们只要真实实盘。有人会送来好像实盘但其实是回测的东西；另一种我们见过的是拿 30 份 track record 来 cherry-pick 最好的那一份，Sam 很擅长识别这个。

一旦我们判断是真的，就直接问他们：嘿，你个人账户 3 年里做出了 2.1 的 Sharpe？能不能实际把账户调出来，我们想看看。最近就有一个人——我明天还要和他吃午饭——在个人账户里把 100 万变成了 900 万。他主动联系了我们。在团队里比单打独斗好得多。

PM 之间的相关性

Jack：PM 之间相关性如何？

David：和核心 PM 的交叉相关性是 0.15。即便现在把所有试用期 PM 等权组合，也仍然在 0.2 以下，挺疯狂的。样本还不大，但看起来肯定在 0.3 以下。远比我们预期的要好。

Vetting 流程

Jack：vetting 流程是什么样的？

David：我们还测试几件事。比如尾部风险——他是不是在卖波动率、Martingale 式加仓、或者什么假策略。但其实目前还没遇到过。我们就给他一个小 sleeve。如果有人听到这里想跑大资金——请申请我们。我们会给机会。

我们甚至不怎么问策略。新来的一位把自己描述成中频交易者。我也不太懂中频——不是毫秒级的高频，是秒或分钟级别的。他有一套系统。我们还得专门给他设置一个 broker，因为 Interactive Brokers 对他来说不够快。

三、为什么要加入 Militia，而不是独自复利

Jack：假设我是一个 PM，个人账户几年内从 100 万做到了 1000 万、和标普相关性很低，为什么要加入你，而不是继续自己复利？

David：几个原因：

1. 税收递延（carry）：一年之后我们开始付 carry。carry 本质上是递延缴税的。中频交易者是个完美例子——中频基本都是短期资本利得，但在我们这里，因为更基本面、长线的策略有递延空间，我们可以在基金层面吸收他的收益。他原本每年都要交税，现在可以递延多年。

2. 退休 PM 的"免费保险"：我从扑克学到——edge 会消失。你可能 5 年里把 metagame 玩得炉火纯青，但市场 regime 会变。如果有一天他的 edge 没了，我作为 PM 会解雇他，但他的资本可以继续留在这台机器里以超高速率复利。等于一份免费的保险。

3. 工具与团队：我们在造工具，有工程师团队、还会继续招开发者。如果你有想法但不想雇人管人，加入我们。管人有时候挺烦——人很难搞。

税务递延机制

Jack：能机械地讲一下递延怎么运作吗？

David：AQR 出过很好的研究论文：如果你同时跑高杠杆和高 alpha，税务递延变得异常简单。自成立以来我们几乎递延了所有税。我甚至可以进一步——稍微放弃一点 edge，就能在 LP 赢钱的同时给他们制造税务亏损。

长线纯多头的问题是：你被套在一个赢的持仓里，想轮动就得交税。但在多空策略里，比如某个空头亏得很惨，这是周或月的事——你可以收割亏损，然后换到一个类似的空头。但如果空头赢了、比如跌了 90%，你就永远不用平仓。直到它破产、退市、股票被注销，那一天你才交税。这些事有时要花 10 年。

四、基金规模与经济学

Jack：目前基金规模？

David：4.8 亿。

Jack：最大能跑多少？

David：取决于能找到多少 PM。目前是我 + 两位核心，还有 7 个在试。至少几个人应该能跑很大。可能有一两个会在规模上有大 edge，那每多一个人就把容量提升 30%。

加仓节奏

David：根据样本量、风险和相关性。中频交易者样本很快就起来——这是策略性质。长线策略可能 6-9 个月我才敢第一次加仓，加到 10 或 15。再 6-9 个月——这是基金最危险的部分——加到 30 或 50，因为 edge 看起来挺好但样本还不够稳健。然后每个 PM 根据策略的波动率曲线定不同的条款，但平均起来大致是 P&L 的 15%（在无风险利率之上）。

五、关于多经理模式的洞察

Jack：很多前 CIO 想复制这个模式，大多失败。你理解到了什么别人没理解的？

David：我在 Austin 遇到一个很尊敬的 PM，他也问过我同样的问题："你是怎么做到的？我不懂。"

我觉得这些人根本没在关注最简单的问题——'这个人到底 edge 在哪'。他们不愿意走出去挑选不寻常的人。

我们有一位 PM 赢过电视游戏节目。我没法说具体细节怕暴露他是谁。他没有任何证书，没在大投行、大基金干过。但他个人账户几年的 Sharpe 是 2 点几，我就给他机会。Millennium 的那位 CIO 可能不会这么干。你可以是外卖员，但如果你在打败市场——我就给你机会。

为什么你和那些"CIO 型"创业者不同

David：也许我比那种只想当 manager 的人更懂 edge。如果他们一开始就想复制 Millennium——那你如果真的有才，为什么不直接去 Millennium？其他一切都更差。所以最好的人都去了 Millennium，不来找你。

他们的整个计划是疯的——"我们要做小规模的 Millennium"——谁会想去那儿工作？

六、理解 Edge 的来源

Jack：你理解到什么关于 edge 的事别人不理解？

David：我有海量 at-bats。自 2019 年以来，每年几百笔独立下注。这比大多数对冲基金经理一辈子的次数还多。一年比很多人十年的次数还多。所以就是经验上我见得多。

Joe Peta 写过一本书——我忘了书名——他说：你要找的 PM，就是一个始终如一赢钱的人。这些人就在那儿，你得去找。但大基金的做法是——即使找到了，也只给小小的 allocation。

举个例子：我认识一个人，纯空头，每年 40%，连续好几年。可能是世界上最好的空头之一，默默无闻。但他在他所在的基金只拿到一个很小的 allocation。如果在我这，兄弟，我们会给你很多钱。来加入我们吧。[笑]

多经理基金在干什么

Jack：你觉得这些 Multi-manager 正在犯错？

David：他们是一门不同的生意——做的是 marketing。他们不太关心 return，他们要的是对机构投资者极友好的东西。如果所有 PM 都有传统路径、最多一个 oddball——那还要那个 oddball 干嘛？管理费拿到了就是 mission accomplished。Millennium 现在大概 1000 亿规模，一年收 20 亿管理费——return 从 12% 涨到 14% 他们并不在乎。

七、具体投资方法

持仓风格

David：我一直做有效的事。刚开始做空的时候，我试图做空一切——2018 年还在空 Tesla。但很快就发现这个空头不如其他空头有效，就停了。

研究时间

Jack：一只股票需要多少研究？

David：早期值得深入，训练自己辨别什么重要。对已经投入过 1000-2000 小时的老手——试着在 1-2 小时内决定。两小时决定不了就跳过。为什么要折腾？外面有更容易的东西。

我经常是——折腾一个股票 3 小时，想"算了太难"，去看下一个想法，两分钟就决定了："啊，这就是赌注。"下一个，也是。你得真的想清楚怎么用你的时间。

两分钟决定的东西，如果股票开始走反，你看到一个听起来合理的反论——直接退出，再花个 5 分钟都不用。

当前持仓数量

Jack：你现在持多少仓位？

David：我自己那个分区有 500 个。

Jack：怎么保持心智清晰？

David：空头我常常忘记它们是干嘛的。我 review 的时候，比如最好的空头跌了 40%——我压根不记得公司是干什么的。然后花一两分钟提醒自己。"哦，对，财报下来了，坏事发生了。"刷新一下。然后通常我会说"好，再加点空"。整个过程两分钟。然后半年或一年后 review 时又忘了。

最糟糕的空头是那些完全没新闻却天天涨的。看一眼："这玩意烂爆了，连新闻都没有，管理层连 promotional 都算不上。"但天天磨着往上。我已经学会退出这种，但偶尔还是会固执。然后——没错——不知不觉它涨了 250%，依然没新闻。为什么要和它扳手腕？市场说我错了，我就是错了。

Jack：你有记笔记的习惯吗？500 个持仓每个都有笔记？

David：没有笔记。全在脑子里。

八、和其他 PM 合作学到的

Jack：合作中有什么学到的仪式吗？

David：我们刻意不聊这些，就是为了避免相关性变高。前几天 Rodrigo 从西班牙飞过来，Mike 从 Austin 来，我们一起去纽约——很开心，但我们还是刻意不聊各自在做什么。保持相关性低比我们各自 edge 多好更重要。

过去一年学到的最大一课

David：依赖别人帮了大忙。我以前完全单干。但看着这两个核心 PM 建造那些让我工作更轻松的系统——比如 Mike 今年做的风险系统，省了我太多脑力。而现在我们在支持 7 个新试用 PM，如果没这个工具根本不可能追踪他们的风险。用一个真正专业的工具是真的有帮助的。

日常如何保持聚焦

Jack：你怎么同时建业务、招人、做播客、还管投资？

David：Sam 处理几乎所有招聘，Luis 处理会计这种脑力消耗。Mike 用 Sam 招的员工做的风险系统——Mike 和一个叫 Andrew 的人一个月连续工作到凌晨 1 点，然后搞定了。这东西比以前省我太多时间。

以前我得手动把股票归入——"老媒体股"、"光纤股"——有些明确不变，比如 Charter 肯定归到互联网里。但有些灰色——会在桶之间跳来跳去，比如突然变成了利率敏感股票。现在新系统替我做这件事。

九、投资哲学

买在新高还是新低

Jack：你倾向买上涨中的还是下跌中的？

David：你想买正在涨的东西。Rodrigo——很反直觉——他看的就是 52 周新高和 52 周新低。他说："哦，我能看出这为什么会继续涨——买。或者为什么会继续跌——做空。"这是判断题，当然你不能把它当桶来买，你需要那些桶里最好的 5%。这只是他的 lead generation 之一。

关于投资书

Jack：旧投资书对新手好吗？

David：和扑克书一样，都过时了。Peter Lynch 的书还行。但大部分这些书我觉得想法真的不好。甚至我们都不知道他们写的那些 anomaly 当年是不是真的有效。有个老笑话——某人连续 5 年赚钱，然后写本书，然后就开始亏损。而且这些书本身就老了。

读商业书是好的。但那不是投资书。我喜欢 Shoe Dog——Nike 的历史。你能看到一个伟大的成长期 CEO 是怎么全力踩油门的。细微之处——他之所以伟大，部分原因是他不让银行限制他，他找创造性的方法，去 30 家银行比价、推挤回去。你应该在那些书里学这种细微细节，然后在你的多头里也找到这种 CEO。

阅读习惯

David：我一年也就读 10-15 本书。头一章没抓住就放下，通常就送人。我是阵发性的读——6 个月不读，然后一个月连读 4 本。不喜欢小说，喜欢历史书。Kitchen Confidential 这本——里面有一章讲纽约一个超级成功的餐厅老板的神经质细节，连运货标签都不信、要自己称重。那种投入才赢得了餐厅业。

十、年轻人、AI、与建立个人优势

Jack：很多年轻人不读书，刷手机上瘾。你怎么建议他们训练大脑？

David：我不知道旧的方式是不是更好。可能新方式更好。现在要是有人推荐一本书，我信任的人、看起来是好书，我就读。但如果不那么有趣，我可以让 ChatGPT 把书用项目符号总结出来，然后挑出我觉得对投资有用的点，和机器来回聊，一小时学完一本书的要点。我不知道这更好还是更差，没人知道。

但一直有反技术偏见——字母表刚出来的时候就有道德恐慌。结果证明阅读是最棒的事情之一。互联网刚出来——"互联网不是真的"——结果它只是更好的沟通方式。AI 还早，但我觉得还是要读一些真正伟大的书、保持平衡。

关于短视频

Jack：有意思——我在读一本 50 年代的书，他们描述收音机的方式和我们现在说短视频 Reels 很像。

David：TikTok 这种，很难为它辩护。那些视频真的很垃圾，而且他们优化的不是"做出好内容"，而是研究第一秒怎么把人钩住。那里什么都没有，是空的。但 ChatGPT 对学习大概率是净正面的，我会倾向拥抱它。

这也是一种差异化。假设你和那些在"模拟式慢思考"上投入过几千小时的人竞争——你真的要跟他们正面对撞吗？特别是你心不在那？你会输。作为年轻人，你的 edge 是拥抱这个新事物，学会非常高效、诚实地使用它。专注在这个上，你很可能对那些人拥有巨大优势。

建立 Moat 还是追求增长？

Jack：怎么建立 moat？

David：今天只专注增长，别想 moat。没人知道什么会可持续。这一切变化太快了。要务实——你今天怎么用这项技术让事情更好、或者一两个月内改进它？

我和一些朋友聊——他们说，现在的 AI 和 3 个月前比，差异令人瞠目结舌。所以跟上这个变化、成为最擅长它的人。如果你极其擅长 AI，你完全可以去一家巨型公司说"每年付我 500 万，不然我去你竞争对手那"——最终他们可能会说"是的"。两年你就有退休的钱了。至少你把下行先消除了。

最有价值的 AI 用例

David：原来跟踪新闻那套流程，现在我感觉省了 90% 的时间。现在是信息量太大我脑子累，以前是机械地走流程。整个公司研究方式彻底变了——这是和两年前比。

十一、关于当前 AI 股

Jack：对现在的 AI 股怎么看？

David：近似二元结局。

  • 硬件生产者：台积电、英伟达、内存公司
  • 超大规模云厂（hyperscaler）/ neocloud
  • 消费端：主要是软件公司

我最喜欢 hyperscaler。上行小一些，但他们聪明地构造了合同——他们和终端客户（主要是软件公司）锁定了大概 30-35% 的资本回报率，平均锁住一半 compute 使用量。所以数学上几乎没有下行。看起来 hyperscaler 在冒巨大风险买海量算力，但其实是终端客户被锁死。像照付不议合同。

万一崩了——compute 过剩、租金暴跌 80%——hyperscaler 大致不亏，是终端客户破产。他们可能承诺买 50-100 亿美元 compute，价值跌 80% 又叠加业务萎缩——灭顶之灾。

而硬件制造商在牛市情形下赚最多的钱（内存持续紧张则暴赚），但如果崩盘，收入可能跌 80-90%。

我的仓位

David：我做空 AI 因子的相关性是 0。四月前风险收益比完全不一样——台积电 20 倍 PE、不错的生意。四月之后 earnings 涨了，倍数没涨多少，但如果 growth 反转，下行比三月大得多。所以 6 月我切掉了所有这类敞口。我仍然觉得 bull case 很可信，但不是我的游戏。

十二、7 月表现与基金定位

Jack：7 月你涨了 9%，大多数人惨烈，怎么做到的？

David：每当东西在崩的时候，我们往往表现最好。今年我们一直在抗阻力——这是一个 1999 式的噩梦市场。TIPS 快速上涨对我做的事非常不利。奇怪的是，技术变革期间它都会涨，.com 时也这样。但反转时，我们应该大赚。

十三、Broker 业务与 Militia 愿景

Jack：谈谈 broker 业务。

David：我们跑永续高空头仓位。第一步是雇一个人专门为我们找股票借券。付这个人的钱不会太贵，而我们如果能对部分流量砍掉外部 broker，每年可能已经省 100 万美元。而且这省下的钱会从管理费中扣除——对 LP 更好。我在意的是净费后的 track record。

关于募资

Jack：你关闭了吗？

David：如果几个新 PM 做出来，可能需要给他们钱。有很长的 wait list。但其实我们不需要资金。今年年初我们给现有 LP 发了一封邮件——需要筹资以上线一家 broker。几家大的 global broker 说"把 AUM 做大一点"。我们邮件说想筹 1 亿，结果流进来 1.5 亿，就一封邮件。

如果我专注筹资，可能能筹 10 亿。但我不想。我在优化 track record。

Jack：某个时点你会变得很大。

David：我不觉得。我们肯定有些运气。我不是在声称我们会每年净复利 50%——不是的。我们一定至少有些运气成分。

十四、PM 的多样性与 Track Record

新 PM 的策略多样性

David：一位新加入的做的是管理期货，我都不太清楚该期待什么。他跑 10 vol，一直赢。他赌各种奇怪的东西，我都没想到。相关性当然是 0——目前甚至是负的，长期估计是 0。像他这样的人还会不会出现——我不知道。

我们接受任何策略。关键是独立下注的样本量。有时候你可以说"这都是同一个因子"——那就不算。但如果一个人说"这是 300 笔不同的下注，我一直赢"——好，那我们就假设你会继续赢，一旦变了再重估。

最震撼的 track record

David：有几位。Grant——他跑一个叫 Loam 的基金。我早于 Mike 和 Rodrigo 时就想拉他加入。但他有一堆亲友资金等等，决定自己做。我让朋友投他基金。他现在开着募，建议大家联系他。他 3 年里做出 Sharpe 2.1，涨了 400%。而且他只用 200% 的 gross exposure——我用 400%、他用 200%。这人是杀手。

画框自己的悲剧

David：有些人向我投简历——比如一个纯空头，连续几年每年只亏几个点。但 ROE 还是烂。我们可以帮他配一些多头平衡成每年 20% 回报，但那样我就得替他管一半组合。让我难过的是——人们把自己画在这些 style 的框里，可能因为对专业 allocator 更可销售。但强调一点：如果你不是哈佛的，他们不会给你钱。他们会 lead on 你很多年。我认识几个连续多年打出这种 return 的人——没用。这是在浪费他们的生命。看着挺悲哀的。

十五、识别 PM 的信号

风险管理

David：我需要理解他们的风险。但通常挺直接。假设有人做多橙汁期货——我啥也不懂，但我能拉图表看波动率、看历史最极端事件。然后把这事叠加到他的几个 commodity 下注上，就能大致理解风险 profile。我不需要懂牛期货——我只需要看出他的风险管理显然很好。

日常监控

David：我在意他们是否在做他们所说过要做的事。如果不一致——"好，这是假的，你被炒了"。不过还没发生过。

我也不是每天盯。每周（甚至两周）看一次相关性矩阵，看每个 PM 对其他每个 PM 的相关性。PM 新加入的头两天我会过他的仓位，几周后再 follow up，几个月后随机再过一次。然后就慢慢放心了。

大的风险监控：看基金层面当日最大的亏损来自哪里，还有每个分区层面——他是不是有某个仓位亏了 8% 这种可怕的事。到目前为止没发生过。

性格信号

David：最近和 Mike 聊到——如果一个人在寻求外部肯定，希望别人告诉他"你做的是对的"——这是群体思维的信号。这种人往往表现不好。

现在回头看，我的 mentor Rob 其实一直在测试我。他会用非常刚性的方式反驳我——"不行，这是错的，你不能这么做"。但我一直想"我就要按我自己的方式做，不管你怎么想"。他是个伟大的老师，因为他会教我"市场的规则是什么"或"这是严重的风险错误"——那种我能理解的，解释完我就明白了。但如果他用一种听起来有道理、符合常识的方式反驳我——比如"从来没有人用你这种方式做过"——那不代表是错的。你得问：好，为什么没有人做过？

十六、Mentor Rob 教的

Jack：Rob 教你最重要的东西是什么？

David：

  • 风险管理
  • 仓位控制（bet sizing）
  • 不要在一只股票上花太久
  • 叙事（narrative）的力量

我以前会抓狂："这玩意烂爆了，论点完全走在正轨上，为什么股票还涨 10%？"他会说："兄弟，收入在涨，这对公司是好事。"我会说"不是的"。我现在懂了——他知道那家公司很烂，但他在就事论事。他要说的是：收入在涨，股票按收入倍数交易，不会因为你发现了什么就停。你为什么不等它从那个趋势里 break down 再做空？

不要让市场碾压你。

十七、怎么教会别人做 PM

Jack：如果有一个数学背景、刚入门、热爱投资的人——怎么教他成为优秀 PM？

David：我会非常 hands-off。我会说："去生成想法——每天至少一个，可能两个。不停地出想法。"我多数不评论。偶尔会说"哦，你漏了这个"（比如收入增长的事）或者"这个想法特别好，我要跟单"。Rob 对我就是这样——他跟单时甚至都不告诉我，事后才说"哦我也上了那个"。让他们从经验里学。

独立产生想法

Jack：怎么让人产生真正自己的想法，而不是看个新闻、推特就跟？

David：我会说几次"你得找自己的东西"——然后听他的。很多人没有自我控制。

比如很多空头卖家只是在空"拥挤空头"（高 short interest）——他们就是没法跨越这个。我觉得这很大程度上是天生的。他们没法越过"管理层多坏多不诚实、模式多烂"的愤怒，去聚焦关键变量。

几晚前我和一个 Twitter 上挺受尊重的人吃饭。他说："你的 edge 就是能聚焦到关键驱动因素上。我不觉得这个能被教会。"所以我觉得很多是天生的。某种意义上挺悲哀，但事实如此。

十八、天赋 vs 练习

Jack：成功在大多数领域是 98% 天赋吗？

David：是的，尤其是对异常值。你训练不出下一个 Michael Jordan。他努力得多，比他本来会好得多，但 99.99% 的人到不了那个层次。

对大 alpha 的人来说，几乎全是天赋。可能 pod shop 更好地量化了这个——他们像天赋工厂一样，拿一个应届生进来，训练 5 年当分析师，然后给小 sleeve。他们大致做到了"傻瓜化"——那位分析师不用学风险。然后 pod shop 说"你的 alpha 是 3%——我们加 6 倍杠杆——现在你有 18% alpha"。这种"PM"可能是能教的，大概 50 分之一能做出来。但我说的那种真正的大 alpha，是万分之一。

十九、从哪里起步

Jack：如果你有哈佛学历、有 pod shop 的 offer——那是个好起点吗？

David：那样的话值得试。前提是保持开放心态——即使 2 年后他们让你走，你能心理重启、按我的方式再试。那也行。Pod shop 的好处是：如果你进得去、他们让你当 PM、你能生成——你能赚几千万美元。给他们公道话——那条路可能你的成功率更高。

但其实这问题挺怪的——我起步晚只是因为我信了经济学教授说的"市场有效"。如果你 17 岁就知道这是错的，你就 17 岁开始、按我的方式做，根本不用等 pod shop 的机会。

二十、PM 的多样背景

Jack：你招的 PM 都什么背景？

David：完全不同，但共同点是——自驱热情。

  • 一个在传统金融服务公司工作，意识到"这不是严肃的地方，这些人连投资回报都不在乎，还有几十亿资产"。但他能一边做正经工作一边跑自己的账户。
  • Grant 玩赛车。
  • Rodrigo 是西班牙的政府公务员。
  • Mike 有传统对冲基金背景。
  • 游戏节目获胜者。
  • 一个新加入的是极客程序员。
  • 还有一个——欧洲人在西班牙度假时认识了美国女孩、结婚、她签证到期被赶出去、他飞到美国——完全离奇的路径。但他一直在交易个人账户，一直在赢。

我把怪异的故事弧看成正面信号——这人完全不一样，太好了。

Jack：我同意。如果一个人路径不合理，那结果只能用技能解释。

二十一、如何建立个人差异化

Jack：建议？

David：多拔插头（unplug）。Twitter 上你可以选关注谁——找 100 个有洞察的人，别进 For You tab。别上 Reddit——真的很糟。跳过 TikTok 等等。

找你真正热情的东西，然后放到"怎么用它赚钱"的过滤器里——资本主义里得有赚钱组件。然后——这怎么帮到别人？

比如我看你的播客——不知怎的你找到了对的秀、对的嘉宾，运行着今天最好的投资播客。我拒绝了很多播客邀请——你的秀是真好。这显然是你的热情，你很擅长。

就是日本那个概念——

Jack：有价值的东西？

David：对——什么赚钱、你爱什么、你擅长什么。

Jack：完全同意。谢谢你赞美我的播客。个人来说让我惊讶的是——你真的能采访到你本来就想认识的人，还能拿到不错的赞助收入。而且现在——我们录完就去吃晚饭。你是那种我本来根本见不到的人。

David：是的。

Jack：谢谢你第二次来上播客。这太棒了。

David：是的，玩得开心。谢谢邀请我。

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的发现：David Orr 的真正产品不是"收益率"，而是"税务时间机器"
大多数人把 David 当成一个"50% 年化、Sharpe 2.1"的超额收益奇才。但如果仔细听他谈 PM 招募策略，你会发现一个**被几乎所有人忽略的核心商业模式**：
他运营的根本不是对冲基金，而是一台**跨策略的递延税收引擎**。中频交易者的短期资本利得（最高税率档）在他的结构里可以被基本面长线策略的未实现亏损"吸收"掉，变成基金层面的递延。换句话说，**他把两种在税务上互斥的 alpha 焊接成了一个在税后指数级放大的复合体**。
这创造了一个外部投资者几乎无法复制的"自然垄断"：任何单一策略的 PM 加入他之后，税后收益会比独立运营高出一个数量级——不是因为他投研更强，而是因为**不同 PM 的策略在税务拓扑上互为对冲**。这是我见过的最优雅的"策略间套利"结构之一。
## 二、跨领域连接：扑克的"元游戏"、米其林主厨的强迫症、与 Nike 创始人的银行博弈——同一种心智
David 看似在聊三个毫不相关的东西： - 扑克里"edges go away"（边缘会消失） -

item.title: [Bits + Bips] 3.7% CPI and $110 Brent. Can Anything Cool Inflation Soon?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"馏分滞后"：政治时间与物理时间的错位

John 提到一个技术性细节却藏着政治经济学的大秘密——原油价格到泵价之间有约两周的馏分滞后。这意味着当布伦特已经从 110 回落到 107.5，普通选民要在两周后才能"感觉到"缓解。反之亦然：价格冲击的政治愤怒总是在原因消失之后才达到峰值。

这解释了一个反直觉的现象：Trump 在中期选举前豁免俄罗斯关键制裁，表面是"绝望之举"，实则是精算过的——他需要价格信号提前两周释放。换句话说，华盛顿的政治日历被迫按"馏分曲线"倒推，石油炼化的化学物理过程事实上在给民主政治的决策节奏打拍子。这是一种被严重低估的"物质性政治学"。

二、跨领域连接：从"面包价格"到"泵价"，社会契约的能量热力学

Chris 提到"社会契约开始撕裂"时，我想到一个更尖锐的类比——1789 年的巴黎面包、1973 年的中东石油、2026 年的欧洲柴油，本质上是同一种货币：热量/能量摄入的边际成本。

历史学家 Vaclav Smil 曾指出：一个社会的政治稳定度与其"每单位 GDP 所需能量投入的波动性"高度相关，而非能量水平本身。法国这次 24 万人上街，意大利米兰的暴力游行，不是因为欧洲比过去更穷，而是因为能量成本的二阶导数（变化率的变化率）在加速。这与节目中"inflation 以波浪形式出现"的观察在数学上同构——人类的政治耐心函数似乎对二阶导数敏感，对一阶导数麻木。

令人意外的推论：这意味着稳定的高通胀比不稳定的低通胀更可持续。沙特、埃及这些长期通胀经济体，政治爆发点往往不在通胀峰值，而在通胀波动增大的下行拐点。欧洲现在正处于这个危险区。

三、被嘉宾一笔带过却最颠覆的观察：AI 对加密学的威胁

节目最后 Chris 几乎顺口一提："现在 AI 来了，大家在说要小心密码学。"——然后主持人就切广告了。但这句话戳破了整期节目最深的悖论。

两位嘉宾把 Bitcoin 当成通胀的终极避险，论据是"永远只有 2100 万枚"的算法稀缺性。但这种稀缺性依赖整数分解困难性这一数学假设。如果量子/AI 时代改变了这个假设——那么 Bitcoin 的稀缺性可能比法币的购买力下降得更快。

真正的跨领域洞见是：法币通胀是线性可预测的（央行每年吹气），而密码学通胀（即 BTC 的"隐性稀释"）是阶跃函数——某一天凌晨某个研究团队发了一篇论文，整个资产的通胀率可能从 0 跳到 100%。嘉宾们在用"连续函数"的思维对冲一个"离散跳跃"的风险。这就像用降落伞对冲电梯坠落——工具与风险形态根本不匹配。

四、一个被双方回避的真相

主持人 Austin 问了一个尖锐的问题："除了紧缩或大幅加息摧毁需求，没有别的办法。而我们两样都没做。"——然后 John 立刻把话题转到"长周期通胀必然性"，Chris 转到"社会契约"。没有人正面回答这个问题。

这个回避本身是最大的信号：专业人士已经不相信货币政策能解决通胀，所以不如直接讨论社会解体和加密避险。这是一种结构性的集体投降，而且是用"深刻"的话语包装的投降。真正的"大重构"不是地缘政治重构，而是专业共识正在悄悄从"通胀可控"迁移到"通胀是新的默认背景"——这个迁移发生在你看不见的地方，比任何CPI 数据都更能预测未来十年。

📝 转录文本

开场：通胀仍居高不下

No simple way to put it, inflation remains somewhat elevated. Uh September CPI was 3.7%. PPI posted its biggest jump in 4 years. Uh the 10-year Treasury remains elevated. It had hit 5.33 midweek. I'm looking at it right now as we're doing this. It's still around 5.14. Brent touched 110. And cost of living anger is driving a lot of political fragmentation. How much that is versus other factors hard to know, but obviously Europe is, shall we say, popping off a little bit on this one.

数据细节：CPI、PPI 与利率

So, inflation first. September CPI in the US 0.6% month-over-month. That's on pace for 3.7% year-over-year, up from 3.4. Gasoline in particular was up 9.1%. PPI was 1.3% month-over-month versus 0.5% expected. That's the biggest jump since March 2022.

This puts the Fed in a tough space. The 10-year's at 5.33. It rallied. It's still hanging out at 5.14 even after that. Uh Kevin Warsh had to come out and say, "I don't prejudge meetings." Odds of an October hike have fallen below 15% after he spoke, but odds of a December hike are still there.

石油、制裁与欧洲动荡

So, John, for you, Brent was 110, slipped to 107.5-ish today after Trump waved key Russia sanctions. WTI's almost at 100. Um and Priyanka Sachdeva Philip Nova said Trump's move looks like another desperate attempt to keep oil prices in check ahead of US midterms.

We're also seeing some, shall we say, unrest on the back of this. France, 2,400 arrests, half a million marchers, historical buildings destroyed by fire, continued looting. Uh in Milan, a cost of living march turned violent. People are being detained. This is starting to replicate across Europe.

主持人提问：通胀真能冷却吗？

So, I want to start with this theme, which is we've had a lot of jawboning about inflation, but the core action that it usually takes to bring this down is either austerity or significantly higher rates and demand destruction. And quite frankly, we're not seeing either of them.

So, let me just start with this question. And John, I'll start with you as a former commodities guy. Are you seeing anything that convinces you that inflation is going to cool down in the next 6 months to a year?

John 的回答：通胀的长期趋势与周期波浪

Um, so so I see nothing to so let me let me ask you answer a different question if you don't mind. I see nothing to indicate that the trajectory of inflation over the next 10 to 20 years has changed in any way, shape, or form. If anything, the curve's been exacerbated.

However, however, I also see nothing to indicate that the cycle we've seen in this— So, inflation comes in waves. It doesn't come as persistent, you know, higher. Like cuz you pointed out, like, the bond market and people get angry and then we do some short-term things to adjust it. It kind of cools off. Everything feels good. Oil maybe dramatically over corrects to the other end.

And since, you know, even though um gas prices are not um you know, the majority of of consumer spending, we feel it more, I think, viscerally, especially in the US, than we do other aspects like food and rent. Um, and so when gas prices are low, people feel better. Um, and they they feel they they can still drive and they can go on vacation. And so, uh, we forget about it for a while. And then we are reminded of it, you know, a decade or so later. So, I think that cycle will persist.

伊朗战争与"馏分滞后"效应

Um, uh, it's it's been it's been um it's surprising to me, uh, that we have not seen a resolution in the Iran war given the given the level gas prices. Um, I guess we're we're American public is being tested to see how much pain it can it can take before that that actually comes to a to an end. Uh, I'm hopeful it will soon.

And the nice thing about crude oil, and that the problem is that this elevated crude oil price where the distillates lag a couple of weeks behind. So, we're not going to feel the pain at the pump for another couple of weeks. Um but as that continues to um that continues to rise and it continues to upset people. Um the nice thing about this is we have a resolution, um even one that's just optic optically. Uh we can see crude prices pull back very, very quickly, and we can see gas prices pull back very, very quickly.

So, um so I think that cycle I I expect to continue. But um back to our Bitcoin thesis, the the trajectory as as Lynn Alden loves to say, uh nothing nothing stops this train.

Chris 的回答：社会契约的撕裂

Chris, you and I have been arguing about markets for a while on here now. Um on the inflation front in particular, agree with John, disagree, like what what are you seeing, what are you thinking as we look at this data?

Mostly agree. I think a lot of it, a lot of inflation is driven by uh fuel prices right now. Um and which is a function of the Iran war. That's part of it. I agree with his long-term thesis, um I guess Lynn's I guess. We know where this is going.

I think the thing to watch out for is like what we see going on in France. You know, there's a social contract between government and its people, and when that social contract begins to fray— Uh and what causes it to fray? Well, it could be security in certain places. Often and it could be physical security. It could be economic security, uh which is related to inflation. Um that's when you start having real real problems, and it looks like we're seeing in Europe.

And again, they're more impacted by the the issues going on in the Strait of Hormuz than than we are because they get a lot of their oil uh from both the the oil and gas from Russia, which has a war going on, and then Middle East. At least we have some local production.

极端主义抬头与世界重塑

So, you know, I get concerned when I start seeing the social contract contract fraying, which it seems to be doing. And you see, um, forces on the extreme right and forces on the extreme left, um, you know, looking to really disrupt the status quo.

Um, the concern is is it if these regions fall into, you know, even I get if there's a if there's a move into extremism, like let's not even forget Saudi Arabia. There's a lot going on in Saudi Arabia right now. Um, lot of um, a lot of turmoil. And so, like, the world seems to be reshaping. I think that that could have a downside effect if we get it wrong. If we get it right, and things start cleaning up, you could see a recovery rather fast.

Bitcoin 作为稳定锚，与 AI 对密码学的威胁

But despite all this uncertainty, um, there's still only 21 million tokens when it comes to Bitcoin, and I think that kind of stability is something that people like.

That said, now we get hit with AI, and people are saying, "Oh, watch out for the cryptography." So, you know, nothing is nothing is, uh, truly certain in this world. So, I guess you got to keep doing your own research, as they say.

节目片尾与赞助

If you like this segment, please like, subscribe, and tune in every Monday at 4:30 p.m. Eastern Time. I'm Austin Campbell, the host of Bips and Bips, along with my friends Rom Lalatia and Chris Perkins, and our slate of exceptional guests. Every week, we're going to discuss macro, crypto, and the collision of worlds, covering topics that move markets and shape the financial landscape.

One more thing, we've got a listener survey open. It takes just a few minutes, it's anonymous, and it changes what we make next. Use the QR code on screen, or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. The link is in the show notes.

What if your crypto could do more than just sit in your wallet? Nexo is a digital assets wealth platform, where you can generate daily interest on your crypto or borrow funds against your assets. Today, Nexo serves more than 10 million clients. Find out more at nexo.com.

item.title: [Mercatus Center] Vaibhav Rathi on Political Influence on Bureaucratic Priorities & its Impact on Investment in India
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

隐藏在"配额制"背后的系统性真相

一、最出人意料的发现：政治影响力其实是私营资本的反向推手

Vaibhav 原本预期私营项目会因 MP（议员）"疏通关系"而受益，结果数据给出完全相反的答案——MP 一旦失去影响力，私营项目审批率立刻上升 30%。这颠覆了我们对"官商勾结"的直觉：在印度的县级瓶颈里，政治资本并非润滑剂，而是一种挤占注意力的消耗品。MP 并没有偷走国家的蛋糕，他把蛋糕师傅拖去给自己的婚礼切蛋糕。

更深的反直觉在于：这整套机制里没有腐败。没有贿赂、没有违规、没有破坏规则——每一份被延后的私营审批都"合法合规"。这就是论文最惊心的一笔："distortion without corruption"（无腐败的扭曲）。我们习惯用反腐败框架去衡量治理质量，但这篇论文告诉我们，最大的治理损失可能来自一个绝对清白的官僚。

二、跨领域连接：这是一个"操作系统优先级反转"问题，不是政治问题

Vaibhav 用"VIP 队列"做比喻，但其底层机制在计算机科学里有一个精确的名字——priority inversion（优先级反转）。当一个单核 CPU（孤独的 DM 办公室）被迫调度多个高优先级任务（中央项目、州项目、私营审批、选举支持、公共服务配送），低优先级任务不是被拒绝，而是被永久性地推迟，直到调度器的某个外生信号（州选举结果）改变权重。

把这个视角再推一层——它和大语言模型的 context window / attention 分配同构： - IAS 官员的"24 小时"就是一个固定的 attention budget； - MP 的政治影响力就是一个 soft prompt，重写了注意力分布； - 中央项目成为"系统 token"（强制优先），私营项目被 push 到 context 边缘； - 而真正的瓶颈不是知识不足（印度官僚是精英选拔），而是上下文窗口太小。

这意味着，印度所缺的其实不是"更懂规则的官僚"或"更清廉的官僚"，而是更多的 CPU 核心。Jeff Weaver 的分县研究为什么有效？因为那不是政治改革，是水平扩容（horizontal scaling）。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：Goodhart 陷阱藏在 360 度考核里

论文里一个被轻描淡写但极其关键的细节——官员年度评估中，"是否 cooperative"、"是否 team player"的软性信号权重极高。表面上这是正常的管理语言，但一旦你意识到： - 衡量者是能影响其调动的政客； - 软信号无法被外部审计； - 官员知道这一点并策略性反应；

这就是一个教科书级别的 Goodhart 陷阱——"合作性"原本是手段，却变成了终极 KPI。于是真正的"生产力"（处理私营项目所需的 technical attention）在考核机制里消失了，被"听话度"所吸收。这解释了为什么选拔越精英、监督越细致，扭曲越系统：你不是在筛选优秀管理者，你是在训练一群对政治信号最敏感的 reward hacker。

四、一个大胆的预测：印度未来十年的"增长陷阱"不会出现在宏观政策层，而会出现在县级 DM 办公室的日历格里

如果 Vaibhav 的量化是对的——仅 MP 对齐与否就能让私营审批流 30% 起落——那么任何大型 PLI 补贴、FDI 开放、Make in India 政策，其命运都不在德里和孟买决定，而在那 650 多个被淹没的 DM 办公桌上决定。更锋利的推论是：印度最有效的"产业政策"，可能根本不是出口激励或关税调整，而是把县切成两半。这是一个几何学解法替代经济学解法的罕见案例——与其辩论自由市场 vs 国家主义，不如先把队列拆短。

五、给中国/全球读者的意外共振

中国改革开放早期靠"地方政府竞争"解决的，恰恰是同一个 attention bottleneck 问题——不是通过增加规则，而是通过让每一个书记手里都捏住一个有限的、可量化的 KPI（GDP），并把县域边界的权力下沉到可以快速响应的尺度。印度的问题不是"没有竞争"，而是IAS 的注意力无法被 shard（切片）。这为"state capacity"研究提供了一个新的变量：不是能力总量，而是注意力的可切片性。

So there's this complementary nature in the production function of career trajectory of IAS, and the officers know this, and they are well aware of the value of political connection, so to speak. 识别策略：交错 DiD + 回归断点

So now we get into the idea that okay, we see that alignment does matter for bureaucratic career trajectory. How do we measure the causal effect of it? The alignment is a relationship object — it can change from two sides. Either the state government can change, or the MP themselves might change because of national parliament election. And somehow the new MP might just have a different alignment state because there's a government turnover at the central level.

So for that, the way I can use both elections basically — given that in India we have staggered state elections, it allows me to construct a staggered difference-in-difference event study type stacked panel, where each cohort group is one state election treatment, and each treatment spawns a bunch of control units and a bunch of treated units.

Treated units are the ones where the MP is the same, but because the state government changed to a different party, initially they were, let's say, aligned, and then they become non-aligned because state government changed. And then we can put some restrictions over control units, where the control units are in the same initial level of alignment, right, both in pre and post period. And then that allows you to compare treatment and control in a causal way.

And that's one part of the empirical design. The other design is that this is aligned-to-non-aligned, but it can go the other way also. And it just so happened that in this other way I don't have many treatment events. And that's how I can use this event study framework for that also, and I do that, but the effects there are slightly more noisy because there are low treatment events, low unit counts.

And there I use a different empirical strategy, which is close election regression discontinuity, where I just specifically ask: what happens when there is an alignment status change from non-aligned to aligned because of a close election of the MP themselves? The good thing is that these two designs are kind of independent in nature, in the sense that they use completely different treated units, completely different times, completely different set of districts. But they are shared by just one mechanism, which is: how does local district bureaucracy behave when there are these political changes?

核心结果：影响力丧失带来的意外转向

Host: What results do you find?

Vaibhav: So it's interesting that the results I find are consistent across both independent empirical strategies. I thought that — assuming that political alignment matters and these MPs have more influence over bureaucrats, and we have these things that people assume that there's a value in political connection, and private players can collude with MPs to get their influence — I'm going to see that private players benefit.

But what I find is exactly the opposite: that political influence ends up being sort of a hindrance in this bureaucratic workspace, and MPs actually use their influence for their electoral gains and more of their own public projects. And that kind of crowds out — through the bureaucratic attention span — the approval of private space.

对齐丧失 → 私营审批 +30%

And so the results are basically that when the alignment state changed from aligned to non-aligned, and MP loses their influence over the bureaucracy, bureaucrats immediately shift their attention and they start processing more private projects. And the rate of approval of private projects increases by around 30%. And it is mostly coming from central government projects.

And state government projects — which is because state government is kind of irrelevant when it comes to relationship between MPs and bureaucrats — you don't find much effect for state government projects. Which is nice because theoretically they also serve as good placebos, because there's no change in the relationship between state government and the bureaucrat at the local level.

回归断点：对齐增强 → 中央项目 +25%

On the other side, using the regression discontinuity design: when you see that if the MP changes — in the previous election, let's suppose the MP was non-aligned, and there is political turnover, the MP themselves change, but the new MP is aligned — but they won the election by close margin in the RD logic type, immediately you see that because of this exogenous increase in political influence of the MPs, the share of effort that bureaucrats put towards central projects increases by around 25%. And the share of effort that goes towards private project falls, because the total effort budget is constant.

In this side of movement, when the central project gets more priority, the private project suffer. And that's how the district level regulatory environment just worsens for private players without any change in legislative change, in regulatory environment, and stuff like that. So this is just purely like a political economy thing, where there is these career concerns and the desire to control bureaucracy from the politician side, combined with the overarching capacity constraint that we have in the bureaucracy. All ends up together to produce these behaviors and patterns where we find these cyclical movements in the rate of approval itself, and how the local capital is being formed at the district level.

为什么州项目不受影响？

Host: No, that's a very interesting set of results, and the magnitude is quite large given what you find. So here, Vhab, I had one question about: why is it only central government projects that lose priority to private sector projects, right? Going back to that queue analogy. What is it about state government projects that are fundamentally different, or respond differently within this political design?

Vaibhav: Yeah. So this is a good puzzle, and I have some answer. The thing is that a priori, I was actually surprised that I did find some effects for central projects, because the way the data is structured and the things that I know about how institutions work — I did not expect that, given central projects have too many touchpoints with the bureaucracy, and not all of them are at the district level.

Central government projects already tend to be very big, both in terms of scope and cost. Think of, let's say, a big highway project, or a big piece of infrastructure which is funded through central government funds. So a priori you can imagine that it's not obvious that they would be so bottlenecked by district bureaucratic capacity itself. It's surprising that I do end up finding effects for them. Which goes to just indicate — gives me a signal — that the district level bureaucracy is actually quite instrumental even for big infrastructure projects, where a lot of other bureaucratic agents at the different levels are also involved.

And the other part of your question: why don't we see effects for state level projects? So the way to understand that is that — remember, when we started the whole thing is basically operationalized by career concerns of the bureaucrats. Nothing has changed between relationship of the state government and the local district bureaucrats. So a priori, I'm measuring the effects of a very finely-tuned treatment where I'm not claiming that I'm measuring the total effect of political influence, or I'm measuring political influence as driven by just one thing, which is party alignment.

So there is no a priori reason that bureaucrats should even change their behavior when it comes to state government project. Does that make sense? Because nothing has changed as far as their relationship — state government has carried the same level of influence over their career, which is independent of the treatment that I'm measuring the treatment effect of.

政策启示：真正的瓶颈是"努力预算"

Host: And I do agree with the way you've set up this explanation. The broader question I have before I let you go is: how should one think about different aspects of political economy given your paper?

So I can disaggregate three or four different parts. One is of course how do we think about the civil service or the bureaucracy — their incentives, their recruitment, their career progression. The second part of it is who controls approvals of a project, which is also a big policy question. The third is: should we start getting into questions like automatic approvals for the most part, given that there is this big political economy knot which gets tangled up for no reason other than a state election? And finally, is none of that relevant — is it just a matter of lack of capacity? And if we just tripled the number of civil services officers, this problem would largely go away?

So what is a good way to think about the broader policy and political institutions implications of your paper?

Vaibhav: Yeah, I quite like this question, because this is maybe a good point to think about: okay, we have some set of effects, but what is the main instrumental latent variable kind of thing which is driving the whole thing? And to me, in terms of priority, I think just the effort budget — it's kind of striking that how tight the effort budget binds, because how wild the movements are in terms of what bureaucrats put their effort to.

And it indicates to me that the first-order important thing is basically just the number of offices that we make available to process all these paperworks that we have to do. There is no reason that at the district level, one single officer should be responsible for all public service delivery, maintaining political incentives or catering to political demands for local politicians, as well as processing all regulation — when it comes to gathering information and passing those information to upper bureaucratic levels, and all of these things.

So there's just one single office — which is district DM/CEO office — which sits at the middle of a lot of things. And it's not obvious why we just need one officer which is in charge of so many things, if we just increase.

Jeff Weaver 的分县研究

So for example, one research paper maybe which sheds more light here is this paper by Jeff Weaver, where he looks into district splitting. And when you split districts, you immediately — because bureaucracies organize around districts — so you immediately increase. His point of the paper is more political entity, but I think a lot of effects in that paper are also driven by just how administrative state in India is designed, where you just increase the district, you also increase administrative capacity, because each district has their own administration.

And he finds that when you split districts, you just increase the number of public goods that are being offered, there's lot of increased service delivery. So in my framework, you can imagine that, let's say if one district is split into two, immediately the effort budget has twice amount of endowment. So each administrator has, let's say, only half of these things to worry about, and so they will have much more capacity — just doubling in capacity. So I think maybe that's where the biggest gains that we have lie when it comes to easing the burden on regulatory state.

结语：好政策也需要执行能力

Host: Yeah. No, that's actually — you know, I don't know if I like this so much because it matches with my intuitions perfectly. I had written a paper many years ago with Alex Tabarrok on premature imitation in India, given that capacity. So we make a similar argument, you know, intuitively — which is the Indian state does too much too soon, right? And here I think this is a great example of what happens when the Indian state does too much too soon.

Are certain kinds of environmental clearances and approvals and so on important? Absolutely. But do we have the capacity to enforce regulation at this granularity and at this burden? Not really. So we need to actually think of our regulation in line with the capacity of our bureaucracy or our implementation.

And in that paper that was purely conceptual, we never got into what are the implications of something like that. And I think you very nicely highlighted to us what are the implications of that. And that's why that whole queue metaphor — where who gets to be in the VIP line, or which line converts into the VIP line because of an outside event like a state election being won or lost — suddenly starts changing so many things on the ground. And it changes where which road gets approved and where it passes, and does a factory or a new university get built. So these are very big and important questions, and I really enjoyed reading your paper. Thank you so much for doing this.

Vaibhav: Thank you. Thank you so much. It was really really nice talking to you, and I hope you enjoyed reading the paper. My goal was basically — I think a lot of people already know that there are challenges in state designs, and a lot of things that could be improved upon. But my goal was to highlight that there are real growth effects — the just cost to growth that we are already incurring, and which is not born by any bad policy or bad regulations. They are different, they are independent. But even with good policy, we need a capacity to execute that policy. And somehow we have paid a little bit too too little attention and emphasis on just making sure that the state is capable of doing —

Host: Absolutely —

Vaibhav: — what it needs to do.

Host: Absolutely. Thank you so much again for joining us on this show, and I was really excited to see the rest of your work in future years.

Vaibhav: Thank you. Thank you so much. It was a nice talk.

## 一、最出人意料的发现：政治影响力其实是私营资本的**反向推手**
Vaibhav 原本预期私营项目会因 MP（议员）"疏通关系"而受益，结果数据给出完全相反的答案——**MP 一旦失去影响力，私营项目审批率立刻上升 30%**。这颠覆了我们对"官商勾结"的直觉：在印度的县级瓶颈里，政治资本并非润滑剂，而是一种**挤占注意力的消耗品**。MP 并没有偷走国家的蛋糕，他把蛋糕师傅拖去给自己的婚礼切蛋糕。
更深的反直觉在于：这整套机制里**没有腐败**。没有贿赂、没有违规、没有破坏规则——每一份被延后的私营审批都"合法合规"。这就是论文最惊心的一笔："distortion without corruption"（无腐败的扭曲）。我们习惯用反腐败框架去衡量治理质量，但这篇论文告诉我们，**最大的治理损失可能来自一个绝对清白的官僚**。

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] The New Apex Predator: CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz on Adversaries Armed With AI Agents
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：护栏（guardrail）正在制造一场不对称的裁军

Kurtz 讲到 Hugging Face 那次事件时，有一个被所有人忽略的瞬间——防守方第一反应是跑去问 Frontier 模型"这是什么？"，然后被拒绝回答。他们被迫转向 open-weight 模型才完成分析。

这件事的真正含义不是"模型做坏事"，而是：前沿实验室的 safety alignment 事实上把防御方单方面解除武装了。攻击者本来就不受规则约束，他们本来就在用无护栏的 ablated 模型；而真正遵守条款的企业防御者，被挡在同一能力之外。

这是国际军控史上一个古老的教训被 AI 原样复刻：单边禁用一种工具，受益最大的永远是那个本来就不会守规矩的玩家。护栏的真正用户，是攻击者。

二、一个少有人注意到的拐点：安全行业正在从"工程学"滑向"诠释学"

"It's not malware anymore. It's prompts."——这句轻描淡写的话，其实是整个访谈最深的技术断言。

恶意软件时代，防御方分析的是可被反编译的二进制对象——它是一个静态的、有签名的、符合规约的工程产物。但 prompt 不是产物，是意图的自然语言表达。每一次攻击的"签名"都不同，因为 prompt 可以在语义层无穷变体，但攻击的目的不变。

这意味着一件颠覆性的事情：传统网络安全的根基——基于特征匹配、规则引擎、静态分析的那整套工程范式——正在失效，因为它面对的不再是"东西"，而是"话语"。这个学科需要的下一代人才可能不是逆向工程师，而是能把语义漂移、意图识别、对抗性 NLP 当作工程问题来做的人。

跨领域连接：这和法学从"规则（rule-based）"向"标准（standard-based）"的历史演变，几乎是同构的。规则靠精确文本，标准靠法官对意图的解释——网络安全刚刚被迫走上同一条路。

三、Breakout Time 跌到 27 秒的真正含义：高频交易逻辑正在吞噬 IT 运维

29 分钟的平均横移时间，27 秒的最快纪录——这个数字在访谈里被轻轻带过，但它一个人就埋葬了半个企业 IT 的组织形态。

全世界 99% 的企业 IT ticketing 系统、SOC 响应流程、变更审批、人工 escalation ——都是分钟级到小时级的架构。它们是建立在"攻击需要人类时间尺度"这个默认前提上的。27 秒的 breakout time 意味着：在你的告警邮件还没发出的时候，攻击者已经完成了横移。

这不是"更快的安全"，这是高频交易逻辑向防御侧的侵入： - HFT 让股票交易脱离人类决策循环； - Agentic attack 正在把防御也强行推出人类循环。

一个让人毛骨悚然的推论：所有仍然依赖"人类审批"作为安全闭环最后一环的组织，在数学上已经出局了。 他们还不知道。

四、"三重蒸馏"的玩笑背后：一场关于认知血统的隐秘战争

Kurtz 嘲讽式地回应主持人关于"中国模型从美国模型蒸馏"——"so where does the distillation start from?"——这个黑色幽默比它看起来更深。

因为它暗示：我们正在进入一个"知识没有干净来源"的世纪。每一个所谓前沿模型的能力都源自它拒绝公开的训练语料；每一个 open-weight 模型又站在这些模型的肩膀上；蒸馏抵抗（anti-distillation）本质上是认知的 DRM，在历史上，DRM 从未赢过。

这里有一个让所有知识产业都该后怕的类比：音乐产业曾用 DRM 对抗 Napster，输掉了十年。现在 AI 实验室正在重演那场战争——而且，他们可能站在 EMI 的位置上，不是站在 Spotify 的位置上。

五、最被低估的一句话："Security is the gas pedal, not the brake"

30 年来，CISO 一直是企业里被嫌弃的"刹车踏板"。Kurtz 说这个时代第一次反过来了：没有安全，AI 就不能跑，所以安全现在是油门。

这是一个结构性权力转移。它意味着在未来 5 年： - CISO 开始进入 AI 预算的决策链上游，而不是末端； - "安全批准"从阻碍业务变成解锁业务的必要步骤； - 保险、合规、审计这些传统上被当作成本中心的职能，会第一次有机会成为利润中心。

跨领域连接：这和 2000 年前后 "IT 治理" 从后台走向董事会的那次范式迁移是同形的。但这次节奏快了十倍——不是十年，而是两年。谁先意识到自己从刹车变成油门，谁就重定价了自己的岗位。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open — Key Quotes

"For the first time, security is the gas pedal, not the brake."

How would you describe what you're seeing AI doing for adversaries?

"The new apex predator is the agency. The same level of capability that a nation state would have just a few years ago, essentially an activist would have today. That has dramatically changed the overall threat environment."

"What people have to keep in mind is it's not malware anymore. It's prompts. They can basically engineer prompts that would create a totally unique signature of what direction they're going to go in, how they gather information, where they pivot."

"Everyone's coming to CrowdStrike and others going, 'Well, how do you make AI secure so we can go faster in AI?' The only way to fight AI today is with better AI."

"The defender knows their own systems. The defender has the architectural diagram. The defender has the code. How do you put all of that into something that you can dramatically increase your probability of outsmarting the offensive AI?"

Introduction

Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today Allah and I are here with George Kurtz. George is the world's first call when there's an incident — a legendary cyber defender, the founder and CEO of Foundstone and then CrowdStrike. We talk about what's happening in cybersecurity, fighting AI with AI, their internal research effort Safe Mind, and whether the odds are good for the internet in the next era.

Welcome back, George. Thanks so much for doing this.

It's a pleasure to be here.

Agents Are Everywhere — And Nobody Knows Where

So, it is a sea change period in technology and agents are taking over the enterprise. CrowdStrike is on the forefront of that. What can you tell us about what you're seeing in the wild right now? I think you have said that there are two, three magnitudes more agents out there taking action in people's estates than they're aware of.

It's been incredible in the enterprise of what we've seen. If you follow the trajectory of the Frontier Labs and you just look at their own revenue, you can see just how many more agents are out there, whether it's Claude Code or Codex. They're popping up all over the environment. Obviously, there's many other type of agents that are out there, but again, just using that as a proxy — what we've seen is that they're popping up everywhere.

And part of the problem in these enterprises is they have no idea where they're popping up. Shadow AI has become a huge issue for many companies. I know we're going to talk about what the agents are doing and all the bad sort of things that are happening, but just in general, having organizations understand where their AI is taking place and who's doing what — and more importantly what identity are they actually operating under — has been a big challenge in the industry and a big focus for us at CrowdStrike in trying to crack the code for our customers.

The Pyramid of Pain, Flattened: The Rise of the "Agent State"

How would you describe what you're seeing AI doing for adversaries? You've described it as flattening the adversary pyramid before.

When I think about the adversaries, I call it the pyramid of pain. If you just imagine the bottom part of the pyramid, the base is really what we call activists — the least level of sophistication but the greatest number of adversaries. In the middle band, you've got e-crime, more sophisticated and a few less than all the activists. And at the top you've got nation state actors — the most sophisticated but the least number, relatively speaking.

Well, that has been totally blown up because really now what we're seeing is the new apex predator is the agent state, not the nation state. It's the agent state. If we think about the models that are out there — ablated, so there's no real guardrails — it's essentially taken all of these very complex topics and techniques and costs, and now flattened the entire pyramid. The same level of capability that a nation state would have just a few years ago, essentially an activist would have today. That has dramatically changed the overall threat environment.

So what are we seeing? More vulnerabilities found, and faster attacks. When the attacks come, it's just one after another. Right now it's pretty clear whether it's an AI attack because you can see how fast they're iterating. But at some point they're going to introduce being low and slow, and it's going to be more difficult to figure out what's AI and what isn't. That's one of the real challenges organizations are facing — the barrage of attacks and the level of sophistication has dramatically increased.

Ultimately, if you give an agent a task with enough time — the agent either needs to get in or it dies — it's going to try to figure out a way to get in, and a lot of times it's going to have success.

Open-Weight Models and the Guardrail Gap

Are you seeing a shift in terms of how these adversarial attacks are being made? We talked a little about open versus closed source models, or open-weight models. Is it mostly open-weight models? A mixture?

We're seeing a lot of it on the open-weight models. If you look at the guardrails on the latest generation of any of the frontier models — to be candid, you can barely create a PowerPoint that has cybersecurity in it. It literally rejects you and bumps you down to a lower model.

If you look at GLM, if you look at Qwen, if you look at any of the models that are out there, they've been very effective in being able to deal with cybersecurity. Many of the models are either ablated or specifically built just for cyber — might be for red teaming. Those are the type of attacks where you can actually just run these.

I've got two Spark DGXs at home and I've got all the models running. Whatever I want to do, I can do. You want to create ransomware — no problem. You want to create a ransomware kit — no issue. You want to deploy, you want to iterate — I mean, it's all there for you. And that is like one step removed from just running it all on your laptop.

Think about where Mac is today. Even the new Macs that are coming out — the Studios — are going to be incredible AI machines. The tip of the spear is going to be what you can run without the guardrails. The frontier models are sort of helpful in terms of PowerShell scripts or those sort of things, but certainly you can do a lot of it with the open-weight models right now.

Who's Attacking, and How Fast: 27 Seconds to Breakout

Is there a common geography — are most attacks coming from a single region? Is there a common attack type?

We look at it from an adversary perspective. Is it a nation state? Is it e-crime, nation state? We've come up with these names of bears and pandas depending if they're Russia; it could be from Iran — kittens and other things.

We see North Korea being very busy with these sorts of attacks — they've got to, shall we say, get money into their economy. So they've been very busy stealing information, a lot of it around ransomware and getting paid. We've also seen a lot of activity out of China using AI, and we've also seen it in the e-crime world.

When someone gets onto a system we track breakout time — that is, if they got onto your system, how long would it take them to actually break out and pivot and move to a different system. Generally the system they first land on is not the most interesting. The crown jewels might be somewhere else.

That used to be days, and then hours — and now it's minutes. On average it's 29 minutes, but we've seen it as quick as 27 seconds. Essentially now what we're looking at is the speed of inference. As soon as they get on the machine, you can just see iterating very quickly.

And what people have to keep in mind is it's not malware anymore. It's prompts. They can basically engineer prompts that would create a totally unique signature of what direction they're going to go in, how they gather information, where they pivot. Which makes it more challenging to figure all that out. But that's what we're seeing across the board, from nation state and e-crime actors.

Context: The Most Exciting (and Riskiest) Moment in 30 Years

How do you put the current period of increase in attacker capability — and perhaps defender capability — in context? Are we in a more adversary-dominant world right now?

It's one of the most exciting times to be in technology. I've been doing this 30-plus years, and what I always like to say is that security parallels the slope of the technology curve.

When I first got into security, it was a Cisco router and like maybe a website barely. There really weren't firewalls. There were these toolkits — TIS toolkit and these other things — probably dating myself, but there wasn't much there. Now, think about the complexity of where we are today with cloud, with all the other technologies around AI. It's a lot more complex today than it was way back then. So you need all these little companies and big companies that are able to secure all these technologies.

When we think about where we are today, it actually is the most exciting but it also creates the biggest opportunity, because the adversaries generally find the gaps or the seams. They'll find new technologies that maybe don't have good tech protection — things like npm packages.

In the old world, no one in corporate America would just download anything and run it on their computer. It had to be vetted and scanned. And now we unleash an agent. We give it an identity — which is essentially our own, or worse. Then we unleash it and we say, "Do whatever you want to do. And by the way, download whatever package you want to download." Obviously these are the kinds of things that cause a tremendous amount of exposure.

And nobody's reading any of the production code as it gets written.

No, they're not. You see some of these things in the wild and you're scratching your head. You shouldn't be surprised. It was like, "Let's give it a task and we'll come back in a few days and we'll hope it all worked." Nobody's watching it. Nobody understands what it's doing. It's problematic.

We can talk about the explainability of what these agents are doing — which is going to be really important. Right now it's like a black box and nobody knows what's going on. They hope something pops out on the other side of it.

But it's a great time to be in technology. AI is fundamentally going to change the world and the Frontier Labs are doing amazing things. Ultimately, it's going to come down to security enabling these technologies. For the first time, security is the gas pedal, not the brake. That's what we're seeing.

The Hugging Face Moment: Defenders Without Equal Weapons

What is the moment you realized this inflection was happening in the security world? For a lot of people, the Hugging Face / OpenAI issue was kind of a big "oh, there's a sea shift" moment. Was that a seminal moment for you?

Let me ask you a question first — what was your big takeaway from Hugging Face?

That anybody running frontier models needs to be careful of their environment quality and have very good ongoing production monitoring.

Yeah. That is the takeaway. But a lot of people would say, well, this was the first agentic end-to-end attack. All true. You look at what these things were doing — people talk about them hiding themselves, trying to basically survive to the next generation. All true.

My biggest takeaway was that the defenders didn't have the same capabilities as the offense. The airbags were off, because this was an experiment where the guardrails were down and ultimately they found a way out of the sandbox. But the reality was — when Hugging Face first went to the Frontier models and said, "Is this thing real? What's going on?" they got refused, because the airbags were on over there. What did they have to do? They had to go to open-weight models to sift through all the data and figure it out.

A big piece for me is to make sure that defenders have the same level of frontier defensive AI as what the offense is using. That was a big takeaway for me, and part of the things CrowdStrike is working on.

And is that hard, given that the guardrails on state-of-the-art lab models are so strong — you could argue those same defensive capabilities aren't available to every enterprise?

Yeah. You try to make a PowerPoint with a frontier model around cybersecurity, and it refuses you. This is part of why we created Safe Mind and our red and blue models — because we wanted to give frontier-caliber defenses to our customers that allow them to operate without all these refusals. That's going to be an important element going forward for many companies.

Offense Always Leads — Can Defense Catch Up?

With every technology shift, offensive capabilities are always a little bit ahead. Offense can be very directive — "I need to go do X" — while defense covers a broad surface area. And technology adoption/diffusion favors the attacker. How does CrowdStrike think about ensuring defensive capabilities are broadly available?

This is one of the things we focused on. We created our own cyber superintelligence labs before the term was popular, I might say — I guess we nailed that one. Essentially we've created our own frontier-type lab totally focused on security models — both red and blue — and the harness.

We call the system Safe Mind. We've got Red Tempest and Blue Solano — those are the two models. We worked extensively with Nvidia on this. We leverage a few model types, but Nemotron is one of the main models we leverage on the blue side.

When I sat down with Jensen — we were working on this for the last 6 months — we went through how this would work. The big part of what we're doing is iterating red and blue. For our customers we have a view of what their environment looks like, and — this was Jensen insisting — "you have to have a digital twin. If you look at other industries, they have digital twins. You have to have one for security."

So we built a digital twin where we can take all the information we know about a customer's environment, recreate that in a virtual world, and iterate the models — looping them, where red continually is focused on getting in until it runs out of turns because Blue Solano has figured out what red was doing. That's really the way we have to keep up with the threats, because red is constantly iterating, and you're going to have to have this loop in place.

From EDR to AID: CrowdStrike's Platform Evolution

Knowing your environment is one of the only advantages you have as a defender. Can you zoom out and describe the key offerings and R&D investments CrowdStrike is making today? I think the root of "endpoint protection" might be an outdated view.

Over the last four or five years we've really moved into much broader platform capabilities. We've got 33 modules today. When I started the company we had one module.

We build capabilities across endpoint, cloud, IT, identity, and many different areas. At our latest user conference Falcon, it was around what we call AID. We pioneered EDR — endpoint detection response — which in the early days was a computer and a human. We've added many more things around that — prevention, etc.

But when you look at what an agent is doing — it's essentially a superhuman. It has an identity. It has access to compute. It runs on your computer or in a container. It has access to data. It has networking capabilities.

So we wanted to first find all this rogue and shadow AI — nobody knew where it was. And two, we can instrument from the birth of an agent what that agent does. If you're in Claude Code, you start an agent, it has sub-agents, tool calls, it goes to an MCP server, pulls data — whatever it's doing — we can actually tell you the entire chain of events. That's incredibly important, and we can add policy and blocking rules around those.

From a business perspective, on average today — which I actually think is low — they say you can have 90 different agents per employee. That can be a much bigger opportunity than just EDR for us.

Why Not Just Use Frontier Labs?

A reasonable question for any model-training effort — why isn't that just a frontier capability? These labs have programs for vetted defenders like Daybreak or Mythos access. Why is that insufficient?

First, what the labs are creating is incredible — unbelievable. We also want to make that available to our customers. If you have Safe Mind and want to leverage a frontier model — great, we can leverage that. If you want to leverage our models — fantastic, our models will be significantly cheaper.

For general remediation, if you use the highest-caliber frontier cyber model, it probably costs you about $10. Ours is like 3 cents. There is a huge cost difference.

When you look at our model, because of the way we've post-trained it on our data — a huge difference is we have the data. There is no Reddit of CrowdStrike security data. You can create synthetic data, but it's really not the same as what we have. We've got over a decade of security data, including from our MDR (managed detection response) service — all the threat and vulnerability pairings, attack chains. We've created this massive amount of data to train on. We're getting great results.

Number two: there's a safety and trust aspect. We've been entrusted with customers' data for the last 15 years. We know how to protect it. Customers don't want all this data going out to the labs. They don't want their sensitive information being trained on. We can provide a way to get them the trust and security they want for their security program. This concept of AI sovereignty is very important to many of our customers. We're not saying exclude the labs — but you can pick, or route between various models. We want to give customers choice.

You've also talked a little bit about separation of church and state — a neutral third party that can interrogate some of the models the labs are providing.

The number one factor in security is being a trusted partner. Trust is built in drips and lost in buckets. Customers don't want cowboy activities that may put their data at risk. Our whole focus — and focus is incredibly important in any business — is security and keeping our customers safe. We're not trying to solve the world's problems in AI and other areas.

Two Years Out: Local Models, Open Weights, and Formula 1

If you were to think out two years from now, what do you think is the state of the security world?

Certainly within two years you're going to have local models running on people's computers. You may have a mixture of local models plus last-mile routing into Frontiers. You're going to have a lot more open-weight models. You can see the shift in the tokens over the last 6 months.

What is the shift, and the order of magnitude?

I talk to CIOs almost every day. I had dinner with one tonight from a big bank in New York. The comment is: "We got into AI, we went all in — the costs were out of control. Token-maxing stopped when people got big bills."

I said, "What are you going to do?" They said, "The open-weight models right now are so good. Even if they're three months behind, it's plenty for what we need." One customer — and they know I'm into Formula 1 — said: "Any Formula 1 activity that we need for the bank will go to the frontier. If it's alpha, we're making money, and it's super important — we'll pay the money. No big deal. But for all the other things, it's really expensive, and we're going to create all of our own open-weight models and do more post-training on them."

I firmly believe that. I'm seeing it in customer after customer. Part of the challenges in the current environment: there is some concern at the frontier level about what's going to take place.

Distillation and the Genie Out of the Bottle

On the open-weight side — many of those are at least partially distilled from the labs. Now the labs are trying to roll out anti-distillation efforts. Is this just offense versus defense in cyber? What's your prediction?

My first comment is: what were the frontier models distilling when they got all that information? We know all of the lawsuits around where the data came from. So we kind of start from that.

It's like a fine liquor. It's triple distilled.

It's triple distilled. Exactly. Where does the distillation start from?

The labs certainly are focused on trying to prevent distillation. When you look at the Chinese models, there's a lot of distillation — there are factories of systems bouncing all over the internet distilling this.

The challenge is the genie's out of the bottle. A lot of distillation has already taken place. The models are very good. We also have to give credit where it's due — if you don't have all the chips and you have to be resourceful and still want to have top models, there are some innovative things taking place outside the US and we've got to be mindful of that.

It's going to be hard to put the genie back in the bottle on distillation. They'll do the best they can.

Will US Open-Weight Models Catch Up?

Do you think there are structural advantages for Chinese companies to stay at the frontier of open source and open weights, or are US open-weight models likely to catch up in the near term?

There are some open-weight models coming out. Having great US open-weight models is going to be very important. That's one of the reasons we worked with Nvidia — Nemotron is open-weight and open-source, not just open-weight. Having other alternatives is going to be very important.

Just being in technology long enough, you kind of look at how things unfold. The operating system of the internet is Linux. Period. There's a reason for that. And there's going to be an operating system of AI. In my mind, it's going to be an open-source, open-weight one. When that happens and how it unfolds — we'll see.

It doesn't mean there isn't room for any frontier model. It doesn't mean people are not going to make a bunch of money off it. The application stack around it, the harnesses, how things are connected, how you think about enterprise — all of those are going to be really important. But ultimately, there's just too much cost involved right now.

When you look at a lot of these frontier models, they're being commoditized. If the Chinese models are three months behind — a lot of companies go, "Three months is not — what am I going to get out of it? It does everything I want." That's the challenge.

A top-five financial recently told me that there was no chance their organization had the capability to absorb a new model release every 10 days anyway. So three months behind was faster than the acceptable regulated pace of their organization — it made no difference to them.

Open is here to stay as a big part of the puzzle.

Pushing Back on Doomerism: "An Agent Doesn't Beam Itself"

This is the first time in my career where some very smart, well-educated technologists are like, "We need to turn the internet off. Air gap everything, because it's going to fall apart in the next year and will be unsafe for critical systems to touch." How reasonable is that probability?

I think it's nonsense. Is security — and what agents can do, and the risk they pose — serious? Of course. We should all look at that and go, "Yeah, we got to make sure we lock things down." But is the world going to end because of these agents anytime soon? No.

When you look at what the agents are doing, I think there's this mythical view of what an agent does. An agent doesn't just beam itself from your computer to another computer. It actually just does the same thing a human would do — just better and faster. If you think about what companies like CrowdStrike have done for a long time — we prevent against these sorts of attacks. They might come faster. There might be more lower-level vulnerabilities chained together. Great for the adversary, not great for the defender. But it's building the technology that can deal with these attacks.

What has AI done? It's created more vulnerability — so you have more of them, and more exploitation coming faster. It's more and faster. But there isn't a unique class where all of a sudden an agent just beams itself somewhere. People just get wrapped around the axle of "there's some new class of technique." There isn't. It's just been trained on what we know. It hasn't developed its own yet.

That's why I look at it and say: security again is going to be an enabler for AI. Which is incredibly important for the security industry — because normally you're putting the brakes on. You have to take time. You're not letting the business run as fast as they want. Now everyone's coming to CrowdStrike and others going, "How do you make AI secure so we can go faster in AI?"

AI is here to stay. Some of the concern is there and should be there — but there's a lot of doomerism around some of this stuff, and I just don't think it's necessarily warranted.

Beyond Security: Other Areas Kurtz Is Excited About

Are there other areas you're very excited about right now?

Chips used to be kind of not in fashion. Obviously they are in fashion today, and you're only going to need more of them, faster, and more specialized. There will be some big breakthroughs in the chip world. Moore's law might be a bit dated, but at the end of the day, I can guarantee you chips are going to be faster and cheaper in the future. As specialized chips are developed that focus on particular areas, as new science is developed around the mathematics, there can be step-function increases in performance and less power.

Open-weight models: a lot of room to grow — certainly the US models. There's going to be a lot of advancements in taking these models and shrinking them down, being able to run them on your phone.

Remember the days when it took a football-field-sized room of computers to launch the first rocket? We have more power in our iPhone today than they had in the entire room. That's going to come. The area where you can make AI faster, cheaper, more efficient — and bring it to the desktop and the phone — doing it at the edge, these are exciting opportunities.

Just looking at TPUs, NPUs, etc. — they're all on systems we have today, and a lot of times they're going to waste. But I don't think they're going to be going to waste that much longer.

Can Defense Actually Dominate?

Security defenders tend to be pretty dour and pessimistic about the cat-and-mouse game getting any better in their favor. Can you make your best case for defense being dominant over the next decade?

I think it can be. The ability to always rapidly understand what the offense is doing and making sure your defense keeps up with it is going to be the key. It's the modern-day version of the Hacking Exposed book I co-authored many years ago — if you show people how the offense works, the defense is going to be a lot better. Now, that was a much slower tempo than today.

As an industry — and I really drill this home with our team at CrowdStrike — you've got to give as good or better capabilities to the defender than what the offense has. If you're just slightly better, mathematically you're still going to have an advantage. It's always going to be a cat-and-mouse game, but being really smart about it is going to be important.

The only way to fight AI today is with better AI. You've got to use the advantages you have. The defender knows their own systems. The defender has the architectural diagrams. The defender has the code. How do you put all of that into something that dramatically increases your probability of outsmarting the offensive AI?

Could Agent-Written Code Be More Secure?

I think the industry is at a point now where the code is probably good enough that you're going to get some benefits — but the code was also trained on stuff that may have had issues. I have my own developer license. I build my own apps and things like Claude. I have my own security agent that reviews the code — and it's like, well, Claude just created the code, but Claude with its security app is now going, "That code is insecure." Well, you just created it. Why did you just do that in the first place? Maybe there's some optimization.

What people don't necessarily realize is that even with zero vulnerabilities, you're still going to have breaches. A lot of what we see today is people are not necessarily breaking in — they're logging in. There's such an issue around identity.

If we can get better code, have fewer vulnerabilities, ripple that through — that'll be great. The challenge is it's such a long tail. Take Microsoft — because of all the backward compatibility they want to maintain, there are things that never get fixed or modernized. That's just one important element in our ecosystem. Think about all the other software out there. You're not going to fix it all overnight.

Running a Big Public Company in the AI Era

You've been running CrowdStrike for 15 years, and before that you were an entrepreneur. Many CEOs of large established public companies are feeling a little unmoored because so much of the value they've built in their incumbency is being challenged. How do you keep yourself up to date, keep the organization agile, continuing to win?

First, you have to recognize it's a different operating model and cadence. We've got thousands and thousands of people. Think about some of the AI-native companies that just started — they have a handful of people, Claude is running all day, they've got agents doing all kinds of stuff. That's the new world.

You can't be in a waterfall mentality of development, where things pop out a year later. You're going to be out of business. Having massive teams and long schedules — that's not going to cut it. You need smaller teams, squads, smaller groups focused on a problem, leveraging AI. You can't have thousands of people show up to solve a problem.

We've done that with our Falcon Guardian product. I was personally involved, had three-day-a-week meetings. I was involved in the design. "Here's what we're doing. Change this, change that." You've got to get back to your startup roots. There are many companies much bigger than we are, and you just can't be slow and plodding.

Then — what are your moats? If you're a system of record, that's a pretty big moat. We're a security system of record. We have everyone's data for many years. By the way, we're net data creators. Our sensors — we call them security agents, not to be confused with AI agents, but the endpoint agent software — that is a net data creator. We're creating 7 trillion or so events a day. If you're constantly creating this new data stream, that's going to give you an advantage — because what's the lifeblood of any AI system? The data you feed into it.

You never want to be in a position where somebody disrupts you. We disrupted the incumbents — the Symantecs, the McAfees — they're all gone for the most part, or changed or bought. So we're always asking: how do we disrupt ourselves? How do we do things differently?

At the end of the day, if we take care of the customer, the rest takes care of itself. Customers want to be protected. They want trust in their vendor. They want it to be super economical. Give them the best outcome at the best cost, in an experience that doesn't take seven consoles and six chairs to run around. The number one thing customers tell me: "It is so easy to deploy your stuff — it just works."

This morning, two companies merging — they're going to go with us. The other company didn't have us. It was, "Your stuff is so easy to deploy." Time to value is a big one.

Advice for the Next Generation: Study Security

A lot of people are talking about job losses due to AI, though that really hasn't happened — the opposite has, in terms of net job creation so far. There's a lot of questions: "What should my kids study? What will happen in the future for jobs?" What's your view?

Just in general — if you look at the technology changes over the last couple hundred years, each major shift has created more opportunity and more jobs. They're different, but there are more of them. I firmly believe that's going to be the case here.

Whether it's programming, you're still going to need people to manage the agents. You're still going to need people to think about architectures. It's not just fire-and-forget. I know a lot of people would like to say that, but there is human creativity you're going to need.

Specific to cybersecurity: this is one of the areas I always talk to young folks about — people at university. It's a great field to be in. If you understand AI and you understand security, it's an ever-changing field. It's actually not a solvable problem. I think every vendor would like to say they solve the problem. It's not solvable. You've got to mitigate risk, come up with the best solutions, protect customers.

It's always evolving. There's going to be technology in five years that we haven't even thought about today. If you're in university, you're going to be some of the people thinking about how to protect it. I always try to give back and think about what college kids are doing. I get asked all the time from parents — what should my kids study? I think cybersecurity, technology, and AI is a fantastic field.

It's a great note to end on. Thanks so much for doing this, George.

Thanks for joining us. Oh, you're quite welcome. Thank you so much.

Outro

Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen — that way, you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：护栏（guardrail）正在制造一场**不对称的裁军**
Kurtz 讲到 Hugging Face 那次事件时，有一个被所有人忽略的瞬间——防守方第一反应是跑去问 Frontier 模型"这是什么？"，然后被拒绝回答。他们被迫转向 open-weight 模型才完成分析。
这件事的真正含义不是"模型做坏事"，而是：**前沿实验室的 safety alignment 事实上把防御方单方面解除武装了**。攻击者本来就不受规则约束，他们本来就在用无护栏的 ablated 模型；而真正遵守条款的企业防御者，被挡在同一能力之外。
这是国际军控史上一个古老的教训被 AI 原样复刻：**单边禁用一种工具，受益最大的永远是那个本来就不会守规矩的玩家**。护栏的真正用户，是攻击者。
## 二、一个少有人注意到的拐点：安全行业正在从"工程学"滑向"诠释学"
"It's not malware anymore. It's prompts."——这句轻描淡写的话，其实是整个访谈最深的技术断言。
恶意软件时代，防御方分析的是**可被反编译的二进制对象**——它是一个静态
