item.title: [a16z Deep Dives] Why Frontier Models Still Can’t Parse a PDF
item.dc:creator: a16z Deep Dives
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、PDF 是人类认知的"化石"，而非数据格式

真正反直觉的事实是：PDF 根本就不是为了"读取"而设计的。Adit 顺口提到的"1990 年代人们在写打印驱动"是整个访谈最被忽视的一句话——PDF 的原始使命是把屏幕上的东西冻结成能忠实打印的像素，它本质上是一种"单向压缩"的介质，就像把源代码编译成二进制后再想反推源代码。

于是真正发生的事情是：整个白领世界用一个只写介质在传递知识，而我们如今要训练模型做"反向工程"。这解释了一个表面悖论——为什么前沿模型能写代码、能证明数学，却在一张扫描的 W2 面前摔跤。它不是智力不够，而是在要求 LLM 去猜一位二十年前写文档的人心里的结构假设（两栏？合并单元格？表格跨页？）。文档解析本质上是一个"心智理论"任务，不是感知任务。这也是为什么专门做这件事的公司反而比超大模型更难被取代。

二、"Agent 比人类更准"是一次悄悄发生的哥白尼时刻

Adit 轻描淡写地提到一个会让整个 ML 社区坐立不安的事实："Agent 在结构化抽取上比人类更准，而我们之所以不知道，是因为 ground truth 本身就是人标的。"

这句话的含义比它听起来大得多——它意味着我们过去十年用来评估 AI 的"黄金标准"系统性地带有人类的疲劳偏差、注意力漂移、以及"写到第 40 行就偷懒"的行为痕迹。换句话说：很多模型在很多任务上，可能两年前就已经超过人类了，只是因为评测它们的尺子本身是歪的，我们一直在用一把弯曲的秤给一个不断变强的物体称重。

跨领域连接：这与心理学中的"复制危机"惊人同构。心理学的 p-hacking 问题，和 AI 领域"benchmark 变成营销"（Adit 原话："they tilt it one degree, add Gaussian blur, 发布者的分数就崩了"）是同一种病——衡量工具被衡量对象俘获。这不是 AI 独有的问题，而是任何"用人造标准衡量超人类产物"的学科迟早都要撞上的墙。

三、专业基础设施随着通用智能变强而更值钱，不是更不值钱

最反主流叙事的洞察：很多人以为 GPT-5、Claude Opus 这类通用模型会"吞掉"所有垂直工具。Reducto 的存在证明了反面——通用智能越强，边角问题的赔率越高。

原因很优雅：当 LLM 从"80% 准确"进化到"99% 准确"，它解锁的不是"少了 19% 的错误"，而是完全不同的使用场景类别。97% 准确率可以做搜索建议；99.9% 才能做医保理赔自动化。而每多一个 9，背后要抚平的长尾问题类型会指数级增加（嵌套 PDF、横跨两页的表、医生潦草字迹、Excel 多 sheet 聚类……）。这就是为什么大模型实验室没动力做这件事：他们要的是"向上的斜率"，而 Reducto 要的是"右侧的尾巴"。

跨领域的类比：这和半导体行业的 ASML 现象完全一致——越是先进制程、越是通用计算需求爆炸，专门做光刻机的 ASML 反而越不可替代。软件堆栈里也会出现同样的分化：越是"模型 = 新 CPU"，越会出现专门做"读取 / 格式转换 / 对齐"的"新编译器"公司。

四、一个让人脊背发凉的数字：80% 的医保上诉被推翻

这不是关于 AI 的事实，这是关于人类官僚系统本身效率的事实。它暗示：当前的"人在环中"并不是"人类守护质量"，很多时候是"人类制造错误、再由另一群人类纠正错误"的循环。AI 不是在替代判断，它是在揭露原本就不存在的判断。

这给了"自动化焦虑"一个全新的框架：很多岗位之所以存在，不是因为它们产生价值，而是因为它们在修复前一个岗位应该做却没做的事。真正被 AI 替代的，不是"工作"，而是"错误级联"本身。

📝 转录文本

开场：从 Memory 到 Documents 的转向

The day we got into YC, we told that we were going to pivot. Nobody thinks about complexity when they upload a document to ChatGPT — you just expect it to work. On the other hand, the tools that you had to solve them were much, much more powerful.

Documents to us are almost these abstractions and artifacts of human work. It's the first time where I find that agents can be better at structured extraction than humans on many tasks. The best version of Reducto is one where you can kind of abstract away the PDF processing problems, even if the PDFs contain these sub-intricacies along the way.

Q: Given the big model labs are also focused on knowledge work, why do you think this is not a problem that they will solve — where it requires an independent company like Reducto to really focus on it?

A: One of the things that's underappreciated is how deep the range of problems gets. Yes, the labs could maybe go into this deep dive of trying to build all these individual tools, but I personally believe that they're on an arms race for [superintelligence].

公司起源：为什么从 Memory 转向 Documents

Adit, welcome to our podcast studio. It's so great to have you here.

Thanks for having me.

I would love to start the conversation by asking: when you and Ronic first started working on Reducto, I think you were working on some memory-related problems. What turned the attention to documents, and why is it still not a solved problem?

So we started in 2023 when models had horrible context windows, and so memory was this top-of-mind thing that you could feel. I remember the day we got into YC, we told Diana that we were going to pivot — which she was surprisingly accommodating about.

The framing retroactively that we have — that honestly I think wasn't actually as lucid back then — is: when you think about it, agents are going to do all sorts of human work. And it happens to be the case that documents to us are almost these abstractions and artifacts of human work. So much white-collar work across healthcare, legal, finance, and insurance is in things like PDFs and spreadsheets. You read from them, you write to them, and they catalog that knowledge.

So if you're going to have agents doing work in healthcare — reading things like patient records — it's really important that you have the same fidelity that you did when a human was looking at it. It's not an "oops" to say, "Oh, I messed up a checkbox." It's: "Oh, that's a patient's outcome."

That's where we got really excited thinking of it as: you're going to process more documents than ever before in history. How do you build this sort of interface that connects synthetic intelligence and human knowledge? That's been a really deep spiral.

The honest answer of how we actually got here is some amounts of right place, right time. Vertical AI apps were first spinning up, our background was in computer vision, and we started talking to a lot of these early AI-native companies — and surprisingly kept finding this recurring trend of people struggling with their document processing infra. Because our background was in CV research, we wanted to look at it from this broader problem of: how would you read it the way that a human would have? And it's spiraled from there.

从传统 OCR 到 VLM：技术代际的更替

I guess maybe break it down a little bit. There has been OCR technology from, I think, 20 years ago.

A while.

Yeah. And Reducto is built on top of visual language models. Maybe do a quick teaser of the difference — where do you see the traditional technology as not good enough, and where are the large models and frontier VLMs really driving to solve these messy problems, and where are they still lacking?

I always joke that I've literally met people that have worked on PDF processing longer than I've been alive. There were people in the 1990s working on drivers to print PDFs — which was the original purpose of the format: how do you faithfully represent all of the characters on the page?

You can break this down into a few epochs. First it was a file processing problem, then you started having these OCR-based IDP companies. Typically what you would have done is: you have something like a W-2, you template out what a W-2 looks like, you have a pixel-level understanding of "the name appears here," and you post-process that text. That's fine for a lot of consistent pipelines.

But the thing that changed in 2023 is: nobody thinks about complexity when they upload a document to ChatGPT. You just expect it to work. And on the other hand, the tools you had to solve them were much, much more powerful. VLMs have this notion of reasoning on the content that historically you wouldn't have had. Those two things kind of came together right around when we were founded.

Ultimately these documents are just images. You have this 9 × 11 grid, and you could have constructed information any which way. It's not just characters on the page — it's: when you have two columns, understanding that you're reading the first column and the second column; when you have a table, it's two dimensions of data but you want to preserve the rows, the columns, the merged cells, and everything in between.

When we first started, we looked at it from a two-part problem: how do you use traditional computer vision to preserve structure, and how to use VLMs as a correction loop — because there were clear accuracy, cost, and latency trade-offs. We care a lot about not just accuracy but determinism and traceability. Our customers need to know where we got an answer from, and traditional CV was really good at that.

But over time, as people have pushed more on multimodality, we've been doing a lot of interesting work on how to build the best VLMs for this type of task. That's where R1 came in: now we have one unified model that does that end-to-end without the trade-offs that historically you would have had. You still have bounding boxes, still very consistent, but it captures everything on the page.

R1：自研基础模型的突破

Since you mentioned R1 — let's talk about that one. You started from using off-the-shelf models but decided to post-train your own foundation model. R1 is reported with better accuracy, higher speed, and lower cost. Maybe talk a bit more about how you achieved the Pareto frontier, and what you think it's going to unlock.

There's a lot to the work that we do. We are fortunate to have some of the best researchers for our domain on the team, and so this isn't like a one-quarter breakthrough. I see it as a culmination of work since the start of the company.

For a while we spent a lot of time catching errors in production — creating feedback loops of "hey, we messed up this table, how do we create a better tabular representation?" We've also been fortunate to work with some of the hardest distributions of data: the largest enterprises, the leading AI-native companies. They've helped us understand the corner cases of where different types of models fail.

So we put a ton of time into not just model architecture but also the data pipelines around it, how we eval the product, and having a really good RL loop around post-training and mid-training the model.

最混乱的数据长什么样

What are some of the messiest types of data and the hardest edge cases?

It depends on the tools you're using. One characteristic of VLMs, for example, is that repetition becomes really annoying. You'll have PDFs where people use periods to separate two different spaces — and when you have 100 periods in a row, VLMs start just repeatedly outputting periods.

But the range of what we see is actually much harder than these last-mile technicalities. In the real world, you'll have content that's — say, a table that spans across two pages, and maybe wasn't scanned perfectly, so the columns are kind of mismatched. You need to start thinking about structure and actively applying specialized pipelines to merge those two together and preserve that context.

When people are capturing things like blueprints and diagrams, these are really dense pages. You as a human need to zoom in to interpret it, so you need almost a patchwork-based approach to understand what was on the page. Those are the sorts of things we wanted to make sure we were incredible at.

准确率、延迟、成本：解锁自动化的三道门槛

Maybe talk about accuracy as well. For every magnitude of accuracy unlock, you actually unlock more use cases in the fully-automated range. A lot of traditional OCR is in the 70–80 range, not even close to 98 or 99. What are you shooting for?

This goes to the work we're doing beyond parsing. Parsing is this core building block of how you even understand what was on the page. For the vast majority of use cases, we can actually be in the high 90s today. There are corner cases — there's doctor's handwriting that I can't read, so I don't even know if we did a good job.

But if you think of an end-to-end task — you're taking in a loan packet — it's not just parsing. You're splitting the contents, extracting individual fields, maybe you're editing a loan application form at the end. Each one of those steps needs to be accurate. If you're taking in a dozen files, you can't have 90% on individual pages, because those mistakes compound.

A lot of the interesting work for us recently is not just on the model layer. We started releasing harnesses around the work we're doing. Deep Extract is a really good example: it's the first time where I find that agents can be better at structured extraction than humans on many tests. We find situations where human-annotated ground truth has a lot of errors that they wouldn't have otherwise known — because it's your ground truth, what is the comparison point?

Humans make all sorts of mistakes: people miss content, they might drop rows, maybe they get lazy and only fill in part of the information. But if you have a harness where the agent is not only extracting the information but correcting itself, reviewing its outputs, you kind of get to unbound that in the favor of perfect accuracy.

成本：一分钱一页之后的世界

So after accuracy and latency, let's talk about cost. Now we're down to a penny per page with very high-quality parsing and extraction. How do you think about what becomes possible?

For a while most AI products were these chatbots where you had a constrained set of sources. If you're going to have agents do work — humans are really good at understanding "hey, I'm missing information, let me go look for more." You ideally want your agents searching the web for your content, looking in your knowledge bases and retrieving more.

Ideally people are not thinking from the lens of "it cost me this much to parse a page, and therefore only these pages go to an accurate pipeline." Today — literally this morning — we crossed our 7 billionth page. At this point we process billions of pages every single month. The thing we want to get to is that every single page that needs to be read by a model is read through Reducto first, and that needs to be frictionless.

One cent per page is our list price, but we are doing a lot to understand: at higher volumes, if somebody wants to process tens of billions of pages, how do we make that work at scale?

Very cool. And congrats on passing 7 billion. I remember you tweeted about how long it took to get to 1 billion.

It just goes faster every time.

Want to have a prediction for when you reach 8 billion?

We said this would come out end of October. I think we'll be past 8 billion by then. We keep breaking our record for pages processed in a week.

增长背后的客户与工作负载

Maybe talk a little bit more about what's driving that growth.

I would categorize the early wave of use cases as different forms of information synthesis — chatbots are ultimately search tools for a lot of people. Early on we started working with a lot of the leading AI-native companies — the Harveys of the world, the Rogos, and so on.

But more and more we've started getting adopted by the largest hedge funds, the largest private equity firms, tech companies — where the use cases are all over the place. In some cases they're building tools where agents are reasoning over data; in some cases they're trying to do actual work. If you're a hedge fund, your pipelines for aggregating information are your competitive edge. If you can be faster and more robust in gathering all the signals that are available — that's alpha. Those are the sorts of things we're starting to see more and more.

Harness：从 Parsing 到端到端工作流

We'd love to talk about the harness you have.

We started seeing a lot of our customers use two or more endpoints together. If you're going to deploy in production, you need not just great parsing accuracy — you need tools for evaluation and review and constructing your individual workflow. We wanted to make all of that easier.

There are little things that are really hard when you think of the real world. If you've negotiated a contract before, you have multiple versions of a redline term sheet in your laptop somewhere, and it's hard for people to understand what is the latest version unless somebody labeled the file "final" or something like that. So you have duplicates of contents. You need to reconcile between disparate sets of information that contradict.

It builds on a lot of the work we've been doing: we put so much time into citing — not only "hey, this is the answer and these are the documents," but "here's the individual word for why we know X was the answer." If you know that on one document, and you know that on another, you can make it easier for agents to actually reason through and understand: "okay, here's how I should land on the truth by looking at both sorts of information and reconciling that."

Codegen 的类比与第二阶问题

I was talking to the team about it recently: if you look at the codegen market in 2023 — when tools were just code-completion tools — they were at a fraction of what they are today. I admire Cursor a lot as a company; I remember one of my friends came to dinner with a shaved head — they'd all shaved their heads for a million in ARR.

And now you look at the market and many of them are past a billion in ARR. But you don't really see that in the professional services markets yet. The question is: why? Is it that there isn't sufficient value? Clearly not — healthcare has so much work that is paper-heavy, in insurance and legal and finance.

I think a lot of it is: there are these second-order problems that are not just intelligence, and we want to help our customers solve those.

技术问题还是文化问题

How much do you think it's a technology problem versus a cultural / speed-of-adoption problem?

There's certainly some part of enthusiasm in tech — these are almost like toys for people in tech to play with. But there's also something to be said about consequences. If you vibe-code something and it's filled with bugs, you get to roll back your PR in a way that is not true if you're making decisions in healthcare. There are stakes there that are very, very real.

I don't think we can pin it on just willingness to adopt. There's a real question of: how do you have sufficient guard rails? How do you give the human confidence in the decisions they're making? That plays into everything we talked about with citations and grounding.

下一步：文档编辑与交互模态

Would love to touch on what's coming next, now that you own your own model and harness.

Number one, we've been doing a lot of work to unlock the full range of interaction modalities. One good example is document editing. I don't know if you've spent much time with Claude for Excel and the different plugins out there, but it's actually surprisingly hard for agents to work with the Office suite — which is weird, because that's where a lot of human work happens.

One good example I really like: localization is a really hard problem. People put a lot of time on it, but translation is really easy — models can take free-form text and translate them. We want to make it easier to apply those translations. If you have a document in English, how do we make it really easy to translate it to Arabic or another language?

So in the next few weeks you'll see us launch a lot on that front. We are starting with a plugin on ChatGPT where you'll be able to edit whatever you want. Think of it as a headless version of Microsoft Word that agents can use.

But it doesn't stop there. In general we want to make that tooling really resilient as you think about eval, monitoring, and observability. More broadly, we want to make it easier for our customers to start improving their pipelines with Reducto — that'll start with things like schema optimization as a first-order problem, but really we want to get to a point where people can apply their context effectively.

为什么大模型实验室不会吃掉这个市场

Given the big model labs are also focused on knowledge work and improving their models' multimodality and vision — why do you think this is not a problem they will solve?

A lot of the work we do is tangential to intelligence. We're not trying to compete with the labs on reasoning quality. One of the things that's underappreciated is how deep the range of problems gets. Even after probably looking at more PDFs than most humans, I still find corner cases that we didn't expect.

Within PDFs, you can have folders of PDFs that contain other PDFs. If you think of even rendering a Microsoft Word file, you'll find that there aren't good open-source tools to represent that faithfully — that's why libraries like LibreOffice often fall short.

Yes, the labs could maybe go into this deep dive of trying to build all these individual tools, but I personally believe they're on an arms race for creating superintelligence for the world. The work we're doing is more like infra around that — that helps make that more useful.

The other thing is: focus is really important. The fact that we can constrain the set of problems we need to be good at is a big part of why we're able to be ahead. We're not making generic models here. The vision encoder for a model powering ChatGPT needs to be able to take a selfie and turn it into a Studio Ghibli image. We know the domain of information we're working around. We need our models to be exceptional on this specific set of tasks.

For our customers, when you're processing at a scale where it's not just accuracy — you need cost and latency at scale — we are able to be orders of magnitude more aggressive on price than a frontier model at a comparable accuracy profile. That makes a huge difference. You can't throw Astra at all of your PDF parsing tasks, but we want Astra-level quality for the work we're doing.

Pipeline vs. One-Shot：为什么不能一次性丢给大模型

This is also where I find a lot of people's misunderstanding lies — that you can just do a one-shot of a model call to get information from a long document. But usually it's a pipeline.

There's actually a really interesting benchmark that Micro1 put out — it was independently run and we got to partner with them. It was focused on long extraction tasks. We tested all the frontier models at the time, Reducto, and some specialized document parsers. We found that frontier models were better than a lot of specialized document parsers at precision — given that they were extracting something, they were more likely to be correct. But the failure mode was actually recall for the frontier models: they would silently drop information. That's the kind of thing that's really hard to catch in production.

When we think about something like Deep Extract, there's a lot happening — it's not just a model focused on extraction. In fact, the harness is kind of agnostic to the model. We create a lot of tools for the model to review its own outputs, to create validation rules. If you have a massive invoice, how do you have a parent agent make sure the items summed up to the total? Those little details — such that it knows when to go back and double-check information. That's the only way we were able to get to near-perfect accuracy there. That applies across all sorts of stuff we do, like document splitting as well.

Benchmark 的真相：当评测变成营销

Maybe touching on the benchmark piece — a benchmark can look great, and we spent a lot of time benchmarking across real-world scenarios. The Micro1 one is representative. But sometimes it's still missing details to the customer themselves. What does a useful eval or benchmark look like when your customers are evaluating Reducto versus open-source or other frontier models?

The number one thing I think they should care about is distribution of data and understanding if it's representative for what they want to do. If you're dealing with really simple documents, odds are a simple pipeline is sufficient — you don't want to look at a generic benchmark for that.

Number two: there are a lot of places where things go wrong in how you decide what to measure. We made a post about this recently — it's generally a mistake to have really strict rules in your benchmarking, because you could represent the same information faithfully two different ways and you don't want to penalize that.

One of the unfortunate things about the AI industry — and I'm not trying to absolve Reducto of this, it's just a general thing — benchmarks have become marketing over time. The downstream side effect is: it's really hard to know what is good in your context when everything is state-of-the-art all the time.

We find sometimes egregious versions of this. I'm not going to name names, but there's a public benchmark we tested where if you take the same documents and add a little bit of noise — tilt it one degree, add a little Gaussian blur — the provider that published the benchmark gets way, way worse than everyone else, but everyone else is kind of consistent. You can draw conclusions from that.

Our recommendation is actually: LLM-as-a-judge is quite strong today, if you're thoughtful about how you think about a rubric. We want to see the industry move closer to people testing on their own data, with tools maybe to make that evaluation easier — but instead of trusting a generic benchmark, you really should be at a point where you know what works best for you.

客户的 "golden data set" 真的 golden 吗

How often do you walk into a customer and they already have a golden data set that they're ready to evaluate?

It's often the case that people have some sort of golden data set, but depending on how they made it, there are all sorts of issues. We find situations where it was human-generated and so the human dropped information. Sometimes it's LLM-generated, but for cost reasons maybe they used Sonnet instead of Opus and Sonnet made some mistakes.

It's increasingly common for people to have at least some form of an eval, but it's really hard to make sure the eval holds. So we try to partner with teams a lot to make sure they feel good about how they're going to test before they even get into any sort of head-to-head comparison.

超越 PDF：Excel、多模态与"文档"的边界扩张

Are you still today seeing the majority of documents being PDFs, or are other formats starting to trickle in?

It's actually kind of all over the place. We support over 40 file types. PDFs are a good flagship, but for us at the end of the day a lot of this is image processing.

You can imagine Excel files can be arbitrarily large — you don't know if it's going to be one massive sheet or multiple spreadsheets with clusters all across. Models, even if they support a large enough context window, actually struggle with that sort of information. So there's a lot you can do in creating a representation of the Excel file that's meant for models to consume, as opposed to just giving the raw file directly.

What does it mean for you when there's more multimodal content — PDFs today can embed multimedia?

I think there's a sort of layers unfolding as you look at complexity. First-order problem: how do you know if a document is complex or not? Second-order problem: how do you know if a given page is hard? But within pages, you have regions that are harder than others.

In finance, one of the most common forms of representing data is time-series data — charts, line graphs, bar graphs. That's really hard. A human is really good at discerning where the trend line is going, but if you ask models, you find they're actually kind of fickle. Being able to understand "okay, this is a line chart" and to not just characterize that revenue went up, but to characterize the individual data points such that you can reason on them — that's a whole sub-domain of problems where we trained a dedicated chart agent. I feel really good about saying Reducto is state-of-the-art there.

We should pull up the benchmark on that one, because it's actually hilarious how bad other models are. When you look at it visually, it's shocking how big the gap can be.

But being able to do that in a way the customer ideally doesn't have to think about it is our goal. The best version of Reducto is one where you can abstract away the PDF processing problems, even if the PDFs contain these sub-intricacies.

And there are nested tables too. In Excel there are multiple tabs. The more we dive into this set of issues, the more I feel like it's an unbounded set of problems.

三年后的 Reducto：从 IDP 到 Agent 基础设施

With that, how do you think about the horizon of the next few years? What does Reducto become?

This goes back to what we were talking about in the beginning. There's so much incredible work happening both with the AI-natives and the enterprises — if you look at what a company like Harvey is doing for legal, but also what people are doing in-house.

I really want Reducto to be this reliable set of tools that both Harveys and the largest enterprises in the world can use to apply their context with models. That means we need to be the best in the world at parsing, but it also means all the little details that they would otherwise have to handle — the infrastructure problems of suddenly needing to process 10 million documents in parallel. Those abstractions matter a lot for our customers.

I generally don't think of the intelligent document processing (IDP) market as our category, because the ambition that exists in IDP is very much not what we are hoping to do. We want to be at a place where agents can help augment human work. I don't have a market-map vision of what that means in the future, but playing a key role in that is a really important thing for the world.

As we always say, there are two important inputs into the models: one is data — which Reducto is turning PDFs and documents into — and the other is just compute. So there's infinite opportunity to create value for language models to behave and perform. Definitely believe there's tremendous opportunity to keep raising that bar.

And that's why we get to work together.

高风险领域的真实后果：Healthcare 的故事

Let's talk more about the consequences of accuracy and how that impacts your customers trusting agents and AI to process documents.

We have this customer that works in healthcare — a really large provider of what's effectively a search tool for doctors to capture information. They work with some of the harder situations in healthcare, to the point where these are physical documents. They will have packets that are inches in height.

It's hard to appreciate how much an error actually matters to the individual. We were talking about individual cases where, because the initial pipeline read something as "chest pain" instead of "chest pain," somebody's claim gets rejected — because the doctor searches "do they have a history of this," and if they don't, maybe they don't need the drug.

That matters, right? Because the doctors are also very overworked in a lot of these health systems — they can't double-check all the information and make sure the OCR was accurate. They're just trusting that the tools they're using are reliable. That's just with the search products. Imagine if an agent was making that sort of adjudication decision. It is so important that you know the inputs you're dealing with are things you can trust, because it builds on everything else.

That's incredible that they're not measuring by pages but by inches of how tall the document is. What's the rough accuracy of the current status of these OCR tools?

In those situations, we actually find cases where it's sub-50%. The best you can do is have some approximation of where information sits, and then a human has to look at it. A given patient's packet could be tens of thousands of pages — so even if you show the best examples, a doctor can't really dig into it. Those are frontier problems that I hope we can solve for the world.

And what is the fallback today if humans miss the "chest pain"?

People make mistakes all the time. There are millions of Medicare claims rejected every single year for prior auth. One of the craziest stats I learned is that in 80% of appeals, the original decision was overturned. Which should be shocking — because clearly there's some inefficiency in how the decision was originated.

80% of appeals?

I found that to be unbelievable, but it extends not just in healthcare. If you look at the backlog that currently exists for USCIS for immigration — so many of these are just paper processes bottlenecked by needing high enough accuracy that warrants a human today. If you had an infinite aperture for accuracy, cost, and latency such that you could just apply frontier models on these tasks, you can make a lot of these processes easier for humans throughout the world.

Having seen some of the filings for immigration — definitely a lot of handwritten notes, images, photos as evidence. I'm sure there's still a ton of efficiency and human-in-the-loop work that can be automated today, but not yet.

最该先消失的工作：数据录入

If AI can really reliably understand, evaluate, and change the documents businesses work with, what should be possible today but hasn't happened yet, as the first few categories of work?

You'd be surprised at how much of data entry is still manual. That's probably the first thing I'm excited about. Humans have a lot to add as you think about reasoning and decision-making. But there are a lot of people in the world who take physical documents and write out what was in the physical documents. It's really, really inefficient.

In America, 16% of tax filers still file via paper mail. All these things that add weeks of work in a way that is kind of rote and routine — those are probably the first set of problems I'm hoping just goes away.

Who are the application-layer companies working on this?

It really depends on the industry. In accounting, we're seeing Basis do incredible work. But this also applies to large enterprises. We work with one of the largest accounting services companies where they do customs and border patrol forms. There's a BPO company that does the back-office work for a lot of these larger companies as well. All of them are excited to move past this category of problems.

Very cool. Can't wait for more of these mundane, soul-sucking human-in-the-loop tasks to go away so we can focus on more exciting things.

Yeah.

Awesome. It's so great to have you, Adit. Thank you so much for coming by today.

Thanks again. This was fun.

item.description:
## 一、PDF 是人类认知的"化石"，而非数据格式
真正反直觉的事实是：PDF 根本就不是为了"读取"而设计的。Adit 顺口提到的"1990 年代人们在写打印驱动"是整个访谈最被忽视的一句话——PDF 的原始使命是**把屏幕上的东西冻结成能忠实打印的像素**，它本质上是一种"单向压缩"的介质，就像把源代码编译成二进制后再想反推源代码。
于是真正发生的事情是：整个白领世界用一个**只写介质**在传递知识，而我们如今要训练模型做"反向工程"。这解释了一个表面悖论——为什么前沿模型能写代码、能证明数学，却在一张扫描的 W2 面前摔跤。它不是智力不够，而是在要求 LLM 去**猜一位二十年前写文档的人心里的结构假设**（两栏？合并单元格？表格跨页？）。文档解析本质上是一个"心智理论"任务，不是感知任务。这也是为什么专门做这件事的公司反而比超大模型更难被取代。
## 二、"Agent 比人类更准"是一次悄悄发生的哥白尼时刻
Adit 轻描淡写地提到一个会让整个 ML 社区坐立不安的事实："Agent 在结构化抽取上比人类更准，而我们之所以不知道，是因为 ground truth 本身

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Do Anthropic and OpenAI Have a Moat? Nick van Eck Says No
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Character.ai 花 16 美元换 1 美元收入——这不是"烧钱换增长"，这是代币庞氏

Chris 顺带一提的那个数字其实是整段讨论里最锋利的一刀，但三位主持人都没有真正剖开它。传统意义上"烧钱换规模"的逻辑是：现在亏钱，未来凭借网络效应/数据飞轮/切换成本获利。但 AI 应用公司的 16:1 支出结构背后没有这三样东西中的任何一样。

那它换的到底是什么？——是"token 消耗量"这个指标本身的叙事价值。风投轮次定价时看的是"每月被烧掉多少 token"，而前沿实验室定价时看的是"有多少应用在消耗我的 token"。于是出现了一个闭环：A 公司烧钱向 B 公司买 token，B 公司拿着"收入增长"去融下一轮，A 公司再拿着"token 消耗量"去融下一轮，两边同时在给对方的 PPT 作背书。

这在金融史上有个名字：相互交易膨胀（round-tripping），90 年代末 Enron 和能源交易所做的事。只不过这一轮用的不是电力合约，是浮点运算。

二、"productive bubble" 这个比喻可能是错的——因为资本寿命差了 20 倍

Chris 和 Austin 把当下 AI 泡沫类比到铁路、电力、互联网，并说"detritus 会抬升人类文明"。听起来很浪漫，但这里有一个被整段讨论完全忽略的技术性事实：

泡沫 核心资本资产 使用寿命
铁路（1870s） 铁轨路基 80–150 年
电气化（1900s） 变压器、输电网 40–60 年
光纤（1999） 暗光纤 25+ 年（直到今天还在用）
AI（2024-） GPU + HBM 3–5 年

铁路泡沫炸死了股东，但留下的轨道一百年后还在跑货运。而一台 H100 在 2029 年只是电费账单。真正合适的历史类比不是铁路，是 19 世纪的捕鲸业：大量资本涌入短寿命的猎捕设备和专用船只，等更便宜的替代能源（煤油）出现，整个产业链在 15 年内归零。CoreWeave 的会计处理方式——把 GPU 当作 6 年折旧的资产——是整个赛道财务模型里最危险的一个假设。

三、市场的分裂不是随机的，它严格按照"用户记忆的所有权"排序

Nick 说 Google、Meta 有现金流所以能撑；Austin 说这是 regime change。但更深层的信号是：这一轮抛售没有均匀打击所有 AI 相关标的，而是精确地绕过了持有用户长期行为数据的公司。

因为前沿模型的能力正在被开源快速追上（这一点他们提到了），但有一样东西开源永远追不上："关于某个具体用户、某个具体关系、某个具体历史"的记忆。Google 搜 20 年、Meta 社交图谱 15 年、Apple 的设备级个人数据——这些才是真正的无法复制资产。

跨领域连接：这其实是生物学里"宿主-共生体"的关系。 前沿模型（Anthropic/OpenAI）是能力极强但没有宿主的游离细胞；Google/Meta 是有宿主的细胞器。进化史告诉我们，游离细胞要么找到宿主（被收购/深度捆绑），要么被淘汰——线粒体曾经是一个独立物种，它存活下来的方式是放弃独立。OpenAI 和 Microsoft 的关系已经在往"线粒体化"演进了，Anthropic 和 Amazon/Google 也是。独立前沿实验室这个物种可能根本不存在稳定生态位。

四、一个被所有人跳过的隐藏主语：他们的真正对手不是彼此，是自己的未来版本

Chris 的 Ford Model T 比喻方向对了但没走到底。他说"大多数人不需要 Roadster"——但真正的含义是：今天的 GPT-5 是在和明天的开源 GPT-4.5 竞争，而不是在和 Claude 竞争。前沿实验室每迭代一次，就是在为自己 6 个月后的开源影子版本挖一次坟。

这是人类商业史上第一次出现这种结构：一个行业的主要竞争者是自己过去的产品。最接近的类比是制药行业的专利悬崖——但药企至少有 20 年专利保护；前沿实验室的"专利"只有大约 9 到 18 个月，而且没有法律强制执行。

所以 Nick 说"他们没有护城河"是对的，但原因不是"竞争太激烈"，而是时间本身就是他们的对手。这是一个和热力学第二定律同构的问题：你要维持能力领先，必须持续注入能量；一旦停止，熵（即开源扩散）必然追上。从这个角度，前沿实验室不是公司，是一台正在对抗熵增的发动机——而发动机不是生意，是成本中心。

五、顺手给一个几乎无人提到的下行路径

讨论里反复出现"第一家 AI 公司破产会很震撼"。但基于前四点，更可能先发生的不是破产，而是体面地被稀释进巨头资产负债表——以"战略合作深化"的名义，股权被不断稀释到 51%、65%、89%，直到某个季报的脚注里出现"全资合并"。到那时候，没有 CNBC 的头条，只有一行 10-K 披露。

这才是 AI 泡沫最像 2000 年互联网泡沫的地方——不是 pets.com 的倒闭，是 AOL-Time Warner 式的"赢家式死亡"。

📝 转录文本

一、AI 交易的分化：市场不再"同一个大脑"

The thing we've started seeing unwinding, at least in part — in fairness, unwinding here is relative, 'cuz it's been hot as hell — is the AI trade.

Um, so part of why I'm looking at this disparity, call it, is the market is no longer thinking with one mind. To the point on correlation earlier, you get moments of correlation one, where either everything goes up or everything goes down. But the interesting state changes are when sort of those factors start to break apart.

And here it appears to me the chain of events — and you guys disagree with me if you think otherwise — was: people started to see some of Anthropic's results. They maybe didn't have the revenue growth that was totally expected there. That led people to start to think about some of the economics and the promises of the core frontier sort of like thesis, which itself led to a sell-off in the stuff most leveraged to that. Take CoreWeave as example, or some of the Cospi and the memory producers. But it didn't seem to me to affect like Google or Meta very much, which have very different expressions here.

So just like with crypto, with the stablecoin / Bitcoin / institutional / degen — are we seeing now market fragmentation there as well? And the reason I ask this is: as we think about macro themes, when you see factors start to break down or break apart, that's when you start to head towards regime changes.

二、"前沿实验室没有护城河"

Of course. I think, right, with all the others, they have massive cash flow businesses. And that's the concern, right, with an Anthropic and an OpenAI — is they have absolutely no moat. They're in the red by tens of billions of dollars a year, and they're not financially viable businesses.

And their last equity valuations were at insane prices, insane multiples, with the peak of peak expectations. And I think SF and like Silicon Valley was drinking a little bit too much of their own Kool-Aid. And we'll see what happens.

三、债务资本市场的关门信号 + 50GW 的算术题

Yeah, I mean just to underscore what Nick's saying. I think part of it is what you were describing, Austin. Part of it is just like people realizing that the debt capital markets are going to get shut off to these companies at some point. There's already a few junk-rated.

And then for me, I think the big realization was — so I forget which bank, one of the big banks put out a report saying they're expecting 50 gigawatts to go online 2027. So if you believe Jensen's number, it's 50 billion dollars a gigawatt. Let's say you cut his number in half 'cuz he's motivated to inflate the value, right? So let's say it's half of what Jensen says. That number represents in 2027 96% or so of all tech investment that we have on annual per year. What we use about 1.6 trillion.

So just, I think people just realize this is not possible. It's the same as when I would argue with people like 5–6 years ago about, you know, Bitcoin's going to keep going up at 10,000% per year. I'm like, but it can't, 'cuz it'll be bigger than the global economy. Like, that's not how compounding works, right?

So I think people just are — to Nick's point — they're just saying: I don't want to be the last person on this train. And look, I'm up 100%, 200% — even if I give up another 50 or 75% run, I won't care, 'cuz I've done so well. And that's very rational.

四、历史尺度的 CAPEX 对比

I think you guys saw the stats — the CAPEX that's gone into AI exceeds that of railroads. Exceeds that of other, you know, major industrial events in our history: electrification, telecoms, highways. By far.

So the question is: when does it end?

五、补贴消费被揭穿 + 碎片化的真正原因

And there's, you know, one other thing I'd point out: there's been levels to the incentive spend, like masking some of this, right? Because you had so many companies that were funded based on consuming these tokens.

I — there was a — that went to funk the week or two ago, I think it was Character or something. And they were spending $16 for every dollar of revenue. Like, that's insane.

And so this will start to unravel really quickly. And open source and open weight models are great for consumers and businesses, and really bad for the financial profile of these companies.

And it's also why you're starting to see fragmentation, right? Because players like Nvidia are going to benefit regardless. Players like Google and others who have other cash cow lines of business that can continue to finance things, albeit at a lesser rate, will continue to survive and have an edge over the medium and long term over some of the frontier model app companies.

六、"好得已经够用了"——Model T 的 AI 版本

Some of that is also, like, to wrap in the earlier point, a statement on the core economics specifically of the frontier labs. That is to say: if you're spending money constantly to remain at the front, you can never have a durable moat. You just incinerate money endlessly.

And part of what's interesting to me is a lot of these models have now gotten what I'm going to call "good enough" for a lot of consumer-level deployments. Like Muse is a great example of that — Muse Spark 1.3, which is the model underneath Muse, like the app that everybody is downloading. It's not the most powerful model on the market, but it's more than good enough for what most people are using it for. That was not true 2 years ago.

Right? It's the thing of like: okay, the Ford Model T may not be a sustainable car for everybody, but the Tesla Model Y might be, and not everybody needs a Roadster at that point. And so I think that has a lot of economic implications for the frontier labs.

七、竞争性任务 vs 非竞争性任务

Yeah, look — I mean, I think you're right. There's going to be, I mean, there's frontier lab models for — I'll just lump everything into competitive versus non-competitive tasks, right?

So for competitive tasks: if I'm using AI to trade, for example, I have no choice. Just like the top hedge funds have to keep paying for cutting-edge research, where a small-medium-sized hedge fund is not paying for satellite technology, for example, right? So there'll be competitive applications that will force a niche of the market to keep paying for that slightly more nanosecond-faster or smarter model.

And then everyone else is going to be like: I can create a tutor for my kids perfectly fine with this model. I can run my home. I can do basic research. And they're just going to be completely unwilling to pay for that incremental unit of value.

八、把 AI 当成资产负债表来看

If AI were to be a balance sheet, on the liability side, you've got real liabilities when it comes to litigation and agents doing bad things. That's going to add up. You've got unit economics that really are questionable at this point. You've got regulatory risk heading into midterms. And then you have a couple of balance sheets across the stack that have really been overextended.

But on the asset side — I mean, this is insane technology. It's breaking — it's essentially recreating mathematics as we know it overnight. Like, if you're a career academic and you're a mathematician, your goals just shifted. And it's going through every single discipline, totally changing it. And it's going to propel us into something that's going to be very, very exciting and interesting.

It's touching all of our lives. Like, you know, how fast was it from when we went from Googling things to going into chat — or, you know, Rob doesn't go to ChatGPT, but I do sometimes. But it's changed our behaviors overnight. It's changed our children. It's civilization-defining technology. So, and that's what the crash —

九、认知失调：游戏规则改变者也可能被定价过高

When the mean reversion happens, I think more aggressively, the cognitive dissonance we're all going to have about that — 'cuz I agree with you, right? I — how can something that is so game-changing start to unravel? And when we have the first major bankruptcy of one of these AI companies, I think it's going to be really hard to fathom how that could be the case.

But I think it goes back to what Nick said: that even something as universally game-changing — anything can be overpriced, Chris. You know that.

十、互联网泡沫的教训：三个被混为一谈的独立问题

Of course. It's also the pattern, to be fair, of the first tech bubble, right? Everybody was right that the internet was a transformative technology. That is 100% correct. If you look at the arc of the world from 1970 until today, the internet's probably the single biggest thing.

But on the other hand, that didn't prevent a bunch of companies from going bust and a bunch of ideas from being bad and a bunch of things from being overvalued, right? Being long-term correct doesn't mean that pets.com was right place, right time.

And so, you know, I also think there's this disambiguation of: Is AI valuable? Are specifically the frontier labs we have right now valuable? And then, are they valuable in the right amounts at the right time? Those are three different questions, and people kind of treat them like they're a single thing when in reality those are discrete statements, right?

Like, airlines are obviously a valuable overall invention. That has not stopped a ton of them from going bankrupt.

That's right.

And there's been companies from the bubble that when you were 97, 98% off their peak, that then did eventually reclaim that peak — but it took 15 years, right? And so I think that's what you're seeing with some of the businesses today.

十一、"有生产力的泡沫" vs "惰性泡沫"

Yeah, I discern between productive and inert bubbles. And there's no question they are in a bubble, but it's a massively productive bubble. The detritus is going to elevate humanity and elevate business to an entirely new level.

And it's not a bad — I don't view bubbles as bad, quite frankly. I think we're not a very logical species. Like, we don't invent an interconnected system — or DARPA doesn't invent it and we don't sit down and say, "Okay, we need a search engine, we need a payment mechanism." No, we have to throw money at things like pets.com to get things like Google. I just think that's how we invest. It's the unfortunate reality of human frailty.

Same with crypto, right? Speculation is what drove investment into all this technology in the first place.

Meme coins have revealed the resiliency of networks like Solana and allow exchanges to now say, "Wow, this thing can actually work in a way that we need it." So, yeah, I'm optimistic no matter what, but it's going to be a bloodbath.

十二、结尾与节目信息

If you like this segment, please like, subscribe, and tune in every Monday at 4:30 p.m. Eastern time. I'm Austin Campbell, the host of Bits and Bips, along with my friends Ram Ahluwalia and Chris Perkins and our slate of exceptional guests. Every week, we're going to discuss macro, crypto, and the collision of worlds, covering topics that move markets and shape the financial landscape.

One more thing. We've got a listener survey open. It takes just a few minutes, it's anonymous, and it changes what we make next. Use the QR code on screen or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. The link is in the show notes.

What if your crypto could do more than just sit in your wallet? Nexo is a digital assets wealth platform where you can generate daily interest on your crypto or borrow funds against your assets. Today, Nexo serves more than 10 million clients. Find out more at nexo.com.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Character.ai 花 16 美元换 1 美元收入——这不是"烧钱换增长"，这是**代币庞氏**
Chris 顺带一提的那个数字其实是整段讨论里最锋利的一刀，但三位主持人都没有真正剖开它。传统意义上"烧钱换规模"的逻辑是：现在亏钱，未来凭借网络效应/数据飞轮/切换成本获利。但 AI 应用公司的 16:1 支出结构背后没有这三样东西中的任何一样。
那它换的到底是什么？——**是"token 消耗量"这个指标本身的叙事价值**。风投轮次定价时看的是"每月被烧掉多少 token"，而前沿实验室定价时看的是"有多少应用在消耗我的 token"。于是出现了一个闭环：A 公司烧钱向 B 公司买 token，B 公司拿着"收入增长"去融下一轮，A 公司再拿着"token 消耗量"去融下一轮，两边同时在给对方的 PPT 作背书。
**这在金融史上有个名字：相互交易膨胀（round-tripping），90 年代末 Enron 和能源交易所做的事。**只不过这一轮用的不是电力合约，是浮点运算。
## 二、"productive bubble" 这个比喻可能是错的—

item.title: [Latent Space] AI in NYC: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native Engineering Team — Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

几个让我意外的隐秘模式

1. "泰勒主义的意外回归"——AI 偷偷完成了 100 年前管理学失败的任务

整段对话里埋着一句最反直觉的话："You can't automate a process that does not exist."（你无法自动化一个尚不存在的流程）

表面上这是关于 agent 部署的工程教训，但往深里看——AI 时代正在悄悄完成弗雷德里克·泰勒（Frederick Taylor）在 1911 年没能彻底完成的事业。整个 20 世纪，知识工作抗拒标准化：律师、分析师、顾问以"每个案子都不同"为由保护自己的黑箱手艺。而现在，当 40 个人用 40 种方法做同一件事，agent 就无法接管。于是企业被迫做它们一百年来都抵抗的事：先 Taylorize 自己，再让 AI 接手。

跨领域连接：这跟军队的"doctrine（作战条令）"是同构的——Tenex 的 meta harness（元框架）本质上是在为 AI 工程建立作战条令，让新兵一上场就能打出老兵的水准。换句话说，CJ 做的不是工具，是"参谋总部制度"的数字化翻版。

2. "10x" 公司的真实差距只有 4x——这不是失败，而是 AI 作为"方差压缩器"的证据

Alex 自己承认：Tenex 最高薪与最低薪工程师的差距只有 4 倍，不是公司名所暗示的 10 倍。他把这当作一个有待解决的问题带过了，但我想反过来读它：

AI 本质上是一个"方差压缩器"，而不是"方差放大器"。叙事上大家都说 AI 让顶尖的人跑得更快、让菜鸟被淘汰；但真实数据显示——当底层模型能力足够强，中位数被拉起的速度远远快于顶尖被拉开的速度。Opus 5.5 让一个二线工程师可以 2x 产出，但同样让一线工程师也只有 2x——因为 token-per-task 的回报正在逼近 Pareto 前沿（这正是他们后面讨论为什么不再担心 token 成本的原因）。

启示：Tenex 的"10x 工程师经济学"叙事与 4x 的实际数据之间的裂缝，恰恰是未来几年知识型劳动市场最被低估的现象——AI 不是在制造超级精英，而是在压扁才华曲线。

3. Token/工资 = 2:1 的公司，其实已经是"反向麦肯锡"

Alex 轻描淡写地给出一个数字：Tenex 的 token 支出和员工支出比例在 1:1 到 2:1 之间。swyx 的反应是"That's pretty high"（挺高的）——但他低估了这件事的历史意味。

典型 SaaS 公司这个比值是 10%。Tenex 是 200%。这意味着这家咨询公司已经不是在"卖人头"了——它的首要投入要素是算力，不是劳动力。换句话说，Tenex 的损益表长得更像一家数据中心、而不是一家埃森哲。

跨领域连接：这是一个历史级的组织形态转折。工业革命时期，制造业的 COGS（销货成本）主体从"原材料"切换到"机器折旧"，催生了福特制。21 世纪的服务业现在正在把 COGS 主体从"工资"切换到"推理成本"——而我们还没有一个管理学理论来处理这种公司。Tenex 实际上是在无意中跑在一场组织架构的 regime change 前面。

4. 一个没人注意到的"内部货币政策危机"

当被问到"一年前的 1 个 story point 值多少钱、现在还一样吗？"CJ 答："we're always trying to calibrate"（我们一直在尝试重新校准）。

这句话被当作操作细节一笔带过，但它其实是人类历史上第一家公司在尝试管理一种"内生通胀/通缩"的内部货币。story points 是 Tenex 的内部法币——它为员工发工资、为客户定价、为增长做衡量。当底层模型每 6 个月让生产力翻倍，这枚货币会相对于"美元/工时"剧烈通胀——除非每季度人为贬值它。

没有央行、没有货币政策工具、没有 CPI 篮子。他们在摸着石头造一个 Tenex 元；而且他们也许不知道，罗伯特·欧文（Robert Owen）在 1832 年用过"劳动时间券"（labour notes），结果因为无法应对生产率变化而崩盘。

最反直觉的洞见：Tenex 面临的最大长期风险不是模型变贵、不是客户流失、不是人才争夺——而是他们的内部货币可能会被底层技术通胀吃掉信用。

一个贯穿全场的隐藏结构

把以上四条串起来：Tenex 看起来是一家 AI 咨询公司，但它实际上在同时运行四个历史级实验—— - 泰勒主义 2.0（流程标准化作为自动化前置） - 方差压缩的劳动力市场（AI 作为均衡器而非放大器） - 以推理成本为主体的损益表（反向咨询业） - 无央行的内生货币制度（story points 作为企业法币）

这四件事里任何一件独立出现都值得写一本书。而他们在同一家 75 人的公司里同时跑着——还没完全意识到。

这才是这段访谈真正值得记住的东西。

📝 转录文本

AI in NYC: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native Engineering Team

Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess · Latent Space

Intro & Reintroducing Tenex

Okay, we're here at AI Engineer checking in with Tenex. Welcome back, Alex.

Thanks. Thanks for having us.

You brought your Director of Engineering, CJ. Welcome to the pod.

Special projects lead at Tenex.

Okay, special projects lead. All right, you're the SWAT team.

Yes, yes.

So you've been on the pod before, and people are vaguely familiar with the Tenex story, but can you sort of reintroduce from the top — what is the 2026, how you introduce yourself?

Yeah, very simply, Tenex is an applied AI partner for some of the biggest companies in the world to help them go from AI absent to AI native. Our belief is that AI is incredible, but it is raw intelligence. And the hardest problem to solve is the final mile to actually diffuse it through the economy. And so our view is to act as the player to help enterprises to figure all of this.

Can I curse on? To figure all this shit out.

Yeah, yeah. Yeah, we have the explicit tag on Apple Podcasts. Although I did recently discover that YouTube doesn't like it.

Oh really?

They're so, like, yeah, you can't say the F word.

So did I just mess up your video? What are you going to do?

I don't care. Okay. We're for adults.

CJ's Path to Tenex: Betting on Output over Hours

CJ, what drew you to Tenex?

So I was actually the first hire. I don't even know if Alex and Armand had the name Tenex quite yet, but I have, like, a graveyard of startups I tried to start before Tenex, ultimately culminating in like my own kind of engineering consulting company. And I spent some time there doing traditional engineering, eventually moved over to doing some of this like AI consulting and just like building more and more with it. I'm a software engineer by trade. And I just felt my output getting better and faster and ultimately getting paid less. Like I was charging hourly to my clients.

And I really liked kind of the ethos of Tenex that Alex had first posted when I saw it on Twitter about kind of looking to reward engineers for their output as opposed to rewarding them for their time. I think, you know, fast forwarding two years, you can see how engineers can now parallelize a ton of work and just have a ton more output. At the time with, you know, Sonnet 3.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, it might not have been that obvious, but I basically took the bet that I think with my skill set and leaning more into AI, I could have much higher output and ultimately have like a higher earning capacity to do that. And since then I've just like fell in love with that model. I think that's what the future of engineering really looks like. And ultimately when AI is solving all these tech problems, companies are gonna pay based on outcome and they're not going to want to pay based on the time that's required to build something.

Yeah. So for more detail on that, people can refer back to our previous pod where you literally pay people by story points.

Yep. And you just have to agree what the story points are. But that also means that some 10x engineers can literally make millions of dollars a year and some others may not make as much just because they're not as productive.

Yeah, exactly. The thesis is that AI is really just a leveraged bet on a human's intellect and work ethic. And so you're just going to have more variance than ever before in earning capacity. The Enterprise AI Adoption Funnel: 90 → 60 → 50 → 5

Right. So coming back to your customers and what you're seeing from the market, what is the most common ask that you guys get? And then what is something that people come to you with and you're like, no, we don't actually want that job yet?

Yeah. So one way I think about this is I think about enterprises adopting AI as almost like these different milestones in a race. And I think, especially at AIE, when I tell people about what percentage of companies have reached these milestones, they're kind of mind-blown by it.

Milestone 1: Rolling out a general purpose LLM. Of the, let's call it 100 enterprises we're talking to today, 90% have rolled out either Claude or Codex to their employees.

Milestone 2: Training and enablement. Actually teaching people how to use it — which never gets the love that it should get, but is arguably more important or as important as the technology itself. I would say that's at like 60%.

Oh, that's pretty good.

Yeah. There's some group there of companies that are like, "our people will just figure it out." But then there's a good chunk that is like, okay, we need to teach our people what skills are. We need to teach our people the features and functionality of these surfaces.

Milestone 3: Coding agents. The crazy thing is, I was asking a few people here, what percentage of enterprises do you think have rolled out coding agents to the engineering/product org in their company? And most people are like, it has to be 70 or 80%. The number is closer to 50%. Every other enterprise that we speak to either hasn't rolled out a coding agent or what they are using is closer to not having a coding agent than having a coding agent.

Milestone 4: Agents in production for non-engineering work. And this is where the biggest diffusion gap is — from raw intelligence to enterprise usage — drops to like 5%. I mean, most enterprises that we talk to that have, let's just say more than a thousand employees, do not have an agent in production that is doing work that is not building software.

FOMO, Back-Office Agents, and the Permissioning Nightmare

And so I think there's a few things. One is, this whole wave is driven by a combination of some small group of people understanding what is possible from this technology — and a way larger group of people driven by FOMO. And by the way, FOMO isn't bad. It creates some forward momentum, but it also means that people will latch onto the things that are most in the zeitgeist. I guess now for the last year and a half, people have been saying it's "the year of the agent" — or however long it is. Every year is the year of the agent.

Enterprises are like: can you help build us an agent for some back office task within the organization? That is one of the most common things. And it's why now a lot of the work we're doing at Tenex is deploying agents into production outside of the engineering org for companies — for repeatable work that they're doing.

The second is permissioning and RBAC. Basically, as every employee in a company has Claude or they have Codex and they need access to certain data, it has turned into an absolute nightmare for CIOs and CISOs. And they don't have basically a good gateway for easily doing — almost like a control panel for data permissioning.

Literally just what can you read, what can you not read.

Exactly. And that is a huge issue. So that's something we spend a lot of time on.

So you make them for people or do you buy something off the shelf?

So basically we started by building bespoke for companies, and now we actually productize that where we have our own gateway solution.

"You Can't Automate a Process That Does Not Exist"

Yeah, exactly. Is there anything else that comes to mind that's like, "we're hearing a lot from customers"?

I think that covered what we're hearing when it comes to the agent deployments. I think one of the pains that just always gets discovered — I phrase it to the team as: you can't automate a process that does not exist.

So when you have 40 people that are all roughly doing the same function, but they're all doing it a little bit of a different way, it's way harder to build an agent that's proactively doing that in the background. You can totally sit down with them, give them the tools, walk them through how they could augment their own workflow. But when you really start to get the leverage is when you have these agents that are surfacing work to you, you're reviewing it, you're throwing it back, and you become more of this — you know, everyone's been talking about becoming an agent manager, and I think we're on the cusp of that. But when you zoom out, oftentimes our recommendation to companies is: hey, first, we need to build a process around this organization within your company. And then here are the steps for us to actually hand off that work to an agent in the background. But if we don't have some form of standardization, it's going to be impossible for the agent to know whether it's doing it right, for us to build evals around this system and actually deliver the value that an agent that is doing this function would have.

Yeah, and I also feel like when we have these conversations around job displacement or job reallocation, we talk about it as this thing happening to people. And one of the reasons I don't like that is I feel like it doesn't give enough credit to people to have agency in their own lives, meaning...

You can adjust.

Yeah, people really should be thinking. When I think about enablement or people re-skilling, I think it is the job of an employer because they want to drive growth in their business, but it is also the job of an employee. And I think when people say that AI is going to replace all of the work that people don't enjoy doing, I think that's a little bit of a cope for the reality of: just, people are going to be put out of jobs because a lot of people don't have the luxury of liking or not liking a job. They do a job to make money.

And also I think people, to the extent that it's possible, should have agency in saying to themselves: okay, what is the stability or replaceability of my job over the next few years, and if I am to try to skill up in a way that I'm better protected, what does that look like? People have agency to say that to themselves and actually take action.

New York vs San Francisco: Bubbles, Billboards, and Arbitrage

Yeah, yeah, yeah. I think that's a good message for people to reflect on. The last piece I wanted to touch on before I let you guys go is just New York. You know, greatest city in the world according to some people. What's the mood generally among the people they talk to, whether it's at work, personally, what's the feeling? I live in San Francisco all day long. Everyone's just in agents all day long. The discussion is Instinks or Grok or Muse. It's not "do you like AI or not," right? And I feel like I want to step out of that bubble for a bit, but it's still New York. It's still progressive. It's still forward-looking.

Yeah. I mean, what I'd say is I feel like, basically, there's a bubble in New York that is a smaller bubble than exists in SF. If SF is like a big bubble, I think we at Tenex feel like we are in a — what I would say is like a microcosm of San Francisco — because of the people that self-select to work at the company. And then also the companies that we're partnered with and the people that we engage with in New York.

But I would for sure say also, it is true that it is a smaller universe than in SF. When you go to SF, it feels all-encompassing where it's like everyone, everywhere you look — there was someone who, similar to AIE, how I was saying earlier when I went on stage: if people go on Twitter or X because they feel like they're on Edge City, they're living in the future, AIE is that on steroids. I feel like SF is similar to AIE. I mean, it's probably the overlap of AIE generally and people who have lived at some point in their life in SF is probably a very large overlap.

We're roughly 1% of the city now.

Actually? For World's Fair, yeah. That's crazy.

Yeah. But to that point, I just think it is in the culture and the DNA of SF where a very big population of people live in the future. I think you can find that group in New York. And I think we at Tenex have found those people. And part of our goal is to drive AI as a hub or New York as a hub for AI in the US, because there is so much commerce here that it is going to be a place where diffusion of the technology actually has such a meaningful impact on the GDP of this country.

I think the bubble is smaller now and we take it almost as a charge of ours to increase our bubble. Maybe I don't know that it's possible to get to SF size, but I do think we can have a meaningful impact on getting more people to live in the future here. There's a physical — you see it on the billboards. It's slowly creeping in.

Oh totally. People used to — remember the Friend campaign where people would spray all sorts of graffiti on that? I think that was a little bit of an intentional rage bait. But now you have the unironic AI billboards and people are like, I guess that's part of life now.

A hundred percent. Yeah, so I think there's an opportunity to bring the edge and the living-in-the-future nature that SF has created because of the economic climate that exists there — because of venture, because of tech companies, and because of the people that are attracted there. But I also think of us as: we're in a smaller pond for AI, but I would argue we're in as big of a pond, if not a bigger pond, for commercial value.

And so I actually — the way I put it is: the reason I do AI in New York is I bring all the people from San Francisco to come here and meet their customers and also get a reality check.

Totally. And I actually think there's a really interesting arbitrage there.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, totally.

Hiring Call

Okay, awesome. Call for hiring. I know you guys are always hiring.

Yep. What are you hiring for? What's changed?

Yep. We're hiring forward deployed engineers at Tenex. Just go to tenex.co. We're also always hiring AI strategists, which are basically technical consultants who are leading client engagements. And the team is 75 strong in New York City. We're continuing to make New York City our home. And then if you are an enterprise who is looking to actually get AI native and you've tried it and it's not working, hit us up. I promise we'll do better work than — not going to name them — but a lot of other traditional consultancies.

Ooh spicy. CJ?

Yeah, I mean, I echo all of that. I'm particularly looking for engineers.

What's a special project? What is that?

A special project involves anything outside of our client work. So I think about my brain right now. It is building that meta harness and system internally — basically, find the bleeding edge of what the models can do and give them tools to augment how well they can do it. And then also internally working on the platform that Alex mentioned. Big goal there: diffuse these background agents and actually get them out to enterprises in a way that's truly, truly helpful to them.

Yeah. And solve a lot of those messy IT problems that we hit on earlier.

Dude, when you have some solutions, we take guest posts on the Latent Space blog. I'd love to welcome some sharing of knowledge. But otherwise, thank you so much for your time. And good to see you again in New York.

Yeah likewise. Appreciate it.

Once a year, once a year.

Hell yeah. Thank you.

# 几个让我意外的隐秘模式
## 1. "泰勒主义的意外回归"——AI 偷偷完成了 100 年前管理学失败的任务
整段对话里埋着一句最反直觉的话："You can't automate a process that does not exist."（你无法自动化一个尚不存在的流程）
表面上这是关于 agent 部署的工程教训，但往深里看——**AI 时代正在悄悄完成弗雷德里克·泰勒（Frederick Taylor）在 1911 年没能彻底完成的事业**。整个 20 世纪，知识工作抗拒标准化：律师、分析师、顾问以"每个案子都不同"为由保护自己的黑箱手艺。而现在，当 40 个人用 40 种方法做同一件事，agent 就无法接管。于是企业被迫做它们一百年来都抵抗的事：先 Taylorize 自己，再让 AI 接手。
**跨领域连接**：这跟军队的"doctrine（作战条令）"是同构的——Tenex 的 meta harness（元框架）本质上是在为 AI 工程建立作战条令，让新兵一上场就能打出老兵的水准。换句话说，CJ 做的不是工具，是"参谋总部制度"的数字化翻版。

item.title: [投资TALK君] ✨【投资TALK君1510期】最强指引！ALL-IN算力，营收1万亿！✨20261020#CPI #nvda #美股 #投资 #英伟达 #ai #特斯拉
item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：这期视频其实暴露了"马斯克帝国"在市场心智里的坍缩

你注意到了吗——整期视频反复说"Spacex 财报"，但聊的全是 Grok 模型、算力租赁、训练推理、Cursor 营收。这不是转录错误那么简单。这揭示了一个被忽略的结构性事实：xAI 在市场心智中已经和 SpaceX 发生了语义性融合，因为它们共享同一个核心变量——马斯克的"叙事发动机"。当一家公司（无论叫 xAI 还是 Colossus）的估值的 80% 来自 CEO 口头下的 ARR 指引，它事实上就已经从一家"算力公司"变成了"叙事期权"。更深的洞察是：马斯克的"非零概率"是一种贝叶斯锚定武器——视频主自己也捕捉到了，"非零概率 = 接近零的概率"。但市场并不交易概率，市场交易锚点。他把 10GW 抬到 13GW 再隐性抛出 20GW，是在以极低认知成本把整条分布曲线向右推——这是一种语言套利，和期权做市商放一张远虚值报价把 IV 拉高是同一套机制。

二、跨领域连接：算力短租市场 ≈ 2007 年的 VLCC 油轮市场

马斯克 all-in 短租、拒绝长约锁定、相信"智能/瓦"永远上升——这几乎是 2007 年希腊和挪威船东们的翻版剧本：John Fredriksen、George Economou 当年也坚信"BDI 永不下跌"，于是在波罗的海干散货指数 11000 点时疯狂下单 VLCC，用现金流最大化逻辑拒绝长约。结果是 2009 年 BDI 跌到 663 点，十年破产潮。结构性相似点有三：(1) 订货到交付的半年-两年前置期，使"看到价格下跌再停"物理上不可能；(2) 单一赛道极度资本密集，退出成本接近总投资；(3) 收入模型是短期现货敞口。视频主用了"芝士店全部卖光"的比喻来形容算力紧缺——这和 2007 年航运圈说"船坞三年内一只新 Suezmax 都排不进来"是一模一样的句式。真正的问题不是短租价格会不会跌，而是：当马斯克自己一个人就带着 13GW 入场，他本人就是在建造那条压垮自己价格的供给曲线。 他的"全押"策略，在博弈论上恰好会触发它所依赖的那个前提的瓦解。

三、被所有人忽略的一个数据裂缝：55/50 的自相矛盾

视频主一笔带过了一个细节——马斯克说未来 13GW 算力中内部/外部"55/50"分配，又说"也可能 40/60，也可能 60/40"。这不是口误，这是认知状态的直接外泄：他没有做过内部测算，他在直播中实时估算。但更惊人的是现状——目前 7B AI 营收里，Cursor（内部产品）只贡献 0.6B，也就是说当下的真实比例是 9:91 外部占优。他宣称未来会把一半算力留给内部，这意味着他相信 Grok+Cursor 在 15 个月内要翻 50 倍。这不是"ARR 翻 10 倍"那么简单——这是说内部需求必须翻近百倍才能撑起他自己给的分配比例。这个数据缝隙比估值泡沫更危险，因为它暗示马斯克要么在用虚高的内部需求为未来的供给过剩找借口（为短租价格崩盘铺叙事退路），要么他真的打算让 Grok 以 Anthropic 级的烈度训练——而后者意味着烧钱速度要再上一个数量级。

四、一个几乎没人提的 Netflix 盲点：注意力的"认知卡路里"重分配

视频主自己非常敏锐地提到了"中国 AI 视频"威胁，但管理层只字不提。这不是傲慢，是 Kodak 1998 年看数码相机时的那种"数据还没出现在报表里"的典型盲点。但真正的洞察不在"短视频/中视频/长视频"的分类上——分类是误导的。真正的变量是"每分钟认知卡路里"：Netflix 一小时剧集给用户的"情绪卡路里"是 X，TikTok 是 2X，AI 生成的个性化视频流可能是 5X。人类每天的"注意力代谢率"是恒定的（约 4-6 小时娱乐窗口），谁的"卡路里密度"高谁就胜出。跨领域连接：这和 1980 年代"精制碳水 vs 全谷物"的食品工业演化完全同构——高密度、低饱腹感的东西短期不可战胜，但长期会反噬整个消费心智。Netflix 当前 18 倍 PE 看似便宜，但如果"注意力卡路里竞赛"进入 AI 加速阶段，它的护城河——昂贵的工业化叙事——恰恰是最先被降维打击的部分。它不是输给对手，是输给了用户的多巴胺曲线。

五、GE 的隐藏身份：被所有人错标的"反石油对冲工具"

视频主提到了，但没点透：GE 的航空服务模式让它在油价上涨（航空公司减班）时仍然增长，在油价下跌时会超额增长。换言之，GE 已经被 silently rewired 成了一个负 beta 石油衍生品。这不是宏观意外，是业务模型的几何属性：引擎卖出的那一刻，GE 锁定了未来 20-30 年的服务现金流，而油价决定的只是"折现时间线的拉伸或压缩"——不是现金流本身。这给了我们一个被低估的组合构造启示：传统 60/40 组合里的"能源对冲"位置，可以用 GE 这类"订单积压型工业服务公司"替代，获得负相关性 + 复合增长的双重收益。这和 Danaher 用服务合约把自己变成"反周期 SaaS"是同一个 playbook，而市场仍在用传统工业股的 PEG 框架给它定价——这就是 33.7 倍前瞻市盈率看起来"略贵"但其实不贵的真正原因。

📝 转录文本

开场

SpaceX 单机救主。我在录这期视频的时候，盘后现在半导体都出现了反弹。那在这一次 SpaceX 的财报里边，老马到底给出了什么样的未来指引？稍后我们一起来聊一下。

那今天主要和大家分享三家公司财报，分别是吉亿、奈飞和最后的 Spacex。欢迎大家来到一个不但只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞、加转发，让更多人可以看到我们这期内容。

一、周二市场回顾

我先快速地回顾一下周二资产价格的走势。周一我没有录视频，整个市场出现了小幅的反弹，那周二是继续出现了小幅的反弹。纳指相对会弱一些，但随着美债收入率，特别是长债收入率这一块的一些下跌，TLT 的反弹，我们可以看到标普的等权指数相当的强，大多数的一些价值股的标的，在这一周，在过去的一周，都出现了比较好的这个反弹。

那么在周二的市场里边，银行板块也上涨了 1.4，公共事业 1.3，REITs 1.8，基本上所有和利率相关的一些价值股板块都出现了反弹。所以标普的等权指数上涨了 1.2%，其他科技股是下跌 0.4，那伴随着同时半导体板块也下跌了 0.4%。但整个市场如果从参与度这个角度去看的话，我相信纳指可能仍然是在减弱的，但是同时标普 500 应该是在扩张的。然后罗素 2000 在周二也出现了 1.7% 的这个反弹，所以罗素 2000 这个参与度和周一去做对比的话，应该也出现了比较好的反弹。

所以现在从三大指数去看的话，纳指仍然是相当的弱，然后排名倒数第二弱的或者排名正数第二，就是罗素 2000，相对最强的其实是标普。

二、GE 财报解读

2.1 整体业绩

那我们先来看一下 GE 的财报。GE 是在周二盘前所发布的财报。那财报本身从数据这个季度的数据或者对于明年的这个指引，GE 都非常的强。这一个季度超出了市场预期，EPS 超出市场预期 12% 至 13%，明年的这个营收指引要往上抬，整个 26 年的全年指引也往上抬。所以这一份财报本身从数据去看是非常好的一份财报。

2.2 油价逆风下的强劲基本面

那 GE 业务本身其实不会有太大的一些波动。主要是因为什么？我们从他们财报会里边来看一下。公司管理层有聊到：虽然各个航空公司的一个航班计划有可能会有所缩减——为什么？这段时间 GE 的格鲁什其实就是因为全球油价的这个上涨，油价的这个上涨使得航空公司的一个航班计划可能会有所缩减。但是我们确实看到了起飞架次的这个增长，其中第三季度还增长了 1%。

你知道 GE 在什么样的宏观环境下仍然实现了 EPS 的增速超市场的预期，然后明年也给了这个指引。也就是说，如果接下去油价出现任何放缓的话，GE 的这个财报本身，最后的结果只会比现在市场的预期给出的这个预期更加的好。

我记得在第一季度财报的时候，就是今年的 4 月份，当时正好是美伊战争开打的那时候，当时第一季度的财报超出了市场预期，但是没有上调全年的这个指引，就是因为油价所带来这个全球地缘政治所带来这个不确定性。而现在我们已经三个季度过去了，可以看到最后的结果，其实这个基本面仍然非常的强劲，就是在这样一个宏观逆风的这个情况下仍然做到了非常好，且明年的这个指引也给下来了。所以接下去只要有油价出现任何的一个反弹，对于 GE 在这一块，在 commercial 这一块的业务其实都是一个利好。

2.3 订单积压与服务模式

管理层有说到，从服务这个角度看，才是他们推动业务的一个核心。从 commercial 这一块主要是卖引擎和卖服务。引擎卖出去之后，卖出去一笔的这个引擎，伴随着是未来几乎是这一个引擎本身终身的一个服务。那么所以 GE 未来的这个增速全部是来自以前所卖出引擎的这个订单。那订单增长了 23%，那订单本身和未来这个营收是有非常强的这个正相关。

我们看右边部分：未来我们可能会受到这些压力——宏观的这些压力——但是从 GE 利航天业务这个角度去看，我们认为 2027 年的这个增长主要将会来自于现有的这些积压订单和航空公司已飞行的循环架次。

2.4 增速与估值

那在这样的一个背景下，我们来看一些数据。市场预期 26 年的营收增速 19%，公司管理层这次给了一个预期了，差不多在 20% 左右。27 年市场预期营收增速 11%，管理层也给了 low double digit，差不多是在 13、14 左右。那最终的结果高于 15% 我也不会感到意外，而且如果油价下跌情况下，可能这个营收的增速会更高。市场的预期，27、28 年就是平均下来差不多每年就在 10%，但实际上最后的一个结果，营收的这个增速可能就在 15% 左右。

所以我在，我记得上次我在聊 GE 的时候，我就认为我说市场对于 GE 未来这个营收增速是低估了，那所以对于他们 EPS 这块的增速也是低估了。

如果一家公司营收的增速每年 10%，那你基本上可以预计它的 operating income 的一个增速、运营利润的增速可能就在 14%、15%。那么假设这家公司有一个 operating、有一个运营效率在那边的话，在这个基础上，然后再做一些回购，那最终的 EPS 每年的这个增速可能就是停留在 16% 至 17% 左右。一家公司如果它的一个 bottom line 平均每年可以增加 15% 的话，五年翻一倍，其实也可以是一家算作是一家合格的增长公司。

而从 GE 这个角度，如果营收增速最终如果每年能够平衡在 15%，那最终的 EPS 这个增速应该是要 north of twenty，就应该是在 20% 以上了。那对于这类的公司，你去看一下它现在如果静态市盈率在 38 倍、39 倍左右，除以 20% 这个增速，那 PEG 在 2 倍。2 倍的 PEG 是相对来说是属于高的，但是 GE 本身所在的这个行业，我认为他们是应该有一个溢价在那边。

对，我们来看一下估值。这是 forward PE，向前看前瞻的这个市盈率。前瞻的市盈率在今天周二的这个收盘之后是在 33.7 倍。你可以看到在 24 年之前，它的 PE 相对会低一些，但是在 24 年的时候，他们进行拆分了，拆分完之后 GE 的这个 PE 最低的时候是 2025 年的 3 月份，当时跌到了 30 倍。那我个人认为一个合理的区间可能就是在 30 倍至 40 倍之间，如果去到 45 倍的话，可能相对会比较高一些。所以我认为现在 GE 的这个估值就是在一个非常合理的一个阶段。如果继续往下跌，接近于 30 倍，在 31 倍到 30 倍左右的话，那就是一个低估的一个区间。

三、Netflix 财报解读

3.1 盘后下跌与营收减速

然后我们来看一下奈飞。那奈飞盘后发布完财报之后，盘后出现了下跌。我看了一下它的财报，其实没有到那么的糟糕。那市场的一个担心很简单——那你从结果去出发的话，市场的一个担心就是他们第四季度这个营收增速将会持续放缓。

那这张图所显示的是奈飞在过去 6 个季度它的一个营收增速。基本上在 25 年底和 26 年初的时候都是在 16% 以上，然后今年的第二季度、第三季度连续下降，从 16% 连续下降到 12% 以上，和第四季度给的这个指引是在 11.5%。所以市场交易的一个逻辑性就是奈飞的这个营收增速持续放缓。

所以在财报会议里边，分析师问的是：你们在明年能不能保证你们的营收增速在 10% 以上，或者在两位数？

3.2 市场预期与估值分析

那我们来看一下市场的预期。2026 年现在马上还有一个季度就要结束了，现在市场预期是 13%，未来的两年市场预期是 11% 和 10%。所以市场的一个担心也不是说不是非常的合理，是合理的。24 年 16%，25 年也 16%，你 26 年一旦放缓到 13%，市场马上做一个线性外推，假设你 27 年是 11%，28 年变成 10%。

那我们假设，未来营收增速 10%，EPS 增速 15%，结合它静态市盈率 19.5 倍，差不多它 PEG 是在 1.3 倍左右。那 1.3 倍的 PEG 相对来说是比较低的。然后我们来看一下它的 forward PE 前瞻市盈率，周二的收盘是 18.35 倍。18.35 倍从历史长河去看其实是相对比较低的，即使在 22 年全部算进去的话，当时 22 年最低的时候是在 15 倍，稍微低于 15 倍一点点。那现在 18 倍其实离 15 倍并没有太远。

那么所以，现在奈飞的这个估值这个角度去看，无论是 PEG 也好，还是前瞻市盈率也好，都是相对比较低的。

3.3 定性风险：中国 AI 视频的长期威胁

市场对于他们美国这一块的业务稍微有一点点担心，管理层也有聊到了美国这一块的业务，他们能够做到更好。所以奈飞这次财报我并没有看到太多令人比较担心的，管理层也看到了美国业务可以做到更好。

唯一从长期、从定性这个角度去看的话，我比较担心的是最近这段时间中国 AI 所做的一些视频的一些兴起会抢了人们很多的一些眼球。而这些视频它也不是——它又不算是短视频，又不算是长视频。而且我们知道从短视频到现在的中视频，到未来 AI 所制作这些长视频，整个行业所发展的速度其实相当的快。

当然这些东西到他们最后能够影响到奈飞可能需要一段时间，在这一次财报会里面也从来没有人去聊这个点。那未来有可能，如果真的要会影响到奈飞的话，可能会从他们某一个季度的财报的数据里面所显现出来。

但是从短中期这个角度去看，市场的一个担心是他们在美国这一块的落地可能没有那么的好，Engagement 可能没有那么的好。那公司管理层也看到了，可能在今年第四季度、包括明年的话，试图去解决这个问题。所以我前面聊的这个定性角度上的一个风险，短时间之内应该还不会完全蔓延开来，或者体现到它那个财报里面。

四、SpaceX 财报深度解读

4.1 整体财报与市场反应

OK，最后我们来聊一下 Spacex 的一个财报。那这一次财报无论从任何一个角度去解读的话，都是非常好的一份财报。三个业务你可以看到营收分别是超出市场预期 24%、8%，和 AI 这一块超出市场预期 20%。总体三个业务全部加在一起，从 adjusted operating income 调整之后的一个运营利润一个角度去看，市场预期是 2.2 个 billion，最后的结果是 2.79 个 billion，超出市场预期 25%。

然后我们来看一下财报会，财报会才是这一次一个重点。老马在里面聊了很多一些令市场惊掉下巴的一些预测。当然了，市场盘后出现了一个上涨，我认为完全离不开的是整个市场的一个 setup——必须市场有一个悲观的 setup，然后这一次 Spacex 的财报出来之后，对于短期数据算力这一块的一个需求非常的强大，所给出这些展望才使得市场出现这个反弹。我认为 setup 在那边和这个财报本身是分不开的。你即使有这个财报，你没有这个 setup 的话，也不见得盘后一定会出现反弹，那因为当下市场对于半导体板块、对硬件板块确实非常的悲观。

4.2 13GW 算力与 20GW 数据中心的指引

好，所以我们一条一条来看。首先第一个，在上一个季度财报的时候，老马说到在 27 年的话，他会有 10 个 GW 算力的这个上限。那这一次老马又说到 13 个 GW，就算上接下去的一个季度加一起的话，到 27 年底会有 13 个 GW 的算力上限。

算力上限和数据中心是两个概念。他说有可能在 27 年底之前，我们会有 20 个 GW 的数据中心。所谓的 20 GW 的数据中心是不包括芯片的，包括芯片的话就是 13 个 GW 的算力的一个落地。所以 13 GW 的算力和 20 GW 的一个数据中心，两者是不冲突的。他所聊的 20 GW 的数据中心是：你把其他数据中心里面所有需要的一些东西全部上线，芯片先放在一边。为什么呢？因为既然整个行业都认为现在的电力本身非常地去难获得的话，那我先把数据中心建完，然后我先把电力弄完，弄完之后芯片本身可能不是那么的紧缺。

然后第三点，他说一个非零概率，我们明年将上线二十几万的算力——原本说 10 个 GW，现在变成 20 个 GW。当然他说一个非零概率，在我对于老马的一个理解里面，所谓的非零概率就是接近于零的这个概率。他只是给了一个非常 aspirational 的一个 goal，那非常令人就几乎难以做到，但是是一个目标，就你如果真的能够做到的话，那非常非常的夸张了。

所以这是第一部分：明年对于整个 27 年，包括最后一个季度，加上 27 年的一个指引在那边。

4.3 ARR 一万亿的夸张预测

然后照这样下去的话，他说到这个数据非常的夸张。他说 Spacex 的 ARR——就是年化的一个收入——在 27 年底能够达到 0.5 个 T 至 1 个 T，就 500 个 billion 至 1 个 T。

我今天在 X 上我做了一个算术：如果老马 ARR 能够做到一个 T 的话，一个 T 的 ARR 它基本上全是卖算力获得的。能够卖掉一个 T 的 ARR 全部卖算力，谁是他的客户？只能是两家模型公司是他的客户。两家模型公司如果是他们的客户，购买了一个 T 的算力的话，那即使我假设这两家模型公司的毛利润只有 50%——且不说他们现在的毛利润是在 80% 以上的，我不去做这个假设——假设他们的毛利润只有 50%，也就是一个 T 的营收对于 Spacex 来说，一个 T 的营收就接近于或者约等于，这两家模型公司全部加在一起会有两个 T 的营收，两个 T 的 ARR。

而现在他们的 ARR 是多少？50 个 B 加上 80 个 B，130 个 B，或者 0.13 个 T。0.13 个 T 到明年年底两个 T 的 ARR，它翻的一个营收不只要翻 10 倍以上了，这是非常非常夸张的一个预测。如果真的能够做到的话，那现在市场根本不存在任何的一个泡沫，因为这就告诉市场说 Anthropic 它的一个营收今年和上年比翻了 10 倍，然后明年和今年这个基础上再翻 10 倍，已经在那么大体量的情况下还能够翻十倍，这已经是非常非常夸张了。

4.4 内部营收结构与"NeoCloud 化"

然后 Spacex 的内部，刚刚过去这个季度 7 个 B、70 亿美金的 AI 营收，只有 0.6 个 B 是来自于 Cursor，也就是大部分的一些营收呢——超过 90% 的这个营收在 AI 这块的营收——全部是来自于卖算力。也就是现在 Spacex 基本上完全变成了一家建数据中心、买芯片、然后去卖芯片，它变成了一家 NeoCloud，超级巨大的一个 NeoCloud，你也可以说它是一个执行力非常非常强的一个 NeoCloud。

然后他们的 CFO 有说到，他期待未来会有更多的一些其他客户。那以现在这个价格，回报周期是小于一的，上一个季度也聊到了小于一年，现在仍然是小于一年。现在价格差不多是 30 至 50 美金 per watt。

4.5 55/50 内外部算力分配之谜

然后接下去一个问题：未来如何去分配这个算力？因为既然如果你未来到 27 年底你要建 13 个 GW 的算力的话，那 13 个 GW 你怎么去分配？你内部需要那么多的算力吗？

那老马说这个问题问得很好，但是老马说差不多 55/50 吧，内部和外部。我不相信这个背后的一个数据，这个 breakdown 是真实的。因为你想，现在它就不是 55/50——现在是多少？现在你想 0.6 营收啊，营收这一块 0.6 个 billion 来自于 Cursor，剩下的 6.4 个 billion 全部是来自于算力上的一个出租或者卖算力。那你怎么可能未来自己这个这个算力，你预期——除非你预期未来的 Cursor 这一块的落地会非常的好。不然的话，这 55/50 的外部和内部算力这个分配其实是不合理的。

从 Anthropic 这个角度去看是合理的，因为他们现在已经有了非常好的这个落地。当然有个前提是老马可以通过卖短期的这个算力来弥补或者来回补自己在 Cursor 这一块的训练、自己在 AI 模型、在 Grok 这一块的训练。这是可以实现的，因为确实短期这个算力现在非常的值钱。所以他有可能通过卖短期的算力来回补自己在训练这一块。模型公司差不多是这样，你只要砸算力下去，你只要在训练这一块砸钱下去，基本上都是会出结果的。

所以针对这个问题，老马的一个回答是 55 是外部和内部，但是从他这个回答的一个语气，我估计他现在是没有这方面的一个思考的，就是它是一个浮动的嘛。他之后也聊了，他说有可能 46/60，有可能 60/40，我现在还不知道。但他说为什么他这么去做——他说"智能/电力"（intelligence/power）是在增加的，就是每一个 power、每一个电力你所能够产生的智能是在增加的，而且未来只会越来越增加，因为模型随着模型越来越聪明之后，你的 Intelligence/Power 只会增加。所以我们决定只做短租市场。

4.6 All-in 短租市场的风险

那这一点和其他的所有的云厂商、星云也好、Hyperscaler 也好，完全是不一样的。同样，我今天也发了一条 X，我说这样去做，你的确短期之内可以最大化你的回报，你也可以最快时间去缩短你的回报周期，但是也必须要承担一个非常大的风险——你假设这一个短租市场的一个价格会持续上升，这其实是一个非常危险的做法。而且你投入这个数据中心的这个体量又那么的大。

那有些人可能会认为：哎，你可以停啊，一旦看到短租市场价格下跌，你可以停嘛。你停不下来的。你怎么停下来？你和英伟达这边的下单，你起码是提早半年就去英伟达那边下单了。然后比如说你在今天你看到了短租这一块的价格出现了下降，然后你把你半年之后的一个单可以停掉吗？停不了的。你必须要提前去下单的。整个现在整个数据中心这个建造里边，很多的这些 component，你早在半年前、一年之前就必须要去下这个订单，包括 HBM。

那所以只做短租市场这个决定本身，我认为风险是相当高的。你可以把 Spacex 理解为是整个市场里面的个超级贝塔，算力这一块的一个超级贝塔，就是压住短期这个算力只会往上，就只会单向上涨，而不会出现任何的一个调整。如果从这个角度去出发的话，你做短租市场、或者选做只做短租市场是最明智的这个决定。

那为什么呢？NeoCloud、为什么星云和大科技——大科技总有钱了吧，你可以说 NeoCloud 他们口袋没有那么的深，那么所以他们只能够用这些中长期订单来锁定未来这个订单、锁定未来这个现金流，然后可以去融资。但是大科技钱袋子够深了吧，大科技为什么不去做？或者大多数业务为什么还是做长租和短租？是因为整个行业会有周期的。

所以我个人认为在算力这一块，老马是出现了一个丰富的情况。而且如果他真的明年上线了 13 个 GW 的算力，而且这 13 个 GW 完全全部用来做短租市场的话，我相信也会把短租市场这个价格给往下压的，除非背后的这个需求真的非常的大，大过了你额外的这 13 个 GW 算力的落地。

4.7 算力紧缺的生动描述："芝士店全空"

好，那然后是一些行业里面所看到的一些现状，我认为这也挺好，这也形容了当下整个算力到底有多么的紧缺。

那老马说到：他说我们甚至和某些云厂商商量，牺牲自己一部分的推理去换训练。因为我们训练所需要的芯片和推理所需要的芯片是不一样的，我们拿一部分的推理芯片和你去换一些算力，算力用来干嘛？用来训练。所以这就说明当下那个市场——而云厂商告诉他们：我们没有，我们没有任何的一个多余的算力给你去做训练。这就说明当下那个市场对于算力有多么的紧缺。

而且他也把当下那个市场形容为是一个芝士商店，就是你去一家芝士商店卖芝士的——卖 cheese——然后你进去你说我要 Mozzarella，然后他说 Mozzarella 没有，你要不要其他的 goat cheese？然后 goat cheese 也没有，然后你要不要其他的？就基本上整个芝士商店里面所有种类的芝士全部被卖掉了。即使你可以妥协，Mozzarella 没有，我买一些其他的芝士——没有，全部卖完。

那老马说的，他说明年有可能 6 个月的回报周期也不是不可能。现在是小于一年，他说 6 个月就能够把现在这一波投资全部赚回来。

我不知道老马选择这么去做能不能够维持多久。但是如果明年他真的能够——我们假设从结果去出发——如果明年他真的能够去落地 13 个 GW 的算力的话，那一定代表从今年到明年年底，那一定代表整个市场从今年现在到明年年底这段时间里边，整个算力仍然是持续紧缺，就需求仍然是大大多于供给，这才会出现这个结果。不然的话，中间有任何需求出现一定程度的放缓，他绝对不可能去落地 13 个 GW，中间他一定会选择进行放缓。当然我说了，某种程度不是他愿意放缓就放缓的，因为背后你的订单必须是提前半年去定的。

4.8 与特斯拉合并问题

最后可能是从特斯拉的投资者也非常关心的一个问题，就是有人问到了，他说和特斯拉之间的这个合并你怎么看的？

老马说道，两家公司都成立了工作小组，他自己是不参与其中的，所以两个工作小组彼此之间会进行一个沟通。他说有人认为一定会合并，那我觉得可能过于自信了。为什么他认为可能过于自信了？他说因为特斯拉是必须要 50% 以上的投资者股权都同意，而不是投票的人里面 50%——是所有特斯拉 50% 以上的投资者都同意，最后特斯拉才有可能会和 SpaceX 之间进行合并。当然他说，如果你问我的话，我觉得是一个好主意。

4.9 总结

最后我们做一个总结：这一次 SpaceX 的财报，如果要去挑一个重点出来的话，老马对于当下短租市场的算力的一个需求进行了非常强的这个倍数，因为他选择拿 Spacex 去 all in 短租市场。

五、活动与直播预告

OK，今天的活动来自于 Seeking Alpha。第一个 Alpha Picks 量化选股策略 YTD 标普 14%，他们的这个策略本身 22.6%。那最近三个所挑选的个股回报还是不错的，都跑赢了市场。

差不多在 4 个月之前，他们推出了另外一个量化选股策略。那这个新的量化选股策略的所选的这些标的全部是集中在价值股身上，所以都会有一个收益率、都会有一个 yield 在那边。你可以看到这个投资组合平均收益率是 2.8%，那即使股价不上涨的话，每年也可以有 2.8% 的一个平均的利息和回报在那边。那在过去的四个月里面，他们所对标的这个指数上涨了 0.12%，而他们这个策略本身上涨了将近 10%，还是不错的。

前面我们第一个看到 AlphaPicks 的量化选股策略，现在正在有一个免费的试用期。如果首年订阅的话，可以立即节省 50 美金。如果对于这两个量化策略都感兴趣的话，现在有个 combo 的价格，原价是 998 美金一年，现在是 719 美金一年。

那最后要提醒一下大家，是在周三的晚上，在我的 APP 里边会有一个会员的直播，大家别忘了。

好，那今天这期内容就到这边。下期见。

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：这期视频其实暴露了"马斯克帝国"在市场心智里的坍缩
你注意到了吗——整期视频反复说"Spacex 财报"，但聊的全是 Grok 模型、算力租赁、训练推理、Cursor 营收。这不是转录错误那么简单。这揭示了一个被忽略的结构性事实：**xAI 在市场心智中已经和 SpaceX 发生了语义性融合**，因为它们共享同一个核心变量——马斯克的"叙事发动机"。当一家公司（无论叫 xAI 还是 Colossus）的估值的 80% 来自 CEO 口头下的 ARR 指引，它事实上就已经从一家"算力公司"变成了"叙事期权"。更深的洞察是：马斯克的"非零概率"是一种**贝叶斯锚定武器**——视频主自己也捕捉到了，"非零概率 = 接近零的概率"。但市场并不交易概率，市场交易锚点。他把 10GW 抬到 13GW 再隐性抛出 20GW，是在以极低认知成本把整条分布曲线向右推——这是一种**语言套利**，和期权做市商放一张远虚值报价把 IV 拉高是同一套机制。
## 二、跨领域连接：算力短租市场 ≈ 2007 年的 VLCC 油轮市场
马斯克 all-in 短租、拒绝长约锁定、相信"

item.title: [Mercatus Center] The Hayekian Triangle: James Buchanan and the Challenge of Self-Government
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

布坎南两篇文章背后的隐藏结构：一个意外的发现

一、这不是矛盾，是"创业者悖论"的政治学版本

表面上看，《自然人与人造人》（1979）和《害怕自由》（2005）像是乐观与悲观的分裂人格。但如果你把布坎南的另一篇文章《经济学家应该做什么》放在中间作为桥梁，你会突然看到一个被所有评论者都忽略的结构——

布坎南其实在描绘一个"创业者悖论"：越是具备"自我建构能力"的人，越会在面对不确定性时渴望"被托管"。

这不是分裂，这是同一枚硬币。能力越强，意识到的可能性空间越大；可能性空间越大，选择的焦虑就越深；焦虑越深，就越想把方向盘交出去。这就像硅谷创业者在IPO前夜疯狂寻找导师、冥想大师、"父亲型"投资人——不是因为他们不够强，恰恰因为他们"artifactual"（自我塑造）的能力让他们看到了太多可能的自己。

跨领域连接：这与心理学家Barry Schwartz的"选择悖论"（Paradox of Choice）结构完全同构，但走到了更深的政治层面。Schwartz告诉你：选择太多会让消费者瘫痪；布坎南则预言：选择太多会让公民投靠利维坦。超市里的果酱实验，放大到国家尺度，就是福利国家的扩张史。

二、一个让人意外的观察："害怕自由"其实是一种成功综合症

对话中Pete提到"19世纪末，自由主义西方达到了前所未有的自治、财富与和平——而恰恰在那一刻它最脆弱"。这句话值得停下来品味。

真正反直觉的洞察是：古典自由主义的失败不是因为它做得不够好，而是因为它做得太好。

当自由把绝大多数外部敌人——饥饿、瘟疫、暴政、短命——都击退之后，人类面对的最后一个敌人就剩下自己选择的后果。而这是最难承受的敌人。中世纪农民不需要"害怕自由"，因为他从未拥有过；他害怕的是领主、瘟疫和冬天。只有在那些敌人退场之后，"自由本身"才会变成需要害怕的东西。

这就解释了一个被所有政治学家都未能很好解释的现象：为什么福利国家不是在最贫困的时代诞生，而是在最富裕的时代扩张？ 为什么北欧——人类历史上最富、最健康、最平等的社会——同时也是家长制国家最强大的地方？

跨领域连接：这与神学家克尔凯郭尔《焦虑的概念》里的论断惊人一致——他说焦虑不是奴隶的情绪，而是自由人的情绪。亚当没有焦虑，是因为他还没有选择；只有当他被赋予"不吃那个苹果"的自由时，焦虑才诞生。布坎南在不自觉地重演克尔凯郭尔，只是把神学语言换成了公共财政语言。

三、被忽略的致命细节：教育是唯一能同时"扩大"和"驯服"artifactual nature的技术

对话里关于教育的那一段，看似离题，其实是整场讨论的秘密钥匙。

Buchanan说教育不是人力资本投资，也不是消费，而是"spending on becoming"（变成的开销）。Pete和Chris都在正面讨论这件事。但他们几乎错过了一个结构性的洞察：

教育是人类发明的唯一一种制度，它既让人更有能力自我塑造（因此扩大了"natural artifactual man"的可能性），又让人学会与这种能力共处的焦虑（因此可能免疫"afraid to be free"的诱惑）。

换句话说，教育是对冲布坎南两篇文章之间张力的那张唯一有效的保单。

这解释了为什么现代国家对教育有一种近乎病态的控制欲——不是因为它想生产工人（那是经济学的解释），而是因为国家与教育在争夺同一个灵魂的塑造权。国家希望你成为"afraid to be free"的那种人；真正的liberal arts education希望你成为"natural artifactual"的那种人。两者无法并存。

跨领域连接：这就是为什么极权主义政权——从斯巴达到苏联到朝鲜——总是优先改造教育而不是优先改造经济。改造经济能让你听话一个季度，改造教育能让你的孙子都听话。乔治·奥威尔在《1984》里让温斯顿最终"爱老大哥"，走的不是经济路径，是教育路径——改造他对2+2等于几的信念。

四、一个大胆预测

如果布坎南的框架是对的，那么AI时代会是"害怕自由"的终极加速器——因为AI第一次让"把方向盘交出去"从政治决定变成了日常微决策。你每天都在用ChatGPT选餐厅、写邮件、决定周末做什么。每一次微托管都在训练你的神经通路：选择是痛苦的，外包是舒服的。

二十年后，当有人提议把更大的决定——职业、伴侣、公民身份、投票——也外包给算法时，你不会抵抗。你的"artifactual"能力不会消失，但它会萎缩，像不用的肌肉。

布坎南在2005年担心的"害怕自由"，可能在2026年已经不是政治问题，而是UX（用户体验）问题。 利维坦这次不穿制服，它穿的是光滑的黑色玻璃。
