item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的洞察：Nvidia 的"自我阉割"与中立性溢价
真正让我震惊的不是 SF Compute 在做什么，而是**Evan 揭示的一个结构性悖论：这个市场之所以能存在，恰恰是因为所有有能力做它的人都做不了**。
Nvidia、CoreWeave、Crusoe、Lambda、Fireworks、Modal——每一家都掌握着做这件事的技术和资源，但他们必须**主动放弃**才能做。因为一旦下场，他们就失去了做市所必需的"中立性溢价"（neutrality premium）——没有中立性，就没有可信价格，没有可信价格，就没有融资曲线，没有融资曲线，整个行业的资金成本就降不下来。
这让我想起**瑞士银行业的发源逻辑**：瑞士之所以能成为资产避风港，不是因为它更强大，而是因为它主动放弃了参与欧洲大陆政治博弈的权利。SF Compute 本质上在做的是——**成为计算市场的瑞士**。"we have to be Switzerland" 这句话不是比喻，是公司的根本架构约束。
更深一层：这揭示了一条规律——**最有价值的基础设施位置，往往需要主动"自残"才能获得**。Visa

item.title: [Business of Sport] Why Domestic Cricket Critics Are Missing the Bigger Picture | Warwickshire CEO
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、酒店即板球：£4700万的"反向补贴机制"

Stuart Cain 最诚实的一句话被埋在中段："Trust me, I'm not" interested in being a hotel。这句自嘲背后藏着一个被观众普遍误读的商业模型——Edgbaston 的酒店投资不是地产项目，而是板球的"隐藏税收"。它不是靠板球养出的利润去扩张酒店，而是反过来：用酒店去反哺一个本质上结构性亏损的 Red Ball 核心产品。

这与大学体育系的"耐克合约 + 校园地产"模式同构，也与欧洲百年剧院靠咖啡厅和会议租赁养话剧的逻辑完全一致。真正令人意外的是：Cain 承认开 Edgbaston 一天要烧 7.5–10 万英镑，而 Worcester 开新路球场几乎不花钱——规模在这里不是优势，而是债务。大球场必须"跑得更快才能站着不动"（run harder to stand still），这颠覆了所有"规模经济"的直觉。

二、板球是唯一把"产品生命周期"倒置的运动

这段访谈最打破常规的洞见不是 Cain 说的，而是他无意间描绘出的一个结构：Phoenix（儿童/家庭）→ Blast（大学与社交饮酒）→ 50-over（成熟期）→ County Championship（退休/半退休）。他本人用了红酒的类比。

但这意味着什么？几乎所有其他职业体育（足球、橄榄球、NBA）都在卖"部落忠诚"——锁定你 7 岁，希望你 70 岁还在穿同一件球衣。板球则承认同一个人在不同人生阶段应该消费不同的"产品 SKU"。这与消费品行业的"消费升级阶梯"（啤酒 → 葡萄酒 → 威士忌 → 陈年酒）、以及奢侈品集团的"品牌金字塔"（LVMH 从香水到高定）完全同构。

真正惊人的是跨领域连接——板球可能是第一项把自己重构为"品牌组合"（brand portfolio）而非"单一品牌"的主流运动。所以 Cain 说他们专门从零售餐饮业挖营销人才，而不是传统体育营销人员。这是一个范式转移的信号。

三、郡锦标赛的"亏损领导者悖论"与体育城市化的拐点

Cain 回答"为什么还要搞郡锦标赛"时的真实逻辑，与好莱坞独立电影经济、F1 的 F2/F3 喂养系列、NBA 发展联盟是同一个长尾产业链结构：最不赚钱的格式制造最值钱的资产（测试队球员 → 天空体育愿意付的转播费 → 整个生态的现金流）。

但真正隐秘的洞见藏在他引用 Neil Rimmer 的那段：体育场正在取代商业园和购物中心，成为新一代城市更新的核心催化剂。伦敦奥林匹克公园、热刺北伦敦、埃弗顿码头、曼城、维拉公园、Edgbaston、Nighthead 的 Sports Quarter——这不是巧合，而是一个后购物时代的城市治理拐点。

购物中心作为"公共空间"的时代结束了（亚马逊干掉了它），人们重新需要仪式性聚集场所，而体育场是少数能同时提供食物、娱乐、身份认同和社区感的空间。Cain 把 Edgbaston 从"六英尺砖墙围起来的 Willy Wonka 工厂"改造成社区中心的做法，本质上是在重新定义体育场作为公共基础设施的角色——这比他说的"多样性"和"社区外展"要深远得多。

四、一个被忽视的制度趋同：会员制 ≈ 德甲 50+1

Cain 把板球的会员所有权模式比作德甲，这个类比值得停下来想一下。越古老的运动项目（板球 1850s、德国足球、英格兰赛马），越倾向于分布式治理；越新兴的职业化运动，越向高净值个人所有者倾斜。这与互联网从去中心化（1990s）走向平台垄断（2020s）的轨迹正好相反。

这暗示：成熟治理结构不是终局，而是一个钟摆。板球可能正在示范一种"后私有化"的所有权模型——既有会员制的合法性，又通过 The Hundred 的 51% 控股安排释放了资本流动性。这个模型可能比英超的沙特/美国私募模式更有长期韧性。

📝 转录文本

Why Domestic Cricket Critics Are Missing the Bigger Picture — Warwickshire CEO

(Business of Sport, interview with Stuart Cain)

Opening — The Hidden Economics of English Cricket

What funds English cricket? It's test match cricket. So unless Warwickshire can create people like Chris Woakes and Jacob Bethell to support that England test team and the England white ball teams, then the game doesn't benefit.

We're building a hotel — £47 million for the new stand. People go "oh, you're more interested in being a hotel here." Trust me, I'm not. The only reason I can fund the cricket is if I find different ways of making money to throw that money to buy players, to invest in the academy, etc.

It frustrates me a bit, if I'm straight with you, because if you look on the pitch, Somerset nearly won the County Championship — they haven't got a Hundred franchise. Off the field, we've got very different infrastructures. It'll cost me £75,000 to £100,000 a day to open Edgbaston. It won't cost Worcester the same amount of money to open New Road that only hosts 3,000 people. Yes, we've got a bigger ground and a bigger capacity, but it costs more to run that.

If you look at Birmingham as a city now, it's really quite vibrant. Villa doing really well in European competition, the Blues on the Sports Quarter, us winning the County Championship, Jude Bellingham investing in the Birmingham Phoenix. And if you add all that to stuff like Ozzy Osbourne and the Peaky Blinders — move over Manchester, you've got Birmingham now.

[music]

County Championship 2026 — "The Ninth Time in Our History"

Fascinating. Stuart, good afternoon. Welcome to the Business of Sport.

Thanks for having me.

Kicking this off, I get to say congratulations. County Championship Winners 2026.

Yes, we are. The ninth time we've won it in our history. I think the first time we entered it was back in the 1850s, so we need to try and increase the hit rate a bit more. But yeah, we won it in '21 after COVID, and winning it again this year was brilliant. The team were amazing — a couple of two-day finishes, some really good ground-out victories. Brilliant effort.

A few wins by an innings. Was that two?

Yeah, there were a couple of days where I saved a few quid on the hotel bills because they didn't have to stay away for four nights — they were coming home after day two. So I'll have to cut the budget a bit for next year and see if they can do the same again. A couple of two-day finishes and innings victories. The bowling unit this year was particularly strong — great to see Chris Woakes still firing, Ethan Bamber coming through. But we had some really gritty performances with the bat as well. If you're playing on wickets that are great for bowlers, they're going to be tough for batters. Sometimes our batters got a bit of criticism, but they got the runs when they needed to and we pulled it off.

It was a competitive finish, wasn't it, the last few weeks?

Yeah, really good — Notts, Somerset and us all in the mix. It kept everyone talking about the championship way after the Hundred, which was brilliant. Somerset would have won it for their first time ever, Notts have only won it a couple of times — they won it twice, I think, if they'd have won it. So there was a nice backstory to all three of us really.

People didn't really see us coming. We came up on the rails a bit, and it was that penultimate game where Notts and Somerset both slipped up a little bit and we managed to get the victory. That was the one where we suddenly thought, "Ah, we're not quite there yet, but we're about 14 points clear — just focus on our own game." Then you sit there wondering, is it better to be a couple of points behind and challenging, or is it better to be on top defending? We did it anyway.

Doesn't really matter.

It kind of doesn't matter now, does it? It was a good day when we celebrated on the Saturday.

What Winning Means for a Members' Club

What does it actually mean for the county when you win?

It's the prestige of it, really. The County Championship is the epitome of cricket — that's what it was all about, that's where it started. And we're a membership organization. Seeing the faces of the members on the Saturday when we won — we let all the fans come onto the pitch, the members came onto the pitch after the game, mingling with the players, getting photographs with the trophy. That hour or two on the pitch was brilliant. There were four or 5,000 members there that day, and hopefully they've got a couple of memories that will last forever. That's what it means for us — winning the ultimate tournament in cricket. Four-day Red Ball cricket. That's what it's about.

Cricket vs Football vs Rugby — The Ownership Difference

How does it compare to other sports you've worked in?

I've worked in football and rugby union. I was involved with rugby league with the World Cup, so I've been around a few different sports. The nuts and bolts are the same: can you create pathways and academies that produce players? Can you build that high-performance environment to succeed? Can you build a business around it — selling tickets, hospitality, shirts?

The business model is not materially different. What's different in cricket is the passion of the members and the way the members own the cricket club. It's got much more of a connection and a family feel than perhaps football and rugby does. I worked at Wasps, I worked at Rangers, I worked at Wolves — the chair or the owner made the decision really. Whether that decision was at odds with the fans or not, the chair had got the skin in the game. They owned it, they were putting millions of pounds a year into it, they made a decision, and then you as an executive had to defend that decision to the fan base.

In cricket, it's a different setup. You are owned by the membership, and ultimately the membership can decide if they don't like you — they'll vote you out. You've seen that at Lancashire, where things have gone on. So you're always very conscious that it's a membership organization and you're just passing through — you'll do your five, six, seven, eight, nine years and then somebody else will come and do it. But the legacy of Warwickshire — it's been around since the 1880s. That tradition is perhaps more front of mind in cricket because of the ownership model.

Demutualization and the Bundesliga Analogy

Fan ownership vs private ownership — that balance is challenging, isn't it?

If you look at the Bundesliga, it's commercially successful as well as having fan involvement at board level. I look at the cricket model a bit like that. People ask me, "You've worked in football, rugby — you've had chairs, high net worth owners — and you've had committees in members' organizations. Which is better?" I go: neither are better or worse, they're just different.

I used to have one chair — he'd ring you every morning at half past seven. You could set your clock by it. I didn't need an alarm clock. The chair would just wake me up, and whatever was on his mind that morning became your agenda for the day. It didn't matter how important your day was — if he had a bee in his bonnet about something, that was it.

A members' organization in cricket is more committee-based. You do have to take a bit longer to make decisions, but at least that acts as a check and a balance.

Why the Hotel — Diversification as Survival

One of the things the game will have to work out: it's getting more and more expensive to develop a stadium. We're building a hotel — £47 million — and a new stand. People go, "Oh, are you more interested in being a hotel?" Trust me, I'm not. The only reason I can fund the cricket is if I find different ways of making money to throw that money over the fence — to buy players, invest in pitches, invest in the academy.

Diversifying is important, but you need capital to diversify. That's where some cricket clubs will say: okay, we need to change. We're fortunate — our financial position means we didn't need to sell all of our Hundred. We've still got 51% control. We've still managed to fund the hotel redevelopment and the stand redevelopment through a combination of Hundred money, some private partnerships, and some funding from the mayor — the West Midlands Combined Authority.

As long as you can still find those ways of financing your business, the cricket model works. If you run out of road in those traditional ways — retail finance, local authority finance, or investment from a catering partner or merchandising partner — that's when it'll get tough. That might be where Yorkshire are at. We're at a point where we think we can sustain the business as long as we can keep test match cricket at Edgbaston — we can sustain the business until at least the mid-2030s.

The Importance of Test Cricket at Edgbaston

Why is test match cricket at Edgbaston so important?

Test match cricket really funds the majority of the cricket game. We host test matches as a contribution — the ticketing revenue goes back to the ECB, which is redistributed to the professional game and the recreational game. We keep a large chunk of the ticketing revenue and the F&B and hospitality revenue. That provides the cash flow for us to operate.

You're working in cycles. We had an India test last year — that's a strong test. Then we had a Pakistan test this year, which isn't quite as strong. Then we've got the Ashes next year. You're planning on five-year cycles — knowing you'll have a couple of years with really strong cash flow from the test matches, which helps subsidize the business in the years when it's not quite so strong. If we didn't have test match cricket, it would probably be difficult to sustain a stadium as big as Edgbaston with 25,000 people. That long-term allocation of test match cricket — and we have the Vitality Blast finals day here as well — gives us some certainty around our cash flow, which allows us to think about capital investment differently.

Planning Horizons — 1–3 Years for Cricket, 5–10 for Business

Edgbaston has to be fit and proper to host top-level cricket — top-level sport. While you're investing now heavily, you're playing a future-proofing game. To consistently guarantee our future revenue streams — required to invest back into cricket but also to build as a business — we have to make these investments now, even if they're not directly performance-related.

On the performance side, cricket's not like rugby or football. You can't buy your way to success because there isn't a transfer market. There might be a player you really want, but they might be on a three-year contract somewhere else. You might have to play a waiting game. You tend to plan your cricket on one-to-three-year cycles, but you'll plan your business on five-to-ten-year cycles — which is why it's really important to work with the ECB on how test matches are allocated. The seven test match venues need enough of the pie to sustain themselves, because that money isn't just for us — it's reinvested back into the wider game, into counties that don't have test match cricket, and into the recreational game. It's important to all of us that that money flows through the ecosystem.

The "Haves and Have-Nots" — Infrastructure Costs Are Relative

On-field equality, off-field disparity?

It frustrates me a bit if I'm straight with you — because if you look on the pitch, Somerset nearly won the County Championship, and they haven't got a Hundred franchise. Northamptonshire won the Blast last year, I think. The game on the field is relatively equal in terms of playing performance.

Off the field, we've got very different infrastructures. It'll cost me £75,000 to £100,000 a day to open Edgbaston. It won't cost Worcester the same amount of money to open New Road, which only hosts 3,000 people. New Road is a beautiful ground — they love going there. One of the best venues in England for cricket. You look over the wicket, you've got the river and the cathedral. It's beautiful. But their business model is materially different.

At those smaller grounds you have smaller infrastructure costs, smaller staffing costs, smaller operating costs. It's all relative. Yes, we've got a bigger ground and a bigger capacity, but it costs more to run that. We have to make more to stand still than some of the other venues do. You've got to give the ECB credit — the way they allocate money around the ecosystem means those smaller clubs can operate on smaller operating costs but still invest in cricket to compete.

What Really Moves the Needle on the Pitch

You need to create winning squads — through the pathway, ideally. Through strong recruitment. We've invested a lot of money in data analytics and recruitment to try and get slightly more science into the way we plan our squads. So while not directly spending on players, you can directly spend around the recruitment structure to identify the best players.

Representing a Diverse Region

One of the big things for us is representation. We're in the middle of Birmingham, in Warwickshire — a very diverse region. One of the things that frustrates a little is that we don't represent the diversity of the region as strongly as we should. We've got over 400 young boys and girls in our pathways, and probably 50 or 60% come from diverse communities in Birmingham, Coventry, the Nuneaton area, etc.

Our ambition now is to get those kids playing in the first-team squads as Bears. So that Warwickshire and the Bears truly represent the people we serve. I don't think we've been as good at that as we could have over the last few years, but we've got some brilliant young players coming through. Dinesh Perera and Hamza Shaikh — Hamza just moved to Leicester this year — but you've got Tazeem Ali still with us, Vance Johnny coming through the ranks. Some really exciting young local players. Jacob Bethell was one of our players, taking the world game by storm. Creating Bears with proper connections to the city and to Warwickshire means people look at them and go, "Hey, I could do that." That'll encourage them to pick up a bat and a ball.

Edgbaston Was a "Spaceship" to the Local Community

When I first joined, Edgbaston was a cracking job — it was in the middle of COVID. There were no fans, no workforce. You sit in the office going, "This is brilliant, easy!" But when you could get out and talk to people, I started knocking on doors in the city and region. Most people said: "Listen, Edgbaston's a bit like a spaceship. It kind of lands six or seven days a year, causes havoc on the roads, and disappears again." It was a bit like Willy Wonka's chocolate factory — literally a six-foot brick wall built around it. If you're a local kid, you got to peer over the wall and wonder what happened in that weird, magical place where this thing called cricket was played.

We've literally knocked all the walls down. We've redeveloped the outside of Edgbaston. We had prayer for 5,000 people at the stadium. There were people who literally lived 50 metres, 100 metres away — I could stand in the hall and see their chimney pots. They'd lived there for 15, 20 years but never once crossed the threshold of Edgbaston. Once we started knocking the walls down, having the vaccine centres, having prayer, opening the stadium for community groups — suddenly people are coming: "Actually, you know what, this is all right." The more open and transparent we can be, the more youngsters we can attract into our pathways and nurture into professionals.

Birmingham's Sporting Renaissance

Lots of good sports teams up there — how does Warwickshire relate?

We work closely. Knighthead invested in Birmingham Phoenix, and they also own Birmingham City FC — they're about to build the Sports Quarter. So we're quite heavily involved with them. We know the guys at Aston Villa really well. A rising tide raises all boats.

If you look at Birmingham as a city now, it's really quite vibrant. Villa doing really well in European competition, the Blues on the up, Sports Quarter, us winning the County Championship, Jude Bellingham investing in the Birmingham Phoenix. Add Ozzy Osbourne and the Peaky Blinders — move over Manchester, you've got Birmingham. You've got culture, drama, music, sport. Coventry City getting promoted into the Premiership is brilliant for Warwickshire because we stretch down into Stratford, Warwick, Coventry.

Joining the Dots Across Sports

Cricket's a summer sport, football is predominantly autumn-winter. Can I get Villa Bears, Blues Bears, Wolves Bears, Coventry Bears coming to watch the cricket? Can I get them going to watch the football clubs? There's a professional women's netball team — the Panthers — we're working with them about how to link Villa, Blues, Bears and Panthers women's teams and Phoenix–Panthers to create a more vibrant women's professional sports scene in the city.

Introducing the Phoenix — Keeping 51% Control

The good thing is we maintained 51%. We always said to our members this was about Warwickshire being able to control the cricket, because we've always played a part in the politics and governance of cricket as one of the founding counties. The membership understood what we were trying to do — it wasn't like we were selling our soul.

We've been able to build a relationship between our membership and the Phoenix that perhaps doesn't exist with some of the other teams. Most of our members — some will never like it, and I respect that, it is what it is — but most are starting to understand that the Hundred isn't a bad game of cricket if you want something slightly different. Go to Edgbaston on a Friday night for the Phoenix: 15 to 20,000 people, people who don't tend to come to cricket generally. The challenge is: how do we get them to come watch the Bears in the Blast? Then when they reach a point in their lives, how do we get them to mature into four-day cricket and 50-over cricket?

Cricket as Red Wine — The Inverted Fan Lifecycle

I look at County Championship cricket as connoisseurs' cricket, really. It's a bit like red wine — you don't really drink it as a kid, you grow into it.

Which is weird, right? Because it's the reverse of how sport generally tries to acquire fans.

If I was treating it like a business, we've got a really interesting lifecycle. A young fan — seven, eight, nine, ten — loves the Phoenix, comes with mum and dad. Then they come to a Blast game as they get older — university friends or mates for a few drinks, social cricket. Then they try the 50-over game. We play at Rugby School, very different to Edgbaston. Then you reach a point in life where you've got four days spare — not everyone has Thursday to Sunday — but as you approach retirement, you've got the time. You could build a pathway for someone from seven years old to their 50s, 60s, 70s and beyond.

In other sports — rugby, football — you're really saying: "Can I convince you to come and watch the same team, the same format, the same competitions for the next 50 or 60 years?" There's a tribalism which is great, but in cricket there are different forms of the game for different times of your life. You might love coming to the Blast when you're single; when you're married with a couple of kids, it might be easier to bring them to the Phoenix. At least you're still watching cricket, still coming to Edgbaston, still convincing the kids to pick up a bat and ball and follow the England team.

Managing a Portfolio Business

For years, Warwickshire was Warwickshire. There was some complexity in explaining different formats, but that was about it. Now the Phoenix is its own entity — it's only five years old and it's got to develop its own DNA. It's very different to the Bears in many ways. Most of the eight owners — the three or four who haven't got majority control — are still working out: how do we build something that lets us promote the Blast and the Phoenix at the same time? You're selling Blast tickets in May–June, then Hundred tickets in July–August.

We've got to learn how to package, present and market both. That takes a different marketing skill — brand portfolio marketing. Look at Ford: the manufacturer is the manufacturer, but there's a dozen different cars in that portfolio, all aimed at different segments. Cricket as a sport is trying to get more sophisticated in its marketing — we'll probably recruit from outside sport. We recruited someone for Phoenix marketing who'd cut their teeth in retail restaurants, where the business had six or seven brands. They knew the portfolio piece — people are going out to eat on a Friday night, but there are seven different brands for seven different audiences. That skill set will probably help us more than a traditional sports marketer who's been chunking out ticket sales for the last 5–10 years.

Why the Hundred Mattered Financially

Why has the Hundred been so important to English cricket's business side?

It's difficult to say, because the ECB did a brilliant job of trying to sustain the 18 counties and the recreational game. A lot of the venues have small stadia — three to five thousand capacity. Generating enough revenue to operate is difficult. Our electricity bill in 2023 was in the hundreds of thousands; it's now in the millions. We have over a thousand people at Edgbaston on a match day. National Insurance, we pay the real living wage not the minimum wage. If we're all doing the same things, the cost of operating has got a heck of a lot more expensive.

Where the ECB deserves credit is the £500 million or so invested in the game through the Hundred investors. If you're a non-host venue, you get more than if you're a host venue, which is probably fair. Worcester will earn more than Warwickshire in terms of capital received. The ECB has put together pretty robust guardrails — it has to be about debt repayment or capital investment. They're trying to keep that money to create a sustainable form of the game in the future.

That's good news for the County Championship — where the culture war kicks in — because people go, "It's Red Ball cricket, that's what it should be about, you shouldn't be playing the Hundred." Well actually, if Derbyshire, Worcestershire, Northamptonshire invest their receipts from the Hundred wisely, hopefully that means they've got much more financially sustainable businesses and can flourish playing County Championship, 50-over and T20 cricket for years. Without Hundred money it would have been trickier — you're relying on ECB central distribution or your own cash flow. If the Sky deal changed in a couple of years, it would create a very fragile operating environment.

Collaboration Among the 18 Chief Execs

The ECB manages that ecosystem really well. The game relies on the governing body to generate the revenue that flows through — probably more so than football and rugby. There's a closer relationship between the governing body and the 18 counties.

They call us the Bears; they call Worcestershire the Pears. If you're a Bear, you're never going to become a Pear — same way a Birmingham City fan is never going to become a Villa fan. You can chat and share best practice. We get together regularly as the 18 chief executives. The ECB's just putting together blueprints for marketing the Blast. We share ideas: "Kent did that really well, could we do that at Warwickshire?" Or: "Warwickshire tried this, didn't work — a few red flags before you try it."

Jude Bellingham as Celebrity Investor

Was there jealousy around securing the Bellingham association?

Jude's been brilliant for us. We did worry a little — is he a Birmingham fan, will that alienate Villa or Coventry fans? We did some research and most people said: "Bellingham is just a Birmingham lad." Hopefully in years to come he'll be a bit like David Beckham — he transcends what club he was at.

Jude and his dad are both really active. They came to some games. We're hopefully going to see them to talk through the high-performance review — we didn't have the best season on the pitch, and he's really interested in how we analyze that. Him and his brother would like to get more involved in insights, analytics and the psychological side of the game. He's a really active investor, which is positive.

Jude as a celebrity investor was spot on for us — it was authentic. He played cricket as a kid. We've got some grainy video footage of him and his brother playing cricket — I think it was Hagley Cricket Club, Stourbridge way, when they were seven or eight. There's real authenticity — both location (he's a Birmingham lad) and the fact that he loves his cricket.

The Tape Ball League

He's involved in the Tape Ball League. Tape ball is a great way of getting into the cities — literally a tennis ball wrapped in tape, from the subcontinent where they play in the streets. We launched the tape ball league with influencers; Dinesh Perera and Jacob Bethell managed a couple of teams. Jude spearheaded it. The association got kids who wouldn't normally be interested in cricket to take a look. Because it was social-media-based, all the content was on social channels — you didn't need a Sky Sports subscription. You could watch on YouTube, engage on Instagram and TikTok. We got kids who love football and Jude to take a look at cricket. Now the challenge: how do we build that into a much bigger initiative across the city and region, and get those kids to cross the Rubicon and come watch a game?

When On-Field Performance Dips — Judging a New Format

Birmingham Phoenix finished last in the men's, second-last in the women's, but Warwickshire won the Championship. How do you balance expectations?

For the investor — Knighthead have owned Birmingham City for four or five years, and anyone who follows a club knows they've had knocks along the way. They said: "Hey, we're not ones to talk about making decisions in high-performance sport. We've learned along the way. We need to trust you to look after the cricket. If it wasn't great this year, understand why and convince us what you're going to do to make it great again."

We've gone through that review. There are changes we're going to make, some things we'll sort out, and you go again. In franchise cricket, because of the auction, there's more churn in the player base — you can change things more quickly than in traditional cricket. We've got a cunning plan.

The Phoenix allows you to develop commercially off the pitch even if you don't perform on it, because it's positioned as a lifestyle product. It's about entertainment, families. Of course you want to be winning — we should be winning and we weren't good enough this year, and we're going to change that. But those who come can still have a great time even if you haven't won. You'll go home: "Yeah okay dad, we lost, but it was still a great day — the DJ was good at halftime, the entertainment was good." It's rooted in high-quality cricket — a world-class tournament — but we've built something around it that makes it attractive to families.

The Role of the Blast in a Hundred World

What's the role of the Blast now?

The Blast is still really important. Two sides to it. First: it's county versus county. The best domestic county players playing each other in the world's top short-format competition. There are great rivalries. I went to Somerset two years ago in the quarter-final — we should have won that game. I walked out that stadium and we lost. I've never been as grumpy in my life. I saw the chief exec of the ECB walking out and refused to talk to him.

Rivalries are being created in the Blast. Somerset–Bears is becoming a real rivalry fixture; Bears vs Pears this year is a rivalry fixture. Giving youngsters coming through county pathways a chance to play the world's most popular short white-ball format — T20 cricket — is really important.

Building Bridges Between Formats

What we've got to do is think about better bridges. Having watched the Blast and seen a player do really well — can they get wild cards into the Hundred? There is a wild card process at the moment, but you could build a bridge Blast-to-Phoenix. Then you're getting into: we've just watched the best of the best from the counties play; now we're watching the best of the best from around the world. Can my best county players hold their own against some of the world's best in the Hundred?

There's definitely a role for two, and there's a narrative. Commercially: the Hundred's only four home games — that's not a summer of cricket. You need your six home games at Edgbaston for the Blast in May–June to really fly. Then a breather for a couple of weeks, then four home games of the Phoenix in late July–August. Ten white-ball games plus the One-Day Cup 50-over games, interspersed with four-day games, gives you something to work with. The 100 games in isolation would be too short a season for white-ball cricket.

Why the Narrative Shift Matters

You need the Blast and the Phoenix to create a summer of cricket. The finals day is now in July — it used to be: play the group phase, then a break, play finals day in September. You lost that narrative. You might lose your overseas players. You've lost the squad that got you to the quarterfinals and the momentum.

Now you've got the Blast playing May–June with its own narrative, completed June–July, then it goes into the Hundred. The Blast story is done — you know the heroes and villains, who won it, you've seen the rivalries, watched it on Sky, been to a couple of games. Then a breather, then the Hundred narrative, which is very different. Two real stories to be told. As a game we've got to make sure the Blast is successful — if you're Worcestershire or Somerset, you need those six home games to fire to generate the revenue to sustain the club throughout the year.

Attendance Across the Formats

What attendance ranges do you expect?

One-Day Cup (50-over) — we play most games at Rugby School. Out-ground cricket, like the Cheltenham Festival. 2,000–3,000 people. Brilliant day out, great atmosphere, beautiful ground.

County Championship — played at Edgbaston. 3,000–5,000 people, predominantly Warwickshire members.

Vitality Blast — about 10,000ish people at a Blast game.

The Hundred — 15,000–20,000.

Test match / One-Day Internationals — maxes out and sells out. Mid-20s.

The County Championship Paradox — Loss Leader or Source Code?

Devil's advocate: the County Championship attracts the least interest, least commercially valuable demographic. Why do we have it?

That misses the picture. We're a members' organization — four or five thousand members, three to five thousand come to watch County Championship cricket. The people who own Warwickshire come to watch County Championship cricket. We've got to make sure we've got a winning team to keep the members who own the club happy.

Then: what funds English cricket? Test match cricket. Most of the revenue attached to the Sky deal probably comes from the Hundred, the Blast, test match cricket and ODIs. Unless Warwickshire can create people like Chris Woakes and Jacob Bethell to support the England test team and the England white-ball teams, the game doesn't benefit — that's when you lose broadcast revenues, sponsor revenues, ticket receipts.

People look at the County Championship wrongly. It should be the birthplace of that test squad. The ECB is trying to build closer links with the counties — probably a bit too disconnected between the Championship game and the test match team. If we can connect that, you could say to a young kid, Jacob Bethell at 16 or 17: "You could be a white-ball superstar and play franchise cricket. Or if you really want to pit yourself against Australia in the Ashes — up there with the Ryder Cup and Wimbledon — then develop your Red Ball skills, play some County Championship cricket, get picked by England, become a global superstar." That's a real pathway, and it all starts in the County Championship.

The Jigsaw View

If I didn't invest in our County Championship squad, perhaps we wouldn't have developed Jacob Bethell or Chris Woakes. If we hadn't developed those, would the England team have been successful? Would Sky have been willing to pay as much?

It's wrong when people look at County Championship as a loss leader. Not everything is about making money. As a chief exec, if I can look at my Warwickshire P&L and link all the pieces of the jigsaw — if I can fund winning teams for men and women that can win the County Championship, compete in the Blast, compete in the 50-over cup — then I'm doing my job. If one costs more money than it makes but another makes more than it costs, and those balance out, and we've got the hotel business coming online, the catering partnership with Levy, the ECB revenues from test matches — if I can make all those parts fit together, I should be able to create a sustainable winning men's and women's team.

The Collar and the Cap

What's good about cricket is there's a collar and a cap. With the Phoenix there's a limit on how much you can spend through the auction. There's a natural mechanism that stops me, Surrey or Lancashire spending three, four, five times more than any other team. We'll all spend slightly differently, but the collar means I've got to invest enough to pay players decent wages and build a squad; the cap means I can't over-invest. That's one of the beauties — anybody can win any tournament. The Blast is 20-odd years old; I don't think many teams have won it twice. There's real parity.

The Women's Game — Investment with a 3–5 Year Horizon

Women's cricket is really important — you can't say you're an inclusive sport if you haven't got a professional women's team or a proper girls' pathway. We lobbied the ECB hard — they did listen, and they wanted to do it themselves. They launched the eight tier-one professional teams a couple of years ago.

Like most women's professional sports, it's still finding its feet. We've got to think about building specific audiences. We're lucky — Knighthead invest in the Panthers (netball) and Blues women's (football); Aston Villa invest heavily in their women's team. There are things we can do together to develop that women's sport ecosystem in the city and region.

Role Models and Earning Potential

Dinesh Perera will be a real star. Issy Wong is back in the England scene — a real star. Role models are emerging who'll attract other girls to pick up a bat and ball. With the Hundred and the Phoenix, you can earn good money as a women's professional cricketer. Youngsters will look at that and go, "Actually, I could earn a living playing cricket."

If you're a 12–14 year-old girl, talented, deciding at school between women's football and women's cricket — a couple of years ago you couldn't see the opportunity in women's cricket. Now with the Women's IPL, the Women's Hundred, the establishment of women's professional county teams, you could earn a good six-figure salary as a young female athlete travelling the world playing cricket. We're on a really exciting journey. It'll take three, four, five, six years to get the pool of elite players up to a level big enough to sustain further growth — which is why it's right to go the slightly restricted route of 8–10 professional teams until the talent pool grows.

The Doubleheader Format Is Working

Attendance at doubleheaders?

We saw the same as you. Slightly more for the men's game, but if we sold 15–20,000 for the men's, we might get 8,000–10,000 for the last half-hour of the women's game. 6,000–8,000 would come in for the start of the women's game because they wanted to watch both. In isolation, still good numbers.

As the summer went on, people came in slightly earlier. Rather than turning up for the last 20 minutes almost by chance, they made a conscious effort to come an hour earlier. The ambition: 15–20,000 tickets sold, everybody arrives at 3pm, watches the women's game as a complete fixture, breather of half an hour, then watches the men's game. For the price of a ticket to watch two world-class professional cricket teams, it's really good value for money.

The Scheduling Problem — Pressure on the Wicket

Can of worms: calendar and scheduling.

The bloke who has to do it at the ECB must sit in a very dark room with a big computer. Five years ago, before the Hundred and before the growth of women's cricket, Edgbaston would host: seven County Championship games, four 50-over games, seven Blast games, plus a men's test and a couple of men's ODIs. Add the Phoenix games on top. Add women's professional cricket. Add a bigger men's international schedule. The pressure on the wicket is phenomenal.

Our ground staff do a brilliant job. You see more hybrid pitches now — the squares last longer because they're half plastic, half turf, like football and rugby pitches. But you have to keep all-grass wickets for some games — test match venues in particular.

Second Grounds

Lancashire have just opened a second ground, Farington. Surrey are looking at a similar thing. We've got a formal relationship with Rugby School where we're playing 50-over games. It'd be interesting to look at whether we could take a County Championship game there, and some women's games. Most of the big international test venues are looking at a second ground to help manage pressure on the wickets.

The Weather App Phenomenon

I came from a world of football and rugby where the weather doesn't matter. I've got about four different weather apps on my phone now — I look at the most optimistic one when I wake up. The one that says there's not going to be any rain — I look at that one all day and ignore the three that do say rain. Sitting there praying it'll be all right, because the quality of the pitch and the weather is so important.

Scheduling as a Marketing Problem Too

At Wasps there was one team called Wasps playing one form of 15-man rugby, in either the Premiership or the European Cup. The only thing you talked about advertising-wise was whether it was Saturday, Sunday or Friday, and whether it started at 3pm or 5pm. At Warwickshire–Edgbaston we're asking: "Would you like to come and watch Warwickshire Bears or Warwickshire play in the T20, the 50-over, the Championship, or the Phoenix in the Hundred?" That's a very different marketing proposition — brand portfolio management. Scheduling has implications on facilities and on how you communicate to cricket fans about what they're watching when, and more importantly how you communicate to non-cricket fans.

Dropping "Birmingham" from the Bears

You dropped Birmingham from Birmingham Bears?

When I joined, Birmingham Bears played the Blast T20; Warwickshire played the 50-over cup and County Championship; and Birmingham Phoenix played the Hundred. My ears are still ringing from the abuse I got from members going: "We're not Birmingham, we are Warwickshire." Then you'd have arguments about what Warwickshire was — there's a political map of the county and a geographical map, both different. Even getting the members to agree about what Warwickshire was was a battle.

I got the message loud and clear. We dropped the Birmingham — it's just the Warwickshire Bears now. The Bears play in the Blast — "Bears" is the shorthand for Warwickshire. A bit like Birmingham City being known as the Blue Noses or the Blues. We've tried to make it belong to the county again, as opposed to Birmingham. That aligns better with the ECB's central proposition for what the Blast is — county versus county, the best county players.

Cricket in the Cultural Fabric

How does cricket contribute to the social fabric?

You can look at it from two angles — the economic impact, and the sport and community.

Economic Impact

When a test match is at Edgbaston, every hotel is full, restaurants are busy, taxi trade is doing well, bars are doing well, the world's media are writing about the city. The economic impact when the World Cup was on in 2019 was about £65 million — more than Aston Villa or the Blues. Not because we're better or worse — just different. If you're a Blues or Villa fan with a season ticket, you live in the city. If you come to watch England play India or the Ashes, you're travelling further, staying in hotels. The economic impact of test cricket is massive, and the global awareness is really important from an inward investment point of view.

I joined in COVID. The first-ever large-attendance sporting event after COVID was played at Edgbaston — the New Zealand test. The only reason we did that was we got the full support of the mayor Andy Street in driving through regulatory approvals. He recognized that even with 12,000 people inside (because of spacing requirements), that's 12,000 people needing hotel rooms, eating somewhere — a way of kickstarting the city's hotel and hospitality industries recovering post-COVID.

Sport as the New Driver of Urban Regeneration

I was at a conference recently about regional regeneration and development. What are sports people doing at a conference about property development? But Neil Rimmer, chief exec of the West Midlands Growth Company, said something I'd never thought about. 30 or 40 years ago, people built business parks to regenerate parts of cities. Then shopping centres and retail parks. Now, whether it's the London Stadium at the Olympic Park, Spurs regenerating a part of London, Everton at the docks, Manchester City regenerating that part of Manchester — Aston Villa regenerating Villa Park, Warwickshire regenerating Edgbaston with the hotel and new stand, Knighthead investing a couple of billion dollars into a new sports quarter — most of the economic regeneration coming out of Birmingham is linked one way or another to a sports stadium. I'd never even thought of that before. Different people are looking at sport through a different lens — as a catalyst for economic change.

Cricket as a Golden Thread

On the community side: if I can get more people picking up a bat and ball, being physically and mentally well through cricket, reaching diverse audiences across the region, then getting them to come together socially at Edgbaston — cricket should just be a golden thread. It shouldn't care what gender you are, what race you are, what religion you are, your level of physical ability. Anybody should be welcome to come and sit at Edgbaston and just watch the cricket. That's our aspiration — and that helps build a few bridges in, let's be frank, a world that is increasingly fragmented.

Closing

A great way to wrap it up. Thank you — really cool to have you.

Pleasure. Thanks for listening to me waffle on for an hour or so.

Not at all. Really appreciate it. Great to hear and congratulations again.

Thank you mate. I've still got the trophy by the bed, so I might have to return it one day.

No, get a replica. Brilliant. Thanks.

Thanks. Cheers.

item.description:
## 一、酒店即板球：£4700万的"反向补贴机制"
Stuart Cain 最诚实的一句话被埋在中段："Trust me, I'm not" interested in being a hotel。这句自嘲背后藏着一个被观众普遍误读的商业模型——**Edgbaston 的酒店投资不是地产项目，而是板球的"隐藏税收"**。它不是靠板球养出的利润去扩张酒店，而是反过来：用酒店去反哺一个本质上**结构性亏损**的 Red Ball 核心产品。
这与大学体育系的"耐克合约 + 校园地产"模式同构，也与欧洲百年剧院靠咖啡厅和会议租赁养话剧的逻辑完全一致。真正令人意外的是：Cain 承认开 Edgbaston 一天要烧 7.5–10 万英镑，而 Worcester 开新路球场几乎不花钱——**规模在这里不是优势，而是债务**。大球场必须"跑得更快才能站着不动"（run harder to stand still），这颠覆了所有"规模经济"的直觉。
## 二、板球是唯一把"产品生命周期"倒置的运动
这段访谈最打破常规的洞见不是 Cain 说的，而是他**无意间描绘出的一个结构**：Phoe

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] How AI Is Repricing Every Software Company
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Vanta 正在"反向定价"——它是 AI 时代第一家公开承认"我吃掉 token 成本"的公司，这不是认输，而是一场精心设计的"去金融化"反击

大多数讨论 AI 定价时都在争论 token、credit、outcome 哪种模式胜出。但 Christina 揭示了一个被所有人忽视的结构性真相：一旦你按 token 收费，你就自愿把自己放到了与 Anthropic/OpenAI 的同一张比价表上。用户会立刻问："你这个 token 是不是 Claude 的 4 倍价？那你有没有 Claude 的 4 倍好？"——这是定价学中最致命的"参照系陷阱"。

这里有个让人意外的推论：token 定价本质上是把应用层公司"商品化"的加速器。它表面上让你看起来像 AI 公司（高增长、使用量计费），实际上把你的毛利永远锚定在模型厂商的成本曲线上。Vanta 选择"吃掉成本、保持 SaaS 定价"，不是因为传统，而是因为她看穿了这件事：在模型成本每 12 个月下降 10 倍的世界里，吃亏是一次性的，而被商品化是永久的。

二、跨领域连接：Billboard 失守 ≈ 2011 年的"下拉刷新"按钮 ≈ 今天的 post-training 营销 —— 都是"形式还没演化到位时的伪创新"

Christina 自己说漏了一个精彩的类比：她把"把 model 交付给客户"比作"2011 年我们还没发明下拉刷新"的那个时期。但这个比喻其实可以延伸成一个更宏大的框架——

凡是在新技术扩散早期出现的"看起来专业但本质是炫耀"的做法，几乎都会在 24 个月内被更简洁的形式取代。 Post-training 一个模型给企业客户，就像 2010 年给手机 app 加一堆 skeuomorphic 皮纹纹理一样——它满足的是"我们认真做了 AI"的信号传递，而不是用户的真实需求。

更隐秘的连接：Billboard 合同用蜡笔写、没有多年锁定条款的那个故事，其实和 token 定价是同一个认知失败——都是在"社会证明 (social proof)"面前，忘了问"合同到底写了什么"。Vanta 在 billboard 上吃过的亏（以为锁了多年其实是 placement order），和整个行业现在在 token 定价上吃的亏（以为抓住了 AI 红利，其实把毛利让给了 lab），是同一种结构性盲视：用叙事代替结构审视。

三、系统性真相：法国公司全线切换中国模型，不是地缘政治，而是"业务连续性"——这预示了 AI 时代最被低估的 moat 是"主权冗余"

当 Christina 以为法国人用中国模型是反美情绪时，被纠正："不，是因为 Trump 把 Fable 对非美国人关闭了，我们意识到不能把业务建在单一美国模型上。"

这是整个访谈最被低估的 10 秒钟。它揭示了一个所有 AI 应用公司都在回避的问题：你的"AI 原生"架构，正在变成你的"主权依赖"架构。

跨领域连接：这和 1970 年代石油危机后，日本汽车厂商决定在美国本土建厂（避免贸易战）是同一逻辑；也和 2000 年代半导体厂商从"台积电单一依赖"转向"多 fab 策略"同构。AI 应用公司下一轮分化不会按"谁用的模型最好"展开，而会按"谁的 model routing layer 最抗冲击"展开。

而最深的洞察藏在 Christina 的策略里：她不 post-train，不绑定单一模型，吃掉 token 成本——这三件事表面独立，实际上是同一件事：保持对模型层的最大可替换性。 她在构建的不是一个 AI 产品，而是一个"模型无关的信任层"。当 CrowdStrike、Wiz 这些公司还在用传统 security 范式打仗时，Vanta 已经把自己定位成"AI 时代的信任中介"——而信任中介的核心价值，恰恰来自于它不绑定任何一方。

这是一个让人意外的终局猜想：Vanta 真正的 TAM 不是 security compliance，而是"AI 时代的第三方可信验证"——未来每个企业都会被要求证明自己的 agents 没干坏事，而 Vanta 正好站在"证明这件事"的管道中央。她说"expansive"是未来五年的关键词时，可能连她自己都还没完全意识到有多 expansive。

📝 转录文本

开场：Token 定价的陷阱

"We have talked to our customers a lot about token based pricing and I think what we've generally heard — people are real smart."

If you try to charge them based on tokens, they are very quick to say: "Oh, you've just marked up a Claude token 4x — are you 4x as good as Claude? I don't know, let me go try it out." You actually put yourselves in a competitive position against the models. And so what we've seen on token pricing is: if you're trying to mark up at all, users are very smart and you will lose on that comparison.

Vanta 简史：从 SOC 2 到信任平台

So, Christina, I've been so excited to do this with you. I think it's been five years since we last did it. So a lot a lot has happened — a lifetime ago. You've been very successful in the intervening 5 years. Can you give us the one-minute history of Vanta?

Started Vanta about 8 years ago — which was about 8,000 years ago, you're like 17 centuries ago — with the premise of: can we help companies build and earn trust? Build trust meaning start security programs and compliance programs, or mature them, and then go get credit from their customers through audits like SOC 2 or ISO 27001 and HIPAA, questionnaires, trust centers. But basically this idea of: can we build a security company by helping companies implement security, because it's what their customer is asking for.

We're initially known for SOC 2. We had a billboard — we do have a billboard on the 101 that... we're mostly known for making billboards, I joke. But it started very compliance-, very audit-centric. The idea was always: that's just one way to get a company started on this. Since then we've gone into different areas of security, different ways of earning trust with your customers. Today we're about 16,000 customers global with about five products.

如何赢下这个品类？执行、集成、数据底座

How did you win? This was a new category when you started.

Execution. Software is a blessing and a curse — and this is more true now than it was 5 years ago — you're really only as good as the last thing you shipped. You can be first and start it, doesn't really matter. Someone can vibe-code your thing in a weekend. You've got to constantly be shipping new products, new features that make the experience better for customers, and running on that differentiation.

The other thing we really invested in when it got competitive was integrations — pulling in data from other tools. Now you can connect Vanta to one of 400 tools. We pull a ton of data out of those tools, and that's what powers the automation, the agent, the AI, all of that. We call it our trust graph. It's really just a security data lake, and it is bigger and broader than any other provider — including some of the security providers — because we touch areas they don't. In retrospect, that data foundation has let us build new things faster.

Then on the go-to-market side: just push good billboards. Like shockingly good — "compliance that doesn't suck too much" — which got really popular on r/accounting, which none of us knew was a bucket-list item in our lives. But when r/accounting likes your things, you're like, okay, something worked.

最惊险的时刻：SaaS 末日论下的认知失调

What was the scariest moment? The last 12 months — SaaS apocalypse — you're like, "Great job building a system of record, you're now screwed, you're now worthless."

You're worth like... good job playing the game, here's some steak knives. Parts of that are true and parts are not. But again, in the vein of "you're only as good as the last thing you shipped" — great, so what is the agent? You have all this data in a system of record. Fine. What the heck are you doing with it?

认知失调：旧估值模型 vs 新估值模型

Vanta is a business growing very fast by historical standards, with very high margins. Four years ago that was considered the best business model ever. Nothing changed about that — if anything you're growing faster and margins are still really high. And yet the market has decided that the multiple for a business like yours is a third of what it used to be, or a quarter.

Cognitive dissonance — you've got to hold two things in your head:

  1. In the fullness of time, an 80%-growth business with 80% margins will be good — and actually better than, over the same time period, a 160%-growth business with 30% margins. One of these will return more cash in the fullness of time.
  2. But today the latter is valued at 3x, 4x, 10x the multiple of the former.

There's a part where you're like, "Hey guys, everyone's being irrational here." Then there's the game on the field — if you need to be financed, you're looking at investors today, many of whom are AI maximalists: "We'll invest in the labs and we'll basically invest in tractors in Iowa" — robo-tractors in Iowa and a lab, and nothing in between. Interesting point of view.

From a talent perspective: you hire ambitious people who want to do things, and if it feels like they're not in the right boat, they're going to change boats. The talent war part is very real. You've got to live with: in the fullness of time, this will all sort itself out. And you have to live for the fullness of time.

Vanta 是不是一家 AI 公司？

"The siren song right now is: sell tokens via agents for security and compliance."

So, do you think of yourself as an AI business?

We do. When we benchmark where we are from an agent-in-product perspective against "AI applications," we have yet to find someone further along. You could say we're doing a bad job looking — that's the obvious critique — but we are constantly going to the set of names you imagine when you think "AI applications," and generally finding they're not yet where we are, where an agent is doing most of the work.

The agent is chat-based, but there are long-running agents. Our agent is auto-generating UI on the fly — sometimes you want chat, sometimes you want UI, so we just have an agent that builds UI, the user does something, comes back in the flow, keeps it going. Very much optimized around keeping the user in the flow loop.

一个具体例子

Someone just left your company and you didn't take them out of all their accounts. "I just wrote a custom agent for you that will go do that. Do you want me to turn this on? Great. Do you also want me to remove access from these three people? Great. Do you want that running always?"

It's not just "here's a red alert that someone didn't meet the monitoring step." It's: "Would you like me to go do this? Do you want me to do this once? Do you want me to do this always?" The agent will just be doing more of this work with the user's permission.

Token 定价、毛利与"输出 vs 结果"

In the course of that we end up using a lot of tokens. People are real smart — if you try to charge them based on tokens, they are very quick to say: "Oh, you've just marked up a Claude token 4x — are you 4x as good as Claude?" You put yourselves in a competitive position against the models.

We're eating the token cost right now. We're taking lower margin, and honestly, we concentrate on usage. That experience where the agent is going off and doing things — we fundamentally believe that is a much better user experience. We have maybe 25% of our customers in that flow right now. If we can get that to 75%, we have much better net retention. If we need to sort out pricing later, we'll sort it out later. This is a usage phase and a deployment phase of this technology. Just go nail that; you can figure out commercialization after.

关于定价的终局

Everyone wants to get to outcome pricing — or if you talk to a pricing person, they'll tell you it's actually output pricing. In another life I was a microeconomics professor; I love this conceptually. The hard part is: what are the outcomes?

Support ticket closed — maybe that's the output; the outcome is actually "my Sonos now works." Even ticket closed is relatively unobjectionable. A lot of companies, included, are trying to figure out: what's that neat unit of work we can all agree on? Document drafted, alert closed, account offboarded? Sure, but then there's so much cognitive overhead — "if I do this with the agent I pay this, but if I do that..." No one wants that.

Token charging puts you up against Claude. People try to obscure that by charging credits and having a credit-token exchange rate — but users are smart, and they're like: "I see what you're doing. I see you've obscured it."

用 AI 建设 Vanta 自身：遗留代码库的挑战

How would you grade yourself on building the business using these tools?

It's so much easier to throw coding agents at a small codebase than a large one — that's a token-input thing. One thing we've invested in in the last year — and Notion has spent a bunch of time on this, they were nine months ahead of us — is modularizing parts of the codebase so the agent can understand smaller parts fully and be really effective.

If you chuck it at an 8-year codebase sight unseen, it doesn't have the context window to understand everything and will do silly things. Then you need a high-context engineer to babysit it — which sort of invalidates the point.

Companies have always had this problem. They've just talked about it as: "Oh, when we onboard a new engineer it takes them a while to figure out the codebase." Agents have made it: "Great, now we want to onboard 9,000 new engineers tomorrow."

On a scale of 1–10 for "this changes everything"? 8 or 9. The principles are still the same — everything is hard, people matter — all the tropes are still the tropes. But the way you do stuff should be quite different.

采用 AI 的"101 课程"：先用起来

What's been hard but fruitful?

Just getting people to use it. Sounds obvious, but: definitely use it yourself. Build for your company personally. Does not matter — just understand where the models are, where they're good, where they're bad, what harness means. Do that at least every two weeks because it changes so quickly. You have to have a visceral understanding of what works and what doesn't, so when somebody comes and says "we're going to fire all of our SDRs because I built one agent," you can be like: where is that true and where is that false?

Onboarding Wizard 的教训

If you're a larger company, you clearly run a security and compliance program. You come to Vanta for visualization, automation, monitoring, real-time dashboards. The hard part is you've got to get all that existing stuff — controls, risks, data, policies, procedures — into Vanta.

Classically, SaaS companies build an onboarding wizard: four steps, a progress bar, confetti. We set out to build better onboarding this year, and the first couple of product reviews, the team kept bringing onboarding wizards. "Stop with the onboarding. Go use an LLM. Stop." But they kept bringing onboarding wizards.

The experience they finally shipped is basically Claude — a big canvas: drag all your messy files in, drag in all your screenshots. We make sense of it, ask you questions, and then you're set up. Why were these smart, motivated people bringing onboarding wizards? Because they said: "We don't know if we can get the drag-your-files thing to work. We know the onboarding wizard will work because we've built those before — and we don't think we're allowed to fail on this project."

"Oh, that's the thing. Great — we're going to bet the LLM flow is going to work. We will make it work. We will hill-climb all we need to. Burn the boat and just make this thing work."

100 亿、人才战争与估值

Now every business needs to be a $100B business. What's that like?

It's funny — I think about: should I adjust the pitch and say "well, inevitably the baseline here is Vanta's $50 billion, the real question is can you take us to $250 billion"? Should I just start saying that? Probably not, but the answer is not definitely not.

There's a Vanta principle: do what it says on the tin — do what you say you're going to do. You can put ambitious things on the tin — that's not it — but don't overpromise and under-deliver. Give context: here's what we do as a company, good, bad, and different. Then talk about business metrics — we show candidates everything. Walk them through what we're doing and how it grows over time. Counter the vibes with data and trustworthy vibes versus YOLO vibes.

薪酬

How much more do you pay the top person at Vanta than you did five years ago?

Total comp — probably a factor of 10. And honestly, I think it should be higher. My general comp philosophy: you never pay the top people enough. There's a bunch of people you pay much more than their contribution.

What are those top people doing that's so valuable? High agency. Get-done. Sounds milquetoast, but yes — a high-context person who understands the company, the customers, the domain, making generally reasonable decisions, sometimes bad ones, iterating on their bad ones, and just moving — is so valuable.

Will it be 10x again in five more years? Accelerating. The counterforce is: when will investors get concerned about dilution and stock-based comp? We had that conversation in 2022–23; we're definitely not having it now.

估值与 tender

I've historically not cared about valuation and multiple — even done things to demonstrate my not caring. I care about ARR and ARR growth. I've been through enough valuation environments — 2010s, 2021, 2022 — seen the multiple roller coaster, so I don't put a bunch of stock in that.

Tenders? We haven't done them historically, but that is the game on the field. Does this feel unhealthy? Totally. But my opinions about it sort of don't matter — they're normalized and people expect them as part of comp. If you're not giving it, you've got to give them a bunch of other stuff to make up for it.

过度炒作与被低估的

Underhyped: Knowing the company and the customers relative to knowing the skill set. It is still really hard to hire, train, onboard, make effective people who join a company. We value and compensate "knows the Vanta pieces" more than vertical skill. As labs and fast-rising AI companies build out go-to-market teams, they're very much evaluating "you're a good salesperson" — I think that's slightly off.

Overhyped: - Token-based pricing. - Low margins for the sake of low margins. - Custom-training models for the marketing value. If you talk to inference providers and they give you true CRM, they'll say: the reason to post-train is cost. There's no quality reason. There's a marketing reason — for investors, mostly for investors actually.

The pitch for post-training: "You are putting a stake in the ground of being a real AI company that customers — like, investors — will notice." There's a secondary one in large enterprises: it's easier to deploy wall-to-wall if you hand them a model specific to them. But: does everyone really want to be handed a model? It feels a little like 2011 before pull-to-refresh — we haven't figured out how this actually works. Handing models is not the right reasonable iteration, not the right solution.

FDE 们

I think FDEs are crazy — or actually, I think it's a great talent arbitrage, the same way "chief of staff" often is: it's professional services. But if you called it a professional services role, that's a very different talent profile than FDE in the current discourse. You're not going to get the Harvard CS grad who's high-agency and wants to learn how to build a business to be pro-serv person #4 or #12 at a company. The company we all think does this well is Palantir — they have eight-figure contracts. We're using FDEs where contracts are five and six figures and those economics are probably upside down.

旧金山晚餐桌上的话题

Talent war pieces — nine months ago it was the joy of going around the table complaining about Cursor and their taking of everyone. There's always a "Cursor of the moment."

FDEs — do you actually do this? Is it working?

Personal agents right now — which ones do you have, what's actually useful?

中国模型与法国客户

I was with our customers in France a couple weeks ago. I was very surprised that a lot of French software companies in Paris are using Chinese models predominantly. I initially thought it was sort of nationalism, maybe anti-American — and stupidly suggested that. Someone very quickly corrected me:

"Absolutely not. We basically all switched to Chinese models when Trump closed Fable off to non-Americans, and we just realized there's a huge business continuity risk. We can't trust that if we build a business on one of these American models it'll always be available. So we stopped doing that."

Vanta 的 $250B 愿景

If you dreamed about where this could go...

We think of Vanta as a security company. Started with compliance, but the best version of compliance is proving the security you have. You've got to have good security.

We're moving into a bunch of security domains. Platform pitch: we've already got the data, the intelligence via the agent — we can start stacking security-focused products on top. As we understand the security of all these companies, the pressure on them to prove they're legitimate and industrial-grade is going to go up. That was a founding thesis 8 years ago; it feels even more true now. Whether working with enterprises, governments, regulators, lawmakers — you have to prove your software is industrial-grade in lots of ways. Vanta is the thing that connects both sides of that marketplace.

安全的未来

These models are so much more persistent than people. They'll try nine quadrillion things, where a person would give up after 9,000. In the course of that, they find things and chain things together.

A lot of the discourse is around zero-days. What's actually happening is these models chain 17 benign-ish things together and really find something. The OpenAI talk at RSA about Hugging Face is basically that: persistence plus putting together things that on their own people would have said "low severity, I'll fix it in 90 days."

That turns prioritization on its head. Saying everything is critical isn't helpful. If you're fixing things at machine speed, you sort of don't have to prioritize. That's where we're going to get to. It'll be rocky.

The ultimate product vision — a constant penetration test, a white-hat agent trying to break in all the time, and every time it finds something, a buddy agent patches it. We can do that in compelling ways for the bulk of our customers. CrowdStrike will do it better for an enterprise — choosing where you play matters.

个人动机的演变

How has your motivation changed?

In the beginning I had a lot more of the feeling: "People think I can't do this, I think I can, and I'm going to show them." I still have that — "you don't think Vanta's going to be $250B, let me show you" — but there's less of a dark edge. More: "Oh cool, we got here. Now we're just going to see how far we can run" in a way that feels a bit more fun and joyful.

Most surprising skill I developed: I like go-to-market more than I ever would have guessed. I was a terrible public speaker — got most nervous in front of my own team because I cared most what they thought. Exposure therapy was helpful.

The trope "no one remembers what you say but they remember how you felt" — it is so annoying but so true. If I just get up and it's content I feel like is content-less, I'll feel that way and it will be obvious to everyone. Try to put real content in and hold in my head: no one's going to remember any of these facts. Heart matters more than mind. The key: authenticity. People can tell when you're going through the motions or misleading yourself.

智能体先行的权衡

We've tried to build in an agent-forward way. We don't want to build a bunch of SaaS UI — "you want reporting? Our agent will go make charts for you on demand based on all of our data." We're not going to put Tableau inside of Vanta, which is probably what we would have done in 2021–22.

But: a US enterprise we were trying to close basically said, "Hey, maybe we want your AI features, maybe we won't — but can you turn them off for now?" Why? Because it's way easier to get a non-AI tool through procurement, and we want you in — turn it on after we're in. And we don't really have an off switch. You're like, "Gross, we don't want to build that off switch — we'd rather spend the time on something useful." But those trade-offs are real.

投资视角

Where would you be focused if you were investing right now?

Oh, I do not envy the job at all right now. On the investor side it feels more echo-chambery, more judged on incremental returns and paper returns than on the company side.

The labs and inference providers, apparently — high entry prices. The discourse and the certainty around open-source model providers, and the lack of tooling and companies around them, feels disconnected. We've all decided open-source will be very real, but the ecosystem around them is so much less built out than around the big labs. That feels off. A bunch of lab playbooks should apply to open-source models, and it's just less mature.

Green shoots: - A bunch of people starting security/cyber companies. - Attacking rev / go-to-market technology. - Robotics is probably underplayed — the models are getting real damn good there.

政府与现代化

Over the past couple of years Vanta has spent more time with governments — federal, state, local, inside and outside the US. There's an appetite for modernization. The AI piece has created more FOMO in government officials: they may have always known they didn't have modern processes, but it feels more imperative now.

The broader point: all the conversation around AI has upped the priority of a lot of modernization. CISOs' jobs are changing because of AI — "given AI and the risks from agents, I'd like to overhaul my enterprise risk program and I would like budget for that." Three years ago people would say "we'll talk about it maybe." Because it's attached to AI, they're much more likely to get budget today.

招聘推销

Why come work at Vanta right now?

Fun stage. 16,000 customers using a product, using agents. When you ship things, they're in use by real people getting real feedback instantly. It has product-market fit. You're going and experimenting with fast iteration loops, but early enough that you can still move.

Billboard 大战：完整版

I was always a billboard skeptic — the tracking is terrible, "founder ego" was why someone would do a billboard. I feel cool because my company has a billboard. So I was anti-billboard.

Mid-summer 2021, SaaStr conference, felt like a big deal at the time. Our marketing team decided to try out-of-home. I was super skeptical but — fine, whatever, try it.

Sarah, our PMM, came up with "Compliance that doesn't suck too much" and pitched our head of marketing, who didn't like it — thought we were negging our users. Sarah believed in it and came to me — which she usually doesn't do, she's not a go-around-her-boss person. I read it and immediately texted Andrew Reed, our investor: "What do you think? You have good internet-meme taste." He loved it. Let's run it. Worst that happens: people think we're obnoxious and forget in six months.

We stand up the billboard somewhere near Burlingame. Goes over so well. We tweet it. Tweet goes viral. Ends up on r/accounting as a funnel.

Why did it work? It's our brand at its best: we take our work seriously but we don't always take ourselves seriously. It was a little obscure — but sufficiently obscure that if you got it, you felt like you got a secret.

失守

22 market crashes. Turns out there's a lot of billboard inventory on the 101. We get this great spot where 101 and 280 intersect — great spot for not that much, especially in retrospect. We joke: "Oh yeah, we've locked it up for years." Even on a podcast I said the contract was locked up for years. It was not locked up for years. But that billboard got famous.

People would contact Sarah: "How do you do billboards?" We'd refer them to our guy. Referred this guy millions of dollars of business. "It's him. It's him. It's him."

Turns out in the background we did not have a multi-year contract — which I should have checked, certainly if I was going to say that on a podcast. Not really do what it says on the tin. The contract was basically: "You've put the billboard up. That's it." Not a contract at all.

Multiple years go by. Sarah's at dinner with a friend who works at a startup. Friend says, "Oh, it's so sad you guys gave up that billboard spot — why'd you do that?" Sarah: "Pardon?" "Oh yeah, we just signed for your spot."

Sarah's like: "What?! We'll go back. Contract — contract." Contract written in crayon. There is no contract. It's a placement order. Called the guy — "Yeah, you know, it's a placement order, they paid more." Swapped it out underneath us.

I go to the founder of said company: "Hello — how much can I pay you? I am an extremely inelastic buyer here." "Nothing." "How about I double? He was paying like $1.5M — how about I give you $3M just to get this spot?" "We're actually cash flow positive." Literally no inelastic seller.

We lost the spot.

Things that made me think "Oh no, Vanta's screwed" — honestly, losing that billboard, I was like: we did probably just lose a billion of market cap. Bad omen — and some vibesy market-cap decrease just happened here.

结语：高兴奋 + 低信任的时代

What might I have missed? You see it in the data-center conversations, in the personal-agent stuff: we just don't trust software companies, tech companies, the way we used to. It's getting worse year over year. Hard to imagine it inflecting back up to the useful optimism of 15 years ago.

Companies showing they are trustworthy, industrial-grade and secure — through metrics and definitions — is more important than ever, and will get more important. Vanta at $250B is in the center of all those transactions.

AI has ushered in extremely high excitement but low trust. Vanta's job: preserve the excitement, but increase the trust — legitimately, not just on vibes.

What will satisfy the market to trust again? In B2B context, it's a real data piece: specific improvement curves, promises with contracts behind them. Rational, the way enterprise markets often are. On the consumer side it is vibes — and that one seems very hard to turn.

Do you trust the big consumer platforms with your data? No. It's not that there's anything particularly interesting in my email or chats — my life's not that interesting — but I'd rather just Google, or just Apple, or just insert-company-here have that information.

五年后的安全

Faster. More intense. More offensive — hopefully — in that: yes, we'll have more attacks, but you need more white hats pushing back. To get to that speed, you've got to get the human decision-making out — or humans architect systems and write rules, but don't make every single decision. Writing evals. Maybe that's all we're doing in the future — all writing evals all day long.

One word for the next five years of Vanta? Expansive. We have this incredible base of customers, of data, and now we get to go build things on top of that. It took 8 years to get here. We could go just build stuff on top of it for the next five or eight.

"It's so cool that we did this 5 years ago. So here we are again. Thanks so much for your time."
