底板被降，天花板由人来抬：设计即新代码

I'm going in a world of AI, agentic AI, I have this capacity to prompt as a human and say, I want to make something that looks like, feels like, and does X. And this magical technology takes off and does it. And I end up with a product. Sometimes the product is great. Sometimes the product sucks, but it's improving the ability for these tools to do that. Historically, I would have needed a product manager, a designer, a bunch of engineers to do the actual building of the product, whether it's a software product or a hardware product. Increasingly though, it seems like AI is doing more and more of those tools. Can you just give me your view on the future of human creativity in this era? This future era that we're walting into, the singularity we're falling into. Where does human creativity play a role? And where do the gaps still need to be filled for taking human creativity to the realization moment?

It's the case, I think, that uh we're lowering the floor with AI, making it so that all of the production, whether it's code or it's uh motion, video, design, whatever you name it, uh if it's digital, you're lowering the floor to make it happen. Um everyone can be part of that and it's more democratized. Ironically, and I I used to believe uh even a few years ago, I said it our annual user conference config. I said the ceiling will be raised by AI. You'll be able to do greater things than me before. That was wrong. Uh the ceiling has stayed the same. AI is not raising the ceiling. Humans are raising the ceiling though. uh the creatives, the designers out there, when they choose to focus, invest their time, and to be bold and try to do something that no one else has ever done before, that's when we see the ceiling raised. And at that point, uh it's a question of do you care about being in the center distribution? Do you care about like a mean or average result? Uh is that sufficient for your task? or do you need something that shows that you care that you took the time to actually like go make this thing? Do you need to go and be beyond uh what is the minimum bar? And in the world of software design and product I mean we're seeing exponentially more software than ever before. It's exactly what you'd predict. The exponential continues. Uh you look at app store uh numbers. the app store numbers are exactly that same exponential and we're seeing that the usage and utilization of apps flat. So people are using just the amount same amount of apps but the amount of apps that you can get it's like bigger than ever and growing. And I think it just speaks to okay there's a need to differentiate yourself if you're building any kind of software. Well how do you do that? It's not code because anyone can create code now. That's not the hard part anymore. So my view is design is the new code. It's the layer above. You have to make it so that your design is differentiated and you have to have a point of view and a good brand in marketing. And the point of view I think is the part that is probably missed the most.

That's the human part.

It's not just the human part. It's also the part that humans are uncomfortable having. Uh, I think that folks are scared to say something that's not consensus.

It's so true. I mean, this is what the greatest artists, the greatest business leaders, the greatest politicians have always demonstrated is the willingness to to be brave to say and do the things that no one else would say or do. And that's what changes the world.

And I would also add comedians to the mix too.

And comedians,

comedians are underappreciated. I had Tony Hinchcliffe fight our thing last year because he's like one of the few guys that is willing to say and do things nowaday in the cancel culture era

but comedians often like speak truth in a way that people otherwise couldn't hear

willing to say things

and uh it's not about political correctness. It's about do you have a message that can rise above the noise and do so in a sustained way? Because look at social media right now. Like every unique point of view, everything interesting, it gets diffused into like the ether of social media instantly. And so unless you've got uh something that allows you to kind of keep generating content and a message that is really uh evergreen because it's so outside of the over 10 window, you're not going to be able to actually break through and have any attention. And the attention economy is ruthless.

Is this also what human creativity is? If you're not doing something that's never been done before, you're not creating something. You're mimicking something. You're copying something. You're xeroxing something. But to do something new is to create. And newness requires doing things that have never been done before

by definition.

By definition,

and uh therefore you are operating outside of this distribution of training. It's not even about operating outside the mean of the distribution which is where you start if you're just prompting without any like any kind of advanced scaffolding around it. Uh but you're actually doing something that is breaking through and it's unique and I do think that will be rewarded by the market. Everyone's going to see it. I think it's even rewarded by the attention market of organizations. I'm already hearing from so many like uh I got another deck made by AI today.

"Written with AI"：Figma 的信任标签

Totally. And I don't even know if the person who made it, I like don't know if they read it. Do they even know what's in their deck?

And at Figma, we actually made it so that uh it was just a simple thing, but we said, "Hey, if you are uh using AI in your writing of any kind, just put at the top written with AI." Very simple, very easy to follow. Uh and you know, people made jokes about internally, but people do it. And it makes it so that we can all trust that when we see something, we know that it's been cared for enough that it's like worth your time to process. And I uh I think that we're going to see some bifurcation here around trust. Uh and one way to get trust is to do something with your hands. The other point that's important is if you have a vision or if you have a point of view in your head of how something should be designed or look aesthetically or from an experiential standpoint, you're I I think it's great to start with building with AI. It gives you something to get past like the blank page, blank canvas problem. You can then react to it and say, "Here are all the things I don't like. I'm gonna I'm gonna go fix these things. I'm going to change them up." because it's really helpful to have a back and forth. But if you don't if you have your own vision and you're trusting AI to implement it, you're doing it through the lens of AI and like AI has kind of like its own distribution

the model fit by it. Yeah.

Yeah. And so you're not going to get exactly what you want. Now if you're able to do both and that's what we're trying to enable in Figma make code a material on the canvas make it so that you can go start by building you can build to think if you like uh but also when you want to think and work with your hands you can do that too

right

回望 Photoshop：图层争议、滤镜革命与真正的颠覆者

I remember the early days of Photoshop just having been a user avid user from the early days people freaked out when layers happened and then they freaked out when all the filters came out and when Kai's power tools came out, everyone was like, "What's the role of the photographer anymore?" It's like you're destroying the art of photography, the creativity of photography. But it unleashed a new era of creativity because now these new artists emerged that could use these filters and use these layering tools and capabilities to reimagine what's possible on a canvas. And it was basically a new toolkit. doesn't mean that the old creatives mapped perfectly to the new creative system and tools, but there was an explosion in creativity and human potential that arose from this and we pushed boundaries in all sorts of ways. Feels like we might be entering that era again.

I'm a big believer in that and I think that part of it is what I described about market dynamics. In order to get attention, order to get engagement, in order to get people to care, you have to do something new. uh you have to actually be daring and try things that are bold. The resistance to change is real and there's a great thing you can Google actually for your point. Look up the mailing list for when layers was introduced and it's like people going this is the worst thing ever. Uh and you can find it if you Google it's like on a a mailing list that's publicly available and you can see all their reactions. Totally. Um, but obviously it became the future and I think that uh there's also still photographers in the world who are doing incredible work. But the bigger disruption, if we're going to be real, it was the camera phone. Uh, that was what made it so that people stopped buying cameras that were dedicated to the task of photography because the best camera is the one that's on you and started treating photography in a different way with Instagram and their camera phone. Uh so it transformed for a lot of people and I can't tell you if it's better or worse as a result. Uh but there was change.

创造力、神经科学与"问题解决"的双螺旋

There's one view on human creativity that human creativity is basically connecting dots in the unconscious that you've had, seen or experienced all of these things in your life or in your set of inputs, sensory inputs and from those inputs you connect dots and then you extrapolate a forward view of things that hasn't perhaps been seen in the world before. Do you agree with that view on creativity and is it distinct from actually what AI does? And again, I want to go back to the uniqueness of the human in an AI era.

Well, I I think that um one thing that happens with humans is they're always seeking novelty. Like our reward function is different than like an AI. Also, our loss function. Like if I was to open this bottle of water and splashed all over you and you got mad at me, like you bet I'm not gonna do that again. But an AI like you know with RL you gota like really tell it a bunch of times uh uh that no you don't do that. Um

robots stop kicking me.

Yeah. Well and maybe that'll change with architectures over time but like overall the brain is different uh than the current systems that we've made with AI. And I I think that uh it's unknown. We don't know much about neuroscience uh overall. I'd love to get to the point where like we all know more about neuroscience, but something is fundamentally different there when it comes to creativity. And I also think design is different than creativity. It's not just creativity. It's also problem solving like I mentioned earlier. And the combination of the two is I I just find it fascinating because you have a user, you're trying to solve their needs, you're trying to do so in a way that stands out as creative and it connects with them. And also like you have to connect to wider systems, the marketing brand, the culture, the business problems uh and so on. and and like holding all that in your head at different levels of abstraction while trying to like deliver a screen or a flow uh that like from a search based standpoint can be a comatorial explosion is just pretty cool. It's pretty fascinating.

新媒介的生成：Weave 与"把粘土捏到位"

I'm actually personally really excited about the idea of reinventing existing art form and media where AI can enable more dynamic generation where the creator steps up a level, sets a bunch of parameters, but doesn't actually necessarily render the final product, but the final product sort of like in a video game

is rendered on the fly with the user in front of it. But the creator, the creative team behind a video game, for example, is building all of the object. They're building the story line. They're building the narrative flow. And the realization of that is much more dynamic, but I feel like it's going to find its way. It's going to leech its way into many more totally different media.

And we we have products around that too. Like in Figma Design, you can have now generative tools and shaders where you can do very much that or we have a product called Weave. And weave is basically a nodebased system. You can connect model outputs into uh other inputs and such. And the whole idea is like it's not bad to generate with AI, but you need a way to craft that clay. You need a way to mold it. And uh with weave, people do like the most amazing video and photo work. Uh and overall just like the the outcomes that are achievable with it are incredible. Uh so yeah I think that if you've got the intention if you actually care to do the work um you can always get to a better result and people you know new model drops there's like this AI psychosis moment that people are in for a few days and it's like I think also aided by algo feeds

totally

the best results rise to the top everyone's like this model is everything

and then a few days later it's it's okay okay I know the

kind of like main tropes of the model. Um, and you adapt fast. Like the novelty is gone. It no longer is a thing that's that's kind of like rewarding you or firing off your dopamine system or whatever. And instead, you're like, "Okay, well, yeah, it always does that thing. How do I move past it?" And that seems to be the continued loop we're in. Uh, which is sort of fascinating because models keep getting so good when it comes to these formal domains, math, cyber security. uh like the IQ points just stack and stack and stack and then for creativity and for design it's very incremental progress overall. Uh maybe that will change at some point, but I think the fact that these are non-verifiable domains has something to do with it.

一些让他惊喜的 AI 艺术案例

And it's probably the fact that maybe that is the human role in the AI toolkit, which is conceive, create, design, and let the AI do more of the work, but it gives you the ability to do much more work. Any art or media that you're particularly excited about or interested in that's kind of emerging right now?

You know, I I find it fascinating uh when people do sort of like new AI experiments. For example, uh put this in the media category. Um there was a designer artist type that made a web page the other day. Uh and it was like a letter to Figma actually. So it caught my attention because I was, you know, getting the Figma hit on the algo feed. And every time you moved away from it uh and came back, it got slightly more degraded and it was basically a comment on attention. I thought that was really cool.

Oh, cool.

Um

that was a piece of art.

I thought so. It was web page.

Yeah.

But like I thought that the technique and the way that they went about it was really neat and like not something that many others have done. I've seen a few other things like that, but overall I thought it was a very cool way to do it. Um, and it was also just a very well-ritten letter. Uh, I like the letter, too. But I Yeah, I see stuff like this. Um, and you know, back in the day, I remember um seeing people do like NFT art with AI when NFTs were a thing, you know, so this like 2019 or something like that. But the way they did it

sometimes was uh really remarkable.

loving Holly Hernand's work around uh taking her voice and making it so that her voice was something that people could use in almost open source way uh that was quite incredible and ahead of its time. Um and I think this like sort of play between uh what is me, what is the collective and what is it that is unique and ownable versus what is not. Uh is is quite fascinating. I've always been fascinated by that intersection.

消费者还是创作者：AI 时代的那道选择题

Yeah, that's cool. Just as we wrap up, a lot of the commentary on AI that's negative is that it takes away human agency, human potential gets capped out. Can you just talk a little bit about your view on the the potential of every human to be a creative, to be a designer, and how AI might perhaps magnify every every person, not just the quote creatives where they're in some elite class of artists in some special building, but the ability for every human to create and the ability for every human to design and produce things in the world and where you sit with that right now?

I I think it's even broader. I think it's it's um as a human in general, pre AI, post AI, you have a choice. Do you want to consumer create? Do you want to take the easy path or do you want to like climb the mountain? And what I'm seeing happen right now a lot is people are letting AI think for them. Uh less at Figma, but like more just like in my interactions with the world. Uh I just see a lot of this at the moment. And that's one path you can take. But the other one is actually you use AI to further your understanding of the world to learn to do things you never would have dared to do before because they were would have taken so much time to learn or it's so hard. Uh and to really expand like the potential ways that you can like live as a human. Uh that to me the latter is the interesting part.

Yeah.

The former like why would I want something else to think for me? like my entire life has been about like figuring out how to think and um I don't know I just hope that people use AI to create good and to like go be a force for it rather than just kind of like joining the hive mind.

Everyone can be a maker.

Everyone can be a maker. Everyone can go do bold things. Uh it's about willpower and it's about curiosity. And if you're curious and you're willing to do the work, uh I believe

be brave and speak your truth.

Yeah. Exactly. And then I think that you can go do incredible things. Uh we will probably see a vastly different setup in the future where things that we can't imagine are possible and things we take for granted are no longer in sort of the realm of what humans do every day.

结语：数学的祛魅与一点失落感

uh how exactly that will look. I don't think either of us can tell, but it is the case that both were on the precipice of great change. And nothing hit home for me more than the math drop last night uh from OpenAI of 700 plus papers on all sorts of very famous problems. Uh that that was a show of something. Uh I had a lot of emotions. I don't I don't know how to process I thought it was the greatest day of discovery in human history.

Oh, I mean factually, yes.

And also like something about it was like brilliant and exciting and something about it was kind of sad.

Yeah.

And I I don't know how to articulate the sadness, but it felt like we lost something and gained something at the same time.

I don't know. I lift my head up and I look at the next frontier and I think that the frontiers are brighter and wider and more accessible than they've ever been. So, I'm pretty excited.

Oh, I'm excited, too. And I think that the world will look amazing and uh I'm an optimist. I think there's gonna be a lot of challenges and we'll figure them out.

Yeah.

Uh how exactly and what the challenges will be in their full form, we have yet to see. But yeah, I do think that like math is uh something that somehow has a quality of mystery to it like an unsolved problem. Uh is it you know is this conjecture true or false? How? why uh grappling with that mystery is something that is special and uh I I'm both excited for the progress and like all the things it'll make possible and also like I don't think it's wrong to like mourn the loss of a little mystery.

Right. Fair enough. Dylan, this has been a great chat. Should we go have another drink?

Sounds good.

Let's do it.

Thanks, man.

Thanks. I'm going all in.

item.description:
## 一个 CEO 的罕见"公开收回"：天花板从未被 AI 抬起
这期对话里最被忽略的瞬间，是 Dylan 当众承认自己错了。他在 Config 大会上曾说 "AI 会抬高天花板"——现在他改口："I was wrong. The ceiling has stayed the same. Humans are raising the ceiling."
这不是语义上的小修正，而是对整个"AI 作为放大器"叙事的釜底抽薪。**AI 不是放大器，而是压平器。** 它只负责抬升地板——让所有人都能生产足够合格的中位数内容。真正的天花板，仍然只能由那些愿意"说出共识之外的话"的人撑起来。
这解释了一个表面悖论：当 App Store 的上架曲线继续指数增长时，用户使用的 App 数量却是**平的**。生产力的爆炸没有带来消费的爆炸，只是让所有人都挤在同一个中位数区间里卷。差异化的议价权，第一次从"你能做什么"迁移到了"你敢做什么"——这是**勇气溢价**，不是能力溢价。
## 跨界连接：Dylan 口中的"AI psychosis moment"，就是药理学里的耐受曲线
Dylan

item.title: [a16z] Why a $1M Startup Wasn’t Worth Building in the Age of AI
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"时间拓扑学"：为什么税务项目注定失败，但不是因为产品差

Jean 的税务项目有近百万美元年收入、技术跑通、客户也愿意付钱——按前 AI 时代的标准这是一门体面的生意。真正杀死它的是一个很少被明说的变量：业务的时间节律（temporal cadence）。税务是年度性的、口碑窗口和销售窗口在时间上错位（人们在报完税三个月后才夸自己的会计，而那时谁也不换会计），决策只能一年做一次。

这里有一个让人意外的推论：AI 创业的"可规模化"本质上不是 TAM 问题，而是频率问题。 一个产品被使用的频率决定了"复利飞轮"每年能转多少圈——而 AI 模型本身的能力提升是连续的，日度产品可以每月吸收一次模型升级并转化为留存，年度产品只能一年吃一次红利，还要和在位者赛跑。这跟 Charles Fine 在《Clockspeed》里描述的供应链"时钟速度"是同一个物理：慢时钟物种在快时钟捕食者面前永远在失速。EdTech 一年卖两次、婚礼一辈子一次、殡葬一辈子一次——AI 时代，这些市场的创业难度会被系统性低估。

二、"Humans are slow routers"——这句话比它看上去更危险

对话里一闪而过的这句，其实是整段访谈最颠覆性的论断。它把企业看成一个分组交换网络：Slack 里问"有谁认识那家公司财务部的人？"本质是一次广播包，每一个人类节点都要加载消息、处理、回复，总延迟是 O(人数 × 注意力切换成本)。Jean 的产品哲学是：在企业内部用 AI agent 做链路层路由，把人之间的信息发现从广播变成有权限的点对点查询。

跨领域连接：这正是 1990 年代互联网骨干从共享以太网升级到交换式以太网的历史重演——不是网线更快了，而是不再让每个节点都监听每个数据包。企业协作软件（Slack、Teams、邮件抄送）本质上仍是 1990 年代的"共享介质"。谁先在企业里架好交换机，谁就定义下一代工作操作系统。而讽刺的是：Slack 当年打败邮件靠的也是同一个物理学——让信息不再广播到每个人的收件箱。它正在被自己打败过的东西（agent 中介的点对点）颠覆。

三、Jevons 悖论的隐秘版本：隐私本身也在被 Jevons 化

Alex 聊到 EA 替他读邮件时，自嘲他本人其实不愿让人类助理读所有邮件，但愿意让 AI 读。这不是一次性的个人偏好，而是一次隐私经济学的相变：当"读完一封邮件"的边际成本从几分钟人类注意力变成一分钱 token，被审视的信息量不是不变、也不是略增——而是像 Jevons 当年的煤一样，上涨三个数量级。

出人意料的推论是：我们正进入一个"过度监视是常态、但没有观察者在场"的奇怪均衡。 福柯的全景监狱假设中心塔里住着一个人；AI 时代的全景监狱里住的是一个你亲自付钱雇的、承诺不记忆的概率程序。你愿意被它看，是因为它看得越多，你从中套出的价值越多——而这个"价值"（例如发现 Jean 举的那个饭店老板的进货价异常）在人类工时成本下本来就没打算创造。所以 Town 的真实对手不是 OpenAI，而是此前根本不存在的那些工作：无人问津的季度账单比价、从未写过的会议前情提要、从未发过的生日提醒——AI 不是在抢人类的饭碗，是在把那些从未被量化、从未被雇佣去做的"幽灵劳动"实体化。

四、一个尚未被充分讨论的赌注：Town 卖的其实不是产品，是"低转换成本"

一般创业公司拼命堆高用户的 switching cost 来形成护城河。Jean 却反过来用"switching cost 低"当卖点：你的 context、记忆、数据资产完全属于你，离开 Town 只需一天。这是一个反直觉到几乎违背 SaaS 教科书的立场。

但它对应了一个历史模式：当底层技术在剧烈进化、而买家极度害怕锁定时，"开放"本身会成为最硬的护城河。 这正是 1990 年代 Linux 相对 Solaris、2000 年代 AWS 相对 Oracle、2010 年代 Kubernetes 相对专有编排的胜利模式——在不确定性最高的时候，可逆性比不可逆性值钱。Jean 等于在跟潜在的大企业客户说："在你不知道三年后哪家 lab 会赢的情况下，别锁定在 OpenAI 的垂直产品里，锁定在一个可以替换 lab 的中立层。"这个立场的隐含预言是：未来几年 AI 应用层会发生一次大规模的"大逃亡"——那些建在 FDE（Forward-Deployed Engineer）模式上的定制软件会随着模型能力上升而迅速贬值（因为模型自己就能生成等价的定制），而把价值沉淀在"上下文所有权"而不是"代码所有权"上的产品会赢。

五、彩蛋：Camel Camel Camel 的 2000 万用户 = 现成的未来

William Gibson 的那句"未来已经到来，只是分布不均"在这段对话里有一个具体得近乎鲁莽的注脚：一个 18 年历史的 Amazon 比价网站，静悄悄地在美国有 2000 万人用。 这个数字应该让所有在争论"agent 什么时候起飞"的人安静下来——时间多于金钱的那部分人类早就在用低配版 agent 了，只是形式简陋到你没把它算进 agent 浪潮。真正要发生的事不是"agent 兴起"，而是"camel camel camel 的用户体验被扩张到金钱多于时间的人群"。这才是广告业真正要失去的那一块——不是搜索流量，是人类的疏忽红利（breakage）：信用卡积分、优惠券、动态定价、会员费闲置——所有这些产业的盈利模式都隐含假设"消费者太懒不会最优化"。当每个人都雇得起一个最优化器，这个假设同时崩塌。

📝 转录文本

开场：一个意外的推荐

Alex Rampell: I get pinged by Ben Horowitz about "like I found this amazing tool. It's called Town. It like changed my life." I was like, wait, that's Jean Denis' company — but he does SMB tax. That doesn't make any sense.

Jean Denis: This was not going to be a venture scale company. No one had built great AI around these very common knowledge worker workflows — like meetings, meeting prep, getting people to be prepared for their day.

We're trying to build a product that works with people to find more and more opportunities for them to deploy AI to be better at their job. It's going to cost you like a dollar a month to run that thing. But the interesting thing is the one month out of a year where it finds something — it's going to find like hundreds if not thousands of dollars for you.

The product experience can't just be a text box. You have to just show the value prop to someone and do it for them. We will use whatever supplier we think is the best for you in the moment.

Humans are slow routers. That's right. And I think the future looks like a lot less human in the loop than we see today. And I think our job is to —

介绍

Alex: Hi everyone. I'm Alex Rampell, partner here at Andreessen Horowitz, and I'm here with Jean Denis, the CEO and founder of Town.

Jean: Thanks for having me.

Alex: So what I find cool is that we worked together when you were the CTO of Plaid, and I had led our investment in Plaid here.

Jean: Yes.

Alex: And I heard you were leaving and going to start a company. And then I remember you told me you're working on an SMB tax tool.

Jean: Yes.

Alex: We had coffee here in Menlo or Palo Alto — and I got a little, uh, not happy about… I was so excited, then it's like, SMB tax tool? That's rough.

Jean: Now, all cards on the table, right? You didn't — I know, yeah — tell me that at the moment.

Alex: I know, I know. But I have to maintain a very happy face at all times. You never know.

And then — this is what I find so funny about this — is that, you know this whole story: I get pinged by Ben Horowitz about "I found this amazing tool. It's called Town. It changed my life. It's so great." And I'm like, that's good, right? And it's an app, so therefore it falls under my fund. And I was like, wait, that's Jean Denis' company — but he does SMB tax. That doesn't make any sense. I'm so confused. And that's what I texted you. And then, next thing you know, a week later we became partners, which I'm extremely excited about.

But maybe tell us what Town does — and I think it's going to be incredibly interesting for everybody — how you got to this point from the origination story. You left Plaid, you started doing SMB tax. Kind of walk us through the founder's journey from there to here.

从离开 Plaid 到做税务

Jean: I left Plaid. I took a few months off with family because I knew that if I was going to be a founder, I was going to have no more time off for a while.

And then I started exploring, in the very B2B way, what would be interesting markets where AI could really change the product experience. And for a variety of reasons, tax made a lot of sense. There's a lot of text in tax, and LLMs are very good at text. You deal with a lot of structured formats as inputs — like financials and lease documents. And it just felt like a medium where we could take this process of putting together a business tax return — it's pretty different from a personal tax return — and automate it.

And I did what engineers do: we did technical due diligence to prove to ourselves that it could be done. And the feeling was like, yes — within the next two years, the process for a small-to-medium-sized business of going from your financials and a bunch of documents about your business to a finished tax return — that could be automated with AI.

And we spent a year building that. And I think there's a knife edge in it, but it worked from a product perspective but not from a go-to-market perspective. Meaning: even though I have no doubt that tax prep will be automated, how do you reach millions of businesses efficiently and sell that product? That had a lot more question marks than we anticipated.

And basically, after one year, we had what I would describe as a good business pre-AI. That is, if I showed you the revenue number and the revenue growth in our first year — a little bit below a million — and if I showed you what I thought we could do in year two — we thought we could get to two and a half to three million in revenue — I think pre-AI, you would have been like, that makes a ton of sense. But post-AI, it just… this was not going to be a venture scale company.

And also — I think even more importantly — we realized that the incumbents were going to be able to use the technology to automate tax prep for their existing customers faster than we could grab market share. And that's a key thing if you're a founder: you have to think about — it's your advantage, if you're a new entrant, that you're faster moving. You can build a different product. You can use different go-to-market approaches. But there's a ticking clock on the wall, which is how quickly can you get real word-of-mouth, network effects, and market penetration before the incumbents (who have other advantages — they have distribution advantages, for example) catch up and copy what you're doing effectively enough.

And it felt for tax like we wouldn't be able to get to hundreds of millions of revenue before our competitors — the incumbents — because you can only sell tax once a year.

关掉一个"没失败"的业务

转向 Town：为什么是邮件和日历

Alex: From there to — obviously the name didn't change, it's still Town.

Jean: We basically explored about four ideas pretty seriously. It's not worth going through all four. What led us to what became Town was this question: why has no one built a great agent that works out of email and calendar?

And we started asking that question — one, because when we were building the tax product, a lot of customers were telling us, "Hey, it's amazing that you're automating tax. But I also spend a lot of time setting up meetings with my customers. When I go into the meetings, I forget what the meeting was about. Clients always ask me the same tax questions. Wouldn't it be awesome if you could pre-draft answers for me?"

And so we realized from these needs that these weren't very complicated things to do, but no one had built great AI around these very common knowledge worker workflows — like meetings, meeting prep, meeting outcome, answering pretty simple emails that happen all the time, getting people to be prepared for their day.

So we just started exploring that idea. And we did it at the time that Opus 4.5 was happening, and agents, at least for coding, were able to do more and more autonomous work. And I would say that very simple insight, plus the model suddenly being able to be more agentic, meant that we got product-market fit very quickly.

And you know, product-market fit is a magical thing. Once you have it, you kind of want to hang on for dear life and keep pulling at the string forever and ever. So we didn't actually sit back and ask ourselves, how big could the TAM be, or will everyone want to do this, or what does it mean to win? We were just like, hey, we're getting a ton of pull from users. Let's go after this for a few months really hard and learn about the market and see what the opportunity could look like.

And as we did it, we started to realize — well, most businesses run out of email and their calendar, right? Especially any role at a business that's external — that's sales or business development or recruiting. The way companies work together is through email, mostly. So we're like, oh, the TAM's got to be big. And it's not just in the US — it's everywhere in the world.

And then when our customers start telling us what they liked about the product, we realized, oh, there's depth to what they're asking us to solve for them. This isn't as simple as just hooking up an LLM to your email. There's a lot more that goes into making this experience better and better. So we started feeling like, on the product end — I'm not saying necessarily we had line of sight to a moat, but there was enough complexity that we thought, hey, we could really dig into this and build a great product experience.

And basically, we did that from December of last year until April. And we just kept going — every day the product grew by a percent or a percent and a half, and our customers kept asking us for more, and the roadmap was very clear. And we got pulled until the point we were like, hey, enough with this closed beta — we're ready to launch the product out into the world.

"App 的价值在下沉，Computer 成了新单位"

Jean: So the way I think about most AI products today is that the capabilities will be very similar. Meaning most harnesses in the work context will be able to do the same things. And so the differentiator — I think what has been the main differentiator in Silicon Valley for a long time, which is you have different product features that are ahead of market — it's going to be more and more difficult to sustain that kind of an advantage.

And we can put a pin in this one, but we can have an interesting conversation about — I think the unit of value in software has changed from the app to the computer. But what that really means — it's gone from an app to anything that a human can do. And a human can do almost anything with a computer. So we're abstracting away the app layer totally. And I think the value will drop in the app layer.

So if the capabilities aren't different, then how do you build a successful company? And I think our take on that is — we are betting that as AI gets better, it can better customize the product for each user, very specifically to their need. Meaning: if you're an electrician that signs up for Town and you're onboarding, the things we recommend to you that we can automate are very specific to electricians. And if you're a venture capitalist, they're very specific to a venture capitalist. And if you're an EA, it's specific to an EA in that industry, and so on and so forth.

And so how do you do that? Well, the models aren't yet good enough where, when you just ask the model, "Hey, recommend for Alex, who's a VC, things that you could automate with Town," I think you get pretty good surface-level suggestions, but not really deep ones.

So what we do — and because we don't look at user data, right? Part of being enterprise ready is you can't look at user data. So what we do is we look at aggregate metrics of who are our power users on the platform today, and then we go talk to them. And when we talk to them, they tell us the kinds of things they've automated. And so we might talk to 10 power users that run restaurants, and we'll see when we talk to them, there's five things in common that they all do. And then we'll sit internally and we'll build prototype automations — we call them routines — for restaurant owners that we think are really good, like the one about wholesalers. And we'll use that as the seed.

And so when someone joins, we look at your email and inbox, and we're like, "You seem to be a restaurant owner." And then we have templates of what we think really good problems and potential solutions are for restaurant owners, that we've kind of hand-carved from those interviews, and we put those in front of you. And you sign up and you start using the product.

And then AI is getting better, and we're talking to more restaurant owners. And now we don't have just five, we have 15 things that we can do for restaurant owners. Still a little bit manual, but you can speed it up. You can schedule interviews automatically. You can ask the restaurant owners — you give them an Amazon [card] — you get a free Amazon card, and you're doing an AI-recorded interview of them and what they do with your piece of software. So you're no longer operating at the speed of humans. You're operating at the speed of AI. And this library is getting better. And then the models get better. And so now the recommendations use the library less.

And what we think is: over time, through this approach, we'll be able to offer 80/20 very customized software for people. And people aren't just one role in the future. Yes, you're a restaurant owner, but also you run finance for your restaurant too, because you don't have a separate person doing that. And also you have a vacation rental that you rent. And so really, you want your Towny to be good at those three things. And also, you have two kids at school, and it can help you schedule their activities for the summer. So it's custom software all the way through. And our belief is that you can use AI to build that.

FDE 方式 vs. 自动化方式

Jean: I think the other strategy that you see in the market — which is, I think, what the labs do — is an FDE approach. And this is very different. FDE is like, I'll have a human go into your business, understand how your business runs, then they'll build custom software with AI that uses my lab's AI, in order to serve you better.

I think the FDE approach, if you're an enterprise that's willing to spend 5 million a year paying OpenAI for FDEs, it looks really good right now. But I think over time, as the models get better, the FDE approach actually gets much worse. And our approach, which is much more around automation and using AI to build the custom software, will scale much better.

And so the bet we're making is: we start with PLG, SMB, mid-market, and enterprises that are very tech-forward, because there our approach scales really, really well. We'll let other people fight in the enterprise for this much more handcrafted software. And the bet we're making is: the things that we learn in the flywheel that we can get will make us more successful in the long term than these more custom approaches.

Alex: That's right.

Jean: We're competing against suppliers. So you got to ask yourself: is that naturally the right state of the world?

So the small answer, which is not the good one, is: we believe very different things about the experience of the user initially around email and the calendar, that for whatever reason none of the other players have really focused on. And there's a lot of complexity to email and calendar which makes our product much, much better there. But that's a small answer, because obviously someone at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google could wake up and decide to do that.

So the better answer actually is to think about our customers and what they want. And when we talk to a mid-market firm — so that's a firm with 500 to 1,000 employees — about Town, what we tell them is: "Hey, listen, do you know which model provider is going to be the best model provider over the next three to five years? What's your opinion on that?" And they don't know.

And you're like, well, if you buy the OpenAI product, well then you'll always have OpenAI models in that product. And what if OpenAI is not the best model provider, doesn't have the best intelligence for you for the next three to five years? Then, as AI does more and more for you, you may be at a competitive [disadvantage]…

Alex: What if they hike the rent?

Jean: Yeah, all of that.

And so the first thing is, we're just like: look, we're neutral. We will use whatever supplier we think is the best for you in the moment. And that's a big part of it. It's also not just general intelligence — like, which supplier is better at voice, is better at video, is better at slides at that time. We feel like it is our job to determine, from all the AI capabilities — frontier model, open weight — what is the right thing for you as a business. And you can save money there, but also you can de-risk ever having made the wrong partner. There are companies that picked OpenAI two years ago, and then Anthropic was better at coding for a 12-month period, and those companies had to use both, because they realized to be competitive they needed Claude. If you're a smart business, you really think about the neutrality of who's providing intelligence for you and who's routing. So that's one reason.

所有权：context 作为新资产类别

Jean: I think the second reason, which is very important: our stance is that you own — and truly own, as a business — the data and memories and context that's being created on Town.

In the old world, pre-computing, if you're a business you had different assets. You had physical assets, and you had maybe human assets. And increasingly now — maybe people call it context — but there's a set of assets which is all the things that AI knows about your business to help you run your business effectively. And I think you should own that entire bucket. And I think you should own it so much that, if there was ever a better solution than Town, switching to that other solution would take you a day.

And that's what I'm selling. I'm selling: you want to own that asset. And I think if you look at anyone who's deploying FDEs to build software for you, what they're trying to do is make it more difficult for you to switch at any point to someone else.

So first, you want neutral intelligence. But I think you also want the app layer on top of the intelligence to be one that you feel comfortable you could move to something else — and in the new world, that's really owning this context layer and having someone who makes it available to you.

Now that means Town — the risk that I'm taking is that the switching cost for my customers is easier. But that's my selling point. And look, if I can't have the best product in the market, then that's okay — then that just means I'll lose. But that's my competitive stance against the labs.

And the third part for me is just on training. If you're a large enough company, the labs won't train on you. But it's the way you operate your business — if that ever makes it into the weights of someone that's reselling to someone else, then basically you're selling what makes your business successful to someone else. And you really don't want to do that. So we — on the training layer — we don't train. That's just not part of our philosophy as a business.

第四个差异点：Agent 之间的路由

Jean: And then the final one on competition is: we believe different things about the world and about the relationship between a human and AI, where we are probably more forward-thinking than even the labs are.

The team's product for Town has a mode around basically building an internal CRM where we're trusting agents to decide what information at the company would be available to other employees at the company. Let me give you an example: you're in Town and you say, "Does anyone know someone in the finance team at this potential customer?" And Town is able to look at — talk to the agents of other employees at your current company to find someone who's connected to that lead that you want.

That's a really powerful product. But from a privacy perspective, you really have to design it really, really well to work. And the way I think about that is: we are really thinking about how do you get humans to operate at the speed of AI, and not at the speed of humans.

So the "speed of humans" version of that question that I just asked is: you would go in Slack or Microsoft Teams and be like, "Does anyone know someone at that team?" and then everyone at your company would have to read that message and think about it, and you get an answer.

Alex: Yeah, exactly.

Jean: And with us —

Alex: Humans are slow routers.

Jean: That's right. And for us, you're going to get that answer immediately — because we've decided that for that kind of a question, we will trust AI to mediate the security and privacy of that request within a company. And we believe things like that that can really speed up a company that I'm not seeing anyone else do.

When you're building a startup, you always have to think about: what does the future look like? And I think the future looks like a lot less human in the loop than we see today. And I think our job is to get companies to be comfortable with that universe, because the economic benefit for them far outstrips any risks that they would see in that experience today.

So those are the differentiators. Data ownership and neutrality are so important. And look at what's happening to Rogo, what's happening to Harvey — if you look at OpenAI, they're building vertical companies that are competing with that. And from a competitive standpoint, you're like, "Oh man, those labs are really unstoppable." But if you're a neutral business choosing who to work with, you've got to think about: well, how far up the stack are they going to go? So I just think strategically, it shouldn't make sense for most large companies to really be beholden to any one lab.

一个 Goldilocks 区间：被 lab 注意到的危险

Alex: It seems like it's also like there's the Goldilocks zone of relevance here, which is: if you had a trillion dollars in revenue, I would obviously be very happy as a shareholder, you'd be very happy as a CEO and co-founder — but you'd probably be the number one target for OpenAI and Anthropic. If you have zero dollars in revenue and nobody uses your product, they just wouldn't care.

But if you're — this is kind of like coding fell in the wrong side of the Goldilocks zone, arguably. Like, the way that — if you were a coding agent right now, like, who's adding $10 billion a week? Or, who knows what it is for, like, Anthropic adding so much — it's so relevant for them, they cannot — to use a double negative — they cannot not ignore it. Or sorry, they cannot ignore it. Just single negative.

Whereas for what you're doing, where — this sounds like an insult, it's not, right? It's just like, this is probably not the biggest thing. I think it actually is the biggest thing longer-term, but short-term it's not coding, right? It's not like, "Oh my god, I have to do this or else it's game over for me," because, like, OpenAI — it seems like they learned that lesson from Anthropic, where OpenAI had 50 bets and then Anthropic went all-in on code and that did really, really well. So there's also this element of just focus and relevance, which — it seems like they're not going to focus like, "You know, healthcare really big, law really big, coding really big" — these big bets they almost have to make. Whereas these kind of horizontal ones that are spread out, it seems a little bit harder for them to commit to.

Jean: I think for the SMB and MG market, I would agree with you. But the market for AI doing more for a business and helping the business be more successful is bigger than the coding market.

Alex: Yeah, for sure.

Jean: And so for me, it's a question of when, not if. In the current environment, it's not going to move the needle at those companies, but I think in 12 months it will. And so it's going to move very, very fast.

Alex: Yeah. It's just, right now, you cannot not — this is the one that I was looking for — you cannot not be in the coding market.

Jean: Correct.

Alex: Right. Whereas this is something where it is like the iPhone / BlackBerry. There's a diffusion point here.

硅谷过度炒作 AI？世界的其他地方其实在低估

Alex: And actually, this is another question I'd love to ask you. I have a theory, I'd love to see if you agree with it. Silicon Valley almost overhypes AI — if that's even possible. I don't think it is possible to overhype AI because every week it's better. The rest of the world, I think, is almost underhyping AI.

And I'm kind of curious: how do you think about — people talk about crossing the chasm — but this is not a great example, where it's not like this is a technology that only exists here. It's nowhere else in the rest of the world. No, people are using it throughout the world, just not evenly distributed. But I guess, how do you think about where are we kind of short AI? What pockets of the economy, either geographically or by profession —

Because this is the cool thing about having a very horizontal product and a very horizontal PLG product: where people are finding Town from all over the world. I remember you told me, "It's like, wow, we're big in Japan." It wasn't intentful. It wasn't like, "Let's go get big in Japan." It just became big in Japan. So you're finding this everywhere. Are there pockets that have surprised you, and there are pockets where you're like, wow, there's actually a lot more opportunity here than people have thought of?

Jean: I'm thinking about individual anecdotes. I'm thinking about this business that rents surfboards on an island to people, and then uses Town to inspect surfboards and little beach buggies — whether they've been damaged — to decide whether afterwards a person should get their deposit back.

Alex: That's pretty cool.

Jean: Yeah. But it's like — that is not on my bingo card. It's not on my 128x128 bingo card. It's like, just nowhere on there.

Really, what's happening is: there is a tinkerer at that small business who — there was something that was annoying to them, and then they figured out with Town how they could automate comparing these pictures and deciding whether to release people's deposits. And what makes it work there is the tinkerer.

And so my answer to you is: actually, we're seeing use in all the weird spots of the economy. And the unlock is: is there someone over there that gets AI enough to want to tinker a solution to their problem?

And the problem is: there aren't enough tinkerers in the world, or there aren't enough people that have the time to be tinkerers to help their business. And I think that's why AI is not diffusing. The reason why it's not diffusing is because, even though in Claude or in ChatGPT, there have existed for the last 12 months features that at a lot of small businesses you could use to save you so much more time — instead, what you're doing is you're using them as a replacement, as like a better Google search. And you're like, what's happening?

And it's because the product experience can't just be a text box. What we have to do is — you can't teach someone, you have to just show the value prop to someone and do it for them. I think that's the real unlock.

And so whenever — for our product — what makes someone stick with Town is: they've connected their email, their calendar, and ideally one really important system of record for their business, and then they've built one custom integration. That is, they've built one thing that didn't come out of the box that was magical. And I'm trying to just get rid of the custom integration. As soon as you connect your system of record, can I deliver value to you in a way that feels very you — that really helps you?

And that's the opportunity, and that's why you don't see it spread evenly. In Silicon Valley, we're all working at companies next to engineers, and so we're much closer to this innate problem-solving and tinker — we have tinkerers everywhere in our firms. So yeah, our firms are using AI effectively, and most of the world just doesn't have that. And that's the real problem. If you can fix that — if you can make a non-tinkerer into getting the same value as a tinkerer in the world of AI — you could be a ginormous business today, because AI can solve so many business problems. You don't need more intelligence. The intelligence is there. It's just, how do you deploy it effectively at scale?

哈佛教授和那位"早期采用者"的悖论

Alex: Yeah. And it feels like it's an integration problem. It's a product marketing problem.

Jean: Yes.

Alex: Because — and this is really interesting to me as well — I met a professor at Harvard, very, very smart woman. She's like the number two person there. And I'm talking to her about AI. She's like, "Yeah, I tried this a few years ago. It was okay, not great." And I was like, "No no, it's really good now." So I had ChatGPT rewrite her dissertation that she wrote 20-some years ago, but everything is now current, like take everything today. And she was like, "This is amazing. What AI is this?" And I'm like, "It's ChatGPT." She's like, "It's free?!" Yeah.

She's like, "How is that?" It's like, because this is moving so quickly. And you know, a lot of people, they judge things on the present. I think that's the other thing: Silicon Valley tends to judge like where it could be.

Jean: And that's where sometimes you oversell reality — reality distortion field, this that and the other — but you see where this could go. And a lot of other people — they see it as it is today. And it's like the slope of this stuff is also such where — if you follow this curve — I mean yes, where it is today, it feels like people aren't taking advantage of it, partially because they were almost ironically early adopters.

Alex: Yes.

Jean: They tried something two years ago. They were like, "Yeah, this hallucinated, this didn't really work that well." And then they've kind of ossified that version of the reality. And if they try it again now — I've done this experiment like 10 times. So it's like, "Where did you get that AI? That's not the AI that I have." It's like, yes it is. You just have to try it again.

The product space is moving so fast, this is going to keep happening. So I think the winning platform is one that continues to adapt the business to the best AI. That's the problem, because the AI will just keep improving and improving forever. And people's mental model of what's possible and not possible, what's difficult and not difficult, will [be] backwards.

I mean, just with computer use and browser use today — like, in the last two and a half months, the assistants can do things that were near-impossible six months ago. And they can do them 90% of the time, whereas before they were doing it like 30% of the time. Most people have not experienced that. And that's why, when you do a demo with Town of it shopping for something for you, or it's using your software to do something that you're like, "Wait, don't you need a UI to do that?" — people are like, "Wow, I had no idea I could do this."

But I don't know how you market that to people. Because if you told people, "Oh, Town now has computer use," that doesn't mean anything. It needs to be much more concrete, like, "Hey, I can make posters for this event that look just like the ones that you've been making in Canva. Hey, I can do it using your Canva subscription, right? Because you're already paying for it. And do you want me to just do that?" And the person will be like, "Yeah, let's do a pass at that." And then five minutes later, when for 25 cents it's shown you something that's super valuable, that needs to go like, "Hey, do you want me to do that before every event like this that I noticed in your calendar?"

And then what happens is: you separately change the design of your small business or your mid-market firm. And then it should be like — you shouldn't even have to ask, but the next time it makes flyers, the flyers should look like the new design, because it should have noticed that for you. And next, when it can do video effectively, it should be like, "Hey, do you also want me to make video assets so you can advertise this on Instagram?" It just needs to suggest things that feel increasingly impossible in today's technology, but really it's just following the curve of what the models will be able to do for you.

Agent 流量：敌对还是协同？

Alex: Well, you've probably seen that agent traffic — and this is largely not assistant agent, but just agent traffic at large — has vastly surpassed human traffic. So that's kind of point one.

And then the other thing that's been in the news a lot is about this kind of adversarial versus — call it maybe synergistic — approach to agents, kind of this new generation of agents. Not agents as in like ChatGPT is just searching something on the internet, but actually doing proactively things on your behalf.

So, like, Amazon has obviously adopted a somewhat adversarial approach, which makes sense because they're an advertising company. And there was this covenant that existed on the internet for a long time: I go to Yahoo Finance to look up a stock quote. Yahoo pays money to go get a feed of stock quotes from the NASDAQ or something, but my eyeballs then hit an E*Trade ad, and the covenant is like, "I, Yahoo, give you, Alex, a free stock quote if you give me your eyeball."

And that covenant has been broken. So people that have hit that broken covenant are adversarial. But it feels like there's a big opportunity to be synergistic. It's like, wow — it's like the new SEO. If I can be on the receiving end of agent traffic and not block it — not figure out how do I stop this, but, how do I welcome it? — it seems like a massive opportunity on the other side there too.

Jean: Yeah. I mean, Amazon's loss should be Walmart's gain, right? Walmart — they don't have the advertising business, and so their incentives are going to be different.

And I think — to your point — distribution has changed. The part that's interesting about the agent, by the way, is: how does distribution change if you no longer trust your agent themselves not being interested in things? Say you use the Meta agent, and Meta has large advertisers, and then you ask it — and say, like, United Airlines advertises a lot more on Meta than, you know, "Nobody Airlines" — and then you ask it to do a flight. What happens if you feel like it's no longer giving you the neutral thing? Because this is the thing: there's still human incentives to promote products and marketing. And so what does that look like in the world where the human's eyeballs are no longer looking at things? That's a very open question.

I'm a firm believer in: you want a neutral agent that is yours, that you have no doubt — the only source of money for the agent is your wallet as the user, and then whoever is creating that agent, their incentive is to give you the best information for you as a human with no distortion in terms of the great forces of marketing. And then you as a human, you have taste, and you express your taste as you make the choices that you do. And you can ask your agent, "Hey, what are people talking about on Instagram?" or, "What's being advertised on…" — you can ask that question, because there, you want to be flavored by the world of advertising and marketing. But again, you want your agent to be neutral vis-à-vis that.

你享受的摩擦 vs 你讨厌的摩擦

Jean: The other thing that is interesting to me conceptually: there are experiences — friction — that you enjoy as a human, and friction that you don't. So me walking around SoHo in New York City shopping — it's friction that I enjoy. I like that I have to walk between stores. I like that there are other humans waiting in line, because I can copy their styles. I like the friction. It's part of that shopping that is enjoyable. I like doing it.

Then there's friction that I don't enjoy. I want to order toilet paper at home. I don't — you know what I mean? I just want the same toilet paper that I've been ordering for a while. Just get it in there as quickly as possible, and as cheaply as possible.

And so I think sometimes when we think about agents too much, we think too much about reducing friction and toil and making things as efficient as possible. But humans don't always optimize for efficiency.

And so the Amazon example for me on the ad is: actually, I think there are times when I'm on Amazon — like when I'm buying Legos for my kids — where I do want ads of other construction toys for my son, because I may realize, one, it's not Lego-branded and I don't know about it and it's interesting, and then I want to ask my agent for some reviews of it — is it popular with the kids? — and maybe I want to buy it. And in that experience, I think Amazon can make a ton of money, and there will still be value for places that are aggregates of supply with advertising and marketing. But there's a lot of times where you're optimizing for friction, where you don't want that stuff.

So if I were Amazon, and I had the 80 billion or whatever — 70 billion dollars a year — advertising business, the question that I would ask is: I don't think you want to block agents, because I think a headless Amazon could be a huge huge business. But I think it puts more pressure on them to create a separate experience where you do want the ads and that's really good, and making that worthwhile to go on, for on its own. And I think I would still go to Amazon for those things, you know, at the end of the day.

But the AI is moving so fast that it's going to change distribution and human habits at a rate where I don't think anyone can predict where the winning platforms will be in those spaces. And there's going to be huge losers. And Amazon might lose a huge chunk of their advertising business trying to fight the future.

Muse 的例子：当货币化与 agent 体验分离

Jean: The other one that's interesting is Muse, for me. I don't know if you've seen the discussion around Muse. Free quotes, free personal agent. Cool. People are like, "Well, one day they're going to have to put ads in Muse." But actually — if maybe they never have to put ads in Muse. Maybe Muse just gives them data that allows them to target you better on Instagram. And when you go to Instagram, you're on Instagram because you don't want efficiency — if you're on Instagram, you want to be entertained, right?

And if they can target better on Instagram because of the information from Muse, and Muse is still free — and on Instagram now, when you see the good that you like, they can also get you to pay for it using a wallet that they've accumulated on you from Muse. Or Muse can look online for different variants of the thing. It's like a really nice flywheel. And what it means is that you've divorced the monetization from the agent experience for this personal use case.

And that's where a property like Amazon is at a disadvantage, I think. It might be with agents — like, having just been the aggregator of supply just may not be a good business model in the world of agents. It just may no longer be. And so there's really not much they can do about it. They're going to lose. And probably the counter-move for them, honestly, is they should have a personal agent.

Alex: Yeah.

Jean: They should have a Muse competitor. Like, that's actually the counter-move for them. It's not to blog [block] Muse, it's to have a Muse —

Alex: Have a better Muse —

Jean: A better Muse, and have the exclusive on shopping for that, and hope that's enough of an incentive, and put it as part of Prime. But I don't know if they're able to do that.

Camel Camel Camel：18 年前就有的 agent

Alex: Well, the fun thing is like with Amazon — so there's a website called Camel Camel Camel. It's a price engine for Amazon. So you basically say, "I want to know when Dr. Pepper — right now it's $8 — tell me when it's $6."

Jean: And then buy it.

Alex: Basically — the second it's $6. No, it doesn't do the buying. It just emails you, and then you have to do the buying. Yeah. 20 million people use this website.

Jean: 20 million people.

Alex: Yeah. 20 million people in America. This is just —

Jean: And it's an affiliate website —

Alex: And this has been around for 18 years. So, my — so Jesse and I wrote a post about this, where the best way to predict the future is to observe the present. Again, going back to it's not evenly distributed. And this thing is the future. Because the other way of thinking about agents is: there are people that have more time than money —

Jean: Yeah, that's right.

Alex: People that have more money than time.

Jean: Yep.

Alex: And people that have more money than time — they're not going to use Camel Camel Camel. People that have more time than money — they are. But wait a minute, what if you now can give everybody who has more money than time, give them all of the tools, and the agent does it? Like, of course they're going to use that. It's an IQ test.

So these things are definitely going to be a lot more pervasive. And again, sometimes you don't even have to picture what might happen — you just have to look at, you know, coupons. Yeah, coupons. You shouldn't use a coupon if you're wealthy, because it takes too much time. You're going to spend like two hours hunting for the right coupon. But guess what? And that's another covenant that's being broken, because it was a very neat way of dividing the world.

Jean: Yeah. I mean, AmEx premium membership, it's the same way. Now it'll just optimize all of your —

Alex: The breakage model is dead.

Jean: Yeah.

Alex: And so we're all going to abuse all of our Chase and AmEx benefits, and then we're going to have to change it. It's not cost effective for — because then it's going to be adversarial.

This is kind of the adversarial versus synergistic thing. So the through-line in all those is: I just think supply aggregation is a lot less valuable than it used to be. [It used to be] very valuable because human attention was limited, and now supply aggregation is a lot less valuable because human attention can be automated away.

收尾

Alex: Yeah, this has been an awesome conversation. Thank you again for coming in today. And go Town.

Jean: Yeah, thanks so much, Alex. It's always great to chat.

Alex: All right, thank you.

## 一、被忽视的"时间拓扑学"：为什么税务项目注定失败，但不是因为产品差
Jean 的税务项目有近百万美元年收入、技术跑通、客户也愿意付钱——按前 AI 时代的标准这是一门体面的生意。真正杀死它的是一个很少被明说的变量：**业务的时间节律（temporal cadence）**。税务是年度性的、口碑窗口和销售窗口在时间上**错位**（人们在报完税三个月后才夸自己的会计，而那时谁也不换会计），决策只能一年做一次。
这里有一个让人意外的推论：**AI 创业的"可规模化"本质上不是 TAM 问题，而是频率问题。** 一个产品被使用的频率决定了"复利飞轮"每年能转多少圈——而 AI 模型本身的能力提升是**连续**的，日度产品可以每月吸收一次模型升级并转化为留存，年度产品只能一年吃一次红利，还要和在位者赛跑。这跟 Charles Fine 在《Clockspeed》里描述的供应链"时钟速度"是同一个物理：慢时钟物种在快时钟捕食者面前永远在失速。EdTech 一年卖两次、婚礼一辈子一次、殡葬一辈子一次——AI 时代，这些市场的创业难度会被系统性低估。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽视的统计幻觉：AI 盈利"狂飙"背后的几何学

主持人提到标普500第三季度 EPS 增速31%，但其中33%来自美光一家公司；FactSet 给 Meta 标注的 6.6% 贡献度其实是会计幻觉——Meta 真实的调整后 EPS 同比是负28%。

这意味着市场叙事中的"AI带动盈利爆发"，相当一部分是单一存储芯片公司的周期弹性 + 对比基期的会计扭曲，而不是广度上的全面繁荣。换句话说，拥挤的AI叙事其实是"少数几个人在屋里跳舞，门口挤着一群人拍照"。而人们看照片的时候，容易误以为屋里挤满了跳舞的人。

跨领域连接：财险公司其实是通胀预测的"地下情报员"

Travelers 这家公司的财报，表面只是一张行业数据表。但如果把它放到更大的系统链里：

汽车/房屋保费增速 → CPI权重项 → 美联储决策 → 利率曲线 → 价值股与科技股的轮动

汽车保费已经从同比+20% 一路跌到 -0.6%；房屋保费从 +19% 跌到 +5.4%。这意味着 CPI 里最顽固的"黏性成分"正在无声松动——这恰恰决定了未来价值股何时让位给科技股。

有意思的是，几乎没有宏观策略师把财险 loss ratio 当作宏观先行指标，但它比 10Y 收益率、PMI 更"去政治化"、更干净。这就像用冰川融水监测气温：绕开所有的政策噪音，直达变量本身。

滚动调整的真正含义：指数稳定是一种"幸存者偏差"

7月半导体跌、9月价值股跌、10月科技+半导体再跌，但指数始终在高位附近。这是市场的内部通风机制：在不让指数崩塌的前提下，悄悄把每个板块的筹码轮流换手。

真正反直觉的是——恐慌贪婪指数到18、纳指多数均线参与度跌到30%以下，账面数字叫"恐慌"，指数却只跌了一点点。这个叙事与结构的背离本身就是罕见信号：筹码交换已经深度发生，但大多数人以为自己还站在山顶。

一个被忽略的悖论：马斯克为什么要给自家行业"降温"？

视频顺带提到马斯克对卫星行业喊话——但 SpaceX 本身就是全球最大的卫星星座。让整个行业情绪低迷，对自家融资/估值并不利。

这背后可能不是商业攻击，而是叙事空间清场：他要让市场在"太空"这个赛道上只剩一个故事——SpaceX 的能源故事（27年前 10 GW 数据中心）。这是一种高阶的叙事资源管理——先把别人的故事边缘化，再让自己的故事成为唯一的解释框架。

最反直觉的洞见：Netflix 可能是 AI 浪潮里最大的"隐性受害者"

讨论 AI 对内容产业的冲击时，人们习惯谈制作成本、版权、脚本自动化。主持人注意到的角度更本质：AI 生成的短视频正在变长。

如果 AI 短视频把时长从 60 秒拉到 15–30 分钟，它们就不再是 TikTok 的替代品，而是 Netflix 的替代品。

更吊诡的是——AI 最大的受益者（算力公司）和最大的隐性受害者（流媒体）在同一个指数、同一批 ETF、甚至同一只基金里被打包持有。市场的 Mag 7 叙事里，这种"内生对冲正在失效"的风险几乎没有被定价。你以为自己在用 Nvidia 对冲 Netflix，但其实你买了一张会自己掐自己的股票组合。

开场：为什么拖到今天

大家好。其实今天这期内容，在周六或者周日早些时候就应该可以上线的。为什么我没有录制完让它上线呢？主要是因为我想看一下周日晚上期货市场开盘之后，到底有没有出现下跌。

整个周末，社交媒体上充斥着一些"周一会发生黑色星期一"的预测——那一部分也和周六的时候 Hyper Liquid 期货市场、半导体这一块出现下跌是有关系的。但是在整个周末、周日的时候，已经把周六这个跌幅全部收复回去。

所以今天这期内容呢，我原本是有必要的话来给大家做一个"心理按摩"。但因为周五市场还是出现下跌了，所以——该准备什么还是准备什么，就来和大家分享一下。

本期主题

主要聊几部分。

首先第一部分，我们通常在聊美股里边有没有泡沫。我说过很多次，我再强调一遍：泡沫的话主要分为两种，一种叫做估值泡沫，一种叫做盈利泡沫。估值泡沫，现在从很多个角度去看，静态市盈率也好，动态市盈率也好，都是没有泡沫在那边的。

所以当我们被一些消息或者预测被动地给喂这些消息和预测的时候，我们应该多问一句：为什么认为市场里面会有泡沫？你认为未来盈利泡沫会出现在哪里？

纯粹地去预测泡沫，或者拿一些 K 线图去预测泡沫，或者刻舟求剑去预测泡沫，没有任何的意义。

我认为市场里面最难的，就是对于未来需求的这个预测。就好比从23年 GPT 上市到现在，整个华尔街里边没有任何一家机构能够准确地预测到一年之后英伟达的盈利会停在哪里——基本上一年之前对于英伟达盈利的这个预测，普遍都是低了 30%~50% 以上。

当我们聊 AI 有没有泡沫，最重要的一点就是泡沫会什么时候发生。泡沫发生的一个时间点，一定是需求小于供给，或者供给大于需求。所以很多时候，我觉得花一些精力去了解 AI 市场里面的一些风险，我认为是有必要的——风险，任何一个投资一定会有风险，花时间下去去研究背后的风险是有必要的。但是任何的一些观点，认为 AI 有泡沫也好、没有泡沫也好，只去聊风险而不聊未来这个机遇，或者只去聊供给端而不去聊未来这个需求端，你都不可能得出最后的一个结论，好吗？

市场有没有见底

那回到当下的市场，可能大家最关心的一个问题，就是短期之内市场有没有见底。

那我不知道市场有没有见底，但是从很多市场的一些参与度啊、指标这个角度去看，当下的市场是在一个相当恐慌的一个阶段。那在这时候，我认为就像三月份——今年的三月份和上年的三月份一样——我不认为我们应该交出自己手里的筹码。这就是我的观点，好吗？

过去一周资产价格走势

我们先快速地回顾一下过去一周资产价格的走势。

  • 美债市场：利率出现了下跌，TLT 出现了相对比较大幅度的反弹。

恐慌贪婪指数与"接受下跌"

而随着科技板块的下跌——因为科技板块的下跌会把指数带下来嘛——我们看到 Fear and Greed Index 恐慌贪婪指数截止到上周五的收盘 18。

那在今年 3 月份的时候最低好像是在 11、12 左右，对吗？我记得在上一年 3 月份的时候，当时最低的时候应该是个位数。

基本上每一次的下跌都会有人问我一个问题：市场有没有见底？什么时候会见底？在什么点位会见底？没有办法——这是没有办法去避免的。

那无论今年的 3 月份也好、还是上年 3 月份也好——其实这个问题你们问我都问错人了。为什么？因为无论是今年的 3 月份还是上年的 3 月份，我都没有猜到那个地步。而我无论是今年还是上年的 3 月份，我所做的就是从左侧开始慢慢地加仓加下去。

市场里边仍然会有相当大一部分的人认为自己可以在市场最低点满仓进去、在最高点满仓出来——这是不可能做到的。也许你一次可以做到、两次可以做到，但是没有人能够在这个市场里面持续这样去做到。

如果我们是从价值投资这个角度去出发，首先我们应该做到的是接受下跌。我在周六还是周日的时候，引用了彼得·林奇的一句话。他举了例子：他说在过去这十几年里边，每一次市场的下跌——大概有 9~10 次下跌吧——那 9~10 次标普都是下跌了 10% 以上了，每一次的下跌他自己的投资组合和自己的仓位都下跌比市场的幅度还要大。那但是他这样也过来了。

这句话背后的含义就是：接受市场下跌。

情绪面有多低：银行板块的罕见跌幅

从价格这个角度去出发，那市场的情绪面到底有多低呢？我在周五看到这条新闻，我觉得挺有意思。新闻聊的是美国大型银行，其实 KBWB 这个 ETF 创下了 2008 年以来最严重的单周连跌，就从八月份以来整个指数下跌了 13%，单单整个九月份就下跌了 10%。

其实我们感受不到，可能不是很多人把自己的仓位放在银行板块里面——但银行板块单 9 月份的下跌幅度真的已经非常的大了。因为 10% 指数的下跌，对于一个 ETF、对于一个价值股的 ETF 来说，其实是一个非常大的跌幅了。从概率这个角度去看，也是一个小概率的事件。

滚动调整：市场内部已经换过一轮

所以如果我们把九月份价值股板块的下跌、和十月份科技股板块的下跌、包括我们从六月份开始、七月份开始半导体的一波下跌全部到现在的话——我认为整个市场我们看到是：

  1. 宏观的风险；
  2. 比如说未来有可能两家模型公司出现一个上市、对于市场的一个吸血的行为。

但整个市场其实我们一直是看到出现一个滚动调整：

  • 七月份先是半导体出现调整；
  • 然后九月份随着利率的上涨，价值股板块出现了下调；
  • 然后整个十月份、在过去的两周，我们看到了科技——因为科技股大科技其实在过去一两个月是相对强势的（我记得九月份 Mag 7 是上涨了 6.6% 还是 7%，非常强势，主要是以 Meta 为主）——那到了过去两周，大科技也下跌、半导体也下跌。

你会发现整个市场里面其实是在一个滚动下跌的过程里边——虽然指数在高位，但其实内部一直是有不同的板块在轮动下跌。

第三季度财报：从两个角度去理解

那最后，我们第三季度的财报已经开始了，所以基本上每一期视频我都尽量和大家聊一些公司的财报。从各个角度我们去理解——两个角度：

  • 第一个角度：AI 现在到底有没有泡沫。这个泡沫的关注点，我说了不是一个供给端的问题，而是需求端的问题——需求端现在到底就供给和需求现在到底错配有多么的厉害。主要就是试图对未来需求去做一个自己的判断，或者做一个自己的展望。所以通过不同公司的财报，我们去判断 AI 有没有需求端这一块问题。
  • 另外一点：整个经济，消费者有没有问题。

这是我希望在财报季度，通过不同公司的财报所带给大家的。然后每一个周末的话，我会从 FactSet 数据去出发，我们看一下整体的财报季度、个股的一些表现、板块的一些表现到底如何。

稍后和大家分享一下不同板块现在的估值在什么位置——可以得出我前面这个结论：你可能会发现很多个板块其实现在的估值都是低于 5 年的平均和 10 年的平均。所以现在绝对没有一个估值泡沫在那边。有没有盈利泡沫是一个见仁见智的问题了，对吗？但是要回答这个问题，一定是对于未来的需求端有一个非常明确的判断，才能够去回答这个问题。

Travelers 财报：保费增速的宏观信号

另外，我们回到上一周发布财报的一些公司。有一家公司叫 Travelers，它是一家保险公司，是一家财险公司。从 Traveler 这家公司的财报，我们可以看到什么？我们可以看到保费的增速、汽车保费和房屋保费的增速——这两个增速其实也影响到了 CPI 或者 PCE 数据。

汽车保费增速（同比）： - 第一季度 0.9% - 第二季度 0.1% - 第三季度 -0.6%

其实从上一年 2025 年我就说汽车保费增速同比开始出现放缓。在 25 年我们聊通胀的时候，通胀里边还是保持在相对高位的——什么？就是汽车保费。但是我说汽车保费非常明显地开始每一个季度开始出现下降。

当汽车保费开始每一个季度出现下降，对于保险公司来说，未来他们的盈利能力、loss ratio（赔付率）就会出现一定程度的问题。那之所以在 24 年、25 年保险公司（特别是财险公司）盈利非常的好——为什么？是因为他们涨价涨得太厉害，或者说他们收费收得过多了，所以他们的利润率非常的好。而当你的保费增速没有出现非常明显——特别是第三季度，保费增速竟然是一个负增长的时候——那接下去盈利这一块就会有压力在那边了。

所以第三季度汽车保费这一块的增速同比负的 0.6%。这个汽车保费增速持续放缓的趋势并没有发生改变，应该接下去还会继续往下跌，直到有一个季度我们看到汽车保费开始见底了、同比增速开始出现一定程度的反弹——那我们知道对于通胀来说，接下去可能就会有一个向上的压力或者负面的动力在那边。但是到现在为止，我们可以看到汽车保费增速放缓的趋势还是比较明显，仍然在持续下去。

房屋保险增速： - 25 年：Q1 19% → Q2 18.9% → Q3 17.5% → Q4 16.2% - 26 年：Q1 9.3% → Q2 6.4% → Q3 5.4%

今年明显房屋保费也出现了非常明显的增速放缓。这一个放缓的趋势和汽车保费一样，还是在不断的放缓之中。

第三季度财报总结：Micron 一家顶 1/3

然后我们对于第三季度的财报先去做一个总结。截止到上周五，是 9% 的公司发布完财报。

这一个季度的财报，首先整体标普 500 EPS 增速、市场预期是比较高的，是超过 30% 以上了。但是这 31% EPS 这个增速有很大一部分是来自于——首先 FactSet 数据——是来自于三家公司：

  • 美光：贡献度 33.42%
  • Meta：贡献度 6.6%
  • 英伟达：贡献度 2.5%

也就是说，现在第三季度标普500 EPS 这个增速——这个 growth rate——其中里边有正好 1/3 是来自于美光一家公司。如果撇除掉美光的话，标普 500 第三季度就是 20% 这个增速。这就说明美光那个体量非常大、增速非常大，所以美光贡献了 33%。

Meta 的数据陷阱

那当我看到 Meta 这组数据的时候，我就知道 Meta 这组数据应该是有问题的。什么意思？因为我知道从运营利润这个角度去看，Meta 应该是出现一个同比增速放缓，不会对于第三季度 EPS 增速是一个正面的贡献。

我们来看一下： - 上年第三季度 GAAP EPS：1.05 - 今年第三季度 GAAP EPS：5.85 - 从会计准则这个角度去看，同比增速 457%

但是不可能一年和上年做对比的话 Meta 的盈利增速有那么的高。那问题出现在哪呢？问题就出现在：在上年第三季度的时候，Meta GAAP earning 它是被低估了，所以这个 1.05 是被低估的——因为有一次性的调整。但是在你算会计准则的时候，你并不会把一次性的调整给算进去。

所以很多时候我们在看一家公司的时候，我们就需要看什么？Non-GAAP earning 或者调整之后的 EPS： - 上年第三季度：9.41 - 今年第三季度（市场预期）：6.79

所以从同比这个角度去看，今年 Meta 同比增速是一个负 28%，而并不是前面 FactSet 数据所总结的、对于整体标普 500 EPS 的贡献要达到 7%。

所以我们把 Meta 给去掉的话，那基本上一家公司——就是美光一家公司——占了 1/3 标普 500 第三季度的 EPS 增速。

板块 EPS 增速：AI 相关 vs. 传统

然后我们从板块这个角度去看一下。就像我前面说的，第三季度市场预期整个标普 500 EPS 增速 29%。

和 AI 相关的四个板块： - IT：同比增速 66%（美光也在里边） - Communication Service 通讯服务：50%（里边有很多大科技） - Material 材料：27% - Industrial 工业：14.2%

传统企业板块： - Real estate：8.6% - Utility：7.5%（其中一些也和 AI 相关，但大多数还是 Utility 本身） - Consumer Discretionary 非必需品消费：3.2% - Consumer Staples 必需品消费：3.2% - Financials：3% - Healthcare：-2.6%

当然了，非必需品消费板块里面也有两家大科技，但这两家大科技不足以把整个非必需品消费一起带起来。

所以你会发现：OK，标普 500 EPS 增速确实第三季度非常的高，但是能够把标普 500 的 EPS 带到一个高位的，还是一些和 AI 相关的板块。而非 AI 板块的增速其实就是在 10% 以下。

当然了，有一个板块是秒杀了其他所有的板块（包括和 AI 相关的板块）——就是 Energy 能源板块，同比增速 127.6%。那主要就是和能源价格上涨有关，但是这个板块我们都知道它的波动会相对大一些。

估值：标普及板块的前瞻市盈率

接下去就是估值。我们看一下前瞻市盈率： - 标普 500：19 倍 - 5 年平均：19.8 倍 - 10 年平均：19.1 倍

所以即使我们去看标普 500 现在的前瞻市盈率，其实也是低于 5 年平均和 10 年平均。

低于 5 年和 10 年平均的板块： - Consumer Discretionary 非必需品消费：23.4 倍（5 年和 10 年分别为 26 倍、25.5 倍） - IT：20.4 倍（5 年、10 年 25 倍、23 倍）——当然，IT 本身或多或少受到了美光的影响 - Real estate 房地产板块：17 倍（5 年、10 年 18 倍、18.6 倍） - Material：17 倍 - Utility：也低于 5 年和 10 年的平均

高于 5 年和 10 年平均的三个板块（都是过去这一周相对会比较强势的）： - 工业板块 - Consumer Staples 必需品消费（上一周上涨 5%，可口可乐今年应该有 30%~40% 的涨幅） - Healthcare 医疗板块：19.3 倍

等权指数：Micron 影响被稀释后依然不贵

讲到这边，很多人可能会有一个质疑：那标普 500 的估值本身或者前瞻市盈率本身，是不是高估了？那即使是低于 5 年 10 年的平均，是不是因为美光的存在被高估了？

前段时间我和大家分享过等权指数标普 500 的前瞻市盈率，现在也是在一个相对的低位。所谓的等权指数就是——即使美光单一，因为美光的市值很高、美光 EPS 增速体量又非常大——那所以如果按照 market cap 去做一个权重的话，你会发现：哦，美光对于标普 500 的盈利影响非常大。但是如果去看等权的话，你美光增速再高也没有用，因为你美光的占比就是 1/504。

好吧，这就是我视频一开始说的：我说从任何一个角度——前瞻市盈率也好、静态市盈率也好、动态市盈率也好、还是标普的等权前瞻市盈率也好——现在估值本身是没有泡沫的。我们要去讨论泡沫，我们就必须要对于未来市场的需求去做出判断。如果说我们听到有人告诉我觉得市场里面有泡沫，我觉得自然我们应该问的问题是：你看到了未来盈利有哪些风险在那边？

本周财报前瞻

最后是本周将要发布财报的一些公司。

周二： - 盘前：GE。GE 在过去两三个月以来，价格上相对低迷，主要就是因为油价在一个高位——GE 里边一半的业务和油价相关。其实在整个今年第一季度的时候就受到了一定程度的影响。它基本面本身非常强劲。 - 盘后：奈飞、SpaceX、ISRG。 - ISRG 这家公司本身我还挺好奇的，我看一下它那个基本面到底有没有向好。上一个季度财报发布完之后，我认为它的基本面可能还没有见底——就是从医疗公司对于他们器材采购的角度去看，似乎未来会有一些花费上削减的问题。但是上一个季度财报不是那么的确定、不是那么清晰，所以这个季度财报其实可以更新一下。 - SpaceX：那我不是非常清楚。在上一周我说过，我说我不是非常清楚为什么老马要去针对星链——为什么？因为 SpaceX 本身就是一家巨大的星链。那现在整个行业里边，如果星链行业不是非常的好、大家对于星链情绪面比较低迷的话，不见得对于 SpaceX 是一件利好。因为接下去 SpaceX 按照老马说法，有可能在 27 年要建造 10 个 GW 以上的数据中心。 - 奈飞：那奈飞本身过去这一段时间股价是低迷的。但是我认为从基本面——我认为奈飞未来有一个 headwind 在那边。就是最近这段时间大家应该有看到，国内有很多的一些短视频的出现，而这些短视频的出现基本上都是用 AI 去制作的。而且这短视频现在变得越来越长，所以未来对于人们花在短视频或者花在中视频上的时间可能又是一个消耗——就是慢慢的短视频在向奈飞的长视频去靠近。这方面的风险我认为是需要去考虑的。

周三盘后：特斯拉、Meta、IBM、Lam Research、TI。后面三家公司都是和 AI 基建相关的，前面两家公司和 AI 应用相关。

周四盘前：诺基亚。这也是我持仓之一了。诺基亚本身，我特地去再次回顾了一下上个季度他们的财报——其实我对这家公司仍然是非常看好。那如果在周一到周三市场相对会比较弱的话，我可能会愿意加仓诺基亚。现在诺基亚的仓位其实比较小。

周四盘后：Blue Energy（这家公司我也有），还有 WDC，也是这段时间相对走势会弱一些的 AI 基建公司。

市场带着这样的悲观情绪面进入科技公司财报，我个人还挺期待的。即使你要出现一个 sell the news 这种情况，那起码在财报之前也得先出现上涨，然后发完财报之后才可以出现下跌。

结尾：订阅活动与下期预告

最后，今天的活动来自于 Seeking Alpha。

第一个：Alpha Picks 量化选股策略 - 标普 500 YTD：14% - 他们这个策略：22.6%，还是不错的，还是 OK 的。 - 过去两个月里面所挑选的三只个股到现在也还是不错。

第二个：量化选股策略（针对增长与收入） - 差不多 4 个月之前他们开了另外的一个量化选股策略——前面是针对所有的一些指数去进行挑选，这边是针对一些增长与收入、相对比较保守的标的。 - 平均会有一个平均收益率在那边，有一个 yield、一个 dividend 在那边。 - Benchmark 上涨了 0.12%，这个策略本身上涨了 9.9%，还是非常的不错。

第一个量化选股策略现在有一个免费试用期，同时第一年可以节省 50 美金。如果大家对这两个量化选股策略都感兴趣的话，现在有一个 Combo——这是一个新的 Combo 的价格，原价是 998 美金一年，现在是 798 美金一年。那我会把这些订阅的链接放到置顶留言里面，大家感兴趣的话可以去看一下。

好吗？那今天这期内容就到这边。下期见。

item.description:
## 一个被忽视的统计幻觉：AI 盈利"狂飙"背后的几何学
主持人提到标普500第三季度 EPS 增速31%，但其中**33%来自美光一家公司**；FactSet 给 Meta 标注的 6.6% 贡献度其实是会计幻觉——Meta 真实的调整后 EPS 同比是**负28%**。
这意味着市场叙事中的"AI带动盈利爆发"，相当一部分是**单一存储芯片公司的周期弹性 + 对比基期的会计扭曲**，而不是广度上的全面繁荣。换句话说，拥挤的AI叙事其实是"**少数几个人在屋里跳舞，门口挤着一群人拍照**"。而人们看照片的时候，容易误以为屋里挤满了跳舞的人。
## 跨领域连接：财险公司其实是通胀预测的"地下情报员"
Travelers 这家公司的财报，表面只是一张行业数据表。但如果把它放到更大的系统链里：
**汽车/房屋保费增速 → CPI权重项 → 美联储决策 → 利率曲线 → 价值股与科技股的轮动**
汽车保费已经从同比+20% 一路跌到 **-0.6%**；房屋保费从 +19% 跌到 +5.4%。这意味着 CPI 里最顽固的"黏性成分"正在无声松动——这恰恰决定了未来价值股何时让位

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Did Revolution at Home Cost Russia the War With Japan? - Sarah Paine
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：俄国的"后勤倒置"——向外投送的军队，变成了向内压爆的炸药

Paine 轻描淡写地提了一句——"预备役在欧洲俄罗斯的集结地远远超过了正规军的数量"——但这句话其实埋着整个 1905 年革命的物理学密码。

常识告诉我们，军队是政权对外的拳头；但当这支拳头准备挥向八千公里外的满洲时，它必须先在沙皇自己的客厅里聚集。于是一个荒谬的构造出现了：沙皇身边密度最高的武装人口，是最不想为他打仗的人。这不是政治学问题，这是系统拓扑学——你在哪里堆放势能，决定了它往哪里释放。

这与 2023 年 Prigozhin 的瓦格纳北上有惊人的同构：向外的战争机器一旦在国内发生停顿，就会反向成为政权的最大威胁。普京那年的教训，是尼古拉二世 1905 年教训的重演。差别只是，普京的"玻洛涅瓶"（下文详述）更厚一点。

二、克劳塞维茨的 Bologna 瓶：一个来自 17 世纪玻璃工艺的政治预言

Paine 顺手扔出的那个比喻——外壁硬如锤，内壁一划即碎——其实是物理学里真实存在的"鲁珀特之泪"（Prince Rupert's Drops）：淬火产生的巨大内应力让玻璃表面坚不可摧，但内部储存着自爆的能量，一旦刺穿表皮，整体瞬间崩解为粉。

这不是一个修辞，这是一个关于预应力系统的精确描述。而独裁政体恰恰是预应力结构：

  • 表面硬度 = 国家暴力机器、宣传、恐惧
  • 内部张力 = 没有合法性缓冲层（议会、工会、公民社会）去吸收冲击
  • 临界点 = 任何单点刺穿都会释放全部累积能量

跨领域连接：这与材料科学中的"脆性—延性过渡"完全对应。拥有议会、独立司法、工会的国家是延性材料——会变形、会抗议、会罢工，但不会碎；没有这些缓冲机制的国家是脆性材料——看上去更硬，但一旦裂纹开始扩散，就是雪崩式失效。

所以 1905 年真正击碎沙皇的，不是血腥星期日那几颗子弹，而是俄国从未淬炼过"延性"的制度金属学。

三、被忽略的真正黑色幽默：日本有议会，俄国没有

这一行只有半句话，但它颠覆了我们对那场战争的全部叙事框架。

我们习惯讲"东方专制 vs 西方立宪"的故事。但在 1904 年，真实的分野是：日本（亚洲）有议会，俄国（欧洲）没有。Paine 列出的三个无议会国家——俄罗斯、奥斯曼、黑山——构成一个被我们完全误读的地缘政治集合：这不是"东方 vs 西方"，而是"无政治减震器国家俱乐部"。

这就引出一个更深层的洞察：日俄战争在制度层面不是"西方对东方"的战争，而是"有缓冲层的政体对无缓冲层的政体"的战争。日本输得起一场失利——他们有议会可以吵、可以换内阁、可以把怒火导入议程；俄国输不起任何一次挫折，因为所有政治能量都没有合法的释放渠道，只能堆积到沙皇一个人的心理素质上。

四、最后一个"啊哈"：独裁的终极脆弱性是心理学的，不是军事学的

Paine 结尾那句话被一笔带过，但它是整段分析的皇冠：

"他个人的 Bologna 瓶看起来不太行……在独裁体制里，是他的决定决定一切。"

这是一个被低估的论断：独裁国家的国家意志 = 一个具体人类大脑的皮质醇水平。

  • 北越能打几十年——因为"北越"是一个分布式决策系统
  • 乌克兰能抗——因为抗战意志分布在泽连斯基、军队、每一个基辅市民之间
  • 尼古拉二世崩了——因为"俄罗斯是否继续打"等于"尼古拉今天睡得好不好、妻子对他说了什么"

这给我们一个反直觉的结论：独裁体制的硬度，是单点依赖的硬度；民主体制的硬度，是网络的硬度。所以独裁政权在表面指标上永远看起来更坚决（因为意志不被稀释），但在抗冲击能力上永远更脆（因为意志不被备份）。

这甚至可以上升到一条普适原理：凡是意志未经分布式冗余的系统，其崩溃模式都是 Bologna 瓶模式——锤击无效，一划即碎。

从这个角度看，1905 不是"革命的开始"，而是一次全世界第一次公开观测到的、独裁体制脆性断裂实验——而 2022 年之后的俄乌战争，是同一个实验的续集。玻璃仍是那块玻璃，只是实验员换了一个。

📝 转录文本

Political Backwardness and the Missing Legislature

This place was one of the more backward places politically in Europe. Some things never change. And the people were becoming more urbanized, more highly educated. They wanted more political say. They had zero.

And so they started hitting the streets, right — demonstrating, strikes, and petitioning the Tsar, because they wanted a legislature, which isn't outlandish. Only three places in Europe didn't have a legislature in this period, and that would be Russia, the Ottoman Empire, and Montenegro. And Montenegro isn't very big. Japan had a legislature. So, what's Nicholas's problem?

A War Nobody Could Find on the Map

Meanwhile, by the end of the year in 1904, that war is really not going very well, and Russians are not thrilled about fighting in a place that they can't even identify on the map.

So the reserves are rioting at the places where they're concentrating in European Russia to be sent out to Asia. And in European Russia — i.e., where the Tsar lives — reserves grossly outnumbered the regular troops. And this is scary numbers for an unpopular Tsar with an even more unpopular wife.

Bloody Sunday and the Collapse of Legitimacy

So when the Russian people have a big demonstration that's peaceful, and they're heading towards the Winter Palace to present a petition to the Tsar, he isn't even in town. His troops panic and they open fire and they kill a lot of people.

And this severely damages the credibility, the legitimacy of the Tsarist government, and makes them look terrible. And so Nicholas very shortly starts compromising and sets up a very weak legislature.

Clausewitz and the Bologna Flask

So, Clausewitz has interesting terminology — it has to do with this thing over here, a Bologna flask. What it is is a flask that you can literally use like a hammer and hammer a nail. It's really strong. But if you get to the inside of it and just scratch it, the thing shatters.

And Clausewitz is using this to describe war termination: where you're going at an enemy and you have no idea — is it going to act like a hammer, or is it going to shatter?

So the question is whether the first shock of battle will steel the enemy's resolve and stiffen his resistance — which is what happened to Putin and Ukraine — or whether, like the Bologna flask, it will shatter as soon as it surfaces, crash.

Good question. And it's hard to know, right — in wars, assessing the other side: will they fight forever (which is what the North Vietnamese did), or are they going to be like Nicholas II?

The Autocrat's Personal Flask

So, his personal Bologna flask apparently wasn't doing very well — and he's an autocrat. So in where he lives, it's his decisions that matter. And so when the autocrat decides "game up," it's game over.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.
